children.text: The CCBHC Model: A Payment-Driven Reform

The most important behavioral health payment reform of the past decade is the Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic (CCBHC) model. It was created by Section 223 of the Protecting Access to Medicare Act of 2014 — based on the Excellence in Mental Health Act — and launched as an eight-state Medicaid demonstration that began operating in 2017.

The defining feature of a CCBHC is its payment method: instead of fee-for-service, CCBHCs are reimbursed through a Prospective Payment System (PPS) — a rate calculated from the clinic’s actual cost of delivering a required, comprehensive set of services. Critically, that cost basis includes the services fee-for-service neglects: care coordination, case management, peer and family support, and 24/7 crisis response. States can also add quality bonus payments, layering a value-based incentive on top of the cost-based rate.

In exchange for this enhanced, flexible payment, CCBHCs must meet federal certification standards — including providing a comprehensive range of services (such as crisis services available 24/7, outpatient mental health and substance use treatment, case management, peer supports, and primary care screening) and offering routine outpatient care within 10 business days. The model essentially says: we will pay you adequately to deliver real, comprehensive care, and in return you must actually deliver it.

children.text: A Growing National Model

The CCBHC model has expanded well beyond the original eight states. The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act created a pathway to add new states to the Medicaid demonstration on a recurring basis, and in June 2024 the federal government announced ten additional states joining the demonstration, including Vermont. Many other states have adopted the model outside the formal demonstration through Medicaid state plan amendments or grants.

Evidence and policy momentum have both grown: expansion of CCBHCs has been associated with increased access to mental health and substance use care, and the model enjoys notable bipartisan support — relatively rare in health policy. Its combination of guaranteed comprehensive services and adequate, flexible payment has made it a leading template for reforming the behavioral health safety net.

Vermont’s inclusion in the 2024 cohort connects this national reform to the state-specific systems covered next in this course. Vermont already has a distinctive community behavioral health infrastructure (its Designated Agencies) and opioid treatment system (Hub-and-Spoke); CCBHC funding is a new layer atop that foundation.

children.text: Payment Reform as the Engine of Better Care

The thread connecting this lesson to the rest of the course is that good clinical models need good payment models to survive. The Collaborative Care Model needed Medicare billing codes to spread. Integrated care needs payment for coordination. And comprehensive community behavioral health needs something like the CCBHC prospective payment to fund the services fee-for-service ignores.

Value-based payment is not a panacea — it brings its own challenges around measurement, risk, and the capacity of small providers — and behavioral health still trails the rest of medicine in adopting it. But the direction is clear: aligning payment with outcomes and comprehensive care is widely seen as essential to closing the behavioral health treatment gap.

For anyone analyzing behavioral health policy, the key question to ask of any reform is: how does it pay for the care, and does that payment reward the activities that actually help patients? Payment design is not a back-office detail — it is one of the most powerful levers for improving behavioral health care.

Good clinical models need good payment models to survive. Fee-for-service starves coordination and crisis care; value-based and prospective payment are how the system learns to fund what actually works.

title: Behavioral Health Payment and Value-Based Care

children.text: Where Genomic Knowledge Comes From

Every clinical genomics application in this course — interpreting a variant, calculating a risk, matching a drug — depends on knowledge that had to be discovered somewhere. That somewhere is, increasingly, the biobank. Biobanks are the engine of population genomic research, the resource that turns raw human genetic variation into the knowledge clinicians use. Understanding them explains where genomic medicine's evidence base actually comes from.

A biobank is a large, secure repository of biological samples (like blood and saliva) from volunteer participants who consented to donate them for research, along with the genomic data derived from those samples and — crucially — linked to the participants' health records, lifestyle data, and environmental exposures. It is the combination that gives biobanks their power: genomes connected to real health outcomes across large populations.

This linkage is what enables discovery. With a genome alone, you cannot learn what a variant does; with hundreds of thousands of genomes linked to lifelong health data, patterns emerge — which variants associate with which diseases, drug responses, and traits. Biobanks are how the field moves from individual sequences to generalizable knowledge.

A biobank is a large repository of consented biological samples and genomic data, linked to participants' health, lifestyle, and environmental data. That linkage of genomes to real outcomes at population scale is what generates the knowledge clinical genomics depends on.
The Major Biobanks

A handful of national biobanks dominate the landscape, each holding genomic and health data on hundreds of thousands of people. The UK Biobank is a landmark — about 500,000 participants with whole-genome sequence data plus more than 10,000 variables including imaging, physical measurements, activity tracking, and lifestyle questionnaires, all linked to health records. It has become a globally used resource powering thousands of studies.

In the United States, the NIH All of Us Research Program has enrolled over 500,000 participants and is generating clinical-grade whole-genome sequence data. Internationally, programs like Singapore's PRECISE, Biobank Japan, and Korea's National Project of Bio-Big Data are building comparable resources. Together these initiatives are generating unprecedented volumes of high-resolution genomic data integrated with deep clinical and environmental information.

A critical difference between them is diversity, which foreshadows a major equity issue. UK Biobank participants are about 95 percent white (94.6 percent) — even somewhat over-representing white participants relative to the UK population. All of Us, by explicit design, prioritizes recruiting from populations historically underrepresented in genomic research. This matters enormously because genomic knowledge derived from a non-diverse cohort applies less well to everyone else — the foundation of the "diversity deficit" the equity lessons address.

children.text: What Biobanks Discover: GWAS and Polygenic Risk

The signature discovery method enabled by biobanks is the genome-wide association study (GWAS). A GWAS scans the genomes of large numbers of people, comparing those with a condition (or trait) to those without, to find genetic variants statistically associated with it. With biobank-scale data, GWAS have identified hundreds of thousands of variant-trait associations across virtually every common disease.

These associations feed a powerful tool: the polygenic risk score (PRS). Most common diseases (heart disease, diabetes, many cancers) are not caused by a single gene but by the combined small effects of many variants. A PRS sums up the effects of those many variants into a single score estimating a person's genetic predisposition to a condition — fundamentally different from the single-gene, high-penetrance variants of the hereditary-conditions lesson.

Polygenic risk scores are an emerging frontier of precision medicine — potentially identifying people at elevated risk for common diseases before symptoms, enabling earlier prevention. But they carry serious caveats: they are probabilistic (a high score is elevated risk, not destiny), their communication to patients is challenging, and — critically — they perform far worse in populations underrepresented in the biobanks they were derived from. A PRS built mostly on European-ancestry data is less accurate for everyone else, which is exactly why biobank diversity matters so much.

body.content:
Researchers run a genome-wide association study across a biobank of hundreds of thousands of people, finding the many variants associated with coronary heart disease. They combine those variants' effects into a polygenic risk score.
A person's PRS can then estimate their genetic predisposition to heart disease, potentially flagging high-risk individuals for earlier prevention. But because the underlying GWAS was conducted mostly in European-ancestry participants, the score is markedly less accurate for people of other ancestries — a direct consequence of biobank composition.

children.text: Consent and the Ethics of Biobanking

Biobanks raise distinctive ethical challenges, starting with consent. Because biobank data is used for countless future studies that cannot all be specified in advance, participants typically sign "broad consent" — agreeing to let their samples and data be used for a wide range of future research purposes, rather than consenting to each specific study. This enables the open-ended discovery biobanks are built for.

Broad consent is ethically contested. It trades the specificity of traditional informed consent (where you know exactly what you are agreeing to) for the practical flexibility research needs. Critics note that biobank consent documents can frame research narrowly (in terms of disease and treatment) while obscuring the full range of lawful uses — raising questions about whether participants truly understand what they agreed to. Maintaining public trust requires transparency about how data is actually used.

Other ethical questions include return of results (if a biobank discovers something clinically important about a participant, does it tell them? — practices vary), data governance and privacy (these are vast repositories of the most personal data imaginable), and benefit sharing (do participants and their communities benefit from discoveries made with their data?). These connect directly to the next lessons on genetic privacy law (GINA) and consent and equity — biobanks are where many of those issues become concrete at scale.

body.message: Biobank participants typically give "broad consent" for unspecified future research, since the studies cannot all be known in advance. This enables open-ended discovery but means participants do not know exactly how their data will be used — and consent documents can obscure the full range of uses. Maintaining trust depends on transparency, and the model raises ongoing questions about return of results and benefit sharing.
body.title: Broad Consent Trades Specificity for Flexibility

children.text: Why Biobanks Matter for Clinical Genomics

Biobanks close the loop of clinical genomics. The interpretation bottleneck from earlier lessons — knowing what a variant means — is solved largely by biobank-scale data: a variant seen across hundreds of thousands of people with known health outcomes becomes interpretable (recall the GA4GH data-sharing lesson, which exists partly to pool exactly this kind of data). Biobanks are the source of the knowledge that makes individual genomic results meaningful.

They are also where the future of precision medicine is being built — polygenic risk scores for common diseases, new drug-gene associations, novel disease genes, and the multi-omics research of a later lesson. The clinical applications of tomorrow are being discovered in the biobanks of today. And they make vivid the equity stakes: because discovery happens in these cohorts, who is in them determines who benefits from the resulting knowledge.

The takeaway is that clinical genomics rests on a research foundation, and biobanks are that foundation. They generate the evidence, raise the central ethical questions of consent and trust, and embody the diversity problem that determines whether genomic medicine serves everyone or only the populations who were studied. The next two lessons take up the policy and ethics — genetic privacy and discrimination protections (GINA), and consent and equity — that the rise of biobanks and clinical genomics makes urgent.

children.text: Who Is Actually Responsible When a Hospital’s Finances Fail?

When a hospital makes a disastrous financial decision — overbuilds, mismanages its debt, or quietly slides toward insolvency — the question of accountability eventually lands in one place: the board of directors. Hospital executives run the institution day to day, but the board holds ultimate responsibility for its financial health and its faithfulness to its mission. Understanding board financial oversight is understanding the last line of defense in hospital finance, and the legal duties that make board service a serious obligation rather than an honorary title.

This responsibility is rooted in the concept of fiduciary duty — the legal obligation to act in the best interest of the organization and the community it serves. For the governing board of a nonprofit hospital, the fundamental fiduciary duty is to ensure the organization’s fidelity to its core mission, and all board members are liable and accountable for their actions. A board member who rubber-stamps management without genuine scrutiny is not fulfilling a ceremonial role poorly; they are breaching a legal duty.

For nonprofit hospitals especially, this oversight carries public weight. These organizations hold billions in tax-exempt assets and enjoy tax exemptions justified by their community benefit. The board is the body that holds the institution to that bargain — ensuring the hospital is financially sound enough to survive and mission-driven enough to deserve its privileged status. Board financial oversight sits at the intersection of finance, law, and public trust.

Key Concept: A hospital board holds ultimate fiduciary responsibility for the organization’s financial health and mission. Fiduciary duty — the legal obligation to act in the organization’s best interest — makes board members accountable and liable for their oversight, not merely advisory.
The Three Fiduciary Duties

Fiduciary duty is traditionally broken into three components, and every board financial decision can be tested against them. The duty of care requires board members to exercise reasonable care and diligence — to stay informed and understand the financial reports, budgets, strategic initiatives, and risks that materially affect the organization, and to make decisions thoughtfully rather than carelessly. A director who never reads the financials or asks a probing question has failed the duty of care regardless of good intentions.

The duty of loyalty requires board members to put the organization’s interests ahead of their own — avoiding conflicts of interest and never using their position for personal gain. This is why hospitals require conflict-of-interest policies and disclosures: a board member who steers a contract to their own company, even if the deal seems fair, violates the duty of loyalty. The duty of obedience requires the board to ensure the organization stays faithful to its mission and complies with the law, including the obligations that underpin its tax-exempt status.

Duty of Loyalty: put the organization first, avoid conflicts of interest
Duty of Obedience: uphold the mission and comply with the law

right.label: What Violates Each Duty
points: Care: rubber-stamping management without scrutiny
Loyalty: self-dealing or undisclosed conflicts
Obedience: straying from mission or breaching legal/tax obligations

body.title: The Three Fiduciary Duties in Practice

body.message: A board member who means well but never reviews actual financial statements, or who approves a deal benefiting a relative without disclosure, has breached their fiduciary duty. These duties are legal standards measured by conduct and diligence — not by sincerity.

children.text: The Board’s Core Financial Responsibilities

Fiduciary duty translates into a concrete set of financial responsibilities. A hospital board has six core financial duties: to specify financial objectives, to review and align management’s financial plan with those objectives, to enhance the organization’s creditworthiness, to ensure capital is effectively allocated, to monitor financial performance, and to verify the financial statements. Notice how these map onto earlier lessons — creditworthiness ties to the debt-financing and bond-rating material, and capital allocation to the capital-planning material. The board is the body that governs all of it.

The most important ongoing duty is monitoring financial performance — and here the duty of care has a sharp, practical edge. Genuine oversight requires reviewing actual financial statements, not summaries or verbal updates: the treasurer’s report should always include the current balance sheet and income statement so the board can see the institution’s true position. A board that accepts a reassuring slide saying "finances are fine" has not exercised oversight; one that reviews the statements, tracks the ratios from Module 1, and questions variances has.

children.text: The Tools of Oversight: Committees, Audits, and Form 990

Boards cannot exercise oversight on instinct; they rely on structures and documents. The most important structure is the audit committee — and best practice, drawn from the principles of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, holds that if a tax-exempt hospital lacks a separate audit committee, it should establish one composed of members completely independent from management who receive no consulting or advisory fees. The audit committee oversees independent external audits, internal controls, and risk, providing the board an objective check on management’s financial reporting. Other Sarbanes-Oxley-inspired practices include auditor independence (periodic rotation), whistleblower protection, and document-retention policies.

The central oversight document for a nonprofit hospital is the IRS Form 990, the annual information return that publicly discloses the organization’s finances, governance, and compensation. Board review of the Form 990 before filing has long been a best practice — and the IRS itself has concluded that nonprofits with a board review process are more likely to be in compliance with tax laws. For hospitals specifically, Schedule H reports the Section 501(r) policies covered earlier: community health needs assessments, financial assistance, emergency care, and billing and collection practices. The 990 is where the board’s stewardship of the tax-exempt bargain becomes public and auditable.

Modern boards increasingly rely on dashboards and reporting tools that present real-time financial and compliance data, letting them track the key ratios and metrics continuously rather than quarterly. But tools do not replace judgment. The IRS scrutiny of nonprofit hospitals’ tax-exempt status has intensified, and a board that cannot demonstrate active, documented oversight of both financial performance and community-benefit obligations exposes the institution to real regulatory and reputational risk.
Why Governance Determines Destiny

It is tempting to treat board governance as a formality far removed from the real work of running a hospital. The evidence says otherwise: board configuration and oversight practices are associated with hospital financial performance. One study of hospital boards found that structural features such as meeting frequency and term limits were associated with financial performance — though not always in the intuitive direction: boards meeting fewer than six times a year posted higher margins than those meeting more than twelve times. What matters is the quality of oversight, not the number of meetings. Governance is not separate from finance; it is the mechanism that steers it.

body.analogy: A hospital board is like the flight crew’s oversight of an aircraft. Management flies the plane day to day, but the board is responsible for ensuring the instruments are accurate, the fuel reserves are adequate, the route is sound, and the airline’s rules and the law are followed. A board that simply trusts the pilot and never checks the gauges is not being polite — it is abdicating the very responsibility that justifies its existence, and everyone on board bears the consequences.
body.concept: The board’s financial oversight role

children.text: The duties also create a structural tension the board must manage: the same body responsible for financial soundness is responsible for fidelity to a charitable mission, and these can pull against each other. A board fixated only on margins may neglect community benefit and the duty of obedience; a board fixated only on mission may let the institution slide toward insolvency, failing the duty of care. Good board financial oversight holds both — keeping the hospital financially viable precisely so it can fulfill its mission, recognizing that an insolvent hospital serves no one.

This is why board financial oversight is the right capstone for the governance side of hospital finance. Every concept in this course — margins and ratios, payer mix, cost accounting, capital and debt, value-based payment — ultimately rolls up to a board that must understand it well enough to govern it. The board does not need to be expert in every detail, but it must be diligent enough to ask the right questions, independent enough to get honest answers, and loyal enough to act on them in the organization’s and community’s interest. When hospital finance fails, it is most often because that oversight failed first.

points: A hospital board holds ultimate fiduciary responsibility for the organization’s financial health and mission; fiduciary duty is a legal obligation that makes board members accountable and liable, not merely advisory.

Fiduciary duty has three components: the duty of care (stay informed and decide diligently), the duty of loyalty (avoid conflicts of interest and self-dealing), and the duty of obedience (uphold the mission and comply with the law).
Good intentions do not satisfy fiduciary duty — these are legal standards measured by conduct, so failing to review actual financials or disclose a conflict is a breach regardless of sincerity.

The board has six core financial responsibilities: specify financial objectives, align management’s plan, enhance creditworthiness, allocate capital effectively, monitor performance, and verify the financial statements.
Genuine oversight requires reviewing actual financial statements (balance sheet and income statement in the treasurer’s report), not summaries or verbal reassurances.

Key oversight tools include an independent audit committee (a Sarbanes-Oxley best practice), auditor independence, whistleblower protection, and board review of the IRS Form 990, where hospitals report Section 501(r) policies on Schedule H.

Board configuration and oversight practices are associated with hospital financial performance, though not always intuitively — one study found boards meeting fewer than six times a year posted higher margins than those meeting more than twelve times, so quality of oversight matters more than quantity.

The board must balance financial soundness against charitable mission, keeping the hospital viable so it can fulfill its mission, because an insolvent hospital serves no one — and when hospital finance fails, oversight usually failed first.

children.text: From Capability to Care

This course has covered what genomic medicine can do — diagnose rare disease, predict risk, guide drug choice, screen newborns and prospective parents, and push toward a multi-omics, AI-assisted future. But capability is not the same as care. A health system can have access to all of this technology and still fail to deliver it to patients, because the hard part of genomic medicine is not the science — it is the implementation. This final lesson is about turning genomic capability into a functioning clinical program.

This matters because the gap between what genomics can do and what most patients actually receive remains large. The technology has advanced faster than health systems' ability to use it. Building a precision-medicine program means solving a set of practical problems — workflow, the electronic health record, workforce, reimbursement, and equity — that determine whether genomic medicine reaches real patients or stays trapped in research and specialty centers.

Encouragingly, the field is maturing: by 2026, a large majority of surveyed health systems (around 76 percent) report having formal precision-medicine programs. But building one well requires understanding the specific barriers and how leading programs overcome them. This lesson synthesizes the course into the practical question every health-system leader faces: how do we actually do this?

Capability is not care — a health system can have all the genomic technology and still fail to deliver it. The hard part of genomic medicine is implementation: workflow, EHR integration, workforce, reimbursement, and equity. By 2026 ~76% of surveyed health systems report formal precision-medicine programs.
The Electronic Health Record Problem

A foundational and underappreciated barrier is the electronic health record. Genomic results are useless if clinicians cannot find and act on them at the point of care. Yet in most health systems, genomic data is poorly integrated: results are often stored as static PDF reports that a clinician must hunt for, rendering them effectively invisible during a time-pressured visit. A cancer-risk variant buried in a PDF from two years ago does no good if the physician never sees it when it matters.

The technical roots of this problem connect directly to the interoperability themes of the broader HTR curriculum: genomic data does not flow cleanly across systems, and there is semantic misalignment across standards like HL7 FHIR and SNOMED CT. The fragmentation that plagues health-data exchange generally is especially acute for genomic data, which is voluminous, complex, and not well represented in legacy EHR structures. Solving genomic care requires solving genomic data integration.

The strategic response is clinical decision support (CDS) — building genomic information into the EHR so that it actively surfaces at the right moment. Rather than expecting a clinician to remember a patient's pharmacogenomic profile, a well-designed system alerts the prescriber automatically when they order a relevant drug (recall the pharmacogenomics lesson). This makes genomic data actionable in the workflow rather than buried in it, and it is a central focus of leading programs precisely because it determines whether genomic data changes care at all.

children.text: Workforce and Workflow

The second major barrier is the workforce. Genomic medicine done well depends on expert interpretation and counseling, but the availability of genetic testing has far outstripped the supply of trained genetic counselors and genetics specialists. There are simply not enough experts to personally counsel every patient who could benefit from genomic testing. This bottleneck is structural — you cannot train genetic counselors fast enough to meet the demand that cheap sequencing has created.

Programs address this in several ways. Clinical decision support (again) helps non-specialist clinicians interpret and act on genomic results without needing a geneticist for every case. Education raises the genomic literacy of primary-care and specialist physicians (the purpose of courses like this one). And new care models — pharmacist-led pharmacogenomics services, telegenetics, and triage systems that route the complex cases to scarce specialists while handling routine results otherwise — extend limited expertise across more patients. The goal is to scale genomic expertise without requiring a specialist in every room.

Workflow integration ties this together. Genomic medicine fails when it is bolted onto clinical practice as extra work; it succeeds when it is built into existing workflows so that the right information and the right action happen at the right time without heroic effort from busy clinicians. The three recurring barriers that stall programs — cost, lack of reimbursement, and workflow complexity — are all, at root, about fitting genomics into the realities of clinical practice rather than expecting practice to bend around genomics.

body.message: Cheap sequencing has created demand that the supply of genetic counselors and geneticists cannot meet — you cannot train specialists fast enough. Programs scale expertise through clinical decision support (so non-specialists can act), clinician education, and new care models (pharmacist-led PGx, telegenetics, triage). Genomic medicine succeeds when built into existing workflows, not bolted on as extra work for busy clinicians.
body.title: Testing Has Outstripped the Genetics Workforce

children.text: Reimbursement, Value, and Where to Start

The third barrier is economic: cost and reimbursement. Genomic testing and the staff time to explain it cost money, and reimbursement has historically lagged, partly due to demands for proof of clinical utility. This creates a chicken-and-egg problem — payers want evidence of value before paying, but generating that evidence requires doing the testing. Sustainable programs must navigate the reimbursement landscape and build the economic case deliberately.

The good news is that the economic evidence is increasingly favorable, especially for pharmacogenomics. Cost-effectiveness analyses of pharmacogenomic clinical decision support have found it cost-effective — one analysis reported an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of about $39,477 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY), well under the common $100,000/QALY willingness-to-pay threshold. Many CPIC-guided pharmacogenomic interventions are cost-effective or even cost-saving by avoiding adverse drug reactions and ineffective prescriptions. This is why pharmacogenomics is often where health systems start.

Indeed, the practical wisdom for building a program is to start where the value is clearest and the workflow simplest. Leading programs prioritize high-impact, well-evidenced applications first — pharmacogenomics (immediate prescribing impact, growing evidence base, CDS-friendly), oncology (where genomic testing is already standard of care), and maternal-fetal/reproductive health. Starting with focused, high-value use cases builds the infrastructure, evidence, and clinician confidence to expand, rather than trying to do everything at once. Begin narrow and prove value, then broaden.

body.content:
A health system launching precision medicine does not begin by sequencing everyone. It starts with pharmacogenomics: building clinical decision support so that when a clinician prescribes a drug with a known gene-drug interaction, the system automatically flags the patient's relevant genetic result.
This is high-value (preventing adverse drug reactions), evidence-backed (cost-effective at roughly $39,477/QALY, often cost-saving), and workflow-friendly (the alert fires at the moment of prescribing). Succeeding here builds the EHR infrastructure, clinician trust, and economic case to expand into oncology, reproductive health, and beyond. Start narrow; prove value; broaden.
body.title: Where a Program Starts

children.text: Bringing It All Together

Building a precision-medicine program is the synthesis of everything in this course. The technical lessons (sequencing, variant interpretation, pharmacogenomics, risk) define the capabilities. The ethics-and-policy lessons (consent, secondary findings, GINA and privacy, equity) define the framework within which those capabilities must operate. The population-screening lessons (newborn screening, carrier screening) model genomics at scale. And the frontier lessons (multi-omics, AI) point to where the program must be ready to grow. A real program weaves all of these together into something that actually reaches patients.

Above all, equity must be designed in, not bolted on. The diversity deficit means genomic tools work less well for underrepresented populations; a program that ignores this will deliver worse care to exactly the patients already facing disparities. Responsible program-building means actively considering who the program serves, ensuring access across populations, interpreting results with appropriate caution where the evidence base is thin, and not letting AI and automation silently amplify existing biases. A precision-medicine program that widens disparities is a failure, however advanced its technology.

The closing message of this course is that genomic medicine is no longer a future promise — it is a present reality that health systems can and increasingly do deliver. But delivering it well requires more than technology. It requires integrating genomic data into the EHR so it is actionable, scaling expertise through decision support and education, building the economic and reimbursement case starting with high-value applications, and designing for equity throughout. The clinicians and leaders who understand both the science and the implementation are the ones who will turn the extraordinary capabilities of genomics into better care for real patients. That is the work — and you are now equipped to do it.

points: Capability is not care — the hard part of genomic medicine is implementation, not science; technology has outpaced health systems' ability to deliver it.
The EHR is a foundational barrier: genomic results are often trapped as static PDFs and invisible at the point of care, worsened by data fragmentation and FHIR/SNOMED misalignment.
Clinical decision support (CDS) is the key fix — building genomic data into the EHR so it surfaces automatically at the moment of decision (e.g., a pharmacogenomic prescribing alert).
Genetic testing has outstripped the genetics workforce; programs scale expertise via CDS, clinician education, and new care models (pharmacist-led PGx, telegenetics, triage).
The three recurring barriers that stall programs are cost, lack of reimbursement, and workflow complexity — all about fitting genomics into clinical reality.
Economic evidence is increasingly favorable: pharmacogenomic CDS is cost-effective (~$39,477/QALY) and often cost-saving, which is why ~76% of health systems now have formal programs.
Start narrow with high-value applications (pharmacogenomics, oncology, reproductive health), prove value, then broaden — and design equity in from the start rather than bolting it on.

body.explanation: Leading programs start with pharmacogenomics built into clinical decision support because it addresses the three barriers that stall programs (cost, reimbursement, workflow) most favorably. It is high-value — preventing adverse drug reactions and ineffective prescribing; it has strong economic evidence — pharmacogenomic CDS is cost-effective at roughly $39,477/QALY, well under typical thresholds, and often cost-saving; and it is workflow-friendly — the relevant genetic result surfaces automatically when a clinician orders an interacting drug, rather than being buried in a PDF. Succeeding here builds the infrastructure, evidence, and clinician confidence to expand. Start narrow, prove value, then broaden.

title: Building a Precision Medicine Program in Practice

children.text: Reading the Evidence: What "Success" Means in Bundled Payment Research

Evaluating bundled payment programs is harder than it appears. The central question — "do bundles save money and improve care?" — demands three separate answers: Do they reduce total episode spending? Do they reduce spending in a way that generates net savings to Medicare after reconciliation payments? And do they maintain or improve the quality of care delivered? These are distinct tests, and a program can pass one while failing another. Most rigorous research now distinguishes between gross episode savings (reductions in FFS claims) and net Medicare savings (what remains after reconciliation bonuses are subtracted).

The methodological challenge is defining the counterfactual. What would those patients have cost if the bundle had never existed? Researchers typically compare bundle participants to matched comparison hospitals or use difference-in-differences designs that control for pre-existing trends. Both approaches can be confounded by the selection effect: providers who voluntarily enter bundled payment programs are not a random sample — they tend to be larger, more integrated, and already more cost-efficient than non-participants. Any evaluation that does not rigorously account for this self-selection risk will overstate the program's causal impact.

With those caveats in mind, the body of evidence on bundled payments is substantial and growing. The strongest evidence comes from surgical episodes — joint replacements, spine procedures, cardiac procedures — where episode costs are large, post-acute care is a known driver of variation, and the bundle gives providers a clear lever to pull. Evidence for medical episodes (pneumonia, heart failure, sepsis) is much weaker and in some cases negative, reflecting the inherent difficulty of coordinating care for patients with complex, unpredictable trajectories.

Net Medicare savings = gross episode spending reduction minus reconciliation payments made to participants. A model can achieve gross savings (claims go down) while generating net losses (bonuses paid out exceed the savings). Evaluations that report only gross savings overstate program value to the federal government.
Surgical Episodes: Where Bundles Work Best

The most consistent evidence for bundled payment effectiveness comes from lower-extremity joint replacement — hip and knee arthroplasty. Multiple independent studies evaluating BPCI and the mandatory Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) model found that participation was associated with significant reductions in episode spending, driven primarily by shifts in post-acute care utilization: fewer discharges to skilled nursing facilities and inpatient rehabilitation, shorter SNF stays when they do occur, and lower readmission rates.

A landmark NEJM study evaluating the first two years of the CJR mandatory model found statistically significant episode cost reductions without deterioration in mortality, readmission, or patient-reported function. Analyses of BPCI orthopedic episodes found per-episode spending declines averaging roughly $1,166, with the reductions concentrated in SNF costs. Importantly, these quality-neutral cost reductions suggest that prior fee-for-service spending included avoidable post-acute utilization that could be eliminated without harming patients.

Cardiac procedures show similarly strong results. Bundled payment programs for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) have demonstrated cost reductions through shorter ICU stays, earlier extubation protocols, and standardized cardiac rehabilitation pathways. The BPCI program for major cardiac procedures generated savings across participating sites, with the highest-performing hospitals combining aggressive clinical protocol standardization with strong post-discharge follow-up programs.

children.text: Medical Episodes: The Mixed and Negative Evidence

The picture for medical episode bundles — heart failure, pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, sepsis — is considerably less encouraging. A 2024 study published in JAMA Cardiology evaluating BPCI Model 2 participation for heart failure (18 BPCI hospitals versus 211 comparison hospitals) found that hospital participation was not associated with improvement in process-of-care quality measures, nor with reductions in 30-day or 90-day risk-adjusted all-cause mortality or readmission rates. In other words, the bundle had no detectable effect on quality or outcomes for this high-volume condition.

Why do medical episodes respond so differently? Several structural factors explain the divergence. First, medical episodes have much higher cost variance — a heart failure patient can cost $8,000 or $80,000 depending on comorbidities and complications that are difficult to predict or control at admission. Surgical episodes have more predictable cost trajectories, making target prices more accurate and financial risk more manageable. Second, post-acute care is a less dominant cost driver for medical episodes, meaning providers have fewer high-leverage levers to pull to reduce spending.

Third, medical episodes require cross-specialty coordination that is structurally harder to achieve. A joint replacement bundle centers on an orthopedic surgeon who acts as the natural care captain. A heart failure bundle involves hospitalists, cardiologists, primary care physicians, pharmacists, and home health agencies — all of whom need to function as a coordinated team across settings they have historically operated in silos. Building those relationships requires organizational trust and shared workflows that take years to develop and are not financially motivated by the bundle alone.

body.content:
A study published in JAMA Cardiology in early 2024 analyzing BPCI participation for heart failure episodes found that bundled payment participation was not associated with improved quality performance or outcomes on key measures including 30-day and 90-day readmission and mortality rates. The researchers concluded that bundled payment models may be most effective for surgical and procedural conditions where post-acute care costs are predictable and reducible, rather than complex medical conditions with highly variable trajectories.
This evidence is consistent with CMS's own evaluation findings and has informed the design of subsequent models, which have increasingly focused on high-cost surgical procedure types with clearer care pathways and more concentrated provider accountability.

children.text: BPCI Advanced: Evaluation Findings Across Five Model Years

CMS has published multiple annual evaluation reports for BPCI Advanced, providing the most detailed longitudinal evidence available on a voluntary federal bundled payment program. In Model Year 5 (2022), BPCI Advanced generated approximately $344 million in net Medicare savings — a roughly 4% reduction in episode spending compared to the risk-adjusted target price benchmark. The model ended on December 31, 2025, and its final evaluation (August 2026) put net Medicare savings at about $800 million across all eight model years, after net losses in Model Years 1–3. Readmission and mortality rates remained stable, satisfying the quality non-inferiority threshold built into the model.

Participation patterns in BPCI Advanced reveal the selection dynamics that complicate evaluation. The model consistently attracted high-volume orthopedic and cardiac programs at large academic medical centers and community hospitals with strong surgical volumes. These institutions already invested in care coordination prior to joining the program and were better positioned to achieve savings from day one. The Penn LDI evaluation noted that physician group practice participation in BPCI Advanced was lower than hospital participation, and that future models need to better engage PGPs if savings are to be extended to the physician setting.

The fourth annual CMS evaluation report (2023) confirmed that savings persisted through the later model years but that per-episode savings rates were compressing over time — consistent with the "ratchet effect" where target prices are adjusted downward as participants demonstrate efficiency. High-performing participants reported that maintaining savings required continuous investment in care coordination and protocol improvement, not a one-time transformation. This finding has important implications for program sustainability and the transition from voluntary to mandatory models.

children.text: What Predicts Success in a Bundled Payment Program?

Research consistently identifies a cluster of organizational characteristics that distinguish high-performing bundled payment participants from those who exit or underperform. Surgeon or specialist engagement is the single most consistent predictor of success. When the physician who performs the procedure is an active partner in designing the episode care pathway — not merely a recipient of hospital-imposed protocols — adoption is faster, variance is lower, and cost reductions are more durable. Programs that treat bundled payment as a finance problem rather than a clinical quality initiative rarely succeed.

Strong post-acute networks are the second predictor. High performers develop preferred relationships with a small set of SNFs and home health agencies, share patient-level data with those partners, and create clear discharge criteria that minimize unnecessary institutional post-acute stays. Facilities that discharge patients to a broad, undifferentiated network of post-acute providers lose the ability to standardize care in the 90-day tail of the episode — where cost variation is highest and provider accountability is most diffuse.

Data infrastructure matters more than most institutions anticipate before joining a bundle. Participants need near-real-time visibility into their episode claims to identify which patients are generating outlier costs and why. Providers who wait for quarterly claims reports to understand their performance cannot make mid-episode course corrections. Successful participants invest in analytics platforms that flag high-cost patterns early — unexpected readmissions, unusually long SNF stays, duplicate imaging — so care managers can intervene before costs accumulate beyond the target.

children.text: Limitations and Open Questions in the Field

Despite the growing body of evidence, several important questions remain unresolved. The most significant is generalizability: can the savings demonstrated by self-selected high performers in voluntary programs be replicated across a broader, less-selected population of hospitals forced to participate in mandatory models? Early evidence from the CJR mandatory model is cautiously optimistic — savings were achieved across a heterogeneous set of hospitals — but TEAM's mandatory extension to five episode types beginning in 2026 will provide the most definitive test yet.

Equity concerns are a second open question. Research has found that bundled payment programs may inadvertently disadvantage safety-net hospitals that serve higher proportions of low-income patients with complex social needs. These patients have higher post-acute care needs and face barriers — transportation, housing instability, medication access — that make care coordination harder and episode costs higher. Standard risk adjustment does not fully account for social determinants of health, potentially making target prices systematically under-set for safety-net populations.

The interaction between bundles and other value-based care models is also poorly understood. A hospital simultaneously participating in an ACO and BPCI Advanced for overlapping patient populations faces complex attribution rules and potentially conflicting incentives. CMS has worked to align these models, but providers operating in multiple value-based contracts simultaneously need sophisticated analytics to understand how their performance in one program affects their financial exposure in another. As the value-based care ecosystem matures, managing this portfolio complexity will become a core healthcare administration competency.

body.message: Many news reports and even some policy briefs describe bundled payment "savings" without clarifying whether those figures are gross (before reconciliation payments to providers) or net (after payments). Programs that reduced episode claims but paid out bonuses exceeding the reduction — as was the case in some early BPCI surgical episodes — technically lost money for Medicare even while appearing successful. Always ask: savings to whom, measured how?

title: Bundled Payment Evidence: What the Research Shows

children.text: What Is an Episode-Based Bundled Payment?

A bundled payment — also called an episode-based payment — collapses the dozens of separate claims that Medicare or a commercial payer would ordinarily process for a single clinical event into one aggregated target price. Instead of a hospital billing for the inpatient stay, a surgeon billing separately for the procedure, a post-acute facility billing for its days, and a home health agency billing for visits, the payer holds all of those costs up against a single benchmark. If the team delivers the episode for less, providers share in the savings; if spending exceeds the target, they owe the difference back.

The logic is straightforward: fee-for-service rewards doing more — more tests, longer stays, more specialist consults — because each service generates a separate payment. Bundling inverts that incentive. A provider who reduces an unnecessary post-acute day or avoids a preventable readmission keeps part of the savings rather than losing revenue. Quality guardrails prevent providers from cutting corners to hit their target: readmission rates, mortality, and patient-experience scores are tracked, and poor quality can disqualify a participant from receiving any reconciliation payment.

Bundled payments sit in the middle of the value-based care spectrum. They are more aggressive than pay-for-performance bonuses, which layer small incentives onto an otherwise unchanged fee-for-service chassis, but less comprehensive than capitation, which hands a provider a fixed monthly sum to cover all care. Bundles concentrate accountability on a defined clinical episode — a joint replacement, a cardiac procedure, a chemotherapy course — making them easier to attribute to specific providers and easier to price than a full-population capitation arrangement.

An episode of care is a clinically meaningful window of time tied to a specific health event — typically an inpatient anchor stay or a qualifying outpatient procedure, plus a defined follow-up period (most commonly 90 days) during which related care is included in the bundle.

children.text: The Mechanics: How a Bundle Is Structured

Every bundled payment model defines three core elements: the anchor event that starts the clock, the episode window, and the care that is included or excluded. In the CMS Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced (BPCI Advanced) model — the largest federal voluntary bundled payment program, which ran from 2018 until it ended on December 31, 2025 — an episode begins either with an inpatient admission identified by a Medicare Severity-Diagnosis Related Group (MS-DRG) code, called the Anchor Stay, or with a qualifying outpatient procedure in a hospital outpatient department, called the Anchor Procedure. The episode ends 90 days after the patient is discharged or the procedure is completed.

The financial engine is retrospective reconciliation. Medicare continues to pay providers their ordinary fee-for-service claims throughout the episode — nobody waits for a single check. At the end of each six-month performance period, CMS totals all non-excluded Medicare claims for each participant's episodes and compares that aggregate with the pre-set target price. If spending is below the target, the participant earns a reconciliation payment (shared savings). If spending exceeds the target, the participant owes a repayment amount. CMS provides preliminary target prices before each model year begins so participants can plan care-delivery changes in advance.

Target prices are calculated from historical Medicare claims data for that clinical episode type in the participant's market, risk-adjusted for patient complexity, and trended forward with a discount rate (the "haircut") that represents the savings Medicare expects to achieve. The haircut ensures the program generates net savings for the federal government even after reconciliation payments are made to high-performing participants.

body.title: How a BPCI Advanced Episode Flows

children.text: Who Participates and What They Are Accountable For

Under BPCI Advanced, two entity types could participate: acute care hospitals (ACHs) and physician group practices (PGPs). A hospital participating as an ACH is accountable for the full 90-day episode cost for every eligible patient admitted. A PGP participates as an episode initiator — responsible for managing costs during the episode triggered by the group's physicians. This distinction matters: hospitals have more leverage over post-acute placement, while physician groups have more direct influence over care protocols and follow-up intensity.

The 35 BPCI Advanced clinical episodes span eight clinical service line groups: cardiac care, cardiac procedures, gastrointestinal surgery, gastrointestinal care, neurological care, medical and critical care, spinal procedures, and orthopedics. Participants do not have to take on all 35 — they can select the episode types where they have the most clinical volume, existing care-coordination infrastructure, and confidence in their ability to manage costs. This flexibility encourages participation but also creates selection effects: hospitals tend to choose episode types where they already perform well.

Quality measurement is built into the financial settlement. BPCI Advanced tracks Medicare Spending per Beneficiary (MSPB) composite quality scores and requires participants to submit quality data. Low quality scores can reduce or eliminate reconciliation payments, ensuring that cost-cutting does not come at the expense of patient safety. Participants are also encouraged — but not required — to engage post-acute providers (skilled nursing facilities, home health agencies) as downstream episode partners who share in savings and absorb a portion of any penalties.

children.text: The Target Price: How CMS Sets the Benchmark

Setting an accurate target price is the most technically demanding element of any bundled payment program. If the target is too high, providers collect windfall payments without changing behavior. If it is too low, providers lose money on every episode regardless of efficiency gains, and they exit the program. CMS attempts to thread this needle by using three to five years of historical fee-for-service claims for the specific episode type in the participant's region, then applying risk adjustments and a discount that ensures the government retains savings.

The target price methodology for BPCI Advanced uses a blend of national and regional data, adjusted for the case-mix complexity of the participant's patient population using hierarchical condition categories (HCCs). High-severity patients receive higher target prices; straightforward cases receive lower ones. CMS also applies a "stop-loss" and "stop-gain" corridor: no single episode can swing the reconciliation more than a defined dollar cap in either direction, protecting both participants and Medicare from extreme outlier cases.

Because target prices are anchored to historical spending, participants who have already reduced episode costs through prior efficiency work start with a lower baseline — a phenomenon sometimes called the "ratchet effect." As participants reduce costs over time, CMS lowers the target price in subsequent model years, requiring continuous improvement just to maintain savings. This dynamic has led some high-performing participants to exit voluntary programs voluntarily once their baseline is compressed, a structural tension that mandatory models are designed to overcome.

body.analogy: Think of the target price like a par score in golf: it is based on what a skilled player should need to complete the hole, adjusted for the difficulty of the terrain (patient complexity). Finishing under par earns savings; going over means you owe the difference. And once you consistently shoot par, the course committee lowers the expected score next season.

children.text: Care Transformation: What Providers Actually Change

The practical care changes driven by bundled payments cluster around three levers: post-acute placement, length of stay, and readmission reduction. Post-acute care — skilled nursing facilities, inpatient rehabilitation, home health — is the single largest driver of episode cost variation for surgical procedures. A hip replacement patient discharged to a skilled nursing facility costs Medicare roughly twice as much over 90 days as the same patient discharged directly home with home health support. Bundled payment participants therefore invest heavily in standardized discharge criteria, preferred SNF networks, and home health partnerships.

Clinical pathway standardization is the second major lever. When a hospital takes on risk for a hip replacement episode, it has a powerful financial incentive to create and enforce a standard care protocol: pre-operative patient optimization (weight, hemoglobin, diabetes control), standardized implant selection, evidence-based rehabilitation protocols, and scheduled follow-up calls. These protocols reduce variance — the expensive outlier cases that blow up episode budgets — and often improve clinical outcomes simultaneously.

Readmission prevention rounds out the triad. A 90-day episode means that any readmission within three months of the initial procedure falls inside the bundle and adds directly to the participant's cost. Participants invest in post-discharge nurse navigator programs, 24/7 patient hotlines, medication reconciliation, and remote monitoring to catch warning signs before they become emergency department visits. These infrastructure investments require upfront capital, which is part of why BPCI Advanced pays preliminary reconciliation payments — to fund the care-coordination capabilities that drive savings.

body.content:
Analyses of BPCI Advanced performance in lower-extremity joint replacement (one of the highest-volume episodes in the model) are a large part of why the model as a whole saved Medicare an estimated net $344 million in Model Year 5 (about $800 million net across all eight model years, per the 2026 final evaluation). Quality metrics including readmission and mortality rates remained stable, indicating that cost reductions were achieved without compromising patient safety.
Participants who succeeded shared common characteristics: strong surgeon engagement, standardized implant formularies, disciplined SNF referral networks, and nurse navigator programs for post-discharge monitoring. Hospitals that treated bundled payments as a physician engagement strategy — rather than a finance department exercise — consistently outperformed those that did not.

children.text: The Future of Bundled Payments: From Voluntary to Mandatory

CMS has moved decisively toward mandatory bundled payment models after learning that voluntary programs attract a self-selected group of already-efficient providers. The Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) model — launched in 2016 as a mandatory program in randomly selected metropolitan statistical areas — was the first federal mandatory bundle and provided critical evidence that bundles can generate savings at scale without quality deterioration. CJR saved Medicare an estimated $63 million between 2016 and 2018.

The next generation mandatory model is the Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM), which CMS launched on January 1, 2026, to run through December 31, 2030. TEAM requires approximately 741 acute care hospitals in selected Core-Based Statistical Areas to accept financial risk for five surgical episode types: lower extremity joint replacement, surgical hip femur fracture treatment, spinal fusion, coronary artery bypass graft, and major bowel procedure. Unlike BPCI Advanced's 90-day window, TEAM episodes end 30 days after discharge, reflecting a sharper focus on the immediate post-acute transition.

Commercial payers have also accelerated their own bundled payment programs independently of CMS. Large self-insured employers — working through coalitions like the Pacific Business Group on Health — negotiate direct bundle contracts with hospital systems for high-volume procedures. The multi-payer environment creates both opportunity (providers can amortize care-coordination infrastructure across multiple payers) and complexity (different episode definitions, target price methodologies, and quality metrics across each payer relationship). Standardization of episode definitions across payers remains one of the field's central operational challenges.

body.message: Bundled payments cover a specific clinical episode, not a patient's entire care. A patient under a bundled payment arrangement for a knee replacement still receives fee-for-service payment for unrelated conditions like diabetes management or a subsequent cardiac event. Do not confuse episode-based bundles with full-risk capitation or population-based payment models, which cover all care for a defined patient population.

title: Episode-Based Bundled Payments: How They Work

children.text: Paying for an Episode, Not a Service

A bundled payment sits conceptually between fee-for-service and the population accountability of an ACO. Instead of paying separately for the surgeon, the hospital stay, the rehab facility, and every follow-up visit, a bundle holds providers accountable for the total cost of a defined clinical episode — for example, a hip replacement and everything that happens in the 90 days after it.

The mechanics are usually retrospective. Providers keep billing fee-for-service throughout the episode, then at the end Medicare reconciles total spending against a predetermined target price. If actual spending came in under the target and quality held, the providers keep the difference; if it ran over, they may owe Medicare back.

Bundling targets a specific weakness of fee-for-service: fragmentation. When no one is accountable for the whole episode, costs leak — especially into post-acute care, where discharge decisions vary enormously. A bundle gives providers a direct financial reason to coordinate the entire arc of care.

A bundled payment sets a single target price for a whole episode of care (often 90 days). Spending is reconciled against that target: beat it with good quality and keep the savings; exceed it and potentially repay. The episode — not the individual service — becomes the unit of accountability.
The CMS Innovation Center (CMMI)

Most of Medicare’s bundled-payment and value-based experiments come from one place: the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI), known as the CMS Innovation Center. It was created by Section 3021 of the Affordable Care Act in 2010 with a specific mission — to test new payment and delivery models that could reduce spending while preserving or improving quality.

CMMI has a powerful and unusual authority: if a model is certified by the actuary to lower spending without harming quality (or improve quality without raising spending), the Secretary of HHS can expand it nationally without an act of Congress. That ability to scale successful models is what makes CMMI Medicare’s primary engine of payment innovation.

CMMI is also why models can be made mandatory in selected regions. Voluntary models suffer from selection bias — only providers who expect to benefit join — so CMMI sometimes requires all hospitals in chosen markets to participate, producing cleaner evidence about whether a model actually works.

body.content: Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced (BPCI Advanced), launched in 2018, let participants take accountability for 90-day episodes across a menu of medical and surgical conditions, with target prices based partly on their own historical spending. It was the first episode model to include an outpatient surgical condition (spine surgery). Like other episode models, it billed fee-for-service throughout and reconciled spending against the target price at the end of each episode.
body.title: BPCI Advanced

children.text: CJR: Testing Mandatory Bundles

The clearest test of bundled payment was the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) model, which ran from April 2016 through December 2024. CJR was mandatory for hospitals in selected metropolitan areas and covered hip and knee replacements — high-volume, high-cost procedures with notoriously variable post-acute spending.

The results validated the core theory. A rigorous evaluation found CJR reduced institutional spending per joint-replacement episode by roughly $812 (about a 3 percent relative decrease), driven largely by a meaningful drop in patients being discharged to costly post-acute facilities instead of home. Critically, CMS found no adverse effects on quality — complication rates, mortality, readmissions, and ED use did not worsen.

CJR demonstrated that a well-designed bundle could squeeze out wasteful post-acute spending without harming patients. Its success directly shaped the next generation of mandatory models, proving that the lever to pull in episode payment is usually post-acute care.

children.text: From CJR to TEAM

The lessons from CJR fed directly into its successor: the Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM), a mandatory episode-based payment model that launched in January 2026. TEAM expands the bundled-payment approach beyond joint replacement to five surgical episode categories and adds enhanced protections for safety-net hospitals.

TEAM reflects how Medicare’s thinking has matured. It is mandatory (for cleaner evidence and broader impact), it spans multiple procedures (not just one), and it explicitly builds in equity safeguards to avoid penalizing hospitals that serve disadvantaged patients — addressing a recurring critique of earlier value programs.

TEAM also illustrates the cumulative nature of payment reform: each model learns from the last. CJR proved bundles work for joint replacement; TEAM extends that proof across more surgeries while patching the equity gaps the earlier models exposed.

body.message: Voluntary models attract providers who expect to win, biasing results. Mandatory models like CJR and TEAM require everyone in selected markets to participate, which gives CMS cleaner evidence about whether a payment model truly works — but also generates strong provider pushback.
body.title: Mandatory models produce better evidence

children.text: CMMI’s Mixed Track Record

For all its importance, CMMI’s overall record is sobering and politically contested. In roughly 14 years it has launched more than 50 models, but CMS's own 2021 strategy review found that only six of its first 50-plus models had produced statistically significant savings, and a 2023 Congressional Budget Office analysis found that over 2011–2020 CMMI increased federal direct spending by about $5.4 billion — roughly 0.1 percent of net Medicare spending — once its operating costs were counted.

Very few models have cleared the high bar required for national expansion. As of January 2025, CMS had certified only four of the 70 models it had tested for expansion — the Pioneer ACO model (whose elements were folded into the Shared Savings Program), the Diabetes Prevention Program, prior authorization for repetitive non-emergency ambulance transport, and Home Health Value-Based Purchasing (GAO, 2026). Many promising-looking models simply did not save money once rigorously evaluated.

This record is essential context, not a footnote. It shows that paying for value is genuinely hard — good ideas frequently fail to deliver net savings — and it fuels ongoing debate about how CMMI should be reformed. But the standouts, like CJR’s bundled-payment success, are exactly why Medicare keeps testing, refining, and occasionally scaling new models.
CMMI’s history is a humbling lesson: most payment experiments do not save money — but the few that do, like mandatory bundles, point the way for the rest of the system.

children.text: Measuring Care From the Patient's Seat

Clinical measures like HEDIS tell you what was done to and for a patient. But they cannot tell you what the care felt like from the patient's side — whether their doctor listened, whether they got help quickly, whether anyone explained their medications. Capturing that perspective is the job of CAHPS.

CAHPS — the Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems — is a program run by the federal Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ). It began in 1995 to build the scientific understanding of patient experience as part of advancing safe, patient-centered care. CAHPS is not a single survey but a family of rigorously developed, standardized surveys.

Each CAHPS survey is designed for a specific setting — hospitals, health plans, clinician practices, dialysis facilities, and more. To carry the CAHPS name, a survey must be approved by the CAHPS Consortium overseen by AHRQ, which is what guarantees the surveys are scientifically sound and comparable across organizations.

CAHPS is AHRQ's family of standardized surveys, launched in 1995, that measure patient experience. Each survey targets a specific care setting and must be approved by the AHRQ-overseen CAHPS Consortium.
Experience Is Not Satisfaction

The single most important concept in CAHPS is a distinction that is easy to miss: patient experience is not the same as patient satisfaction. The two terms are often used interchangeably, but CAHPS deliberately measures experience, not satisfaction.

A satisfaction question asks how happy a patient was — a subjective rating that depends heavily on expectations. An experience question asks whether something that should happen in care actually happened, and how often. Instead of "How satisfied were you with communication?" CAHPS asks "During this hospital stay, how often did doctors explain things in a way you could understand?"

This framing matters because experience questions are actionable and fair. "How often did nurses treat you with courtesy and respect?" points to a specific, improvable behavior, and it is far less swayed by whether a patient simply liked their food or their room. By anchoring on concrete events rather than feelings, CAHPS produces data that organizations can actually act on.

children.text: HCAHPS: The Hospital Survey

The most consequential member of the CAHPS family is HCAHPS — the Hospital CAHPS survey — the first national, standardized, publicly reported survey of patients' hospital experiences. It exists to let patients and the public compare hospitals on experience using the same questions everywhere.

HCAHPS has a long development pedigree. Beginning in 2002, CMS partnered with AHRQ to develop and test it; it was endorsed by the National Quality Forum in 2005, implemented in October 2006, and its results were first publicly reported in March 2008. That careful, multi-year development is why HCAHPS scores are treated as credible enough to drive payment.

The survey organizes its questions into composite topics that reflect the core of the hospital experience: communication with nurses, communication with doctors, responsiveness of hospital staff, communication about medicines, discharge information, care transition, the hospital environment (cleanliness and quietness), and an overall hospital rating.

children.text: When Experience Affects Payment

HCAHPS is not just informational — it has real financial teeth. Results are publicly reported on Medicare's Care Compare website and feed directly into the Hospital Value-Based Purchasing (VBP) program, which redistributes a portion of Medicare payments based on performance.

The weight is significant: patient-experience measures from HCAHPS make up a substantial share of a hospital's Value-Based Purchasing score. That means how patients answer questions about communication, responsiveness, and discharge can swing a hospital's Medicare reimbursement by meaningful amounts each year.

Tying payment to patient experience was a deliberate policy choice: it signals that how care is delivered — not just whether the clinical box was checked — is part of quality. It also raised the stakes for getting the measurement right, because money now rides on the numbers.

body.content:
HCAHPS results are publicly posted on Care Compare and built into Hospital VBP, which redistributes a percentage of Medicare payments based on performance.
Patient-experience scores form a large portion of each hospital's VBP score, so consistent shortfalls in, say, communication or responsiveness can translate into real reductions in Medicare reimbursement — making patient experience a board-level financial issue, not just a satisfaction metric.
body.title: HCAHPS in Hospital Value-Based Purchasing

children.text: Making the Comparison Fair

Comparing hospitals or plans on patient experience is only fair if the comparison accounts for differences that have nothing to do with quality. CAHPS surveys therefore apply adjustments before results are publicly reported.

Two adjustments are central. Patient-mix adjustment accounts for differences in the kinds of patients each organization serves — factors like age, education, and health status that are known to influence how people answer experience questions, independent of the care's quality. Mode adjustment accounts for the fact that people respond differently depending on whether they were surveyed by mail, phone, or another method.

These adjustments are the experience-survey analog of risk adjustment for clinical outcomes. Without them, a hospital serving an older or sicker population could look worse purely because of who it treats, not how well it treats them. The adjustments are what make a hospital's publicly reported scores a fair basis for comparison — and for payment.

body.message: Publicly reported CAHPS scores are patient-mix and mode adjusted precisely because raw responses are influenced by who answered and how they were surveyed. Comparing unadjusted scores across organizations can be misleading — always use the adjusted, reported figures.
body.title: Don't Read Raw Scores as Quality

children.text: Deciding What to Build and What to Buy

The previous lesson established that hospitals plan major investments through a fixed capital budget, where every department’s request competes for limited dollars. This lesson is about how those decisions actually get made — and constrained. Capital planning sits at the intersection of three forces: the financial analysis that tells a hospital whether an investment will pay off, the strategic judgment about what the institution needs to fulfill its mission, and the government regulation that, in many states, determines whether the hospital is even allowed to make the investment at all.

These three forces pull in different directions. Pure financial analysis favors the projects with the best returns. Strategic and mission considerations may favor projects with modest financial returns but high community value. And in much of the country, a state regulator wielding "certificate of need" authority can block a project entirely, regardless of how attractive it looks on the hospital’s spreadsheet. Capital planning is the discipline of navigating all three.

Key Concept: Capital planning combines financial analysis (NPV, IRR, payback, profitability index), strategic and mission-driven prioritization, and — in many states — Certificate of Need (CON) regulatory approval to decide which long-term investments a hospital pursues.

children.text: Certificate of Need: The Regulatory Gatekeeper

Certificate of Need (CON) programs are state laws that require health care providers to obtain government approval before making major capital investments — building or expanding facilities, adding beds, or acquiring expensive equipment. Their stated purpose is to restrain health care facility costs and allow coordinated planning of new services and construction, on the theory that unchecked duplication of expensive services (every hospital buying its own proton-beam machine) drives up total spending. Currently, 35 states and Washington, D.C. operate CON programs, with enormous variation among them.

The dollar threshold that triggers CON review reveals how differently states approach this. In New York, projects by general hospitals exceeding $30 million require a CON; in Iowa, projects over just $1.5 million do. Thresholds are typically lower for non-hospital providers like ambulatory surgery centers than for hospitals. The practical effect is that the same capital project — say, a new surgery center — might sail through unregulated in one state and require a months-long, contestable approval process in another.

CON laws are genuinely controversial, and the evidence is mixed and politically charged. Critics point to research suggesting hospital charges are about 5.5% lower five years after a state repeals CON, and that per-capita hospital expenditures run about 20.6% higher in CON states — arguing the laws protect incumbents and stifle competition. Defenders argue CON prevents wasteful duplication and protects rural and safety-net providers from being undercut. The result is an active reform landscape: in 2024, Georgia advanced reforms exempting certain single-specialty ASCs from review, and New York proposed raising its hospital CON threshold from $15 million to $30 million.

body.message: In a CON state, a hospital cannot simply decide to build based on financial merit. It must first determine whether the project triggers CON review and, if so, win regulatory approval — a process competitors can oppose. A capital plan that ignores CON can be dead on arrival no matter how strong its projected return.
body.title: CON Is the First Question, Not an Afterthought

children.text: The Financial Analysis: Will the Investment Pay Off?

For projects that clear regulatory hurdles, hospitals apply rigorous capital-budgeting techniques to judge financial merit. The most important is net present value (NPV), which measures the dollar profitability of a project by discounting its expected future cash flows back to today’s dollars and subtracting the initial investment. A positive NPV means the project is expected to create value after accounting for the time value of money; a negative NPV means it destroys value. NPV is the gold standard because it answers the question that matters: will this investment make the hospital better off in real terms?

Several companion metrics fill out the picture. Internal rate of return (IRR) expresses a project’s return as a percentage, making it easy to compare against the hospital’s cost of capital. Payback period measures how long it takes to recoup the original investment — intuitive and useful for gauging risk, but flawed because it ignores both long-term profitability and the time value of money. Profitability index (PI) measures return per dollar invested, which is especially valuable when capital is scarce because it ranks projects by efficiency of capital use, not just total return.
