children.text: From Framework to Teeth: Data and Payment

A framework only matters if it is wired into requirements and money. CMS has done this through two main channels: quality measurement and payment incentives. On measurement, CMS has pushed stratification of quality measures by social risk and demographics — the operational expression of "you cannot improve what you cannot see." Stratified measurement turns the aggregate trap from a concept into something programs are expected to confront.

The most powerful lever, though, is payment, and the clearest example is the Medicare Advantage and Part D Star Ratings system. Star Ratings score plans on dozens of quality measures, and the ratings drive enormous bonus payments — billions of dollars annually flow to high-rated plans. Because the money is so large, anything CMS builds into Star Ratings commands the immediate attention of every Medicare Advantage plan in the country.

CMS designed a specific equity mechanism for Star Ratings: a Health Equity Index (later renamed the "Excellent Health Outcomes for All," or EHO4all, reward). It was built to reward plans that achieve good outcomes specifically for enrollees with social risk factors — those who are dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid, receive the Part D low-income subsidy, or qualified for Medicare due to disability. The reward, ranging up to 0.4 added to a plan's star rating, was structured so that a plan could only earn it by performing well for its most disadvantaged members — directly tying bonus dollars to equity.

body.content:
CMS developed a Health Equity Index reward — later renamed Excellent Health Outcomes for All (EHO4all) — to replace the legacy "reward factor" in Medicare Advantage and Part D Star Ratings. It targets enrollees with social risk factors: dual-eligible, low-income-subsidy, and disabled members.
The design adds a bonus (0 to 0.4) to a plan's raw star rating based on how large its disadvantaged population is and how well the plan scores for those members on a subset of measures. The point was structural: make billions in Star Ratings bonuses depend, in part, on closing outcome gaps for the most disadvantaged enrollees.
body.title: The Health Equity Index / EHO4all Reward in Star Ratings

children.text: A Crucial Caveat: Equity Requirements Are Reversible

It would be a mistake to present CMS's equity strategy as a settled, one-directional march. These requirements are creatures of federal policy, and federal policy changes with administrations. The most important current example: in its Contract Year 2027 Medicare Advantage and Part D final rule — finalized in 2026 — CMS reversed course on several equity provisions.

CMS finalized that it would not implement the Health Equity Index / EHO4all reward for the 2027 Star Ratings, instead continuing the historical reward factor that rewards consistently high performance across all enrollees. CMS also removed specific Medicare Advantage health-equity requirements, including the requirement that utilization-management committees include a health-equity expert, conduct annual health-equity analyses, and publicly post those analyses. In other words, a set of equity mechanisms that had been built and announced were rolled back before taking full effect.

The lesson here is not cynicism but realism. The structural insight — that payment and data requirements are the levers that move equity — remains true. But which specific requirements are in force at any given moment depends on current rulemaking. Anyone doing this work needs to track CMS rules in real time rather than assuming a framework announced in one year is fully operational in the next. The durable equity work in an organization should not depend solely on whether a particular federal incentive happens to be active.

body.message: CMS equity provisions can be reversed by rulemaking. The Health Equity Index / EHO4all reward was developed for the 2027 Star Ratings but then finalized as NOT implemented in the CY2027 final rule (2026), and several MA health-equity requirements were removed. Always confirm the current rule before relying on a specific CMS equity incentive — frameworks announced one year may be scaled back the next.
body.title: Verify which CMS equity requirements are currently in force

children.text: What This Means for Organizations

For health systems and plans, CMS's strategy carries a clear practical message regardless of the year-to-year fluctuations. The foundational capabilities CMS has pushed — high-quality demographic and social-risk data, stratified quality measurement, language access, and disability access — are valuable on their own terms and align with everything the evidence in this course supports. Organizations that build these capabilities are well-positioned whether or not a specific federal incentive is active.

It also means organizations should not outsource their equity commitment entirely to CMS incentives. An equity strategy that exists only because a Star Ratings bonus rewards it will evaporate the moment that bonus does — as the 2026 reversal illustrates. The durable approach is to treat equity as core to quality and mission, using CMS incentives as accelerants when they are available rather than as the sole reason for acting.

Finally, CMS's framework is a useful map even when its specific requirements shift. The five priorities — data, disparity assessment, organizational capacity, language and literacy, and disability access — describe a comprehensive equity program that any organization can adopt on its own initiative. The Framework tells you what a serious equity strategy looks like; whether CMS is currently paying for each piece is a separate, and changeable, question.

children.text: What Is the Collaborative Care Model?

The Collaborative Care Model (CoCM) is the most rigorously studied approach to integrating behavioral health into primary care. Rather than referring a depressed or anxious patient out to a separate mental health system — where many never arrive — CoCM treats common behavioral health conditions inside the primary care clinic, using a defined team and a systematic process.

The model grew out of research led by Dr. Wayne Katon and Dr. Jürgen Unützer at the University of Washington in the 1990s and is now maintained and disseminated by the university’s AIMS Center (Advancing Integrated Mental Health Solutions), founded in 2004. CoCM sits at the upper, "integrated" end of the SAMHSA-HRSA continuum because it requires a real change in how a primary care practice operates.

CoCM is built around a small, defined care team and a registry-driven, measurement-based process. It is not simply "having a therapist in the building." It is a specific, evidence-based way of organizing care so that patients are tracked, treatment is adjusted until they improve, and a psychiatric expert’s knowledge is leveraged across an entire population without seeing every patient directly.

The Collaborative Care Model (CoCM) treats common behavioral health conditions inside primary care using a defined team, a patient registry, and measurement-based care — adjusting treatment until the patient actually improves.
The Collaborative Care Team

CoCM relies on three roles working together. The primary care provider (PCP) leads the patient’s overall care and prescribes treatment. A behavioral health care manager — often a nurse, social worker, or counselor embedded in the clinic — provides brief interventions, coordinates care, supports the patient between visits, and maintains the patient registry. A psychiatric consultant reviews the caseload regularly and advises the team on diagnosis and treatment.

The crucial innovation is how the psychiatric consultant is used. Instead of seeing patients one at a time, the psychiatrist holds regular (often weekly) caseload reviews with the care manager, focusing on patients who are not improving. This "leveraged" model lets one psychiatric consultant support far more patients than they could ever see directly — a key reason CoCM extends scarce psychiatric expertise across an entire primary care population.

This division of labor is what makes the model both effective and scalable. The PCP keeps prescribing authority and the patient relationship, the care manager provides the continuity and follow-up that busy primary care usually cannot, and the consultant adds specialist expertise where it is most needed — for the patients who are stuck.

children.text: The Five Core Principles

The AIMS Center defines CoCM by five core principles. Together they distinguish true collaborative care from looser arrangements that may borrow the name without the substance. A program that lacks these principles — especially measurement and treatment-to-target — is not genuinely practicing CoCM.

The principles are: (1) patient-centered team care, in which the PCP and behavioral health team collaborate; (2) population-based care, using a registry so no patient "falls through the cracks"; (3) measurement-based treatment to target, using validated tools like the PHQ-9 for depression and GAD-7 for anxiety; (4) evidence-based care, applying treatments proven to work; and (5) accountable care, with reimbursement and quality tied to outcomes rather than volume.

Measurement-based treatment to target is the engine of the model. The team scores symptoms with a validated instrument at every contact and actively changes the treatment — adjusting medication or therapy — until the patient reaches a defined goal, such as a substantial drop in PHQ-9 score. Care is not "set and forget"; it is continuously steered toward improvement.

The Evidence Base

CoCM is exceptional among integration models because of the depth of its evidence. It began with the landmark IMPACT trial (Improving Mood — Promoting Access to Collaborative Treatment), published in 2002. IMPACT followed 1,801 older adults with depression across 18 primary care clinics affiliated with eight health care organizations in five states (Washington, California, Texas, Indiana, and North Carolina).

The results were striking: compared with usual care, collaborative care more than doubled the effectiveness of depression treatment. Since IMPACT, the model has been tested in more than 90 randomized controlled trials in the United States and abroad, consistently showing better clinical outcomes, greater patient and provider satisfaction, improved functioning, and lower total health care costs. A long-term IMPACT analysis even found reduced cardiovascular risk among treated patients.

This evidence base matters because it answers the skeptic’s question — "Does integrating behavioral health into primary care actually work?" — with an emphatic yes, across depression, anxiety, and co-morbid conditions such as diabetes and cancer. Few interventions in any area of medicine rest on as many randomized trials.

Led by Dr. Jürgen Unützer at the University of Washington, IMPACT enrolled 1,801 depressed older adults across 18 diverse primary care clinics in five states and randomized them to collaborative care or usual care.

children.text: Implementation and Financing

For years, a major barrier to CoCM was payment: the care manager’s follow-up calls and the psychiatrist’s caseload reviews did not fit traditional face-to-face billing. That changed when Medicare introduced specific monthly billing codes for Collaborative Care. CPT codes 99492 and 99493 reimburse the first and subsequent months of CoCM (based on care-manager time and required activities like registry tracking and caseload review), with 99494 and HCPCS code G2214 for additional increments.

These codes were a turning point because they pay for the model as it actually works — team-based, between-visit, population-focused care — rather than forcing it into a fee-for-service mold. Many state Medicaid programs and commercial payers have since adopted similar coverage, and the codes embody the "accountable care" principle by tying payment to the defined CoCM process.

Implementation still requires real change: hiring or training care managers, contracting a psychiatric consultant, building a registry, and adopting measurement-based workflows. But with both a deep evidence base and a payment pathway, CoCM has become the leading template for integrating behavioral health into primary care at scale.

children.text: Who Community Health Workers Are

Much of the equity work in this course points to the same need: someone who can bridge the gap between a health system and the daily lives of the patients it struggles to reach. Community health workers (CHWs) are that bridge. The American Public Health Association defines them as frontline public health workers who are trusted members of, or have an unusually close understanding of, the community they serve. That trust and shared experience is their defining asset.

A CHW is typically from the same community as the patients they work with — sharing language, culture, neighborhood, and often lived experience of the same challenges. They go by many names: promotores, community health representatives, patient navigators, peer support specialists, outreach workers. What unites them is a role grounded in relationship rather than clinical authority. They are not mini-doctors; they are connectors, educators, advocates, and navigators.

This positioning lets CHWs do what credentialed clinicians often cannot. They can meet patients in their homes and neighborhoods, understand the practical barriers behind a missed appointment or an unfilled prescription, and help solve them — and they can earn trust from communities that have good historical reasons to distrust the medical system. For exactly the populations that experience the worst disparities, a trusted person from their own community is sometimes the most effective intervention available.

Community health workers are trusted frontline workers from the communities they serve. Their power comes from shared language, culture, and lived experience — they connect, educate, advocate, and navigate rather than provide clinical care.
What CHWs Actually Do

The CHW role is broad by design, shaped around whatever stands between a patient and good health. In practice, the work clusters into a few core functions. They provide health education and coaching — explaining a diagnosis, demonstrating how to use a glucometer, reinforcing a care plan in plain, culturally familiar language. They provide navigation — helping patients schedule appointments, understand insurance, find a specialist, or apply for benefits.

They also do the social-needs work that ties this whole course together. A CHW is often the person who screens for and acts on social determinants — connecting a patient to a food bank, a housing navigator, transportation, or utility assistance, and following up to make sure the connection actually happened. In the language of earlier lessons, CHWs are frequently the human infrastructure that turns a positive SDOH screen into a closed-loop referral.

And they provide something harder to categorize: advocacy and relationship. CHWs accompany patients to appointments, advocate for them within a confusing system, and offer consistent human support to people who are often isolated. This relational continuity is part of why CHW interventions work — they address not just discrete tasks but the trust and engagement that make everything else possible. The model is most powerful when CHWs are integrated into the care team, not bolted on as an afterthought.

children.text: The Evidence: Outcomes and Return on Investment

CHW programs are sometimes dismissed as feel-good initiatives without rigorous evidence. That dismissal is outdated. The strongest body of evidence comes from the IMPaCT program developed at the University of Pennsylvania's Penn Center for Community Health Workers, which has been tested in multiple randomized controlled trials — a far higher evidentiary bar than most social interventions clear.

Across three randomized controlled trials, IMPaCT improved chronic disease control, mental health, and quality of care while reducing total hospital days substantially and improving patient satisfaction with primary care. These are not soft outcomes — they are the hard clinical and utilization measures health systems care about, demonstrated in the gold-standard study design.

The economic evidence is equally important for sustainability. A widely cited Health Affairs analysis found that every dollar invested in the IMPaCT model returned about $2.47 to an average Medicaid payer within the same year — meaning the program more than paid for itself. This was the first economic analysis of a health-system-based CHW intervention for adults built on randomized-trial data. The combination of improved outcomes and positive ROI is what moves CHWs from a nice idea to a financially defensible investment.

children.text: The Sustainability Challenge

Despite strong evidence, CHW programs have historically struggled to survive — not because they do not work, but because of how they are funded. For years, CHW programs were financed largely through time-limited grants. A grant funds a program for two or three years; the program demonstrates good results; the grant ends; the program disappears. This boom-and-bust cycle has repeatedly destroyed effective CHW programs and wasted the trust they built in communities.

The core problem is the absence of a stable, recurring payment mechanism. Unlike a physician visit, a CHW's work did not traditionally generate a billable, reimbursable service, so it had no natural place in health care's revenue streams. Sustainable CHW programs need an ongoing funding source tied to the value they produce — which, given the ROI evidence, is economically justified but operationally hard to wire into payment systems.

The most promising path is Medicaid financing. In a 2013 rule (effective January 2014), CMS allowed state Medicaid programs to reimburse for preventive services delivered by non-licensed providers, including CHWs, when recommended by a licensed practitioner. Since then, more than half of state Medicaid programs have implemented some form of CHW coverage and payment policy. This shift — from grant-dependent to Medicaid-reimbursable — is the single most important development for putting CHW programs on durable footing, though adequate payment rates remain a real concern.

body.content:
The IMPaCT model, developed at the University of Pennsylvania, is the most rigorously evaluated CHW program in the US, tested in three randomized controlled trials and serving more than 12,000 patients in the Philadelphia region.
Its trials showed improved chronic-disease control, mental health, and care quality with reduced hospital days, and a Health Affairs economic analysis found a $2.47 return per $1 invested for Medicaid. IMPaCT is widely used as a blueprint precisely because it pairs strong outcomes with a documented business case — the combination needed to make CHW programs sustainable.
body.title: Penn Center for Community Health Workers (IMPaCT)

children.text: Building CHW Programs That Last

Translating the evidence into durable programs requires attention to design as well as financing. The trials make clear that CHW effectiveness depends on doing the model well: hiring genuinely from the community, training adequately, integrating CHWs into the care team with clear roles, giving them manageable caseloads, and supporting them with supervision. A CHW program that hires the wrong people, isolates them from the team, or overloads them will not reproduce the trial results.

Sustainability also has a workforce dimension. CHWs deserve professional respect, fair pay, and career pathways — and increasingly a voice in the policies that govern their own field. The APHA has emphasized CHW self-determination, including the principle that CHWs themselves should have a substantial role in decisions about CHW definition, training, and standards. Certification requirements vary by state; some require state-level certification through an approved program, while others do not, and the field continues to work toward consistent standards without over-professionalizing away the community-rootedness that makes CHWs effective.

The bottom line is that CHWs are one of the best-evidenced, most directly equity-relevant interventions available — a workforce explicitly designed to reach the populations that experience the worst disparities. The remaining challenge is not proving they work but financing and structuring them so they endure. The shift toward Medicaid reimbursement, combined with disciplined program design, is what can finally break the grant-funded boom-and-bust cycle and let effective programs persist.

Durable programs need recurring funding, increasingly through Medicaid reimbursement (enabled by the 2013/2014 CMS rule). Plan for sustainable financing from the start, not as an afterthought when the grant runs out.

title: Community Health Workers: Evidence, Roles & Sustainability

children.text: Reaching the People the System Misses

The previous lesson showed how to find disparities by stratifying data. But finding a gap is not closing it — and the groups faring worst are often precisely the ones the health system struggles to reach: people facing language barriers, mistrust born of historical harm, poverty, unstable housing, and social isolation. Conventional clinical outreach frequently fails with exactly these populations. Community health workers (CHWs) are the most effective tool for reaching them.

A community health worker is a frontline worker who is a trusted member of, or has a close understanding of, the community they serve. That trust is the entire point. A CHW from the neighborhood, who speaks the language and shares the lived experience, can connect with patients in ways a clinician from outside the community often cannot. The CHW serves as a bridge between the health and social-service systems and the community.

This makes CHWs core population health infrastructure, not a charitable add-on. They are how a program actually reaches the high-risk, hard-to-engage, disparity-affected patients that risk stratification and equity stratification identify. If care management is the human engine of population health, CHWs are the part of that engine purpose-built for the communities the system has historically failed.

A community health worker (CHW) is a frontline worker who is a trusted member of the community they serve, bridging health and social services to advance equity. CHWs are how population health reaches the high-risk, disparity-affected patients conventional outreach misses.
What CHWs Do: The C3 Roles

The roles and skills of CHWs were standardized by the Community Health Worker Core Consensus (C3) Project, carried out from 2014 to 2018, which defined a national consensus set — ten core roles and eleven core skills. This gave the field a shared definition of what CHWs do, supporting training, certification, and workforce development.

The C3 roles span the bridge function: cultural mediation between communities and systems; culturally appropriate health education and information; care coordination, case management, and system navigation; providing coaching and social support; advocating for individuals and communities; building individual and community capacity; providing direct service (like basic screening); implementing assessments; conducting outreach; and participating in evaluation and research.

Notice how these map onto population health needs. System navigation and care coordination address the fragmentation problem; outreach reaches the patients not coming in; cultural mediation and social support engage the disparity-affected groups; and connecting patients to social services addresses the social determinants that drive most of health. CHWs operationalize the social-needs side of population health that clinicians are poorly positioned to handle.

children.text: The Evidence: It Works and It Pays

CHWs are sometimes dismissed as a "nice to have" without hard evidence. That objection is outdated. The strongest evidence comes from the IMPaCT program (Individualized Management for Patient-Centered Targets), developed at Penn and tested in rigorous multi-center randomized controlled trials — the gold standard, addressing the criticism that earlier CHW economic studies were not rigorous enough.

The results are striking. The IMPaCT randomized trial found the program reduced total hospital days by 65 percent and doubled patient satisfaction with primary care, while modestly improving control of conditions like diabetes, obesity, and mental health. IMPaCT works by hiring and training trusted neighborhood residents as CHWs to address unmet social needs — housing, food, transportation — and to provide social support, advocacy, and health-system navigation for underserved patients.

And it pays. A Health Affairs economic analysis found that Penn's CHW program returned $2.47 for every $1 invested annually by Medicaid, with the savings driven by reduced hospitalizations. This is the rare population health intervention with randomized-trial evidence of both better outcomes AND positive return on investment — a roughly 2.5-to-1 ROI. CHWs are not charity; they are a high-return investment.

children.text: Making CHW Programs Sustainable

Like collaborative care and care management, CHW programs historically struggled with sustainability because there was no clear way to pay for them outside grants. That is changing: a growing number of state Medicaid programs now reimburse CHW services, increasingly via Medicaid State Plan Amendments and other pathways, giving CHW programs a durable financial footing rather than relying on time-limited grants.

Sustainability also depends on doing CHW programs well. The evidence is strongest for structured, evidence-based programs like IMPaCT — with defined roles, real training (aligned to the C3 competencies), appropriate caseloads, integration into the care team, and clear protocols — rather than loosely-defined "community outreach." A CHW program designed and supported like a serious clinical program produces serious results; one treated as an afterthought does not.

For population health, the practical model is to integrate CHWs into the care-management team (the embedded model from the care-management lesson), deploy them to the disparity-affected and high-social-need patients that stratification identifies, support them with training and supervision, and bill the available reimbursement to sustain the program. Done this way, CHWs become permanent infrastructure for reaching the communities the system most needs to serve.

Penn's IMPaCT program hires and trains trusted residents from the communities it serves as community health workers. They help underserved, high-risk patients with unmet social needs — finding housing resources, addressing food insecurity, arranging transportation — and provide social support and health-system navigation.
In randomized trials this reduced hospital days by 65%, doubled primary-care satisfaction, and returned $2.47 per Medicaid dollar — demonstrating that a structured, evidence-based CHW program is both effective and a sound financial investment.

children.text: CHWs and the Equity Mission

CHWs are the natural answer to the equity challenge this module poses. Stratification reveals which groups are faring worse; the determinants lesson showed those gaps are driven largely by social factors outside the clinic; and CHWs are uniquely equipped to address exactly those social factors for exactly those communities, with the trust and cultural concordance that make engagement possible. The equity diagnosis and the CHW intervention fit together.

They also embody the course's recurring themes: they are proactive (reaching people not in care), whole-population (focused on the panel, especially its hardest-to-reach members), team-based (one role in a care-management team), and aimed at the social determinants that drive most of health. CHWs are population health's equity strategy made into a workforce.

The broader lesson is that closing disparities requires more than better data and good intentions — it requires people who can actually reach and earn the trust of underserved communities. CHWs are that workforce, with rigorous evidence behind them and a growing payment model to sustain them. A population health program serious about equity builds CHWs into its core, not its margins. The final lessons turn to measuring all of this — the dashboards and quality improvement that prove whether the whole population health effort, equity included, is actually working.

body.message: The strong outcomes and ~2.5:1 ROI come from structured, evidence-based CHW programs (like IMPaCT) — with real training, defined roles, manageable caseloads, care-team integration, and reimbursement. Loosely-defined "community outreach" without that structure does not reliably produce results. Treat CHW programs as serious clinical infrastructure, not an afterthought.

title: Community Health Workers as Population Health Infrastructure

children.text: Why "Integration" Became the Goal

For most of the twentieth century, mental health and substance use care developed separately from the rest of medicine — in different buildings, under different funding streams, with different records and different rules. This separation, often called fragmentation or "carve-out," produced exactly the problems the first track of this course described: people with serious mental illness dying of untreated physical disease, and people with co-occurring disorders bounced between systems that each addressed only half the problem.

Integrated care is the systematic coordination of physical and behavioral health care. The premise is simple but powerful: the body and mind are not separate, the same patients move through both systems, and care works better when those systems communicate, share information, and ideally operate as one team. Behavioral health conditions are extremely common in primary care, and physical conditions are common among people receiving behavioral health care.

But "integration" is not a single thing you either have or lack. It is a continuum — a range of arrangements from two providers who occasionally fax each other a note, all the way to a single merged team sharing one chart and one treatment plan. Knowing where a given practice sits on that continuum is essential to talking about integration precisely.

Integrated care is the systematic coordination of physical and behavioral health. It is not binary — it exists on a continuum from minimal coordination between separate organizations to a single, fully merged team sharing one record and one plan.
A Standard Language: The SAMHSA-HRSA Framework

In April 2013, the SAMHSA-HRSA Center for Integrated Health Solutions published "A Standard Framework for Levels of Integrated Healthcare." It built on earlier work by Doherty, McDaniel, and Baird (1996) and gave the field a shared national vocabulary for describing exactly how integrated a practice is.

The framework defines six levels of collaboration and integration, grouped into three broad categories: Coordinated care, Co-located care, and Integrated care. Each category contains two levels, so the six levels run from minimal collaboration between fully separate organizations up to full collaboration in a single transformed, merged practice.

The value of this framework is shared language. It lets two partnering organizations honestly assess where they are, set a realistic target, explain their model to funders and regulators, and benchmark progress over time. When this course or a clinic says a practice is "Level 4" or "co-located," everyone is referring to the same defined point on the continuum.

body.title: The Three Categories of Integration (SAMHSA-HRSA)

children.text: The Six Levels in Detail

Each of the three categories contains two levels, giving six steps on the continuum. As a practice moves up the levels, three things increase: how physically close the providers are, how much they share systems like records and scheduling, and how much they change their actual clinical practice to work as a unified team.

It is important to understand that higher is not automatically "better" for every organization. Full integration (Level 6) requires significant investment, cultural change, and financing that supports team-based care. A small rural clinic might realistically aim for strong coordination or co-location rather than full merger. The framework is a map, not a mandate to reach Level 6.

body.title: Higher Is Not Always the Goal

children.text: Coordinated vs. Co-located vs. Integrated

The single most useful distinction in this framework is among its three categories, because they answer three different questions. Coordinated care answers, "Do the providers communicate?" Co-located care answers, "Are they in the same building?" Integrated care answers, "Do they function as one team with shared practice?"

These are genuinely different. Two providers can share a building (co-located) but never coordinate a patient’s care if they keep separate records and never talk — proximity alone is not integration. Conversely, providers in different buildings can coordinate well through shared protocols and warm handoffs. True integration requires changing how the practice actually works, not just where people sit.

children.text: Using the Continuum in the Real World

The continuum is more than a teaching tool — it shapes policy and practice. Federal grant programs, health systems, and states use the framework and related assessment tools to evaluate where practices stand and to set improvement targets. SAMHSA also funded demonstration programs, such as the Primary and Behavioral Health Care Integration (PBHCI) grants, to help organizations move up the continuum.

The specific integration models in the next two lessons map onto the upper levels of this continuum. The Collaborative Care Model and the Primary Care Behavioral Health model are both ways of operationalizing close collaboration and integration — concrete, evidence-based approaches to actually doing team-based care rather than just describing the destination.

For anyone working in or analyzing health care, the takeaway is to ask not simply "Is this practice integrated?" but "Where on the continuum is it, and where does it realistically want to be?" That precision is what the SAMHSA-HRSA framework made possible.

children.text: The Contract Is Where Promises Become Obligations

Once a state selects its MCOs through the procurement covered in the last lesson, it translates the winning proposals into a binding contract. That contract — often hundreds of pages long — is the single most important operational document in Medicaid managed care. It converts the federal requirements of 42 CFR Part 438 and the state’s own priorities into specific, enforceable obligations the plan must meet. If the procurement is where the state chooses its partners, the contract is where it defines exactly what those partners must do.

Three categories of contract requirements form the operational backbone of every Medicaid MCO contract: network adequacy (ensuring enrollees can actually access providers), quality assurance (ensuring the care is good), and reporting (ensuring the state can see what the plan is doing). These three threads run through the entire relationship, and each is anchored in federal regulation. Together they are how a state holds a risk-bearing private plan accountable for serving a vulnerable public population.

Understanding these requirements matters because they are the mechanism that addresses the central tension of managed care. A capitated plan has an incentive to spend less — which could mean a thin network, skimpy care, or hidden problems. Network, quality, and reporting requirements are the contractual counterweights: they force the plan to maintain real access, demonstrate real quality, and show the state real data.

Key Concept: An MCO contract converts federal rules and state priorities into binding obligations across three core areas — network adequacy (access), quality assurance (good care), and reporting (transparency) — backed by enforcement tools like sanctions and liquidated damages.
Network Adequacy Requirements

The first pillar is network adequacy: the contract must require the plan to maintain a provider network sufficient to deliver the covered services. Under 42 CFR 438.68, states must develop and publish a quantitative network adequacy standard (other than appointment wait times — often time-and-distance or provider-to-enrollee ratios) for a defined set of provider types — primary care (adult and pediatric), OB/GYN, behavioral health, adult and pediatric specialists, hospitals, pharmacy, and pediatric dental — plus additional types as CMS determines. The 2024 final rule layered appointment wait-time standards on top of these, as the federal-framework lesson described, so adequacy is now judged by both the state’s quantitative standards and timeliness.

Crucially, network adequacy is not just about counting providers. In setting standards, states must consider factors such as providers’ ability to communicate with limited-English-proficient enrollees, accommodation of disabilities, the availability of triage or screening lines, and the use of telemedicine and other innovative technologies. This reflects a recognition that a "provider in the network" is only meaningful if a real enrollee — who may have a disability, speak limited English, or live far from care — can actually reach and use them. The contract embeds these considerations as binding requirements.

To verify adequacy, states require plans to support a Network Adequacy and Access Assurances Report (NAAAR), documenting an analysis that supports the assurance that each plan’s network is adequate. Combined with the secret-shopper surveys from the federal-framework lesson, this gives the state both the plan’s self-reported network data and an independent test of whether that network functions in practice — closing the gap between paper networks and real access.
Quality Assurance Requirements

The second pillar is quality assurance. The contract must require the plan to participate in the state’s quality apparatus, which federal rules build around several components. Each state contracting with managed care plans must draft and implement a written quality strategy for assessing and improving the quality of care (42 CFR 438.340). Within that, each plan must operate a Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) program, undergo external quality review (EQR) by an independent organization, and meet accreditation and reporting requirements.

These requirements work together as a system. The state’s quality strategy sets the overall direction and goals. Each plan’s QAPI program is its internal engine for measuring and improving care. External quality review provides an independent, expert assessment of each plan’s performance — the subject of its own lesson later in this course. And quality measure reporting (including HEDIS, also covered later) generates the data that feeds all of it. The contract binds the plan into this entire structure, making quality not optional but a condition of payment.

body.message: Because a capitated plan profits by spending less, there is a risk it could cut corners on care. The quality strategy, QAPI, external quality review, and measure reporting exist precisely to detect under-provision and force improvement — turning "good care" from a hope into a measured, enforceable obligation.
body.title: Quality Requirements Counter the Skimping Incentive

children.text: Reporting Requirements and Enrollee Protections

The third pillar is reporting — the data flow that lets the state see what its plans are doing. The centerpiece is the requirement under 42 CFR 438.66 that each state submit to CMS, no later than 180 days after each contract year, a Managed Care Program Annual Report (MCPAR) on each program. That report must assess, at minimum, each plan’s financial performance (including medical loss ratio), the quality and timeliness of encounter data, enrollment and benefit changes, a summary of grievances, appeals, and state fair hearings, network adequacy and access, and performance on quality measures. The MCPAR is essentially the state’s annual accountability ledger for managed care.

Two reporting streams deserve special note. Encounter data — the information about every item or service an enrollee receives under the contract — is the managed care equivalent of fee-for-service claims data, and it is essential for rate-setting, quality measurement, and oversight; the timeliness and accuracy of encounter data is itself a monitored requirement. And appeals and grievances data give a direct window into enrollee experience: enrollees can appeal service denials and file grievances about any dissatisfaction, and states must summarize each plan’s appeals, grievances, and state fair hearings for CMS in the annual MCPAR, so the state can spot a plan that is denying too much care.

These reporting requirements connect to enforcement. Federal rules require states to maintain a monitoring system spanning administration, appeals and grievances, claims, enrollee materials, finance and MLR, information systems and encounter data, marketing, medical and utilization management, program integrity, network management, quality improvement, and LTSS delivery. When monitoring reveals problems, contracts give states enforcement tools: monetary penalties, corrective action plans, suspension of new enrollment, and liquidated damages — predetermined monetary penalties written into the contract for specific failures. These are the teeth behind the requirements.

body.title: The Three Pillars of an MCO Contract

children.text: Why the Contract Is the Heart of Oversight

Everything a state can require of a plan after the contract is signed must be in the contract. This makes contract design enormously consequential — it is the state’s last and best chance to exercise leverage. A weak contract with vague standards and few reporting requirements leaves the state with little ability to hold a plan accountable; a strong contract with clear, measurable, enforceable requirements gives the state real oversight. Because the relationship runs for years, the quality of the contract determines the quality of the accountability for the entire contract term.

body.analogy: An MCO contract is like the franchise agreement behind a restaurant chain. The franchisee (the plan) runs the day-to-day operation, but the agreement dictates the standards it must meet — the menu it must offer (covered services), the locations it must staff (network adequacy), the inspections it must pass (quality review), and the sales reports it must file (reporting). If a location skimps, the franchise agreement’s penalty clauses (sanctions and liquidated damages) are what let headquarters force a fix. A vague agreement means a chain that can’t control its own restaurants.
body.concept: How the MCO contract enables oversight

children.text: The three pillars also illustrate how managed care’s components interlock. Network adequacy without reporting would be unverifiable; quality requirements without enforcement would be toothless; reporting without standards to measure against would be meaningless. The contract weaves them together: it sets the standards (network and quality), requires the data to verify them (reporting), and attaches the consequences for failure (sanctions). Each pillar depends on the others, and the contract is what binds them into a coherent system of accountability.

This lesson sets up the rest of the course in a direct way. The monitoring and oversight lesson that follows explains how the state actually uses the reporting and enforcement provisions established here. The rate-setting module explains how the financial terms — including the encounter data and MLR provisions referenced above — are calculated. The network adequacy and quality lessons go deeper into those specific contract requirements. The contract is the hub; the operational details radiate out from it. Master what the contract requires, and you understand the structure within which all of Medicaid managed care operates.

points: The MCO contract converts federal rules (42 CFR Part 438) and state priorities into binding, enforceable obligations, organized around three core pillars: network adequacy, quality assurance, and reporting.

Network adequacy requirements (438.68) include quantitative standards (such as time-and-distance or provider ratios) for specified provider types plus 2024 appointment wait-time standards, and must consider LEP communication, disability accommodation, and telehealth.
States require network assurance documentation (the NAAAR) and, combined with secret-shopper surveys, verify that paper networks deliver real access.

Quality assurance requires a state quality strategy (438.340), a plan QAPI program, external quality review by an independent organization, and accreditation/measure reporting — a system that exists to counter the skimping incentive of capitation.

Reporting centers on the Managed Care Program Annual Report (MCPAR) under 438.66, due within 180 days of the contract year, covering financial performance/MLR, encounter data, enrollment/benefit changes, grievances and appeals, network adequacy, and quality measures.

Encounter data (the record of every service an enrollee receives) is the managed care equivalent of claims data and is essential for rate-setting, quality, and oversight; appeals and grievances data (summarized for CMS in the annual MCPAR) reveal enrollee experience and over-denial.

Federal rules require a broad state monitoring system, and contracts provide enforcement teeth — monetary penalties, corrective action plans, enrollment suspension, and liquidated damages (predetermined penalties for specific failures).

Because anything the state can require after signing must be in the contract, contract design is the state’s key point of leverage — a strong, measurable contract enables real oversight for the entire multi-year term.

title: Contract Requirements: Network Adequacy, Quality Assurance, and Reporting

children.text: The Gap Between Billed and Collected

In the previous lesson, we saw that a hospital’s gross charges (what it bills at chargemaster prices) are far higher than its net revenue (what it actually collects). This lesson dissects exactly where that money goes. The difference between what a hospital bills and what it keeps is not one thing — it is three distinct categories, each with its own cause, accounting treatment, and policy significance: contractual adjustments, charity care, and bad debt.

Confusing these three is one of the most common errors in hospital finance, and it leads to badly wrong conclusions. A contractual adjustment is a planned discount the hospital agreed to. Charity care is care the hospital chose to give away to those who cannot pay. Bad debt is money the hospital expected to collect but never received. They look similar on a statement — all three reduce gross charges down toward net revenue — but they mean completely different things about the hospital and its patients.

Getting the distinctions right matters enormously. They determine how a hospital reports its finances, whether a nonprofit meets its community-benefit obligations, how much "uncompensated care" the sector claims, and how aggressively a hospital pursues patients for unpaid bills. This is where hospital finance, tax law, and medical-debt policy all intersect.

Key Concept: Three different write-downs separate gross charges from net revenue. Contractual adjustments are agreed payer discounts (not uncompensated care). Charity care is free/discounted care for those who cannot pay. Bad debt is expected payment that was never received. Charity care + bad debt = uncompensated care.

stats.context: U.S. hospitals provided almost $745 billion in uncompensated care between 2000 and 2020 (American Hospital Association)
stats.label: Uncompensated Care, 2000–2020

stats.context: Charity care plus bad debt, measured at cost, in a single year (American Hospital Association, 2022 fact sheet)
stats.label: Uncompensated Care in 2020

children.text: Contractual Adjustments: The Discount You Agreed To

A contractual adjustment (or contractual allowance) is the difference between a hospital’s gross charge and the amount a payer is contractually obligated to pay under its negotiated rate. If a hospital bills $5,000 for a procedure and the insurer’s contract says it will pay $1,200, the $3,800 difference is a contractual adjustment. Crucially, this is not money the hospital ever expected to receive — it is the discount baked into the contract the hospital signed.

This is the single most important point about contractual adjustments: they are not uncompensated care. The IRS is explicit that charity care excludes contractual adjustments with third-party payors, self-pay or prompt-pay discounts, and the gap between Medicare/Medicaid revenue and cost. A contractual adjustment simply reflects the reality that chargemaster prices are fiction and negotiated rates are the truth. By far the largest portion of the gap between gross and net revenue is contractual adjustments — and it represents a planned discount, not a loss or a charitable act.

body.message: Hospitals (and headlines) sometimes describe the gap between inflated chargemaster prices and negotiated payments as money "lost" or "given away." It is neither. A contractual adjustment is a discount off a fictional list price the hospital itself set artificially high — not a charitable contribution and not uncompensated care.
body.title: Contractual Adjustments Are Not "Losses"

children.text: Charity Care vs. Bad Debt: Intent Is the Dividing Line

Once contractual adjustments are set aside, the remaining unpaid amounts fall into two categories that look identical on a balance sheet but differ entirely in meaning. The dividing line is intent and expectation. Charity care is free or discounted care provided to patients who are unable to pay and who meet the hospital’s specified income and asset criteria. The hospital never expected payment — it deliberately provided the care for free or at a reduced cost to those in need.

Bad debt is the opposite: it represents services for which the hospital expected payment but never received it. Bad debt arises when patients who could potentially pay — or who never applied for financial assistance — simply do not pay their bills, whether because they cannot, will not, or never engaged with the billing process. The same unpaid $2,000 hospital bill is charity care if the patient qualified for and received financial assistance, but bad debt if the patient simply never paid and never applied.

left.label: Charity Care
points: Hospital never expected payment
Patient qualifies under income/asset criteria
Deliberately provided free or discounted
Counts toward nonprofit community benefit
Reflects the hospital’s charitable mission

right.label: Bad Debt
points: Hospital expected payment but did not collect
Patient may not have applied for assistance
Results from non-payment, not a granted discount
Treated as a credit loss, not charity
Often reflects gaps in screening or collections

body.title: Charity Care vs. Bad Debt

children.text: Together, charity care and bad debt make up uncompensated care — the overall measure of hospital care for which no payment was received from patient or insurer. This is the number the hospital industry cites to demonstrate the burden of serving the uninsured and underinsured. Note what it excludes: contractual adjustments and the Medicare/Medicaid shortfall are not part of uncompensated care, which is why precise definitions matter so much in debates about hospital finances.
Why the Distinction Has Legal Teeth: Section 501(r)

For nonprofit hospitals, the line between charity care and bad debt is not just an accounting nicety — it is a legal obligation tied to their tax exemption. Under Internal Revenue Code Section 501(r), enacted as part of the Affordable Care Act, tax-exempt hospitals must establish a written financial assistance policy (FAP) and a separate written policy for emergency medical care. The FAP must spell out the eligibility criteria for charity care, how patients apply, and how the hospital distinguishes charity care from bad debt.

Section 501(r) goes further, imposing concrete patient protections. It limits the amounts a hospital can charge financial-assistance-eligible patients for emergency or medically necessary care (they cannot be billed more than the amounts generally billed to insured patients), and it restricts "extraordinary collection actions" — such as lawsuits, wage garnishment, or reporting to credit agencies — until the hospital has made reasonable efforts to determine whether the patient qualifies for financial assistance. A hospital that fails these requirements risks its tax-exempt status.

body.content:
Imagine a uninsured patient treated in the ER who never fills out a financial-assistance application. If the hospital simply sends the bill to collections, the unpaid amount becomes bad debt — and the patient may face aggressive collection actions.

If instead the hospital screens the patient and determines they would have qualified for financial assistance (sometimes called "presumptive eligibility"), the same care is reclassified as charity care. The dollars written off are similar, but the meaning is opposite: one is a failure of process that harms a vulnerable patient and inflates bad debt; the other fulfills the hospital’s charitable mission and its 501(r) obligations. This is why screening patients for assistance is both an ethical and a financial priority.
body.title: Why "Presumptive Charity" Matters

children.text: The Bigger Picture: A Rising Burden

These categories are not static — they move with the economy and with policy. Uncompensated care has been an enormous and growing burden: U.S. hospitals provided almost $745 billion in uncompensated care between 2000 and 2020, including $42.7 billion in 2020 alone (AHA). And it moves with coverage: when pandemic-era Medicaid continuous-enrollment protections unwound in 2023 and more patients lost insurance, hospitals faced more uninsured patients and more unpaid bills.

The strain falls unevenly. Rural and safety-net hospitals, which serve disproportionate numbers of uninsured and low-income patients, absorb the most uncompensated care while having the fewest commercial patients to offset it. As uncompensated care rises, these facilities are forced to cut services, delay investments, or close — exactly the institutions whose communities can least afford to lose them. The scheduled Medicaid DSH cuts, discussed in the payer-mix lesson, threaten to land on top of this rising uncompensated-care burden.

body.analogy: Think of a hospital’s billed charges as a restaurant tab. The contractual adjustment is the standing discount the regular customer’s membership card always applies — expected and agreed. Charity care is the meal the owner deliberately comps for someone who clearly can’t pay. Bad debt is the diner who quietly walks out without paying a bill the owner fully expected to collect. All three reduce the till, but only a careless bookkeeper would record them the same way.
body.concept: Contractual adjustments vs. charity care vs. bad debt

children.text: For the student of hospital finance, the lesson is precision. When you see that a hospital "wrote off" a large sum, the first question is always: which kind of write-off? A mountain of contractual adjustments is normal and meaningless as a measure of charity. A large charity-care figure may reflect genuine community benefit. A swelling bad-debt figure may signal a broken financial-assistance process or a community losing insurance. Three numbers that look alike tell three completely different stories — and knowing which is which is the mark of someone who actually understands how hospitals get paid, and how they don’t.

points: The gap between a hospital’s gross charges and net revenue comes from three distinct categories: contractual adjustments, charity care, and bad debt — each with a different cause and meaning.
A contractual adjustment is the agreed difference between the chargemaster price and a payer’s negotiated rate; it is a planned discount, NOT uncompensated care and NOT a loss.

Charity care is care the hospital never expected to be paid for, provided free or discounted to patients who meet income/asset criteria; bad debt is care the hospital expected payment for but never received.
The dividing line between charity care and bad debt is intent and expectation — the same unpaid bill can be either, depending on whether the patient qualified for and received financial assistance.
Charity care plus bad debt equals uncompensated care; this measure excludes contractual adjustments and the Medicare/Medicaid payment shortfall.

IRC Section 501(r) requires tax-exempt hospitals to maintain a written financial assistance policy (FAP), limit charges to FAP-eligible patients, and restrict extraordinary collection actions until they determine assistance eligibility.

Screening patients for assistance ("presumptive eligibility") can reclassify bad debt as charity care — fulfilling the charitable mission and 501(r) obligations rather than subjecting vulnerable patients to aggressive collections.
Uncompensated care is large and rising — almost $745 billion from 2000–2020, and $42.7 billion in 2020 alone — and it falls hardest on rural and safety-net hospitals.

children.text: From "What Does Care Cost?" to "Which Care Makes Money?"

The previous lesson established that hospitals must allocate overhead to know the full cost of care. This lesson takes the next step: using cost information to answer the questions that actually drive hospital strategy. What does a single case — one knee replacement, one heart catheterization, one delivery — cost the hospital? And which clinical service lines are financially carrying the institution versus quietly draining it? These are the questions that determine where a hospital invests, what it markets, and sometimes what it stops doing altogether.

Two analytical tools answer them. Cost-per-case analysis estimates the cost of treating an individual patient or procedure. Service-line analysis aggregates those cases into clinical lines — cardiology, orthopedics, obstetrics, oncology — and measures the financial contribution of each. Together they turn the abstract idea of "cost" into concrete management decisions, and they reveal a truth that surprises many: a hospital’s busiest services are not always its most profitable, and its profitable services are not always the ones it promotes.

Key Concept: Cost-per-case analysis estimates what treating one patient or procedure costs the hospital. Service-line analysis aggregates cases into clinical lines (e.g., cardiology) to measure each line’s financial contribution — guiding investment, growth, and divestment decisions.

stats.context: Orthopedic surgeons generate an average of roughly $3.3 million in annual revenue for their affiliated hospitals — among the highest of any specialty (Merritt Hawkins 2019 survey)
stats.label: Orthopedic Surgeon Hospital Revenue

stats.context: Contribution margins for total hip replacement ran about $5,889 higher in concentrated hospital markets than in competitive ones (AJMC, Robinson)
stats.label: Hip Replacement Margin Gap

children.text: How Hospitals Estimate Cost Per Case

There is no single perfect way to cost an individual case; hospitals use several methods that trade accuracy against effort. The simplest is the ratio of cost to charges (RCC): a department divides its total cost by its total charges to get a ratio (say, $40 million in cost against $100 million in charges equals 0.4), then multiplies a case’s charges by that ratio to estimate its cost. RCC is fast and useful for high-level departmental monitoring, but because it applies a single average ratio to every case, it is unreliable for individual case-level decisions.

A more refined approach is RVU-based costing, which uses relative value units — standardized measures of the resources (physician time, staff time, equipment, supplies) a procedure consumes. The hospital divides total expenses by total RVUs to get a cost per RVU, then multiplies by the RVUs assigned to a given procedure. This better reflects relative resource intensity, though it can misstate cost when local workflows or patient mix differ from the national averages embedded in the RVU scale. The most precise (and most labor-intensive) method is microcosting, which tallies the actual individual resources consumed by a specific case.

steps.description: Multiply a case’s charges by the department’s cost-to-charge ratio. Fast and good for high-level monitoring; too crude for case-level decisions.
steps.title: Ratio of cost to charges (RCC)

steps.description: Divide total expenses by total RVUs to get cost per RVU, then multiply by a procedure’s RVUs. Reflects relative resource intensity.
steps.title: RVU-based costing

steps.description: Tally the actual resources a specific case consumes. Most accurate, most labor-intensive — reserved for high-value analyses.
steps.title: Microcosting

body.title: Three Common Cost-Per-Case Methods

body.message: RCC and similar average-based methods apply one ratio across every case, masking the real variation in resource use. They are fine for monitoring trends but dangerous for deciding whether a specific procedure or contract is profitable — that requires methods that reflect actual case-level resources.
body.title: Don’t Use Average Ratios for Specific Decisions

children.text: Contribution Margin: The Service-Line Workhorse

Once cases can be costed, the central tool for comparing them is contribution margin. Contribution margin measures the profitability of a case or service exclusive of indirect costs — that is, revenue minus the variable (direct) costs of providing the care, before subtracting overhead like administration, capital depreciation, and the cost of charity care. For a hospital paid a fixed amount per DRG (diagnosis-related group), contribution margin is calculated by comparing the case-related variable costs against the DRG payment for that case.

The reason contribution margin, rather than full cost, is the preferred tool for comparing treatments within a service line is subtle but important. Overhead is largely fixed and will be incurred whether or not a particular case is performed. So when deciding whether one more procedure is worth doing — or which procedures to grow — what matters is whether its revenue exceeds the additional variable cost it triggers. A procedure with a positive contribution margin helps cover the hospital’s fixed overhead even if, after full overhead allocation, it appears only marginally profitable.

The numbers vary enormously by procedure and market. One analysis found contribution margins running thousands of dollars higher in concentrated (less competitive) hospital markets — about $5,259 higher for angioplasty, $4,123 for total knee replacement, $5,889 for total hip replacement, and $7,931 for lumbar spine fusion — than in competitive markets, reflecting the pricing power that comes with market concentration. The same procedure can be a financial winner or a loser depending on the payment rate, the patient’s payer, and the hospital’s cost structure.
Which Service Lines Carry the Hospital?

Aggregate the contribution margins across a clinical line and you get service-line profitability — the financial scorecard hospital executives live by. The pattern is consistent across American hospitals: procedure-heavy specialties such as cardiovascular surgery, interventional cardiology, orthopedics, and neurosurgery consistently rank among the most profitable, while services like primary care, behavioral health, and obstetrics often run thin or negative margins despite being essential. An orthopedic surgeon generating around $3.3 million in annual hospital revenue (Merritt Hawkins, 2019) illustrates why these lines command so much strategic attention.

This profitability is exactly what funds the rest of the hospital. Positive contribution margins on orthopedic and cardiac procedures — especially for privately insured patients — are used to subsidize less remunerative procedures and patient groups, from money-losing behavioral health to charity care. Service-line analysis thus reveals the internal cross-subsidy that mirrors the payer-mix cross-subsidy: a handful of profitable lines keep the doors open for the mission-driven but unprofitable ones.

body.content:
A community hospital might assume its high-volume emergency department or its busy primary care clinics are financial pillars, simply because they are always full.

Service-line profitability reporting often overturns that assumption: those high-activity areas may carry thin or negative margins, while a lower-volume cardiac or orthopedic line quietly generates most of the contribution to margin. Leaders who assume a service line is profitable based on volume, referrals, or "downstream revenue" frequently find those assumptions don’t survive scrutiny — high activity does not guarantee positive margin. This is why CFOs insist on actual margin data rather than volume as the basis for strategy.
body.title: Why Volume Can Deceive

children.text: Turning Analysis Into Strategy — Carefully

With reliable cost-per-case and service-line data, leadership can make deliberate choices: grow the service lines with strong margins, invest in the staff and equipment that expand them, scrutinize lines that consume heavy resources for little contribution, and renegotiate or restructure money-losing arrangements. The purest financial logic says concentrate on the profitable lines and shed the unprofitable ones. Many hospital strategies — the marketing push behind a new orthopedic institute, the expansion of a cardiac program — flow directly from this analysis.

body.analogy: A hospital’s service lines are like a grocery store’s departments. The store may sell mountains of low-margin staples like milk and bread (the high-volume ED and primary care), but it earns its real profit on the prepared foods and specialty items (cardiac and orthopedic procedures). A manager who judged each department only by how many customers it served would mismanage the store; the one who tracks margin by department knows which aisles fund the rest — and which loss leaders are worth keeping anyway.
body.concept: Service-line profitability analysis

children.text: But pure financial logic runs straight into the hospital’s mission and obligations. The unprofitable service lines — behavioral health, obstetrics in rural areas, primary care, charity care — are often the ones a community most needs and, for nonprofit hospitals, the ones their tax-exempt community-benefit obligations require. A hospital that shed every money-losing line would betray its purpose and likely its legal standing. Service-line analysis must therefore inform strategy without dictating it; the goal is a sustainable portfolio, not the elimination of everything that loses money.

There is also a methodological humility required. As the previous lesson showed, overhead allocation is judgment, so a line’s "profitability" depends partly on how costs were assigned. Good analysts distinguish contribution margin (clean, based on variable costs) from fully allocated margin (which carries allocation assumptions), and they incorporate downstream and total-cost-of-care effects rather than viewing each line in isolation. Done well, cost-per-case and service-line analysis are among the most powerful tools in hospital finance. Done carelessly, they can justify abandoning exactly the care a community depends on — which is why the numbers must always be read alongside the mission.

points: Cost-per-case analysis estimates what treating one patient or procedure costs; service-line analysis aggregates cases into clinical lines to measure each line’s financial contribution and guide strategy.

Common cost-per-case methods trade accuracy for effort: ratio of cost to charges (RCC) is fast but crude, RVU-based costing reflects relative resource intensity, and microcosting is most accurate but labor-intensive.
Average-ratio methods like RCC are appropriate for high-level monitoring but unreliable for specific case- or contract-level decisions, which require methods that capture actual resource use.

Contribution margin — revenue minus variable (direct) costs, before overhead — is the preferred tool for comparing treatments, because fixed overhead is incurred regardless and a positive contribution margin helps cover it.
Procedure margins vary widely by market and payer; contribution margins ran thousands of dollars higher in concentrated markets (e.g., ~$5,889 for total hip replacement) than in competitive ones.

Procedure-heavy lines (cardiovascular surgery, interventional cardiology, orthopedics, neurosurgery) are consistently most profitable, while primary care, behavioral health, and obstetrics often run thin or negative margins.
Profitable lines internally cross-subsidize unprofitable but essential ones; high volume does not guarantee positive margin, so strategy should rest on actual margin data, not activity.

Service-line analysis must inform but not dictate strategy — unprofitable lines are often mission-critical and required by nonprofit community-benefit obligations, and "profitability" depends partly on overhead-allocation judgment.

title: Cost Per Case and Service Line Analysis: Finding the Money in the Mix

children.text: Deciding What the Plan Is Responsible For

When a state contracts with an MCO, one of the most consequential design decisions is also one of the least visible: exactly which services the plan is responsible for. It would seem obvious that a comprehensive plan should cover everything, but Medicaid programs routinely pull certain services out of the MCO contract and manage them separately. These decisions — to "carve in" or "carve out" a benefit — shape how care is delivered, how it is coordinated, and whether a member’s care is unified or fragmented across multiple systems.

The terminology is simple. A carve-in is a service that remains within or is integrated into the MCO’s responsibility — the plan provides it and is paid (through capitation) to cover it. A carve-out is a service removed from the MCO benefit package — the plan neither provides it nor receives payment for it, and the state manages that service through a separate arrangement, such as a limited-benefit plan or fee-for-service. Every Medicaid managed care program is, in effect, a set of decisions about which benefits to carve in and which to carve out.

These decisions carry real stakes for members and for the system. Carve-outs can bring specialized expertise to complex services but risk fragmenting a person’s care across disconnected plans; carve-ins promise integration and "whole-person care" but depend on the MCO actually coordinating well. This lesson examines which services are commonly carved out, the strong recent trend toward carving them back in, and the surprisingly mixed evidence on whether integration delivers.

Key Concept: A carve-in keeps a service within the MCO’s capitated responsibility; a carve-out removes it, so the plan neither provides nor is paid for it and the state manages it separately. The mix of carve-ins and carve-outs defines the scope of each MCO contract and how integrated a member’s care is.

stats.context: In 2023, over two-thirds of comprehensive MCO enrollees were also in at least one limited-benefit plan and/or received fee-for-service care outside their MCO (KFF)
stats.label: MCO Enrollees Also Using Carved-Out Care

stats.context: California, Missouri, North Dakota, Tennessee, West Virginia, and Wisconsin as of July 2022 (KFF), plus New York from April 2023
stats.label: Carving Pharmacy Out of MCOs

children.text: What Gets Carved Out — and Why

A handful of services are carved out far more often than others, and they share a common trait: they are specialized, distinct from general medical care, and historically managed through their own systems. The services most frequently carved out of Medicaid managed care are behavioral health (mental health and substance use), dental, pharmacy, and non-emergency medical transportation (NEMT). Behavioral health is the most commonly carved-out service of all, reflecting a long history of separate mental health systems and specialized provider networks.

The rationale for carving out is real. A specialized service may benefit from a vendor with deep, focused expertise — a behavioral health organization that understands serious mental illness, a dental plan with a dedicated dentist network, a transportation broker that manages rides. Carving out lets the state contract with an entity built specifically for that service, rather than expecting a general medical MCO to manage something far outside its core competence. When done well, a carve-out delivers specialized management that a comprehensive plan might handle poorly.

But carve-outs come at a cost: fragmentation. When a member’s behavioral health is managed by one entity, their physical health by another, their pharmacy by a third, and their transportation by a fourth, no single organization sees the whole person. A patient with serious mental illness and diabetes may have their psychiatric care and their diabetes care managed by entities that never communicate. This fragmentation is precisely the problem that the integration movement, discussed next, aims to solve.
