children.text: If It Wasn't Documented, It Wasn't Done

The previous two lessons covered coding and charge capture — but both rest on something more fundamental: documentation. The codes and charges on a claim are only as good as the clinical record that supports them. This gives rise to the oldest maxim in health information: "if it wasn't documented, it wasn't done."

To a payer, the documentation IS the care. Brilliant physicians have been denied reimbursement not because they provided bad care, but because they could not prove what they did. The clinical record is the evidence, and a service that is performed but not adequately documented cannot be billed — or, if billed, cannot survive an audit.

Documentation therefore sits at the center of the mid-cycle, and it is simultaneously a revenue issue and a compliance issue. Get it right and the claim is defensible and fully paid. Get it wrong and you face denials, lost revenue, and — at the extreme — allegations of fraud. This lesson covers both sides: documenting to get paid, and documenting to stay compliant.
To payers, the documentation is the care. The principle "if it wasn't documented, it wasn't done" means a claim is only defensible to the extent the clinical record supports its codes and charges.
Medical Necessity: The Cornerstone

The central thing documentation must establish is medical necessity — proof that the service was reasonable and necessary for the patient's condition. Medical necessity is the cornerstone of reimbursement: payers will not pay for a service unless the record clearly shows it was justified by the diagnosis and clinical picture.

This is where documentation, coding, and payment lock together. The ICD-10 diagnosis code (from the coding lesson) signals medical necessity, but the diagnosis code is only valid if the underlying documentation actually supports it. A payer auditing a claim reads the clinical notes, treatment plan, and results to confirm the service genuinely matched the documented need.

When documentation fails to establish medical necessity, the claim is denied — even for care that was entirely appropriate. This is one of the most common and frustrating denial types, because the problem is not the care or even the coding, but the written justification. Strong documentation closes that gap by telling a clear, patient-specific story of why each service was needed.

A practical shift reinforces this: the 2021 Evaluation and Management (E/M) guidelines for office visits moved away from counting history and exam "bullets" toward basing the visit level on medical decision-making or total time. Documentation now must convey the complexity of clinical thinking, not just check boxes.
Clinical Documentation Integrity

The discipline of ensuring documentation is accurate, complete, and supports the codes is called Clinical Documentation Integrity (CDI) — sometimes Clinical Documentation Improvement. CDI specialists review records, often concurrently with care, to confirm that the documentation accurately reflects the patient's condition and the services provided, and that it supports the codes billed.

A core CDI tool is the query: when documentation is ambiguous, incomplete, or conflicting, a CDI specialist or coder formally asks the provider to clarify — without leading them toward a particular answer. Query practices are carefully governed (organizations decide what clinical indicators justify a query and whether queries become part of the legal record) precisely because a leading or improper query can itself create a compliance problem.

CDI is both offense and defense. On offense, it captures the full, accurate complexity of care so the organization is paid correctly (not under-paid for under-documented complexity). On defense, it ensures that if a payer audits later, the documentation stands behind every code — letting the organization demonstrate its accuracy and its commitment to compliance.

children.text: Upcoding, Downcoding, and Fraud

Documentation defines the boundary between correct billing and fraud, and two errors sit on either side of it. Upcoding is submitting a code for a higher level of service or complexity than was actually performed and documented. Downcoding is the reverse — billing a lower level than was provided and documented, leaving money on the table.

Upcoding is the dangerous one. Consistently billing a higher level of service than the documentation supports is a classic sign of fraud or abuse, depending on whether it is intentional. Related schemes include "unbundling" (billing separately for services that should be billed together) — also a compliance violation.

The legal teeth come from the False Claims Act (FCA), which imposes liability for submitting false or fraudulent claims to federal programs like Medicare and Medicaid. The FCA holds the provider accountable for the final submission, and the Department of Justice and Office of Inspector General (OIG) actively pursue billing fraud. Penalties are severe, which is why documentation-to-code integrity is not optional — it is a legal obligation.

body.message: Billing a higher level of service than the documentation supports — consistently — is a classic fraud/abuse pattern under the False Claims Act, which holds the provider liable for the claim submitted. Downcoding loses revenue; upcoding risks legal liability. The safe path is always: code exactly what is documented.
body.title: Upcoding Is Fraud When the Record Doesn't Support It

children.text: Building a Compliance Program

Because the stakes span both revenue and legal liability, organizations build formal compliance programs around documentation and coding. The hallmark practices include enforced documentation standards (favoring patient-specific narratives over generic templates), regular internal audits, and — critically — "pre-bill" audits that catch patterns of over- or under-billing before claims ever reach the payer.

These programs are shaped by external authorities: CMS rules, OIG compliance guidance, Joint Commission standards, and payer-specific requirements all define what good documentation and coding compliance look like. The OIG has long published guidance on the elements of an effective compliance program, and recent enforcement has increasingly targeted "technology-enabled" failures — for example, copy-paste and templated notes that inflate documentation without reflecting real care.

The unifying principle is integrity: code and bill exactly what was documented and done — never more (which is fraud), never less (which is lost revenue). Good documentation simultaneously maximizes legitimate reimbursement and protects the organization legally. With the claim now coded, charged, and documented defensibly, it is ready to be assembled and submitted — which is where the next module, on clean claims and submission, begins.

A compliance program might run pre-bill audits that sample claims before submission, comparing the documentation against the codes to catch upcoding, unbundling, or unsupported services before they go out the door.
This proactive approach reflects OIG compliance guidance: it is far better to catch and fix a pattern internally than to have the DOJ or OIG discover it later under the False Claims Act, where the provider bears liability for every claim submitted.

children.text: Measuring Quality Straight From the Chart

Every measure in this course so far depends on data — and where that data comes from shapes everything about cost, accuracy, and timeliness. Traditionally, quality measures were calculated two ways: from insurance claims, or by humans manually reading patient charts. Both have serious drawbacks. Electronic clinical quality measures, or eCQMs, are the modern alternative.

An eCQM is a quality measure specified in a standardized electronic format that uses data extracted directly from electronic health records (EHRs) and other health IT systems. Instead of a person reading a chart or a measure relying on billing codes, the EHR itself supplies the clinical data — lab results, vital signs, medications, diagnoses — straight from where care was documented.

The promise is significant: capture quality automatically from the same record clinicians already use, minimizing manual effort and human error while producing more clinically rich, consistent results. eCQMs are the bridge between traditional measurement and the fully digital quality future.

An eCQM (electronic clinical quality measure) is a quality measure specified in a standardized electronic format that pulls structured clinical data directly from EHRs — rather than from claims or manual chart abstraction.
Why Not Just Claims or Chart Abstraction?

To appreciate eCQMs, consider the alternatives. Claims-based measures use billing data the payer already has — cheap and complete, but they only capture what was coded for payment. A blood-pressure reading or an A1c result often never appears on a claim, so claims measures miss clinically important detail.

Chart-abstracted measures fill that gap by having trained staff manually read a sample of medical records and key the findings into data-collection tools. This captures clinical richness but is slow, expensive, sampled rather than complete, and prone to human error. Results often arrive weeks after the reporting period ends.

eCQMs aim to combine the best of both: the clinical depth of chart review with the automation and completeness of electronic data. The shift has been decisive — by 2017, eCQMs had begun to outnumber chart-abstracted measures in CMS quality reporting, and the trend has only accelerated since.

children.text: The Standards Under the Hood: QDM and CQL

For an eCQM to work, every certified EHR must interpret the measure the exact same way — otherwise two hospitals running "the same" measure would compute different things. That consistency requires shared technical standards. Two are central: the Quality Data Model (QDM) and Clinical Quality Language (CQL).

The Quality Data Model is the conceptual model that defines the clinical concepts a measure uses — what counts as a "diagnosis of hypertension" or an "encounter," in machine-readable terms. Clinical Quality Language (CQL) is the language that expresses the measure's logic — the rules for who is in the denominator, who meets the numerator, and what exclusions apply.

Together, QDM and CQL let a measure developer author a measure once, in a standardized way, so it can be executed reliably across diverse certified EHR systems. Measures are typically authored in the Measure Authoring Tool (MAT), and reporting requires certified EHR technology (CEHRT). This standards stack is what makes "the same eCQM" genuinely the same everywhere it runs.

children.text: Value Sets: Standardizing the Data Itself

Standardizing the logic is not enough if the underlying data is recorded inconsistently. One EHR might code a hemoglobin A1c test one way and another EHR a different way. eCQMs solve this with value sets — curated lists of the standard codes (from terminologies like SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RxNorm) that count as a given clinical concept.

A value set is essentially the answer to "which codes mean this?" When an eCQM asks whether a patient had an A1c test, it checks the patient's data against the LOINC codes in the measure's A1c value set. This is why the data-standards lessons elsewhere in this course matter so directly: eCQMs are only as reliable as the standardized coding beneath them.

Get the value sets and coding right, and an eCQM can be computed automatically and compared across organizations. Get them wrong — or document care in unstructured free text the measure cannot read — and the eCQM silently undercounts, making good care look like a gap.

eCQMs depend on value sets — curated lists of standard codes (SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm) that define each clinical concept. An eCQM is only as accurate as the standardized data and coding it reads from the EHR.
The Catch: Data Capture Is Hard

eCQMs sound like a clean win, but implementing them is genuinely difficult. Calculating an eCQM is more complex than chart abstraction: organizations must educate staff, review and adjust clinical workflows so the right data is captured in structured fields, and map and validate that their EHR produces correct results.

The core problem is that eCQMs can only count what is documented in structured, coded form. If a clinician records a key finding in free-text notes, or in a field the measure does not look at, the eCQM cannot see it — and the patient appears non-compliant even though the care happened. Studies have found that some EHR-extracted data elements are captured far less reliably than others, with error rates varying widely across clinical elements.

This is the central tension of eCQMs and a direct lead-in to the next lessons: the measure logic can be perfect, but if the EHR data is incomplete, inconsistent, or buried in free text, the result is wrong. That is why data quality and the move toward FHIR-based digital measures — the subjects of the next two lessons — are so important.

children.text: The Foundation Everything Rests On

The last two lessons built toward a clear conclusion: modern quality measurement — eCQMs and FHIR-based digital measures — computes scores automatically from data in the electronic health record. That makes one fact inescapable. The most sophisticated measure in the world is worthless if the underlying EHR data is wrong, missing, or inconsistent.

EHR data quality is therefore not a side topic; it is the foundation the entire digital-measurement enterprise rests on. A measure can have perfect logic, flawless standards, and elegant FHIR plumbing, and still produce a completely misleading result if the data feeding it is poor. "Garbage in, garbage out" is not a cliché here — it is the central operational risk.
This lesson breaks down what "data quality" actually means, the specific ways EHR data goes wrong, and why this matters so much for quality measurement and improvement.

Because modern measures compute automatically from EHR data, data quality is the foundation of all quality measurement: a perfectly specified measure still produces a wrong answer if the underlying data is incomplete, inaccurate, or inconsistent.
The Dimensions of Data Quality

Researchers have worked to define data quality precisely, and while frameworks vary, a consistent core set of dimensions recurs. The three that matter most for quality measurement — and that name this lesson — are completeness, accuracy, and timeliness, joined closely by consistency.

Completeness asks: is the data actually there? A measure needs the relevant facts recorded for every patient in the denominator. Accuracy (sometimes called correctness) asks: is the recorded data right — does it match reality? Timeliness (or currency) asks: is the data available when it is needed, and does it reflect the current state? Consistency (or concordance) asks: does the data agree with itself and across sources?

Other frameworks add dimensions like plausibility (is the value believable — a blood pressure of 900 is not), uniqueness (no duplicate records), and representativeness. Notably, there is still no single standard taxonomy for EHR data quality, which is itself a challenge — but completeness is consistently the most-assessed dimension, because missing data is the most common and most damaging problem.

children.text: How EHR Data Actually Goes Wrong

These are not theoretical concerns. EHR data quality problems are pervasive and well-documented. Missing data is the headline issue: studies have found missing-data rates exceeding 80 percent for some variables, meaning the fact a measure needs simply is not in the record for most patients.

A second major problem is the free-text trap. The majority of data stored in EHRs is unstructured free text — narrative notes — which automated measures generally cannot read. Important clinical facts (a documented reason a patient declined a screening, a blood pressure mentioned in a note) routinely live in text the eCQM cannot see, so the care vanishes from the measure even though it happened.

A third is copy-paste and note bloat. Copy-paste prevalence has been measured at around 82 percent in residents' progress notes, and more than half of the text in some electronic records is duplicated. Bloated, copied notes propagate stale or wrong information forward, contributing to diagnostic errors, wasted clinician time, and inaccurate billing — and they make it hard to tell what is actually current and true.

children.text: Why It Hits Quality Measurement So Hard

Each data-quality failure maps directly onto a wrong measure result. Incomplete data makes delivered care invisible, so a measure understates performance — good care looks like a gap. Inaccurate data can do either: it can falsely credit care that did not happen, or penalize care that did.

The free-text problem is especially insidious because it is systematic, not random. If a particular clinic documents a key step mostly in narrative notes, that clinic will look worse on the eCQM regardless of how good its actual care is — the measure is really measuring documentation behavior, not care. This is how a quality measure can quietly become a measure of "how well you code," which corrodes trust in the whole exercise.

Beyond measurement, these issues carry real safety stakes. EHR-related medication errors have been found to comprise about 34 percent of all medication errors in ICUs, with a substantial share carrying life-threatening potential. So data quality is simultaneously a measurement problem and a patient-safety problem — the same bad data that distorts a score can harm a patient.

body.message: When required clinical facts live in free text or go unrecorded, an eCQM measures how care was documented and coded, not how it was delivered. A clinic with excellent care but text-heavy notes can score poorly — eroding trust in the measure and unfairly penalizing good clinicians.
body.title: A Quality Measure Can Become a Documentation Measure

children.text: Improving Data Quality

Because data quality underpins everything, organizations serious about quality measurement invest in it directly. The first step is assessment: systematically checking data against the dimensions above using methods like comparison to gold standards, validity and plausibility checks, element-presence checks, and data-source agreement. You cannot fix what you have not measured.

The second is capture at the source: redesigning workflows and templates so that the clinical facts measures need are recorded in structured, coded fields as a natural part of care — not buried in free text or skipped. This is the workflow work that the eCQM lesson flagged: getting the right data into the right field the first time. Natural-language processing can help surface facts trapped in free text, but capturing them structurally up front is more reliable.

The third is governance: clear standards for documentation, controls on copy-paste, ongoing validation of EHR outputs, and the external auditing role played by entities like the EQRO and the HEDIS Compliance Audit covered earlier. Data quality is not a one-time cleanup; it is a continuous discipline. As measurement goes fully digital and multi-source with dQMs, this foundation only becomes more important — which is why it sits at the center of this course rather than the margins.

children.text: The Last Mile of Clinical Genomics

A genomic result is worthless if it never reaches the clinician at the moment a decision is made. The previous lesson covered the standards that represent genomic data; this lesson covers the "last mile" — getting that data into the electronic health record (EHR) and turning it into clinical decision support (CDS) that actually changes care. This is where genomics either becomes useful at the point of care or quietly fails.

The problem is concrete and common. A patient's pharmacogenomic test shows they are a CYP2C19 poor metabolizer (from the pharmacogenomics lesson) — but two years later a different physician prescribes clopidogrel, unaware of the result buried in a PDF somewhere in the chart. The genomic information existed; it simply was not available, in a usable form, at the moment it mattered. Solving that is the work of EHR genomic integration and CDS.

This is genomics' version of the integration and decision-support themes from across the HTR curriculum, and it is genuinely hard — because genomic data is unlike any other data the EHR was built to handle. Getting it right is what separates genomics-on-paper from genomics-that-improves-care.

EHR genomic integration is the "last mile" — getting genomic results into the record in a usable form and turning them into clinical decision support that reaches the clinician at the moment of decision. Without it, genomic information exists but never changes care.
Why Genomic Data Breaks the EHR

EHRs were designed for lab values, notes, and medication lists — not for genomes. Genomic data has an awkward combination of properties: it is very large (like medical images) and very granular (like lab data) at the same time. That combination is exactly what makes it hard to store, retrieve, and analyze rapidly within systems built for simpler data.

The traditional workaround has been to store a genomic result as a PDF report — a static document attached to the chart. This is the core problem: a PDF is human-readable but not computable. The data has no granularity, so it cannot drive decision support, cannot be reinterpreted later, and cannot be reused for any purpose beyond the original report. A CYP2C19 result locked in a PDF cannot trigger an alert when a relevant drug is ordered.

The solution is to store genomic data as discrete, structured data rather than a flat document. Modern EHRs are building genomic modules for this — for example, Epic's Genomic Module introduced a variant ("VAR") database to store SNPs, indels, and structural variants in computable form. Discrete storage is the precondition for everything useful: only computable genomic data can drive CDS, be reinterpreted as knowledge evolves, and be reused across a patient's care.

children.text: Genomic Clinical Decision Support

Once genomic data is discrete and computable, it can power clinical decision support — automated guidance delivered to the clinician at the point of care. The flagship use case is pharmacogenomic CDS: when a clinician orders a medication, the system checks the patient's relevant genomic data and, if there is a relevant gene-drug interaction, returns a recommendation (the CPIC guidance from the pharmacogenomics lesson) right then and there.

The technical enablers are FHIR (the genomics standard from the previous lesson) and CDS Hooks — a standard that lets the EHR call out to an external decision-support service at specific workflow moments (like placing a medication order) and display the returned guidance. A pharmacogenomic CDS service, triggered by the medication order, looks up the patient's genetic data and returns the recommendation to the ordering clinician in real time.

This is the payoff: the CYP2C19 poor-metabolizer result no longer sits uselessly in a PDF — it actively fires an alert the moment clopidogrel is ordered, prompting the clinician to consider an alternative. Real implementations show the effect: when UF Health moved its pharmacogenomic results into Epic's discrete variant (VAR) database — converting 50 CDS rules and more than 11,000 patient results — pharmacogenomic alert firings and provider interactions roughly doubled, from 1,518 to 3,218. Genomic CDS is how the genotype actually changes the prescription.

children.text: The Hard Problems: Reinterpretation and Alert Fatigue

Genomic integration carries two distinctive challenges that ordinary lab data does not. The first is reinterpretation over time. Unlike a glucose value, which is fixed, a genomic variant's meaning can change as knowledge evolves — a variant of uncertain significance (VUS) may later be reclassified as pathogenic or benign. This raises a thorny question: when a variant is reinterpreted, who is responsible for going back to the patient? It has real liability implications for the lab and the ordering clinician, and the EHR must somehow support re-querying stored variants against updated knowledge — something it was never designed to do.

The second is alert fatigue — the same risk from the clinical decision support literature. If genomic CDS fires too many alerts, or low-value ones, clinicians start ignoring them all, including the important ones. Poorly designed CDS is not just ineffective but potentially harmful. Genomic alerts must be carefully curated, high-value, and well-timed, or they become noise that gets clicked through.

These challenges mean genomic integration is not a one-time technical build but an ongoing clinical and governance discipline: deciding which alerts are worthwhile, maintaining them as guidelines change, managing the reinterpretation of stored variants, and handling the liability and re-contact questions. The technology (discrete storage, FHIR, CDS Hooks) is necessary but not sufficient — it must be paired with thoughtful clinical governance.

body.message: Storing genomic data as a static PDF report means it cannot drive decision support, be reinterpreted as knowledge changes, or be reused — so a clinically critical result (like a pharmacogenomic flag) silently fails to surface when it matters. Discrete, computable storage plus well-curated CDS is what makes genomic data actually usable; alert fatigue and the need for variant reinterpretation are the ongoing challenges to manage.
body.title: A Genomic Result in a PDF Is Effectively Invisible

children.text: Genomics as a Lifelong, Reusable Resource

The deepest implication of doing genomic integration well is that genomic data, unlike most clinical data, is a lifelong, reusable resource. A person's germline genome does not change, so a result captured once — properly, as discrete data — can inform decisions for the rest of their life: this year's pharmacogenomic prescribing, next decade's cancer-risk question, a future drug not yet invented. This is the case for storing genomic data computably rather than as a one-time report.

This reusability is also why preemptive pharmacogenomic testing (from the pharmacogenomics lesson) only pays off with good EHR integration: test once, store the results discretely, and let CDS consult them automatically across a lifetime of prescribing. Without the integration, preemptive testing produces a report no one remembers to check. The integration is what unlocks the value of the test.

The honest state of the field is that EHR genomic integration is improving but still imperfect — genomic data and EHRs are, as one review put it, "not yet a perfect match." Discrete genomic modules, FHIR Genomics, and CDS Hooks are maturing, but reinterpretation, alert governance, and standardization across labs remain works in progress. For anyone in clinical genomics, the takeaway is that delivering genomic medicine at scale depends as much on this informatics last mile as on the science — and that getting the data into a computable, decision-support-ready, lifelong form is the goal. The next lessons turn from the individual clinical record to population-scale genomic research in biobanks.

children.text: From Seeing the Gap to Closing It

The last two lessons did the diagnostic work of equity: stratification revealed disparities hiding inside aggregate measures, and the risk-adjustment debate showed how easily those disparities can be re-hidden. But seeing a gap does not close it. This lesson is about the action — how to design quality improvement that actually narrows disparities rather than merely documenting them.

Equity-focused quality improvement is not a separate program bolted onto regular QI. It is regular quality improvement run with an equity lens built in from the start: every focus area, measure, and intervention is examined for its effect on disparities, not just on the overall average. The default question becomes not "did we improve?" but "did we improve, and for whom?"

This matters because conventional QI can widen disparities even while improving the average. If a new intervention is adopted faster by advantaged patients — who have more resources, access, and health literacy — the overall rate rises while the gap grows. Equity-focused QI is designed specifically to prevent that outcome.

Equity-focused quality improvement embeds an equity lens into ordinary QI: the goal is not just to improve the overall average but to narrow disparities between groups. The guiding question is "improved — and for whom?"
A Framework: Make Equity the Default

The Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI) — whose Model for Improvement underpins much of modern QI — has published a practical framework for embedding equity into measurement and improvement. Its core insight is to make using an equity lens the default rather than an optional add-on.

The framework lays out a sequence: identify and prioritize a focus area and a population of focus (especially populations disproportionately affected by inequities); determine the stratification attributes (race, ethnicity, language, social risk); compute the metric for every attribute value; and quantify the disparity against a reference point. This turns "we should care about equity" into concrete, repeatable steps.

Notably, this builds directly on earlier lessons. The framework cannot run without stratified data (Lesson 13), and it presumes good underlying data quality (Lesson 12). Equity-focused QI is the action layer on top of the measurement foundation this course has been building.

children.text: Two Strategies: Target or Close the Gap

Once a disparity is quantified, there are two broad strategic choices. The first is targeted intervention: focus improvement resources specifically on the disadvantaged group experiencing the worst outcomes. The second is gap-closing: explicitly measure and aim to reduce the difference between groups, holding the whole system accountable for the gap, not just the average.

A sophisticated middle path is "targeted universalism": set a universal goal for everyone, but tailor the strategies to reach each group, recognizing that different groups face different barriers. Everyone aims for the same blood-pressure-control target, but the path to get a low-income patient there may require addressing transportation and medication cost that an affluent patient never faces.

The choice depends on context, but the common thread is that the disparity itself becomes a tracked metric. If you only watch the overall rate, you can "succeed" while the gap widens. Equity-focused QI puts the gap on the dashboard so improvement is judged by whether the disparity shrinks.

children.text: Community Engagement: Data Is Not Enough

A recurring lesson from equity work is that metrics alone cannot achieve equity. Numbers can tell you that a gap exists and how big it is, but they rarely tell you why, or what intervention the affected community would actually trust and use. That understanding comes from engaging the community.

Authentic community engagement means more than surveys. It means sharing power and co-creating solutions with the people affected — designing interventions with the community rather than for it. Done superficially, engagement becomes box-checking; done well, it surfaces the real barriers (mistrust, language, hours, cost, transportation) that a purely clinical view misses.

This is also a caution: poorly done community engagement can be harmful, extracting input without sharing power or acting on it, which erodes trust further. The discipline is to combine quantitative disparity data with genuine community input — quantitative to size and track the problem, qualitative and participatory to design a solution that works.

body.message: Stratified data shows where a gap is and how big it is, but not why it exists or what the affected community will actually use. Combine the numbers with authentic community engagement that shares power and co-creates solutions — superficial engagement can do more harm than none.
body.title: Equity Cannot Be Achieved Through Metrics Alone

children.text: What Works: Multicomponent, Real-World Interventions

The evidence on closing disparities points consistently to multicomponent interventions — bundles that combine several strategies rather than a single fix. Effective equity QI typically pairs clinical measures (medication management, monitoring) with support that addresses access and social barriers (care coordination, community health workers, pharmacists).

A concrete example is the RICH LIFE Project (Reducing Inequities in Care of Hypertension, Lifestyle Improvement for Everyone), which tested a multilevel, multicomponent approach to reduce racial disparities in blood-pressure control. Its strategy combined blood-pressure monitoring, drug therapy, lifestyle counseling, and care coordination delivered with community health workers and pharmacists — explicitly targeting the disparity in hypertension control among Black Americans.

The pattern generalizes: durable disparity reduction in conditions like hypertension and diabetes comes from bundles that address both the clinical care and the social determinants behind the gap, run through continuous quality improvement with stratified measurement to verify the gap is actually narrowing. Equity-focused QI is the synthesis of everything in this course — measurement, stratification, honest interpretation, and disciplined improvement — pointed at the goal of equitable care.

children.text: Recording the Money That Comes In

When a payer adjudicates a claim and sends payment, the work is not over — the provider must record what happened. Payment posting is the act of recording each payment (or denial) into the practice management system, applying it to the correct patient account and the specific charges. It is the back-end step where the abstract "claim submitted" becomes a concrete "payment received and recorded."

Payment posting sounds clerical, but it is where the truth about a claim is finally established: how much the payer actually paid, what it adjusted off, what it denied, and what the patient now owes. Done accurately, it gives a true picture of revenue and surfaces problems; done sloppily, it distorts everything downstream — patient balances, AR, and the KPIs that depend on accurate posting.

To post payments, the provider needs to read the payer's explanation of what it did with the claim. That explanation comes in two forms — the ERA and the EOB — and understanding the difference between them is the starting point.

Payment posting records each payer/patient payment or denial into the system, applied to the right account and charges. It is where the true outcome of a claim — paid, adjusted, denied, patient-owed — is finally established.
ERA vs. EOB

The payer communicates how it processed a claim through a remittance. There are two formats. The Electronic Remittance Advice (ERA) is the machine-readable electronic version — it follows the HIPAA X12 835 standard (so "ERA" and "835" are used interchangeably) and can be imported automatically into the billing system. The Explanation of Benefits (EOB) is the human-readable version (paper or PDF) that requires manual entry or OCR to post.

There is also an audience difference worth noting. The ERA/835 is sent to the provider's billing team for posting. The EOB, in the sense most patients know it, is the document sent to the patient explaining how their insurance was applied and what they owe. Both convey related information about the same claim, but they serve different users.

Whichever form it takes, the remittance carries the same essential content: the payment amount, the contractual adjustments, the Claim Adjustment Reason Codes (CARCs) and Remittance Advice Remark Codes (RARCs) explaining any reductions or denials, and the patient's responsibility. The remittance is, in effect, the payer's itemized answer to the claim — and the source document for posting.

children.text: Auto-Posting and the Electronic Payment Cycle

The great advantage of the ERA is auto-posting. Because the 835 is structured and machine-readable, it can post payments, adjustments, and denials to patient accounts automatically — drastically reducing the staff time and keying errors of manual posting from paper EOBs. Most practices auto-post routine payments and reserve manual posting for exceptions and payers that do not support ERA.

The ERA pairs naturally with EFT — Electronic Funds Transfer — the electronic payment that delivers the money directly to the provider's bank account (instead of a paper check). Together they create a fully electronic payment cycle: the money arrives via EFT and the posting detail arrives via ERA, ideally at the same time, enabling complete automated reconciliation.

This electronic cycle is the modern ideal: a claim goes out as an 837, the payer pays via EFT and explains via 835, and the 835 auto-posts. The whole loop runs with minimal manual touch. The transactions from the clearinghouse lesson (837 out, 835 back) are exactly the machinery that makes this possible — payment posting is where the 835 finally does its job.

children.text: Reconciliation: Making Sure It All Matches

Posting and reconciliation are related but distinct. Posting records the payment; reconciliation is the broader quality-control step that verifies everything matches afterward. The most fundamental reconciliation is deposit matching — confirming, ideally daily, that the money actually deposited in the bank (the EFT or checks) matches the remittances posted in the system.

Deposit matching catches a whole class of problems: a remittance posted but the money never arrived, money deposited but not posted, or amounts that do not tie out. Until the posted payments reconcile to the bank deposits, the organization cannot trust its own revenue numbers. This is the financial-integrity backbone of the back end — the point where the books are proven to reflect reality.

Reconciliation also includes payment variance analysis: checking that what was paid matches what the payer contract said should be paid. This is exactly the underpayment detection from the payer-contracts lesson, and payment posting is where it operationally happens — as each payment posts, it can be compared to the expected reimbursement, and any shortfall flagged for recovery.

body.message: Posting records a payment; reconciliation proves it is correct. Skipping reconciliation — especially daily deposit matching of posted remittances against actual bank deposits — means the organization's revenue figures may not reflect reality, with money posted-but-not-received or received-but-not-posted going undetected.
body.title: Posting Is Not Reconciliation

children.text: Why Accurate Posting Matters

Payment posting is deceptively high-stakes because everything downstream depends on it being right. A key metric is the posting accuracy rate — the percentage of audited postings with no errors in patient, claim, amount, or adjustment. Wrong posting distorts patient balances (billing patients the wrong amount), corrupts AR (making accounts look paid or unpaid incorrectly), and breaks the KPIs that drive management decisions.

Accurate posting is also the trigger point for back-end follow-up. As payments post, the system should automatically route exceptions: underpayments flagged for recovery, denials sent to the denial workflow, and remaining patient balances queued for patient billing. Posting is not just record-keeping — it is the dispatcher that hands each claim's outcome to the right next process.

In short, payment posting closes the loop on the payer side of each claim: it records the truth, reconciles it against the bank and the contract, and dispatches the leftovers (denials, underpayments, patient balances) to be worked. Once the payer has paid and posted, what remains is the unpaid balance — which leads directly into the next two lessons on accounts receivable management and patient collections.

children.text: The Rulebook Behind Every Medicaid Managed Care Contract

Medicaid is a federal-state partnership: states run their programs, but they do so within rules set by the federal government, and they receive federal matching dollars only if they follow those rules. For managed care, the master rulebook has a name worth memorizing: 42 CFR Part 438. This section of the Code of Federal Regulations governs Medicaid managed care organizations and defines what states must require of the plans they contract with — from network adequacy to financial standards to quality and beneficiary protections.

Understanding Part 438 is essential because it is the framework within which everything else in this course operates. When a state writes an MCO contract, sets capitation rates, defines network standards, or oversees plan performance, it is implementing requirements that ultimately trace back to Part 438. The companion rules for the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) live at 42 CFR Part 457, applying parallel managed care protections to CHIP enrollees. Together, these regulations are the federal floor for Medicaid and CHIP managed care.

This framework is not static. In 2024, CMS substantially updated it through a major final rule, raising the bar on access, finance, and quality. This lesson covers both the enduring structure of Part 438 and the significant 2024 changes that now shape how states must manage their managed care programs.

Key Concept: 42 CFR Part 438 is the federal regulation governing Medicaid managed care, setting the rules states must follow for network adequacy, finance (including MLR), quality, and beneficiary protections. CHIP managed care is governed by the parallel 42 CFR Part 457.

children.text: What Part 438 Requires

Part 438 is organized around the state’s responsibilities as the entity contracting with private plans. Its core requirements span the operational territory this course will explore. On network adequacy, a state that contracts with a managed care plan must develop and enforce network adequacy standards, including quantitative standards for specified provider types. On finance, it governs how capitation rates must be actuarially sound and sets the rules for the medical loss ratio. On quality, it requires quality assessment and improvement programs and external review. And throughout, it establishes beneficiary protections — enrollment, grievances and appeals, and access to care.

A central financial requirement is the medical loss ratio (MLR). Part 438 provides that if a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR for its plans, that minimum must be equal to or higher than 85 percent, and the MLR must be calculated and reported each year by the plan. The MLR — covered in depth in its own lesson — ensures that at least 85 cents of every capitation dollar goes toward medical care and quality rather than profit and administration. States have been required to submit summary MLR reports to CMS since rating periods beginning July 1, 2017.

Part 438 also imposes detailed network adequacy requirements at section 438.68. States must develop quantitative network adequacy standards for certain provider types covered under the contract, and states whose contracts cover long-term services and supports (LTSS) must develop quantitative standards for LTSS provider types as well. These requirements exist to ensure that the promise of a "network" is real — that enrollees can actually reach the providers their plan claims to offer.
The 2024 Final Rule: Access, Finance, and Quality

In 2024, CMS issued one of the most significant updates to the managed care framework in years. The "Medicaid and CHIP Managed Care Access, Finance, and Quality" final rule (CMS-2439-F) was published May 10, 2024, and became effective July 9, 2024. It advances CMS’s efforts to improve access to care, quality and health outcomes, and health equity for Medicaid and CHIP managed care enrollees — and it applies to both Part 438 (Medicaid) and Part 457 (CHIP). The rule is best understood through its three named pillars: access, finance, and quality.

The most concrete and consequential changes are on access. For the first time, the rule sets specific, enforceable appointment wait time standards: enrollees must be able to get a routine appointment within 15 business days for primary care (adult and pediatric) and for OB/GYN services, and within 10 business days for outpatient mental health and substance use services. These are national floors that translate the abstract idea of "network adequacy" into a measurable patient experience — how long someone actually has to wait to see a provider.

On finance, the rule addresses state directed payments and reduces some state burdens while specifying MLR requirements and adding standards for "in lieu of services and settings" (ILOS) — alternative services like housing or nutrition supports that plans can offer in place of traditional covered benefits. On quality, it establishes a quality rating system for Medicaid and CHIP managed care plans, a kind of consumer-facing report card. Together these pillars push the framework from process requirements toward measurable outcomes and transparency.

body.title: The 2024 Final Rule’s Three Pillars

children.text: Enforcement: The Secret Shopper

A standard means nothing without enforcement, and the 2024 rule pairs its access requirements with a specific monitoring tool: the secret shopper survey. States must use annual secret shopper surveys to determine plan compliance with the appointment wait time standards and to assess the accuracy of electronic provider directories. A secret shopper survey involves a third party posing as an enrollee and attempting to schedule an appointment with a provider listed in the plan’s directory — testing whether the network is real and accessible in practice, not just on paper.

The methodology is specified to make the results meaningful. The surveys must use a random sample, cover all areas of the state served by the plan, and reach a statistically valid sample of providers for the wait-time tests. Crucially, the results must be submitted to CMS and posted on the state agency’s public website — building in transparency and accountability. This directly targets the long-standing problem of "ghost networks," where provider directories list doctors who are not actually accepting new Medicaid patients or who cannot be reached.

body.message: For decades, network adequacy was judged on paper — a plan could list thousands of providers while enrollees struggled to get appointments. The secret shopper survey tests the directory against reality, exposing "ghost networks" and inaccurate listings, and forcing plans to maintain networks that actually deliver timely care.
body.title: Why the Secret Shopper Matters

children.text: Why the Framework Matters

It is easy to dismiss regulatory citations like "42 CFR Part 438" as bureaucratic detail, but the framework is where the public interest in Medicaid managed care is actually protected. Recall the central tension from earlier lessons: capitation gives plans a financial incentive to under-provide care and avoid expensive members. Part 438 and its CHIP counterpart are the legal counterweight — the binding rules that require plans to maintain adequate networks, spend most of their capitation on care, meet quality standards, and treat beneficiaries fairly. Without this framework, managed care would be risk transfer with no guardrails.

body.analogy: If a Medicaid MCO contract is the lease on an apartment, 42 CFR Part 438 is the housing code behind it. The lease sets the specific terms between landlord and tenant, but the housing code sets the floor no lease can fall below — working heat, safe wiring, a real door that locks. The 2024 rule is like the code being updated to add a new requirement that the heat actually reach a measured temperature, with inspectors (secret shoppers) sent to verify it. The code is what makes the lease’s promises enforceable.
body.concept: How the federal framework backs managed care contracts

children.text: The framework also illustrates the federal-state dynamic that runs through all of Medicaid. The federal government sets the floor through Part 438; states build on top of it through their own contracts, which can be more demanding but not less. This is why two states’ Medicaid managed care programs can look quite different while both complying with the same federal rules — and why a major federal rule change, like the 2024 update, ripples through every state’s program at once, forcing contract amendments, new monitoring, and new reporting nationwide.

For the rest of this course, Part 438 is the connective tissue. The procurement and contracting lessons implement its requirements; the rate-setting and MLR lessons implement its financial standards; the network adequacy and quality lessons implement its access and quality provisions; and the oversight lesson implements its monitoring and enforcement expectations. When you encounter a specific operational requirement later, it is worth asking where it traces back to in the federal framework — because almost always, the answer is here.

points: 42 CFR Part 438 is the federal regulation governing Medicaid managed care, setting the rules states must follow for network adequacy, finance (including MLR), quality, and beneficiary protections; CHIP managed care is governed by the parallel 42 CFR Part 457.
Part 438 requires actuarially sound capitation rates and provides that any state-mandated minimum medical loss ratio must be at least 85 percent, reported annually by each plan.
Network adequacy requirements (section 438.68) require states to set quantitative standards for specified provider types, including LTSS provider types when LTSS is covered.

The 2024 "Access, Finance, and Quality" final rule (CMS-2439-F, effective July 9, 2024) significantly updated the framework across three pillars — access, finance, and quality — for both Medicaid and CHIP.
The rule established first-of-their-kind appointment wait-time standards: 15 business days for primary care and OB/GYN, and 10 business days for outpatient mental health and substance use services.
It also addressed state directed payments, added standards for in lieu of services and settings (ILOS), and established a new quality rating system (a public report card) for managed care plans.

Enforcement relies on annual secret shopper surveys — a third party posing as an enrollee to test appointment availability and directory accuracy — with results reported to CMS and posted publicly to expose "ghost networks."

The framework is the legal counterweight to capitation’s under-provision incentives, sets a federal floor states can exceed but not fall below, and is the connective tissue linking procurement, rate-setting, network, quality, and oversight throughout this course.

title: Federal Framework: 42 CFR Part 438 and CHIP Rules

children.text: The Birth of Fee-for-Service: A 1965 Bargain With Medicine

When President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Social Security Amendments of 1965 on July 30, Medicare and Medicaid were created to extend health coverage to elderly and low-income Americans. To win the cooperation of organized medicine — particularly the American Medical Association, which had fiercely opposed government health insurance — the law was structured around a simple payment principle: physicians would be paid a fee for each service they delivered, just as they billed private patients. Fee-for-service (FFS) was not a deliberate policy choice so much as a political accommodation to secure physician participation.

When Medicare services formally began on July 1, 1966, more than 19 million Americans age 65 and older enrolled in the program. Physician payments were based on "customary, prevailing, and reasonable" (CPR) charges — essentially whatever a doctor had historically charged. This created an immediate structural problem: every new claim submitted at a higher charge raised the future benchmark, producing a ratchet effect that drove spending upward with no automatic governor.

For the first two decades, policymakers treated the escalating costs as a managed problem rather than a systemic one. Various fee schedule updates, assignment rules, and charge limits were layered on top of CPR without fundamentally questioning the underlying incentive architecture. By the 1980s, it was clear that the "more services = more revenue" logic was deeply embedded in American healthcare finance — and that it was not going away without deliberate reform.

Key Concept: Fee-for-service is a payment model in which a provider receives a separate, discrete payment for each individual service rendered — a visit, a test, a procedure, a prescription. Volume, not value, drives revenue under this model.

children.text: How Fee-for-Service Distorts Clinical Incentives

The defining feature of fee-for-service is that it pays providers for activity, not outcomes. A surgeon who performs an operation is paid regardless of whether the patient recovers well or poorly. A primary care physician who spends 45 minutes counseling a patient on lifestyle changes to prevent diabetes earns less than a specialist who performs a 15-minute procedure. A hospital that discharges a patient quickly — reducing the episode cost — earns less than one that extends the stay. In each case, the financial incentives and the clinical incentives point in opposite directions.

This misalignment is not a flaw in individual physician character; it is the predictable output of a well-functioning incentive system pointed in the wrong direction. When volume is the revenue driver, rational economic actors — hospitals, physician groups, imaging centers — respond by increasing volume. This dynamic is widely documented. A 2017 survey of 2,106 physicians published in PLOS ONE found that physicians themselves reported approximately 20% of overall medical care as unnecessary, including 22% of prescriptions, 25% of tests, and 11% of procedures.

The consequences extend beyond wasteful spending. Overutilization exposes patients to real harms: unnecessary surgeries carry surgical risk, excessive imaging involves radiation exposure, and over-prescription of antibiotics contributes to antimicrobial resistance. Fee-for-service also systematically under-incentivizes prevention, care coordination, and the management of chronic disease — precisely the areas where the U.S. population most urgently needs investment, given rising rates of diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease.

children.text: Overutilization: The $750 Billion Problem

The scale of waste in fee-for-service medicine is staggering and well-documented. A landmark 2012 analysis by the Institute of Medicine (now the National Academy of Medicine) estimated that the United States wasted roughly $750 billion out of $2.6 trillion in annual healthcare spending — approximately 30% of all health expenditures. That analysis identified six categories of waste: unnecessary services, inefficient care delivery, excess administrative costs, inflated prices, prevention failures, and fraud. Unnecessary services — a direct product of FFS incentives — was the single largest category.

More recent estimates have adjusted the figures but not the conclusion. Overtreatment and low-value care are estimated to cost approximately $200 billion annually in the United States. These are not edge cases or outlier events; they are the normal output of a system designed to pay for doing more. The geographic variation in Medicare spending — a well-studied phenomenon — illustrates this clearly: regions with more FFS-driven care often show higher spending but not better health outcomes than lower-spending peers.

Defensive medicine — the practice of ordering additional tests or procedures primarily to guard against malpractice liability rather than for clinical necessity — compounds the problem. Physicians practicing under FFS are simultaneously incentivized by payment and by fear of liability to order more. The result is a system with two powerful engines pushing utilization upward and few structural forces pulling it back.

body.analogy: Imagine paying a taxi driver by the mile, then asking them to recommend the best route across town. They might genuinely believe the longer route is better — more scenic, fewer lights — but the meter is also running in their favor. In fee-for-service medicine, providers have the same structural conflict: the payment system rewards more care, even when the right clinical answer is less.

children.text: The Outcomes Paradox: Spending More, Getting Less

The United States spends more on healthcare than any other country on Earth — by a significant margin. In 2023, the U.S. spent approximately $14,885 per capita on health, compared to an OECD average of $5,967. That is more than two-and-a-half times the average spending of other wealthy nations. And yet, by nearly every population health measure, the U.S. performs poorly relative to its peer countries.

U.S. life expectancy was 78.4 years in 2023 — 2.7 years below the OECD average and nearly 4 years shorter than the average among comparable high-income nations (82.5 years). The U.S. performs worse than the OECD average on 77% of health status indicators, including obesity rates (43% in the U.S. versus 26% OECD average) and opioid mortality (223 per million in the U.S. versus 30 per million OECD average). The fee-for-service structure contributes to this paradox by over-investing in acute, high-intensity intervention while systematically under-investing in the primary and preventive care that drives population health.

This mismatch between spending and outcomes is not inevitable. Countries that organize care around primary care-centered, capitated or globally budgeted payment models consistently achieve better population health at lower cost. The evidence from international comparison does not indict American physicians or hospitals — it indicts the payment architecture that shapes how those physicians and hospitals behave.

body.content:
Vermont launched the nation's first statewide All-Payer Accountable Care Organization (ACO) model in 2018, moving the state's major payers — Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurers — toward value-based payment simultaneously. Rather than paying providers separately for each service, the model provides a single, globally-negotiated budget for a defined population.
The model demonstrates that shifting the payment architecture — not just layering quality bonuses onto FFS — is what produces durable change in care delivery patterns.

children.text: Early Attempts to Fix the System: Managed Care and the SGR

Policymakers began serious attempts to constrain FFS-driven spending in the 1980s and 1990s. The most influential structural response was managed care — health maintenance organizations (HMOs) and preferred provider organizations (PPOs) that used capitation, utilization review, and gatekeeping to moderate volume. Managed care did succeed in slowing spending growth through the mid-1990s, but a political and consumer backlash against restricted access and coverage denials led Congress to pass patient protection legislation and effectively defanged many of managed care's cost-control mechanisms by the early 2000s.

For Medicare, Congress attempted a different fix with the Sustainable Growth Rate (SGR) formula, enacted as part of the Balanced Budget Act of 1997. The SGR tied aggregate physician payment updates to GDP growth, theoretically preventing physician spending from outpacing the broader economy. In practice, it failed. When physician spending exceeded the SGR target, the formula required automatic fee cuts — often exceeding 20% — that Congress consistently overrode with emergency "doc fix" legislation rather than allow payments to fall. By 2015, the proposed SGR-driven cut was 21.2% — an amount both politically and practically impossible to implement.

The SGR experience illustrated a fundamental truth: you cannot fix a volume-driven payment system by threatening to reduce the per-unit price when volume rises, because those whose livelihoods depend on that volume will always find a way to reverse the cuts. The only durable solution is to restructure the underlying payment model — to make it financially neutral or advantageous to deliver less but better care. That insight became the foundation for the value-based care movement.

body.title: The Path from FFS to Value: Key Legislative Milestones

children.text: Why FFS Persists Despite Its Flaws

Given the weight of evidence against fee-for-service, a reasonable question is why it remains the dominant payment model in American healthcare. The answer involves entrenched financial interests, administrative complexity, and the genuine difficulty of measuring "value" in health. Provider organizations that have built their revenue models, staffing levels, and capital investments around FFS volume face existential risk in a rapid transition to different payment structures. Hospitals whose margins depend on high-acuity inpatient admissions cannot easily restructure overnight.

There is also the measurement problem. Value-based payment requires robust quality metrics, attribution methodologies (to determine which provider is responsible for a patient's outcomes), risk adjustment (to avoid penalizing providers who care for sicker patients), and data infrastructure capable of tracking patients across settings over time. These systems are expensive to build, slow to validate, and contested in their design. FFS, by contrast, is administratively simple: the claim defines the service, the fee schedule defines the payment, and the transaction is complete.

Despite these barriers, the trajectory is clear. CMS has set explicit targets for moving Medicare toward value-based payment, and the commercial insurance market has followed. Understanding why FFS fails — at the level of incentive structure, not just cost — is the essential first step toward understanding why every major reform initiative of the past 15 years has been an attempt to move away from it.

body.message: Fee-for-service is sometimes confused with "privatized" healthcare, but it is actually the dominant payment model within both public (Medicare, Medicaid) and private insurance programs in the United States. The problem is not who pays, but what behavior the payment incentivizes. Both public and private FFS payers face the same volume-driven cost dynamic.

The persistence of FFS reflects entrenched financial interests, administrative simplicity, and the genuine difficulty of measuring and attributing health value — not ignorance of its flaws.

children.text: The Next Step Beyond eCQMs

The previous lesson showed how eCQMs pull quality data directly from EHRs — a big advance over claims and manual chart abstraction. But eCQMs have a limitation: they are tightly bound to a single EHR's data, and they rely on older technical standards. The next evolution, which CMS is actively driving the entire field toward, is the digital quality measure, or dQM, built on the modern FHIR standard.

CMS defines a digital quality measure as a measure that uses standardized digital data from one or more sources, captured and exchanged via interoperable systems, with standards-based specifications and code packages, computable in an integrated environment without additional effort. The key phrases are "one or more sources" and "without additional effort" — dQMs are meant to draw from many data sources and run automatically.

This matters because it is not a niche technical update — CMS has set the strategic goal of transitioning all the quality measures in its reporting programs to dQMs. Everyone working in quality will be living in a dQM world; this lesson explains what that means.

A digital quality measure (dQM) uses standardized digital data from one or more interoperable sources, with standards-based specifications, computable automatically. CMS's goal is to transition all its quality measures to dQMs.
What Makes a dQM Different From an eCQM

eCQMs and dQMs both use digital data and interoperability standards, so the line between them can blur. The clearest distinction is the breadth of data sources. An eCQM is generally tied closely to EHR data — it measures what is in the electronic health record. A dQM can pull standardized digital data from many sources: EHRs, claims, registries, and even patient-generated health data.

This multi-source capability is powerful. Recall the recurring problem of care gaps that are not really gaps — a service happened but the EHR didn't capture it. A dQM that can also see claims and registry data has more places to find evidence of care, producing a more complete and accurate picture than an EHR-only eCQM.

The other key difference is the underlying technology. eCQMs were built on the Quality Data Model (QDM); dQMs are built on FHIR — the same modern, web-based interoperability standard used across health IT — which makes the data far easier to exchange and combine across systems.

children.text: The FHIR Standards Stack

A FHIR-based measure rests on a specific stack of standards, and the names are worth knowing because they appear constantly in this space. The foundation is FHIR Release 4 (R4), the version of the interoperability standard most measures build on.

On top of FHIR sit two implementation guides. The Quality Improvement Core (QI-Core) defines the data profiles — it replaces the old QDM as the model for representing clinical data, and it is built directly on FHIR resources (including US Core). The Quality Measure Implementation Guide (QM IG) describes how to represent the measure itself using FHIR's Clinical Reasoning module. Notably, Clinical Quality Language (CQL) — the same logic language used in eCQMs — carries forward to express measure logic in dQMs.

So the transition is evolutionary, not a clean break. CMS's first operational step is converting existing QDM-based eCQMs into "FHIR eCQMs" that use QI-Core and the QM IG. From there, measures can expand to the multi-source dQM vision. CQL remains the logic language throughout, which preserves much of the existing measurement know-how.

children.text: Why CMS Is Pushing dQMs

CMS is not adopting dQMs for technology's own sake. The motivations are the same pain points that have run through this whole course. First, reduced burden: if measures compute automatically from interoperable data "without additional effort," providers spend less time on manual abstraction and submission.

Second, better data and accuracy: drawing from multiple standardized sources captures care that any single source would miss, addressing the care-gap and free-text problems that limit eCQMs. Third, speed: FHIR's real-time, API-based exchange supports the dream of near-real-time quality insight rather than the retrospective, year-end picture that plagues HEDIS-style reporting.

Fourth, interoperability and alignment: because dQMs use the same FHIR standard as patient access APIs, payer data exchange, and the broader health-IT ecosystem, quality measurement stops being a separate data silo and becomes part of one connected data fabric. That alignment is the strategic prize.

children.text: The Reality: A Hard, Ongoing Transition

The dQM vision is compelling, but getting there is a multi-year, difficult transition. Targets have shifted, and the practical reality is that providers, vendors, and CMS are all working through a long migration: converting measures, upgrading EHRs to support the FHIR standards, building the data pipelines, and validating that FHIR-based measures produce correct, comparable results.

The same data-quality dependency from the eCQM lesson applies with full force here. A dQM that can pull from many sources is only as good as the standardized data those sources provide. If the underlying FHIR data is incomplete or inconsistently coded, a more sophisticated measure simply computes a wrong answer more efficiently. Multi-source data also raises new challenges around de-duplication and reconciling conflicting records.

For anyone in the field, the practical posture is to understand where the puck is going — FHIR-based, multi-source, automated, near-real-time measurement — while recognizing that today's reporting still leans heavily on eCQMs and even legacy methods. The dQM is the destination; the journey is the work of this decade. That is exactly why the next lesson tackles the foundation everything here depends on: EHR data quality.

body.message: dQMs are more powerful because they pull from multiple sources — but that power amplifies the data-quality dependency. If the underlying FHIR data is incomplete or inconsistently coded, a sophisticated dQM just produces a wrong answer faster. Multi-source data also introduces de-duplication and reconciliation challenges.
body.title: A Better Measure on Bad Data Is Still Wrong

points: A digital quality measure (dQM) uses standardized digital data from one or more interoperable sources and is computable automatically; CMS aims to transition all its measures to dQMs.
The key difference from eCQMs is breadth: eCQMs are tied to EHR data, while dQMs can draw from EHRs, claims, registries, and patient-generated data.
dQMs are built on FHIR rather than the older Quality Data Model, making data easier to exchange and combine.
The FHIR stack is FHIR R4 + QI-Core (replacing QDM for clinical data) + the Quality Measure Implementation Guide, with CQL carried forward as the logic language.
CMS's first step is converting QDM-based eCQMs into FHIR eCQMs using QI-Core and the QM IG — an evolution, not a clean break.
CMS pushes dQMs to reduce reporting burden, improve accuracy via multiple sources, enable near-real-time insight, and align quality data with the broader FHIR ecosystem.
The transition is a hard, multi-year effort, and dQMs remain only as accurate as the standardized data they read — amplifying the importance of EHR data quality.

body.explanation: Both use digital data and CQL logic, but the defining difference is data breadth: eCQMs are closely tied to a single EHR's data, whereas dQMs are built on FHIR and can pull standardized data from many sources — EHRs, claims, registries, and patient-generated data — for a more complete picture. This is why CMS is steering all measures toward the dQM model.

children.text: The Question Every Other Lesson Has Been Building Toward

Every concept in this course — payer mix and margins, cost accounting, capital and debt, value-based payment, governance — ultimately serves a single question: can this hospital survive? Financial sustainability is the capacity of a hospital to remain financially viable over the long term while continuing to fulfill its mission. It is not a single metric but a condition: enough margin to reinvest, enough liquidity to weather shocks, enough access to capital to modernize, and a business model durable enough to withstand a relentlessly changing landscape. This capstone lesson examines the forces threatening that sustainability today and the strategies hospitals are using to defend it.

The central threat is deceptively simple and increasingly severe: expenses are growing faster than revenue. In 2025, hospital expenses increased by 7.5% — over twice the rate of growth in hospital prices over the same period. When the cost of providing care rises faster than the payment for it, margins compress, and for many hospitals, health systems, and medical groups, margin pressure in 2026 is intense, with the median hospital operating margin slipping below zero early in the year. The thin margins documented throughout this course are now being squeezed harder than ever.

This is not a temporary post-pandemic hangover; it is a structural challenge driven by labor and drug costs, an aging population shifting payer mix toward government programs, and looming federal funding cuts. Understanding financial sustainability means understanding both why the pressure is mounting and what separates the hospitals that will adapt from those that will close.

Key Concept: Financial sustainability is a hospital’s capacity to stay viable long-term while fulfilling its mission — requiring adequate margin, liquidity, and capital access. The defining threat today is expense growth outpacing revenue growth, compressing already-thin margins.

children.text: The Expense Squeeze

The first force eroding sustainability is cost growth across the board. Recent data shows the squeeze in detail: workforce costs grew 5.6%, supply expenses 9.9%, and drug expenses 13.6% in 2025, according to the AHA’s Costs of Caring report — with supplies and drugs surging fastest. Labor, as the cost-accounting lessons established, remains the largest single expense, but the broad-based rise across supplies, pharmaceuticals, and services means hospitals cannot cost-cut their way out through any single lever. Total expenses rising 7.5% — more than twice the growth in hospital prices — captures the bind: the gap between the two lines is where margin disappears.

These costs are largely outside the hospital’s direct control. Drug prices are set by manufacturers; wage levels are set by competitive labor markets and persistent clinical workforce shortages; supply costs reflect global pressures. Because so much of the cost base is fixed or externally driven, and because (as earlier lessons showed) hospitals cannot quickly shed fixed costs when revenue softens, the expense squeeze translates almost directly into margin erosion. A median hospital operating margin of −0.6% in January 2026 (Strata Decision Technology benchmarks) leaves almost no cushion against further cost shocks.

body.message: Because expense growth is broad-based and largely externally driven — labor, drugs, supplies all rising — no single cost cut restores sustainability. Hospitals that treat cost control as the entire strategy, rather than pairing it with revenue diversification and payment-model change, tend to manage decline rather than reverse it.
body.title: You Cannot Cut Your Way to Health Alone

children.text: The Payer and Policy Threat

The second force is the deterioration of the revenue side, driven by payer mix and federal policy. As the population ages, more patients shift into Medicare; as economic and coverage conditions change, more shift into Medicaid or become uninsured. Both trends move the payer mix toward the below-cost government payers analyzed in earlier lessons, eroding the commercial cross-subsidy that hospital finances depend on. In one nationwide survey of healthcare finance professionals, 66% cited government funding and Medicaid cuts as a leading concern — the single most pressing worry on the revenue side.

That worry has a concrete cause. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) is projected to cut roughly $911 billion in federal Medicaid spending over ten years, with about $155 billion of that falling on rural areas, alongside the DSH cuts covered in the payer-mix lesson. Medicaid work requirements and tightened eligibility are projected to increase the uninsured population, adding uncompensated care just as supplemental payments shrink. For hospitals with heavy government payer mixes, this is a direct, multi-year hit to revenue with no obvious replacement.

Nowhere is the threat more acute than in rural communities. Nearly half of rural hospitals already operate with negative margins, more than 100 rural hospitals have closed or converted in the last decade, and Commonwealth Fund modeling suggests Medicaid work requirements alone could cut safety-net and rural hospitals’ operating margins by roughly a quarter to a third in 2027. For these institutions, financial sustainability is not an abstraction — it is the difference between a community having a hospital and not having one. Mechanisms like state-directed payments and provider taxes have become critical lifelines.
Strategies for Sustainability

Faced with this squeeze, hospitals are pursuing several strategies, and the strongest combine them rather than relying on any one. The first is operational excellence and disciplined cost control — but elevated from a finance-department task to a board-level strategic initiative, treating "operational rigor" and getting at the expense lines as a core competency rather than a one-time cost-cutting drive. This is cost management as an ongoing discipline informed by exactly the cost-accounting tools covered earlier.

The second is revenue diversification, especially the shift toward outpatient care. Outpatient revenue has been growing far faster than inpatient — rising 8.0% versus 6.1% in 2024, per Strata Decision Technology — as care migrates to ambulatory settings and hospitals build outpatient, ambulatory surgery, and service-line capacity to capture it. The third is the development of value-based enterprise models and strategic partnerships, positioning the organization to be paid for keeping populations healthy rather than depending solely on volume that is increasingly capped by government payers. Together these reflect a hospital trying to reshape both its cost base and its revenue base for a different future.
