children.text: The Synthesis: Why Sustainability Ties It All Together

This lesson is the capstone of hospital finance because sustainability is where every prior concept converges. The thin margins and ratios from Module 1 define how little cushion exists. The payer mix and reimbursement realities from Module 2 explain why revenue is under threat. The cost accounting from Module 3 is the toolkit for the expense discipline sustainability demands. The capital and debt strategy from Module 4 determines whether a hospital can fund its transformation. The value-based finance of Module 5 offers the most promising path to a durable model. And the governance of the prior lesson is what steers all of it. Sustainability is not a topic alongside the others — it is what the others add up to.

body.analogy: A hospital’s financial sustainability is like a household living on a fixed income whose bills keep rising. Cutting spending helps but cannot fully close the gap; the household also needs new income sources and must adapt to a changing world. The ones that endure are not those that simply economize, but those that restructure — finding new revenue, controlling costs continuously, and adjusting their whole way of living to the new reality. Hospitals that merely cut, without reshaping revenue and payment, are economizing their way toward the exit.
body.concept: Hospital financial sustainability

children.text: The stakes of getting this right could not be higher, because a hospital is not just a business. When a hospital fails financially, a community loses access to care, jobs, and often its largest employer — which is why financial sustainability and mission are inseparable rather than opposed. A hospital cannot serve its community if it cannot keep its doors open, and it does not deserve to keep its doors open if it abandons its community in pursuit of margin. The art of sustainable hospital finance is holding both truths at once: remaining financially viable precisely so the mission can endure.

Looking ahead, the pressures are intensifying — margins slipping toward zero, hundreds of billions in Medicaid cuts phasing in, an aging population, and relentless cost growth. But the path forward is visible in the strategies the strongest organizations are already pursuing: rigorous cost discipline, diversified and outpatient-weighted revenue, genuine movement toward value-based payment, and disciplined capital stewardship under engaged governance. The hospitals that master the full toolkit this course has assembled — and have the discipline to apply it as their landscape shifts beneath them — are the ones that will still be standing, and still serving their communities, when the next decade of change arrives.

children.text: Food Insecurity Is a Clinical Problem

Food insecurity — limited or uncertain access to enough food for an active, healthy life — affects a large and growing share of Americans. According to the USDA, in 2023 about 13.5% of US households (18.0 million households) experienced food insecurity at some point during the year, and roughly 47 million people lived in food-insecure households, including nearly 14 million children. Both figures rose from 2022 and reached their highest levels in years.

For clinicians, food insecurity is not merely a social misfortune; it has direct, measurable clinical consequences. It is associated with worse control of diabetes and hypertension, higher rates of depression and anxiety, and more hospital admissions. The mechanism is intuitive: a patient who cannot reliably afford or access fresh produce, lean protein, and whole grains cannot follow the diet their chronic disease requires, no matter how good their medication regimen is.

There is also a cruel feedback loop with cost. Food-insecure patients sometimes face a "treat or eat" tradeoff, rationing medications to pay for food or skipping food to afford prescriptions. The result is worse disease control, more complications, and higher downstream medical costs — which is precisely why "food is medicine" has moved from slogan to a serious area of clinical intervention and payment reform.

Food insecurity is a clinical issue with measurable effects on diabetes, hypertension, mental health, and hospitalization. In 2023, ~47 million Americans — including nearly 14 million children — lived in food-insecure households.
Screening for Food Insecurity

Because food insecurity is often invisible and stigmatized, identifying it requires deliberate screening rather than assumption. The good news is that effective screening can be extremely brief. The Hunger Vital Sign, a validated two-item tool, asks whether in the past 12 months the household worried food would run out before there was money to buy more, and whether food bought did not last. An affirmative answer to either item flags food-insecurity risk.

Two questions are short enough to fit into nearly any clinical workflow — intake forms, rooming questions, or a patient portal. The brevity matters: a tool that takes thirty seconds is far more likely to be used consistently than a long questionnaire, and consistency is what surfaces the patients who need help. Food-insecurity items are also embedded in the broader SDOH tools covered earlier, such as PRAPARE and the CMS AHC tool.

As with all SDOH screening, the rule holds: do not screen without a plan to respond. A positive food-insecurity screen should connect to something concrete — a referral to SNAP enrollment assistance, a food pharmacy, a produce prescription, or a medically tailored meal program, depending on the patient's needs and the resources available.

body.content:
Developed by researchers at Children's HealthWatch and validated against the longer USDA food-security module, the Hunger Vital Sign is a two-question screen: (1) "Within the past 12 months we worried whether our food would run out before we got money to buy more," and (2) "Within the past 12 months the food we bought just didn't last and we didn't have money to get more."
A response of "often true" or "sometimes true" to either statement identifies a household at risk for food insecurity. Its brevity has made it one of the most widely adopted social-needs screens in clinical settings, including pediatrics.
body.title: The Hunger Vital Sign

children.text: Medically Tailored Meals: The Strongest Evidence

Among "food is medicine" interventions, medically tailored meals (MTMs) have the strongest evidence base. These are fully prepared, home-delivered meals designed by registered dietitians for a patient's specific medical condition — renal-appropriate meals for kidney disease, low-sodium meals for heart failure, controlled-carbohydrate meals for diabetes. They target the sickest, highest-cost patients, for whom diet is directly entangled with disease control.

The clinical and economic results are substantial. In a widely cited study by Berkowitz and colleagues, receiving medically tailored meals was associated with a 49% reduction in inpatient admissions, 72% fewer skilled-nursing-facility admissions, and about 16% lower total health care costs compared with similar patients who did not receive them. The effects concentrate where they should: among high-need patients whose conditions are most diet-sensitive.

Modeling work has extended these findings to a national scale. A study published in JAMA Network Open by researchers at Tufts University's Friedman School estimated that a nationwide medically tailored meal program for eligible patients could avert roughly 1.6 million hospitalizations and save insurers on the order of $13.6 billion annually. These are projections, not guarantees, but they explain why payers and Medicaid programs are increasingly willing to cover MTMs.

children.text: Produce Prescriptions and Food Pharmacies

A second family of interventions tries to improve diet quality more broadly. Produce prescription programs let clinicians "prescribe" vouchers or debit-style cards redeemable for fruits and vegetables at grocery stores or farmers markets. Food pharmacies — grocery-style spaces inside clinical settings where food-insecure patients can select free healthy food — pursue the same goal through a different channel.

The evidence on produce prescriptions is genuinely promising but more mixed than for medically tailored meals, and honesty about that matters. Several evaluations have found meaningful improvements: a large Tufts-led analysis reported modest A1c reductions (around 0.3 percentage points) along with reduced food insecurity and improved diet, and some physician-supported programs have reported larger A1c drops of roughly a full point. But at least one randomized clinical trial found that a produce prescription subsidy alone did not significantly improve A1c or health care utilization at twelve months.

The likely explanation is that program design matters enormously. Produce prescriptions paired with nutrition education, navigation support, and clinician involvement appear more effective than a subsidy handed out in isolation. The takeaway for practice is not "produce prescriptions don't work" or "they cure diabetes" — it is that food-as-medicine interventions need to be designed and evaluated carefully, with realistic expectations and attention to the wraparound supports that make them effective.

body.message: It is tempting to claim produce prescriptions reliably produce clinically large A1c reductions. The evidence is mixed: some studies show modest benefits (~0.3 to ~1.0 point A1c), but a randomized trial found a subsidy alone did not improve outcomes at 12 months. Present these programs as promising and design-dependent — not as proven, uniform A1c reducers.
body.title: Do not overstate the produce-prescription evidence

children.text: SNAP and the Limits of Clinical Programs

No clinic-based food program can match the scale of the federal nutrition safety net. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) is by far the largest food-security intervention in the United States, reaching tens of millions of people. For most food-insecure patients, helping them enroll in or maintain SNAP benefits is the single highest-impact food intervention a care team can facilitate — yet many eligible people are not enrolled, often due to administrative barriers and stigma.

This points to an important strategic principle: clinical food programs and public benefits are complements, not substitutes. A medically tailored meal program serving a few hundred of the sickest patients does not reach the thousands of food-insecure people in a health system's broader population. Screening that routinely connects patients to SNAP, WIC, and local food resources scales in a way that a boutique meal program cannot.

It also means that food-as-medicine work is inseparable from policy. The reach of the nutrition safety net depends on eligibility rules, benefit levels, and enrollment processes set by federal and state policy. Health systems serious about food insecurity therefore work on two fronts at once: deploying targeted clinical interventions for their highest-need patients, and helping the broader population access the public programs built for exactly this purpose.

children.text: Data Is Necessary but Not Sufficient

The previous lesson made the case for high-quality REaL data and stratified measurement. But producing a beautiful dashboard that displays a disparity is not the same as closing it. The history of health equity work is littered with organizations that mistook measurement for progress — that invested heavily in identifying gaps and then stalled, treating the dashboard as a destination rather than a starting point.

Health systems that actually reduce disparities share a recognizable pattern. They move deliberately from data (the gap exists and here is its size) to root-cause analysis (why does it exist) to targeted intervention (a specific change aimed at the specific cause) to accountability (someone owns the result and is measured on it). Each step is necessary; skipping any one is where most efforts fail.

This lesson is about that pipeline: how to turn a stratified disparity finding into a structured equity action plan, choose interventions that fit the root cause, set measurable targets, and build the organizational accountability that determines whether the gap actually narrows. The tools are not exotic — they are ordinary quality improvement methods, applied with an equity lens.

Identifying a disparity is the beginning, not the end. The systems that close gaps move from data to root-cause analysis to targeted intervention to accountability — and most failures happen when one of those steps is skipped.
The Equity Action Cycle

A practical way to structure disparity reduction is as a cycle that mirrors standard quality improvement but begins with stratified data. The first step is to identify and quantify the gap: take a meaningful measure — say, postpartum follow-up visits — stratify it by race, ethnicity, and language, and name the size of the gap between the highest- and lowest-performing groups. A precise gap ("an 18-point Black-white difference") is far more actionable than a vague concern.

The second and most-often-skipped step is root-cause analysis. A gap in postpartum follow-up could stem from scheduling barriers, transportation, appointment availability, language-discordant communication, or distrust — and each cause implies a completely different intervention. Disaggregating the gap further (Where does it appear? At scheduling? In no-show rates? In which clinics?) tells you what is actually broken. Choosing an intervention before understanding the cause is how organizations waste effort on changes that do not move the gap.

Only then does the cycle proceed to designing a targeted intervention, setting a specific time-bound improvement target, and measuring against it on a regular cadence — iterating if the gap is not closing. This is deliberately the discipline of quality improvement: treat a disparity exactly like any other quality defect, with a named owner, a measurable target, and a feedback loop, rather than as a values aspiration without a mechanism.

body.title: The Equity Action Cycle

children.text: Choosing Interventions That Fit the Cause

The reason root-cause analysis matters so much is that interventions are not interchangeable. An intervention that fixes a transportation barrier does nothing for a gap driven by language discordance, and vice versa. The art of disparity reduction is matching a specific, evidence-based change to the specific cause the analysis revealed.

The toolkit is well established. For access and follow-up gaps: community health worker outreach to the affected population, reminder calls and messages in the patient's preferred language, same-day or extended-hours appointments, and transportation support. For communication gaps: professional interpreter services and language-concordant scheduling and care. For trust gaps: partnership with trusted community organizations and culturally concordant staff. Each maps to a category of root cause.

A critical design principle is to target the intervention to the gap population without stigmatizing them. Disparity reduction often means giving more — more outreach, more support — to the group that is behind, which is exactly the equity-over-equality logic from the start of this course. Universal interventions (a change applied to everyone) sometimes widen gaps, because the already-advantaged take them up faster; targeted interventions aimed at the lagging group are usually what actually closes a disparity.

body.content:
Mass General Brigham used stratified data to identify clear inequities in its own care: lower colorectal cancer screening rates among patients of color and patients with limited English proficiency, and racial and language disparities across diabetes outcome measures.
Rather than stopping at the finding, its system-wide equity leadership organized targeted responses — culturally and linguistically tailored screening-awareness campaigns, mobile Community Care Vans bringing screenings and chronic-disease services into underserved neighborhoods, and equity goals embedded in its strategic plan. It illustrates the full pipeline: stratify, find the gap, analyze who is missed, and deploy interventions aimed at that population.
body.title: Mass General Brigham — Targeted Disparity Reduction

children.text: Disparity Dashboards: Making Gaps Visible and Owned

The operational home for this work is increasingly the disparity dashboard — a tool that displays key quality and outcome measures stratified by race, ethnicity, language, and other equity-relevant factors, in a form leaders and frontline teams can act on. A 2023 framework published in The Lancet Digital Health evaluated the literature on disparity dashboards and laid out principles for using them to drive improvement rather than just display data.

A good disparity dashboard does more than show gaps; it assigns them. It makes a specific gap visible to a specific owner with a specific target, and it tracks movement over time so that progress (or its absence) is unambiguous. The difference between a dashboard that drives change and one that gathers dust is whether the numbers on it are tied to accountable owners and time-bound goals — the same discipline as any effective performance management.

Dashboards also surface the aggregate trap in real time. By always showing measures stratified rather than in aggregate, they prevent the comfortable illusion that a good overall number means equitable care. A clinic that sees its colorectal screening gap on the dashboard every month cannot un-see it — which is precisely the point.

children.text: Accountability: The Factor That Separates Progress From Stagnation

Across the literature on health systems that make measurable equity progress, one factor recurs above all others: accountability tied to leadership. Systems that close gaps consistently link senior-leader performance goals — and, increasingly, compensation — to measurable equity outcomes. When the CEO's and chief medical officer's reviews include a specific equity target, the organization predictably allocates resources, attention, and urgency to meeting it.

The National Academy of Medicine has been explicit on this point: holding the CEO accountable against clear, quantifiable equity goals is described as an essential governance duty, and modifying executive compensation so that a meaningful portion is tied to equity metrics is a key lever. This is not symbolic. Compensation and performance review are how organizations signal what genuinely matters, and equity work that lacks that signal tends to remain a values statement that competes — and loses — against everything that is measured and rewarded.

The contrast is stark and well documented. Organizations that treat equity as a values commitment without accountability rarely produce measurable improvement; organizations that wire it into goals, dashboards, and compensation do. The lesson for anyone doing this work is that the technical pipeline — data, root cause, intervention, target — only delivers when it sits inside an accountability structure that makes closing the gap someone's actual job.

body.message: A published equity statement, a diversity committee, and a dashboard are not enough on their own. The evidence is consistent: measurable disparity reduction requires tying specific, quantifiable equity goals to senior-leadership performance and compensation. Without that accountability, equity work competes against everything that is actually measured and rewarded — and usually loses.
body.title: Values statements without accountability rarely close gaps

title: From Disparity Data to Equity Action Plans

children.text: Two Forces Shaping What Comes Next

Having built up the full machinery of Medicaid managed care across this course — delivery models, federal rules, procurement, rate-setting, networks, quality, and value-based payment — we close by looking forward. Where is this system heading? The answer is shaped by two powerful forces pulling in different directions. One is aspirational: a sustained movement toward "whole-person care" that addresses the social factors driving health, not just medical services. The other is fiscal and political: looming federal cuts and enrollment losses that threaten to reshape the program’s scale and strain its finances. The future of Medicaid managed care lies in the tension between these two forces.

The whole-person-care movement reflects a genuine intellectual shift. There is growing recognition that medical care alone cannot produce health when a person lacks stable housing, adequate food, reliable transportation, or employment — the social determinants of health (SDOH). Medicaid managed care, with its capitated, population-focused structure and (via Section 1115) its flexibility to fund non-traditional services, has become a leading vehicle for acting on this recognition. The direction of travel is toward MCOs that address the whole person and their social context, not just their diagnoses.

But that aspiration now collides with a harsh fiscal environment. Major federal Medicaid cuts and policy changes are projected to shrink enrollment and squeeze financing precisely as states aspire to do more. Understanding the future of Medicaid managed care means holding both realities at once — the expansive vision of whole-person care and the contractionary pressure of cuts that could undermine it.

Key Concept: The future of Medicaid managed care is shaped by two forces — an aspirational shift toward whole-person care addressing social determinants of health (SDOH), and a fiscal/political shift toward major federal cuts and enrollment losses that threaten the program’s scale and finances.

children.text: Whole-Person Care: The Aspirational Direction

The defining aspiration of modern Medicaid managed care is whole-person care — integrating physical health, behavioral health, services for intellectual and developmental disabilities, pharmacy, and social supports into a single coordinated approach centered on the member rather than fragmented by service type. This is the through-line connecting many earlier lessons: the carve-in trend toward integration, MLTSS coordination for complex members, and value-based payment all point toward treating the whole person rather than a collection of disconnected benefits.

Increasingly, that integration extends beyond clinical care to social needs. Medicaid managed care organizations are using Medicaid funds to address social determinants of health, supporting members’ broader needs including housing, nutrition, and employment, in recognition of the adverse health impacts of unmet social needs. The mechanisms are ones this course has already covered: Section 1115 demonstrations (the HRSN waivers), "in lieu of services and settings" (ILOS) authority from the 2024 final rule, and value-based arrangements that reward keeping people healthy. Together they let plans pay for a food prescription or a housing navigator when those interventions improve health more than another clinical visit would.

Effective whole-person care depends on partnership and infrastructure. Plans are increasingly partnering with community-based organizations to connect members with critical resources, recognizing that an MCO cannot itself provide housing or food but can fund and coordinate with the organizations that do. Key elements of doing this well include member- and community-centeredness, structured programming, and realignment of the delivery system. Some states are even beginning to integrate SDOH factors into risk adjustment, so plans serving members with greater social needs are paid appropriately — extending the risk-adjustment logic from clinical conditions to social circumstances.

children.text: The Fiscal and Political Headwinds

Against this expansive vision stand serious headwinds. Recent federal law (H.R.1, also discussed as OBBBA in the hospital-finance course) is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by roughly $911 billion — about 14% — over a decade, and to increase the number of uninsured people by around 7.5 million, with impacts varying widely by state (spending cuts ranging from about 4% to nearly a fifth of federal Medicaid spending in some states). These are not marginal adjustments; they represent a structural contraction of the program’s federal financing.

The enrollment effects are projected to be large and are already beginning. The Urban Institute projects that expansion-adult enrollment in 2028 could be 4.9 to 10.1 million (27–55%) lower than otherwise expected, depending on how much states mitigate coverage losses. The drivers include work reporting requirements and more frequent (six-month) eligibility redeterminations beginning January 1, 2027, which research consistently shows cause eligible people to lose coverage through administrative churn, not just genuine ineligibility.

These pressures cascade through the system in ways this course has mapped. As enrollment falls and financing tightens, the Medicaid segment’s already-thin profitability comes under further pressure. Providers, already reimbursed below fee-for-service levels in many cases, face reduced or stagnant rates alongside more uninsured patients, pressuring them to cut staff and services or close — a particular threat to rural and safety-net providers. The network adequacy, payer-mix, and sustainability problems from earlier lessons all intensify under fiscal contraction.

body.message: Whole-person care asks Medicaid managed care to do more — addressing housing, food, and social needs. Federal cuts and enrollment losses push it to do less, with shrinking budgets and fewer members. How states and plans navigate between this expansive vision and contractionary pressure will define Medicaid managed care for the rest of the decade.
body.title: The Core Tension of the Coming Years

children.text: What States and Plans Are Prioritizing

Facing these crosscurrents, states and advocates are converging on a set of priorities for the years ahead. The most pressing concerns for Medicaid managed care include enrollment oversight (ensuring that eligible people are not wrongly disenrolled amid redeterminations and work requirements), network adequacy (keeping real access as financing tightens), benefit design (deciding what to cover when budgets shrink), and MCO accountability (holding plans to their obligations even under fiscal stress). These priorities are, notably, the very subjects of this course — the machinery built to govern managed care becomes more important, not less, when the program is under strain.

The 2024 final rule’s quality rating system, the strengthened network adequacy and secret-shopper requirements, the tightened MLR and directed-payment oversight — all of these accountability tools take on heightened significance in a contracting environment. When budgets are ample, oversight catches occasional problems; when budgets are cut and plans face negative margins, the temptation to under-provide care, thin networks, and avoid expensive members grows, and robust oversight becomes the main protection for vulnerable enrollees. The future will test whether the accountability framework this course described can hold under real fiscal pressure.

body.analogy: Medicaid managed care’s future is like a household that has finally decided to invest in long-term health — better food, a safer home, preventive care (whole-person care) — just as its income is cut. The wisest response is not to abandon the vision but to protect the investments that actually keep people well and out of expensive crises, while watching spending carefully. The danger is that under financial stress, the household cuts exactly the preventive investments that would have saved money later. States face the same choice: whether cuts fall on the whole-person investments that improve health or are absorbed without gutting them.
body.concept: Navigating between vision and fiscal constraint

children.text: Conclusion: Where the Course Has Led

This final lesson completes a journey that began with a simple question: why do states pay private plans to manage Medicaid, and how is that arrangement governed? The answer unfolded across the course. States moved to managed care chiefly for budget predictability; they choose among delivery models that transfer different amounts of risk; they operate within the federal framework of 42 CFR Part 438; they select plans through procurement, pay them through actuarially sound risk-adjusted capitation bounded by medical loss ratios, require adequate networks and credentialed providers, measure quality through HEDIS, oversee performance through external review, and increasingly push value-based payment and whole-person care. Every piece exists to capture managed care’s benefits while guarding against its central risk: that a plan paid a fixed amount will under-serve the vulnerable people who depend on it.

The future will stress-test that entire structure. Whole-person care represents Medicaid managed care reaching toward its highest ambition — using its capitated, population-based design to address the social roots of health, not just treat illness. The fiscal and political headwinds represent the constraint within which that ambition must be pursued. The same tools that govern managed care in good times — risk adjustment, network standards, quality measurement, MLR floors, oversight — are what will protect enrollees if the cuts arrive as projected. The machinery is not bureaucratic overhead; it is the safeguard that determines whether managed care serves its members or fails them when money is tight.

For the student who has worked through this course, the enduring lesson is that Medicaid managed care is neither inherently good nor bad — it is a powerful financial and delivery structure whose outcomes depend entirely on how well it is designed, paid, and overseen. It can deliver coordinated, whole-person care to tens of millions, or it can become risk transfer with thin networks and under-provided care. The difference lies in the operational details this course has covered. As Medicaid managed care moves into a future of expansive vision and fiscal pressure, those details — the rates, the rules, the networks, the measures, the oversight — will determine whether the system honors its purpose: caring for the people who have nowhere else to turn.

children.text: Consent for a Test That Sees Everything

Ordering a single-gene test is relatively simple to consent for: the patient agrees to look at one thing. But genome and exome sequencing is fundamentally different — it reads vastly more than the reason the test was ordered. A sequencing test ordered to diagnose a child's seizures also, incidentally, contains information about that child's risk of inherited cancer, heart disease, and dozens of other conditions. This is what makes informed consent for genomic sequencing uniquely challenging.

The core issue is that the test generates information the patient did not ask for and may not want. Informed consent for sequencing therefore cannot be a simple "do you want this test?" — it must address what additional information might surface, whether the patient wants to receive it, and what the implications could be. The breadth of sequencing turns consent into a genuine conversation about uncertainty and choice.

This lesson covers two of the most important ethics-and-policy issues in clinical genomics: how to handle the unexpected information sequencing reveals (secondary findings, and the consent that must precede them), and the diversity-and-equity deficit that determines whether genomic medicine serves everyone or mainly the populations who have been studied. Both are practical realities clinicians and programs must confront, not abstract debates.

Genome and exome sequencing reads far more than the reason it was ordered — so informed consent must address what unexpected information might surface and whether the patient wants it. This lesson covers secondary findings, the consent that precedes them, and the diversity deficit at the heart of genomic equity.
Secondary Findings and the ACMG List

When sequencing is performed for one reason, it can reveal medically important information unrelated to that reason — for example, a cancer-predisposition variant found during testing for an unrelated condition. The American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) addressed this by publishing a recommended list of genes for which laboratories should actively look for and report such "secondary findings," because the conditions are serious and medically actionable (something can be done to prevent or treat them).

The current list, ACMG SF v3.3 (2025), includes 84 genes, and is now updated annually. The genes were chosen because variants in them cause conditions that are clinically actionable — for example, hereditary cancer syndromes (like BRCA1/BRCA2), cardiovascular conditions, and others where early knowledge enables prevention or surveillance. The logic is that if sequencing happens to reveal a high-risk, actionable variant, the patient benefits from knowing, even though that was not why the test was ordered.

Importantly, patients can typically opt out of receiving secondary findings — the choice is theirs. Secondary findings are returned through the ordering clinician, who places the result in the context of the patient's clinical picture and family history (echoing the genetic-counseling theme of earlier lessons). The model balances the value of actionable information against the patient's right not to learn things they did not seek.

body.title: How Secondary Findings Work

children.text: Informed Consent for Sequencing

Because of secondary findings and the breadth of sequencing, informed consent must happen before the test, and it must be substantive. Pre-test counseling should cover the purpose of the test, the kinds of results it can produce (including the possibility of secondary findings and variants of uncertain significance, the VUS from the variant-interpretation lesson), and — critically — the patient's choices about what to receive. Consent for sequencing is meaningfully harder than consent for a targeted test.

Several features make it complex. Patients must decide about information they cannot fully anticipate. There are questions of scope (do you want only the result you came for, or also secondary findings?). There are pediatric complexities (parents consent for children who cannot, raising questions about a child's future autonomy — should a child be tested now for an adult-onset condition?). And the results can implicate relatives who never consented to anything. Good consent acknowledges this complexity rather than glossing over it.

The practical upshot is that high-quality genomic medicine is inseparable from high-quality consent and counseling. A program that sequences patients without robust pre-test consent processes is setting itself up for harm and mistrust. This is why genetic counselors and counseling-trained clinicians (from the hereditary-conditions lesson) are central infrastructure for genomics, not an optional add-on — they are how informed choice is actually delivered.

body.content:
A clinician orders exome sequencing to diagnose a child's undiagnosed neurological condition. During pre-test counseling, the family is told the test could also reveal secondary findings from the ACMG list — for example, a variant predisposing to a treatable cancer or heart condition — and is asked whether they wish to receive such findings.
The family is also told the test may turn up variants of uncertain significance, and that any finding could have implications for relatives. They make an informed choice about scope BEFORE the test runs. That conversation — not the sequencing itself — is what makes the result ethically usable.
body.title: Consent in Action

children.text: The Diversity Deficit

The most serious equity problem in genomic medicine is that the data underlying it is overwhelmingly drawn from people of European ancestry. In published genome-wide association studies, roughly 86 percent of participants are of European ancestry, while African-ancestry populations are severely underrepresented at around 1.1 percent, with Indigenous American, Oceanian, and many other groups scarcely represented at all. This is the "diversity deficit," and it is not improving fast enough.

This is not merely unfair — it is medically consequential, and it threatens to widen health disparities. Genomic knowledge derived mainly from one population applies less well to others. Variant interpretation is worse for underrepresented groups (more variants of uncertain significance, more misclassifications). Polygenic risk scores (from the biobanks lesson) are markedly less accurate outside European-ancestry populations. And pharmacogenomic findings (from the drug-gene lesson) can differ across populations, so a guideline built on one group may not transfer. The people least represented in the data get the least benefit — and potentially get harmed.

The fix is deliberate diversification of genomic research — which is precisely why programs like the NIH All of Us Research Program prioritize recruiting underrepresented populations, and why African and other ancestry-specific genomic initiatives matter. Ancestrally diverse data improves gene discovery and risk estimation for everyone, not only the added groups. But despite mandates and awareness, progress has been slow, making the diversity deficit one of the defining unsolved challenges of the field.

body.message: About 86% of GWAS participants are of European ancestry; African-ancestry participation is around 1.1%. This "diversity deficit" means variant interpretation, polygenic risk scores, and pharmacogenomics all perform worse for underrepresented populations — threatening to widen health disparities. The people least represented in the data benefit least and may be harmed. Diversifying genomic research (e.g., All of Us) is essential and still lagging.
body.title: Genomic Data Is ~86% European Ancestry — and That Harms Everyone Else

children.text: Building Genomics That Serves Everyone

Consent and equity are connected. The diversity deficit partly reflects historical mistrust — many underrepresented communities have legitimate reasons to be wary of medical research, and rebuilding participation depends on trustworthy consent, transparent data governance, the privacy protections of the previous lesson (GINA and its gaps), and genuine benefit sharing. You cannot solve the diversity problem without solving the trust problem, and you cannot earn trust without honest consent.

For clinicians and program leaders, the practical implications are concrete: invest in real informed-consent and counseling processes; understand that genomic tools (interpretation, PRS, pharmacogenomics) may be less reliable for patients from underrepresented populations and interpret results with appropriate caution; and support efforts to diversify the data. Knowing the limits of the evidence for a given patient is part of practicing genomic medicine responsibly.

This lesson closes the ethics-and-policy arc of the course: secondary findings and consent define how genomic information is responsibly handled at the individual level, while the diversity deficit defines whether genomic medicine is equitable at the population level. Together with the privacy protections of the GINA lesson, they form the framework within which all the technical capabilities of genomics — sequencing, interpretation, pharmacogenomics, risk scores — must operate to actually help patients. The remaining lessons turn to the emerging frontier and to building a precision-medicine program in practice.

Crucially, patients can typically opt out of receiving these findings, and they are returned through the ordering clinician with counseling. Consent about what the patient wishes to receive must come before the test.

title: Informed Consent, Secondary Findings, and Genomic Equity

children.text: Genomics Is a Data Problem

The earlier lessons established that cheap sequencing solved the problem of reading DNA, and that the bottleneck moved to interpretation. But between sequencing and clinical use sits an enormous, often-overlooked challenge: data. A single human genome is billions of data points, and to be useful that data must be stored, processed, exchanged, and integrated into care — all of which require standards.

Without shared data standards, genomics fragments into incompatible silos: one lab's results cannot be read by another's software, a genomic result cannot flow into the EHR, and data cannot be pooled for research. Standards are the unglamorous plumbing that makes genomic data actually usable across the bioinformatics pipeline, the clinical record, and the research enterprise.

This lesson covers the three layers of genomic data standards that matter for clinical genomics: the file formats produced by sequencing and analysis (FASTQ, BAM, VCF), the clinical-reporting standard for getting genomics into health IT (HL7 FHIR Genomics), and the global data-sharing framework (GA4GH). Each solves a different part of the genomics-as-data problem.

Genomic data only becomes useful through shared standards. Three layers matter: sequencing/analysis file formats (FASTQ, BAM, VCF), the clinical-reporting standard (HL7 FHIR Genomics), and the global data-sharing framework (GA4GH).
The Bioinformatics File Pipeline

Sequencing produces data in a sequence of standardized formats, each a step closer to a clinical answer. The pipeline runs FASTQ → BAM → VCF. Understanding this flow demystifies what happens between the sequencer and the report.

A FASTQ file holds the raw output of the sequencer: the millions of short DNA "reads" plus a quality score for each base. It is the unprocessed starting material — sequence fragments with no idea yet where they belong in the genome. Next, alignment software maps those reads against a reference genome, producing a BAM file (Binary Alignment Map) — the reads now placed in their correct genomic positions. FASTQ shows the raw reads; BAM shows where they belong.

Finally, variant-calling software compares the aligned reads (BAM) to the reference and identifies where the patient differs — the variants — producing a VCF file (Variant Call Format). VCF, developed in 2010 for the 1000 Genomes Project, is the standard format for storing variants (SNPs, indels, structural variants). The VCF is the starting point for the interpretation work — applying the ACMG classification to decide which of the listed variants actually matter clinically. So the pipeline turns raw sequence into a list of variants ready for expert analysis.

children.text: FHIR Genomics: Getting Into the Health Record

A VCF file is fine for bioinformaticians, but it is not how a clinician consumes genomic information, and it does not flow into an electronic health record. To make genomic results clinically usable — orderable, reportable, and integrated with the rest of a patient's data — the field needs a clinical health-IT standard. That standard is built on FHIR, the modern interoperability standard from the broader HTR curriculum.

The HL7 Clinical Genomics Work Group developed the FHIR Genomics Reporting Implementation Guide — a set of FHIR profiles for representing genomic test requests and results in a structured, standardized way. It standardizes the reporting of variants, genotypes, and variant annotations, and can represent both germline and somatic findings, simple and complex variants, and the clinical implications (disease associations, medication recommendations) derived from them.

This matters because it connects genomics to everything else in clinical informatics. A genomic result represented in FHIR Genomics can flow into the EHR, trigger clinical decision support (the next lesson), and be exchanged between systems using the same FHIR machinery that carries the rest of a patient's data. FHIR Genomics is the bridge from the bioinformatics world (VCF) to the clinical world (the EHR) — turning a variant file into an actionable part of the patient record.

The contrast is instructive: VCF answers "what variants does this sample have?" for a bioinformatician; FHIR Genomics answers "how does this genomic result fit into this patient's clinical record and care?" for the health system. Both are needed; they serve different layers.
GA4GH: Sharing Data Across the World

The third layer addresses a problem neither file formats nor clinical reporting solves: the need to share and pool genomic data across institutions and countries, responsibly. Genomic interpretation improves dramatically when data is pooled — a variant seen once is a mystery, but seen in thousands of people with known outcomes, its meaning becomes clear. Yet sharing genomic data raises enormous privacy and governance challenges.

The Global Alliance for Genomics and Health (GA4GH) was created to meet this need. It develops a common framework of technical standards and harmonized, responsible approaches for sharing genomic and health-related data across organizations. Its goal is to let the world's genomic data work together — both technically (interoperable formats and APIs) and ethically (governance and consent frameworks).

GA4GH standards are not academic: more than 500 organizations have joined GA4GH as members, and large genomic initiatives serve as "Driver Projects" that pilot its standards in practice — among them the NIH All of Us Research Program and Genomics England. This global adoption is what enables the large-scale data pooling that powers better variant interpretation — directly addressing the interpretation bottleneck and, notably, the equity problem that databases underrepresent some populations (a later lesson), since broader sharing can broaden representation.

body.content:
A clinical lab finds a rare variant in a patient and cannot tell if it is pathogenic — a "variant of uncertain significance." On its own, the lab has seen it only once.
Through GA4GH-enabled data sharing, that variant can be checked against pooled data from dozens of institutions worldwide. If it turns out to appear in many healthy people, it is likely benign; if it clusters in affected individuals, likely pathogenic. Shared standards turn isolated mysteries into interpretable answers — directly attacking the VUS problem.
body.title: Why Pooling Data Improves Interpretation

children.text: Why Standards Are the Foundation

These three layers fit together as the data backbone of clinical genomics. The bioinformatics formats (FASTQ/BAM/VCF) move sequence to variants; FHIR Genomics moves variants into the clinical record and decision support; and GA4GH moves data across institutions to improve interpretation for everyone. Each layer solves a distinct piece, and all are needed for genomics to function as routine medicine.

The recurring theme of this curriculum applies forcefully here: standardized data is the precondition for everything. Without VCF, every lab's output is incompatible. Without FHIR Genomics, results cannot reach the clinician or trigger decision support. Without GA4GH, the world's genomic data stays in silos and interpretation stays harder than it needs to be. Standards are not the exciting part of genomics, but they are what make the exciting parts possible at scale.

For anyone working in clinical genomics, the practical takeaway is to understand which standard operates at which layer, and to recognize that the field's ability to deliver genomic medicine at scale depends on this plumbing being in place. The next lesson builds directly on FHIR Genomics: how genomic results, once standardized, are integrated into the EHR and turned into clinical decision support that actually changes care at the point of decision.

body.message: VCF is a bioinformatics file format (sequence-to-variants) — it does not flow into an EHR or trigger decision support. FHIR Genomics is the clinical-reporting standard that does. GA4GH is the cross-institution data-sharing framework. Confusing these layers (e.g., expecting a VCF to integrate with the clinical record) leads to broken genomic workflows. Each standard solves a different part of the data problem.

children.text: The Fear That Holds Genomics Back

There is a fear woven through every genetic test: what if this information is used against me? If a genetic result could cost someone their job or their health insurance, many people would rationally refuse testing — even testing that could save their life. Genetic discrimination is not just an ethical problem; it is a practical barrier to the entire enterprise of genomic medicine. People will not participate in something that can be weaponized against them.

This fear is well-founded historically. Genetic information is uniquely sensitive: it is predictive (it can reveal disease risk before any symptoms), it is shared (a result implicates blood relatives), and it is immutable (you cannot change your DNA). Concerns about discrimination by insurers and employers were a genuine threat to public trust in genomics.

The primary legal response in the United States is the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA) of 2008. Understanding GINA — what it protects, and just as importantly what it does NOT — is essential for any clinician, counselor, or patient navigating genetic testing, because its protections and its gaps directly shape the real risks of getting tested.

Fear of genetic discrimination is a practical barrier to genomic medicine — people won't test if results can be used against them. The Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA) of 2008 is the primary U.S. legal protection, and knowing both its coverage and its gaps is essential.
What GINA Protects: Title I and Title II

GINA, signed into law on May 21, 2008, protects Americans from genetic discrimination in two domains, organized into two titles. Title I covers health insurance. It prohibits group health plans and health insurers from denying coverage to a healthy person, or charging higher premiums, based solely on a genetic predisposition to developing a disease in the future. An insurer cannot raise your rates because you carry a BRCA variant.

Title II covers employment, and is enforced by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC). It bars employers from using genetic information in hiring, firing, promotion, or job-placement decisions; from requesting or requiring genetic information from employees or applicants; and from harassing someone based on their (or a relative's) genetic information.

Together, these two titles address the two discrimination scenarios people most feared — losing health coverage and losing employment opportunities because of their genes. For the contexts GINA covers, it provides real, enforceable protection, and it has been important in reassuring patients that a clinical genetic test will not cost them their health insurance or their job.

children.text: The Critical Gaps in GINA

Here is the part every clinician and patient must understand: GINA has major gaps, and assuming it protects against all genetic discrimination is a dangerous mistake. GINA does NOT cover three important types of insurance — life insurance, disability insurance, and long-term care insurance. In these lines, insurers may, in many states, use genetic information in underwriting decisions.

This is a real and counterintuitive risk. A person who tests positive for a Huntington's disease variant or a high-risk cancer predisposition is protected by GINA from health-insurance and employment discrimination — but could potentially be denied life insurance or long-term care insurance, or charged more, based on that same result. Patients considering predictive genetic testing must be counseled about this gap, because it can have serious financial consequences.

GINA has other limits too. It does not apply to employers with fewer than 15 employees. It does not apply to the U.S. military (which may use genetic and medical information in its decisions). And GINA addresses discrimination — it is not a comprehensive genetic-privacy law guaranteeing the confidentiality of all genetic data in every context. These gaps mean GINA is a meaningful floor, not a complete shield.

body.message: GINA protects against genetic discrimination in health insurance and employment ONLY. It does NOT cover life insurance, disability insurance, or long-term care insurance — where insurers may use genetic results in underwriting. It also exempts employers with fewer than 15 employees and the U.S. military. Counsel patients on these gaps before predictive testing; assuming "GINA protects me" is a serious mistake.
body.title: GINA Does NOT Cover Life, Disability, or Long-Term Care Insurance

children.text: Filling the Gaps: State Laws and HIPAA

Because GINA leaves gaps, other laws partially fill them. Some states have enacted their own genetic-privacy and non-discrimination laws that extend protection into areas GINA does not reach — including, in some states, life, disability, or long-term care insurance. The result is a patchwork: a patient's protection against, say, life-insurance genetic discrimination depends substantially on which state they live in.

Separately, the HIPAA Privacy Rule (from the broader HTR curriculum) treats genetic information as protected health information, governing how it can be used and disclosed by covered entities — a layer of privacy protection distinct from GINA's anti-discrimination focus. GINA stops genetic information from being used to discriminate in health insurance and employment; HIPAA governs the confidentiality of that information in the health system. They are complementary, not redundant.

For clinicians and counselors, the practical implication is that the protections a given patient actually has depend on the specific context (which insurance, which employer, which state) and require accurate, individualized counseling. "It's protected" is too simple; the honest answer is "it depends on the type of insurance, your employer, and your state." This is part of why genetic counseling (from the hereditary-conditions lesson) is so important — it includes helping patients understand the real legal landscape before they test.

body.content:
A healthy 35-year-old considers predictive testing for a known familial Huntington's disease variant. A genetic counselor explains that GINA protects them from losing their health insurance or job over the result.
But the counselor also warns that a positive result could affect their ability to obtain life, disability, or long-term care insurance, since GINA does not cover those — and whether any state law helps depends on where they live. The patient might reasonably choose to secure life insurance BEFORE testing. This is exactly the gap that makes pre-test counseling about GINA essential.
body.title: The Life-Insurance Gap in Practice

children.text: Why This Matters for Genomic Medicine

Legal protections like GINA are not a side issue — they are foundational to whether genomic medicine can work. Genomics depends on people being willing to get tested, share their data, and participate in research (the biobanks of the previous lesson). That willingness depends on trust that the information will not be used against them. Strong, well-understood protections enable genomic medicine; gaps and confusion undermine it.

GINA has been broadly successful at its core purpose — it substantially reduced the fear of health-insurance and employment discrimination that once deterred testing, and it remains a landmark protection. But its gaps (life, disability, long-term care insurance; small employers; the military) mean genetic discrimination is not fully prohibited in the United States, and patients must be counseled honestly about the real, residual risks.

The broader lesson is that the policy and legal framework around genetics is part of the clinical reality, not separate from it. A clinician ordering a predictive genetic test must understand GINA's protections and gaps to counsel patients responsibly, because the test result carries legal and financial implications beyond the medical ones. The next lesson extends this policy-and-ethics theme to informed consent and the equity challenges — including the diversity deficit foreshadowed in the biobanks lesson — that genomic medicine must confront to serve everyone fairly.

children.text: The Most Radical Idea in Hospital Payment

Almost every payment reform discussed in value-based care leaves one thing intact: the hospital still gets paid more when it does more. Shared savings, bundled payments, and pay-for-performance all sit on top of an underlying fee-for-service chassis. A global budget throws that chassis out. Under a global budget, a hospital is given a fixed amount of revenue, set in advance, to cover its inpatient and hospital-based outpatient services for the year — regardless of how many admissions, procedures, or tests it performs.

This single change inverts the hospital’s financial incentives. Under fee-for-service, an empty bed is lost revenue. Under a global budget, an empty bed is money saved — because the revenue is guaranteed either way. Suddenly the hospital has a powerful reason to prevent admissions, reduce avoidable emergency visits, invest in care coordination, and keep its community healthy enough to stay out of the building. Revenue is decoupled from volume, and population health becomes a business strategy rather than a charitable afterthought.

Global budgets are not theoretical. They have been operating at the level of entire states for over a decade, producing some of the strongest evidence in all of payment reform — and they are now expanding through the federal AHEAD Model, which Vermont signed in 2025 but left in July 2026. Understanding global budgets means understanding both how the mechanism works and what happened when real states tried it.

Key Concept: A global budget is a fixed, prospectively set amount of revenue a hospital receives to cover its services for a defined period — typically a year. It decouples hospital revenue from the volume of care delivered, reversing the core fee-for-service incentive.

children.text: How a Global Budget Actually Works

The mechanics are conceptually simple but operationally demanding. A regulator or payer sets each hospital’s budget prospectively — before the year begins — based primarily on the hospital’s historical net revenue for inpatient and outpatient hospital-based services. That budget is then adjusted year to year for factors like inflation, population changes, quality performance, and shifts in the services the hospital provides. The hospital knows, on day one, roughly what it will earn for the entire year.

The defining feature is that this is an all-payer arrangement in its strongest forms: the budget applies across payers rather than just for Medicare, which prevents hospitals from simply shifting costs onto private insurers to make up for constrained public revenue. Within the budget, the hospital adjusts its prices (unit rates) during the year so that total revenue lands on target. If volume falls, rates can rise to hit the budget; if volume surges, rates fall. The budget — not the visit count — is the anchor.

body.message: A global budget that applies to only one payer (e.g., Medicare) invites cost-shifting — the hospital simply bills private insurers more to offset constrained public revenue. The strongest global budget models, like Maryland’s, are all-payer: every payer’s rates are regulated, closing the cost-shift loophole.
body.title: Why the "All-Payer" Part Matters

children.text: Maryland: The Proof of Concept

No state has gone further than Maryland, which has regulated hospital rates since the 1970s and in 2014 launched an all-payer hospital global budget under its All-Payer Model. In 2019 it expanded into the Maryland Total Cost of Care (TCOC) Model, which built on the global budgets by adding incentives for providers across the system — not just hospitals — to coordinate care and manage the total cost of a patient’s care, including outside the hospital walls.

The results make Maryland the strongest real-world case for global budgets. The global budget approach generated $689 million in net savings to Medicare over the first three years of the TCOC Model (2019–2021). Over the first four years (2019–2022), total Medicare spending for Part A and Part B declined by an average of $292 per beneficiary per year, or 2.1%. On utilization, the model cut hospital spending by 6.1%, hospital admissions by 16.2%, outpatient emergency department visits by 5.9%, and preventable admissions by 16.8% — exactly the pattern the incentive design predicts.

body.content:
Maryland’s model demonstrated that a state could hold hospital revenue growth to a fixed budget while improving quality — saving Medicare hundreds of millions of dollars and sharply reducing avoidable hospital use.

Its success directly shaped federal policy. Rather than letting the approach expire, CMS announced the Maryland TCOC Model would end December 31, 2025, and Maryland signed a new long-term agreement to continue an all-payer total-cost-of-care approach under the federal AHEAD Model — extending the experiment into a multi-state framework.
body.title: Maryland Total Cost of Care Model (2019–2025)

children.text: Beyond Maryland: Rural Hospitals and the Spread of the Idea

Maryland proved global budgets work at scale, but a different problem made them attractive elsewhere: the financial fragility of rural hospitals. Rural hospitals with low patient volumes are devastated by fee-for-service, where revenue depends on filling beds that are often empty. A global budget guarantees their revenue regardless of volume — a lifeline that can keep the doors open in communities that would otherwise lose access entirely.

Pennsylvania tested this directly. The Pennsylvania Rural Health Model (PRHM), which ran from 2019 to 2024, gave participating rural hospitals prospective all-payer global budgets based primarily on their historical net revenue, aiming to stabilize their finances and improve population health. The evidence was genuinely mixed: the model delivered meaningful financial stability for fragile rural hospitals, but its impact on quality outcomes was less clear — a reminder that guaranteeing revenue solves the solvency problem without automatically transforming the quality of care.

children.text: The AHEAD Model and Vermont’s Path

The federal government is now scaling the global-budget concept across multiple states through the AHEAD Model — originally States Advancing All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development, renamed Achieving Healthcare Efficiency through Accountable Design in CMS's September 2025 redesign. AHEAD is a state-based total-cost-of-care model that includes global budgets for participating hospitals and holds participating states accountable for controlling overall growth in healthcare spending while improving population health. CMS issues an agreement to each participating state, which can receive up to $12 million in funding to build the infrastructure, and the model is designed as a long-term effort running through December 31, 2035.

Vermont signed on to AHEAD in January 2025 — a natural step given its history. For eight years, Vermont ran the Vermont All-Payer ACO Model (VTAPM), a state-led accountable care experiment operated largely through the accountable care organization OneCare Vermont. That model sunset at the end of 2025, and OneCare Vermont announced it would wind down operations at the conclusion of 2025, closing one chapter of the state’s reform story. AHEAD, with its hospital global budgets, was meant to be the next chapter — but after CMS capped the expected additional federal funding near $10 million (from roughly $138 million), Vermont withdrew in July 2026, and its move toward hospital global budgets now rests on state law (Act 68 of 2025) rather than the federal model.

AHEAD’s rollout is staged across cohorts, with performance periods phased in over the following years so that states have time to build the regulatory and data infrastructure global budgets require. Vermont’s transition illustrates both the promise and the difficulty of this work: the VTAPM faced real challenges, including the withdrawal of major insurers and persistent questions about cost control and quality, even as it advanced the state’s reform agenda. Global budgets do not erase those challenges — they restructure the incentives within which a state must still do the hard operational work.

body.analogy: Fee-for-service pays a hospital like a taxi meter — every additional mile (admission, test, procedure) adds to the fare, so there’s no reason to take the shortest route. A global budget pays like a monthly transit pass: the cost is fixed up front, so the operator’s incentive flips entirely toward moving people efficiently and avoiding unnecessary trips.
body.concept: Global budgets vs. fee-for-service hospital payment

children.text: Promise, Limits, and What It Takes

Global budgets are among the most powerful tools in value-based care precisely because they attack the root of the volume problem rather than layering incentives on top of it. The Maryland evidence — real Medicare savings alongside large reductions in admissions and preventable hospitalizations — is some of the most compelling in the field. For rural hospitals, global budgets can be the difference between survival and closure.

But the model is demanding and not a cure-all. It requires a strong rate-setting authority or regulator capable of setting and adjusting budgets fairly, robust all-payer data systems, and trust among hospitals, payers, and the state. Pennsylvania’s experience showed that financial stabilization can outpace quality improvement, and Vermont’s showed that even a committed state can struggle with insurer participation and measurable cost control. Global budgets change what a hospital is rewarded for; they do not, by themselves, build the care-coordination capacity needed to act on that incentive.

The trajectory, though, is unmistakable. From Maryland’s decade-long proof of concept, to Pennsylvania’s rural lifeline, to the multi-state AHEAD Model — with Maryland in performance since 2026 and Connecticut, Hawaii, Rhode Island and downstate New York slated to follow, through 2035 — global budgets have moved from a regulatory curiosity to a central instrument of national payment reform. For students of value-based care, they represent the clearest answer yet to the field’s founding question: what happens when you simply stop paying hospitals more for doing more?

points: A global budget is a fixed amount of revenue, set in advance, that covers a hospital’s inpatient and hospital-based outpatient services for the year — decoupling revenue from the volume of care delivered.

By making revenue fixed, global budgets reverse the fee-for-service incentive: a prevented admission saves money rather than losing it, turning population health and prevention into a financial strategy.
The strongest models are all-payer, applying regulated rates across all payers to close the cost-shifting loophole that undermines single-payer budgets.

Maryland is the leading proof of concept: its Total Cost of Care Model generated $689 million in net Medicare savings (2019–2021), cut Medicare per-beneficiary spending 2.1% (~$292/year, 2019–2022), and reduced hospital admissions 16.2% and preventable admissions 16.8% over four years.
Maryland’s TCOC Model ended December 31, 2025, with the state continuing an all-payer total-cost-of-care approach under the federal AHEAD Model.
The Pennsylvania Rural Health Model (2019–2024) used global budgets to stabilize fragile rural hospitals’ finances, though its effect on quality outcomes was mixed — financial fix, quality flaw.
The federal AHEAD Model is scaling global budgets and total-cost-of-care accountability across multiple states, offering up to $12 million per state and running through December 31, 2035.

Vermont, after running the Vermont All-Payer ACO Model through 2025 (with OneCare Vermont winding down at the end of 2025), signed on to AHEAD in January 2025 but withdrew in July 2026; its hospital global budgets now proceed under state law (Act 68).

children.text: The Central Paradox: Most Spending, Worst Performance

The United States spends more on health care than any other nation on earth — by a wide margin — and gets worse results than its peers on the outcomes that matter most. This is the defining paradox of American health policy, and it sits at the center of any honest conversation about health equity. A country leaving outcomes on the table while spending the most is, by definition, distributing health inefficiently and unjustly.

In 2022, US health spending reached roughly $12,400 per person — more than double the average of comparable high-income countries. Switzerland, the second-highest spender among wealthy nations, spent only about two-thirds as much per capita. Yet the US trails its peers on life expectancy, infant mortality, maternal mortality, and the burden of avoidable death.

It is tempting to assume this means American medicine is simply low quality. That is not quite right. For a patient with good insurance and good access, US specialty care is among the best in the world. The failure is systemic — in who gets access, how fragmented and administratively costly the system is, and how little is invested in the social conditions that actually produce health. The money buys a lot of high-intensity treatment and very little population health.

The US spends roughly twice what peer nations spend per person on health care, yet ranks at or near the bottom on life expectancy and other core outcomes. The problem is not the quality of care for those who can access it — it is the system as a whole.
The Numbers Behind the Gap

The scale of the spending-to-outcome mismatch is easiest to see in a few headline figures. On spending, the US is a clear global outlier. On outcomes, it is consistently last or near-last among the wealthy democracies it is usually compared to.

US life expectancy at birth was about 78.4 years in 2023 (rising to roughly 79.0 in 2024) — but the average across comparable high-income countries is around 82-83 years, a gap of three to four years. Infant mortality tells the same story: about 5.6 deaths per 1,000 live births in the US in 2023 versus an OECD average closer to 4.0. And maternal mortality is in a category of its own, with US rates several times those of peer nations like the UK, France, and Canada.

These are not rounding errors. A three-to-four-year life expectancy gap with peer nations, sustained while outspending them two to one, represents an enormous quantity of preventable death and suffering — and the burden falls hardest on the populations already facing the steepest disadvantages.

children.text: Mirror, Mirror 2024: Last Among Peers

The most comprehensive recent comparison is the Commonwealth Fund's "Mirror, Mirror 2024: A Portrait of the Failing U.S. Health System." It compared the health systems of ten high-income countries — Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and the United States — across 70 performance measures in five domains: access to care, care process, administrative efficiency, equity, and health outcomes.

The United States ranked last overall. It was not merely below average; it was an outlier separated from the pack, trailing far behind on affordability, administrative efficiency, equity, and health outcomes. The top performers were Australia, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom. The report's framing is blunt: the US is the only high-income country where the health system fails to deliver affordable, equitable care despite spending the most.

The equity finding is especially relevant here. The US ranked lowest of all ten countries on equity — meaning the gap between higher- and lower-income Americans' experience of the health system is wider than the comparable gap in any peer nation. The US does not just underperform on average; it underperforms most for the people with the least.

body.content:
The Commonwealth Fund has run its cross-national comparison for over two decades using its International Health Policy Surveys plus administrative data. The 2024 edition evaluated 70 measures across ten wealthy nations.
The US placed last overall and last on equity, access, and outcomes, while spending the most. Australia, the Netherlands, and the UK led. The report concluded that the US is a true outlier — high spending paired with the weakest performance among its peers.
body.title: Commonwealth Fund "Mirror, Mirror 2024"

children.text: The Disadvantage Reaches Even the Advantaged

A common assumption is that the US average is dragged down entirely by its poorest and most marginalized residents — that well-off, insured Americans enjoy outcomes as good as anyone's, and only the disadvantaged pull the numbers down. The landmark 2013 National Academies report "U.S. Health in International Perspective: Shorter Lives, Poorer Health" complicated that comforting story.

The report did confirm that the US disadvantage is severe for low-income and minority populations. But it went further: it found that even relatively advantaged Americans — people who are white, college-educated, insured, who do not smoke and are not overweight — appear to be in worse health than their counterparts in other wealthy countries. The US health disadvantage, in other words, is broad, not confined to the bottom of the distribution.

This matters for how we interpret equity. It means the US has both a distribution problem (enormous internal gaps by race, income, and place) and a level problem (the whole curve sits lower than it should). Closing internal disparities is essential, but even Americans at the top of the ladder are not getting what their counterparts abroad receive — a sign that the systemic failures run deeper than any single disadvantaged group.

body.message: It is wrong to assume US underperformance is entirely explained by the health of poor or minority Americans. The 2013 National Academies report found that even advantaged, insured, healthy-behavior Americans fare worse than peers abroad. The US has a population-wide disadvantage layered on top of severe internal inequities — both must be addressed.
body.title: Avoid the "it's just the poor" misconception

children.text: Why the Gap Exists

No single factor explains the paradox, but the contributing causes are well documented. The US lacks universal coverage, leaving tens of millions uninsured or underinsured and delaying care until conditions become severe and expensive. Its system is uniquely fragmented and administratively costly, burning a large share of spending on billing, claims, and coordination rather than care.

Just as important is what the US does not buy. Peer nations spend a far larger share of their public budgets on social services — housing, income support, early childhood, education — relative to medical care. Because so much of health is produced by social conditions rather than clinical treatment, that allocation matters. The US over-invests in high-intensity medical intervention and under-invests in the upstream conditions that prevent illness in the first place.

Finally, the US tolerates internal inequality that peer nations constrain through policy. Wide gaps in income, wealth, and neighborhood conditions translate directly into wide gaps in health — and a system that does not actively narrow those gaps lets them compound. The result is a country that can deliver world-class rescue care to some while leaving its overall population behind.

children.text: Two Honest Ways to Describe the Same Gap

Suppose Group A has an adverse-outcome rate of 20% and Group B has a rate of 10%. The rate difference — the absolute disparity — is 10 percentage points. The rate ratio — the relative disparity — is 2.0: Group A's rate is twice Group B's. Both descriptions are simultaneously true of the identical underlying data, and each is more informative in a different context.

The rate difference answers "how many more people in Group A are affected, in absolute terms?" The rate ratio answers "how much more likely is Group A to be affected, relative to Group B?" A disparity that looks modest on one scale can look large on the other: a rate difference of 2 percentage points sounds small, but if the reference rate is only 1%, that same gap is a 3x rate ratio. AHRQ's National Healthcare Quality and Disparities Report — the federally mandated annual disparities report — uses both scales at once: it counts a gap as a disparity only when the absolute difference between a priority population and its reference group is statistically significant and the relative difference is at least 10%.

Absolute disparity (rate difference) and relative disparity (rate ratio) are both legitimate summaries of the same underlying gap. Reporting only the smaller-looking one is a framing choice, not a neutral default.

body.title: Worked Example: Two Ways to Report the Same Gap

children.text: Notice the second and third rows: an identical 10-point rate difference (row 1 and row 3) produces very different rate ratios (2.0x vs. 1.2x) depending on the baseline rate, and a small 2-point difference (row 2) can still be a 3x ratio when the baseline is low. This is why AHRQ's NHQDR tests the relative difference alongside the absolute one — the relative scale surfaces gaps that a raw percentage-point comparison can hide.
Summarizing Disparity Across Many Subgroups

A single rate ratio compares exactly two groups. Real populations usually split into many subgroups at once — several racial and ethnic categories, multiple income bands, several education levels — and tracking a dozen separate two-group ratios over time gets unwieldy fast. Jeffrey Pearcy and Kenneth Keppel addressed this directly in a 2002 Public Health Reports paper written to help track progress toward the original Healthy People 2010 disparity-elimination goal.

Their proposed Index of Disparity (ID) is a modified coefficient of variation computed across all subgroup rates relative to a chosen reference rate, expressed as a single percentage that can be tracked over time. Applying it, they found that gender disparity in cardiovascular disease deaths declined between 1989 and 1998, while racial and ethnic disparity in the same outcome stayed essentially unchanged over the same period — a single index number carrying two very different underlying trends, disaggregated by which grouping variable you choose.
