children.text: The Change Healthcare breach is a systemic risk illustration, not just a company failure. A single vendor providing payment processing for hundreds of thousands of providers meant that one successful ransomware attack disrupted care delivery nationally. It is the strongest argument yet for aggressive third-party risk management and the elimination of single points of failure in healthcare infrastructure.

points: The HIPAA Security Rule, published February 2003 with compliance required by April 21, 2005, governs electronically protected health information (ePHI) — not paper records — for both covered entities and their business associates.
Three safeguard categories structure compliance: administrative (policies and training), physical (facility and device controls), and technical (access, audit, integrity, and transmission controls).

Risk analysis is the most commonly cited Security Rule deficiency — a 2016–17 OCR audit found only 14% of covered entities substantially meeting the requirement, and OCR's Risk Analysis Initiative (launched October 2024) generated eight enforcement actions by April 2025.
Physical safeguards are often underestimated: BYOD devices that handle ePHI are in scope regardless of ownership, and unencrypted portable devices remain a persistent breach cause.

The 2025 NPRM — the first major Security Rule update in over two decades — eliminates the required/addressable distinction, mandates encryption at rest and in transit, requires MFA, and adds biannual vulnerability scanning and annual penetration testing.
In 2024, hacking/IT incidents accounted for 99.45% of all breached records, with the Change Healthcare ransomware attack alone affecting about 192.7 million people.
OCR collected $9.94 million in HIPAA settlements in 2024 across 22 enforcement actions, signaling sustained regulatory pressure despite the administration change.

Organizations should begin preparing for the final Security Rule now (final action projected for July 2027) — audit all addressable specifications, verify encryption coverage, and establish formal vulnerability management programs before the 240-day compliance clock starts.

body.explanation: The 2025 NPRM's most consequential structural change is eliminating the longstanding required/addressable distinction that allowed organizations to document why encryption was not "reasonable and appropriate" for their situation. Under the proposed rule, encryption of ePHI at rest and in transit becomes an explicit requirement with no cost-based exception — meaning organizations that previously documented away their encryption obligation will need to implement it regardless of their rationale.

children.text: HL7 v2 Origins and Dominance

In March 1987, a group of hospital CIOs, software vendors, and healthcare informaticists convened at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, convened by Dr. Sam Schultz, to solve a problem that was quietly strangling the modernization of American hospitals. Each clinical system — laboratory, radiology, pharmacy, admissions — had been built in isolation, and connecting any two of them required a bespoke, hand-crafted interface. With N systems in a hospital, you needed as many as N-squared custom integrations. The first version of HL7 (Health Level Seven) emerged from that 1987 meeting, and Version 2 was published the following year in 1988, adding billing and lab results workflows. HL7 v2 was not the most elegant technical design ever produced, but it was pragmatic, vendor-agnostic, and — crucially — it shipped at exactly the moment hospitals needed it.

Nearly four decades later, HL7 Version 2 remains the dominant messaging standard in global healthcare. HL7 International reports that 95% of U.S. healthcare organizations use HL7 v2, and the standard has been adopted across more than 35 countries. Every major EHR, laboratory information system, radiology information system, and pharmacy system supports HL7 v2. This is not simply legacy inertia — it is a reflection of how deeply the format is woven into clinical operations that cannot afford downtime, data loss, or ambiguity.

The enduring dominance of HL7 v2 is a case study in how standards succeed in high-stakes industries. The format works. It is human-readable enough that a trained analyst can eyeball a raw message and diagnose a problem. It is compact enough to perform well over slow network connections. And it arrived before the internet era, meaning it was designed for point-to-point TCP connections — the network topology that hospital infrastructure was built around. Newer standards like HL7 FHIR offer dramatically better design and web-native interoperability, but replacing HL7 v2 requires replacing thousands of carefully tuned, mission-critical interfaces. Most health systems will run HL7 v2 alongside FHIR for many years to come, not replace it outright.

children.text: Message Structure: Segments, Fields, and the Pipe-Delimited Format

HL7 v2 messages are plain text, structured hierarchically using delimiter characters rather than XML tags or JSON keys. The vertical bar (pipe, "|") separates fields within a segment. The caret ("^") separates components within a field. The tilde ("~") separates repetitions of a field. And the ampersand ("&") separates sub-components. This means a raw HL7 v2 message looks, to the uninitiated, like line noise — but to integration engineers, each position carries precise clinical meaning. Every message begins with an MSH (Message Header) segment, which encodes the sending application, receiving application, message type, timestamp, and a unique message control ID. If any segment is the "shipping label" of the HL7 envelope, it is MSH.

After MSH, a patient-level message will typically contain a PID (Patient Identification) segment carrying demographics: medical record number, name, date of birth, sex, address, and contact information. The PID segment is the foundation for patient matching across disparate systems — a notoriously difficult problem given that the same patient may have different identifiers in the EHR, the lab system, and the insurance system. For clinical orders and results, the OBR (Observation Request) segment describes what was ordered — the test, the ordering provider, the specimen collection time — while one or more OBX (Observation Result) segments carry the actual result values, reference ranges, and abnormal flags. A single lab panel can generate dozens of OBX segments, one per analyte.

A realistic HL7 v2 lab result message (ORU^R01) might look like this: "MSH|^~\&|LAB_SYS|MAIN_HOSPITAL|EHR|MAIN_HOSPITAL|20240315143022||ORU^R01|MSG00123|P|2.5" on the first line, followed by "PID|1||MRN123456^^^MAIN_HOSPITAL||JOHNSON^SARAH^M||19820714|F" identifying the patient, then "OBR|1|ORD987654|LAB987654|85025^COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT^CPT" describing the CBC order, and finally a series of OBX lines such as "OBX|1|NM|718-7^HEMOGLOBIN^LN||13.8|g/dL|12.0-16.0|N|||F" carrying the hemoglobin result with value, units, reference range, and a normal flag. Parsing that string correctly requires knowing not just the delimiters but the HL7 data type and table definitions for every field position. This is why integration engines and parser libraries exist.

children.text: Common Message Types and Clinical Workflows

The ADT (Admit, Discharge, Transfer) family of messages is the heartbeat of hospital operations. When a patient arrives and is admitted, the registration system fires an ADT^A01 message to every downstream system — the pharmacy, the dietary system, the billing engine, the clinical documentation platform — so that each knows a new patient encounter has begun. When that patient moves from the emergency department to the ICU, an ADT^A02 transfer message propagates the location change. When they go home, ADT^A03 closes the encounter. And whenever patient demographics are corrected — a misspelled name, an updated insurance ID — ADT^A08 broadcasts the update. These four event types (A01, A02, A03, A08) alone account for the majority of ADT message volume in most health systems, and their reliable delivery is a prerequisite for accurate care coordination, billing, and quality reporting.

The ORM (Order Message) and ORU (Observation Result Unsolicited) pair forms the backbone of the diagnostic cycle. When a clinician places a lab or radiology order, the EHR sends an ORM^O01 to the laboratory or radiology information system. The receiving system acknowledges with an ACK (acknowledgment) message, then begins processing. When results are available, the lab system returns an ORU^R01 carrying OBX segments for each result. This bidirectional ORM-to-ORU loop happens millions of times per day across U.S. hospitals. For scheduling, SIU (Scheduling Information Unsolicited) messages — ranging from SIU^S12 (notification of new appointment) to SIU^S15 (notification of appointment cancellation) — synchronize scheduling modules across EHR, radiology, and referral management platforms. MDM (Medical Document Management) messages, particularly MDM^T02, carry transcribed clinical notes, operative reports, and discharge summaries from dictation and transcription platforms back into the EHR.

Understanding these message types is essential for anyone troubleshooting an integration failure or designing a new interface. When a provider complains that lab results are not appearing in the EHR, the problem is almost certainly in the ORU pipeline — perhaps a malformed OBX segment, an unrecognized LOINC code in OBX-3, or a mismatch in the patient identifier that prevents the result from attaching to the correct encounter. When the pharmacy does not know a patient has been admitted, the ADT^A01 message likely failed delivery or was silently dropped due to a message profile mismatch. Tracing the HL7 message type immediately narrows the diagnostic search space from the entire hospital IT ecosystem to a specific interface and segment.

children.text: The HL7 v2 Interoperability Problem: Standards That Do Not Standardize

HL7 v2's greatest strength — flexibility — is also its deepest flaw. The standard defines message structures but does not enforce vocabulary, implementation choices, or local customizations. Two systems that both claim compliance with HL7 v2.3 can be entirely incompatible in practice. One laboratory might encode hemoglobin results using a local code "HGB" in OBX-3, while another uses the LOINC code "718-7^HEMOGLOBIN^LN". Both are technically valid under HL7 v2.3. The receiving EHR, however, may only be configured to recognize LOINC codes — meaning the first lab's results will be received but silently fail to map, leaving clinicians staring at an empty result field while the data sits orphaned in an integration engine queue. This kind of silent failure is more dangerous than an outright error.

The Z-segment mechanism exemplifies this tension between flexibility and interoperability. Every HL7 v2 segment beginning with the letter "Z" is a locally defined, proprietary extension. Vendors use Z-segments to transmit data that either does not fit in standard segments or that they prefer to keep in custom structures — patient consent flags, scheduling metadata, insurance authorization codes. A ZIN segment from one vendor and a ZIN segment from a different vendor may share a name but carry completely different fields. Receiving systems that encounter an unknown Z-segment are typically configured to ignore it silently. This means critical data encoded in Z-segments by the sending system may simply vanish at the receiving end unless both parties have explicitly agreed on the custom structure, documented it, and implemented it — which requires ongoing bilateral coordination that rarely scales across a health system with hundreds of interfaces.

The practical consequence of HL7 v2's implementation flexibility is a phenomenon called "interface engine proliferation." Because each connection between two systems requires custom translation logic to reconcile differences in field usage, code sets, and Z-segments, health systems have accumulated integration engines — Mirth Connect, Rhapsody, InterSystems HealthShare, Cloverleaf — running thousands of individual channel configurations. A large academic medical center may operate a very large number of active HL7 interfaces, each one a small bespoke software artifact. This creates a massive, hidden infrastructure burden: every upgrade to an EHR or lab system can break dozens of interfaces, each of which must be individually tested and repaired. The interfaces collectively represent years of engineering effort and institutional knowledge that is rarely documented adequately.

body.message: HL7 v2 interfaces frequently accept and acknowledge messages (sending back an ACK) that they then fail to process correctly due to code mapping errors or unrecognized Z-segments. This means clinical data — lab results, medication orders — can appear to have been delivered successfully while actually being lost or misfiled. Integration monitoring tools that check beyond ACK status are essential for detecting these silent failures.
body.title: The Silent Failure Risk

body.analogy: Imagine if the United States had a national standard for electrical outlets that specified the shape of the plug but not the voltage, frequency, or current rating — and allowed any manufacturer to add extra pins labeled with whatever letters they chose. Every device would technically use the "standard" outlet, but you would need a custom adapter for every device-outlet combination. That is HL7 v2 interoperability in practice.
body.concept: HL7 v2 defines message structure (the plug shape) but leaves vocabulary, coding systems, and local extensions (the voltage and custom pins) to each implementer — creating the illusion of standardization while preserving the reality of point-to-point incompatibility.

children.text: HL7 v2 and FHIR Coexistence: The Long Transition

HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources), published in 2014 and now at Release 4 and beyond, was designed to address almost every limitation of HL7 v2: it uses RESTful APIs and JSON/XML, enforces structure through defined resource types, mandates standard terminologies, and is natively web-compatible. The question is not whether FHIR is technically superior to HL7 v2 — it clearly is. The question is how to get from here to there without disrupting the billions of clinical transactions that depend on HL7 v2 every day. The answer, increasingly, is that they will coexist for decades. HL7 International has explicitly recognized this reality by publishing the official HL7 Version 2 to FHIR Implementation Guide, a project maintained by the Orders and Observations working group that provides standardized mappings from HL7 v2 messages, segments, and data types to their FHIR R4 equivalents.

The transport layer for HL7 v2 — MLLP, the Minimal Lower Layer Protocol — is another dimension of the legacy that will persist. MLLP wraps HL7 v2 messages in a simple envelope using start-of-block (ASCII 0x0B) and end-of-block (ASCII 0x1C) characters, then transmits the wrapped message over a persistent TCP connection. MLLP has no inherent security or encryption; it relies on TLS or IPsec at the network layer for protection of PHI in transit. IANA registers port 2575 for HL7, though in practice each interface listens on whatever port the two parties agree — and it requires a persistent, stateful TCP connection between sender and receiver. Every major integration engine — Mirth Connect, Rhapsody, InterSystems, Cloverleaf — maintains MLLP listener and sender components as core capabilities. As long as legacy systems speak only MLLP, the integration engine's job is to receive MLLP HL7 v2, transform it to FHIR, and deliver it to modern API endpoints — acting as a universal translator at the boundary between eras.

The v2-to-FHIR mapping project (available at build.fhir.org/ig/HL7/v2-to-fhir) defines, for example, how the fields of an HL7 v2 PID segment map to FHIR Patient resource attributes: PID-3 (Patient Identifier List) maps to Patient.identifier, PID-5 (Patient Name) maps to Patient.name, PID-7 (Date of Birth) maps to Patient.birthDate, and so on. Similarly, an ADT^A01 message maps to a FHIR Bundle containing a MessageHeader, Patient, Encounter, and related resources. These mappings allow integration engines to serve as automated translators — converting the legacy pipe-delimited messages arriving from a 20-year-old laboratory system into standards-conformant FHIR resources that can be consumed by a modern clinical decision support platform or a patient-facing app operating under 21st Century Cures Act API mandates. The coexistence of v2 and FHIR is not a failure of modernization; it is the realistic, pragmatic path forward for an industry where patient safety cannot tolerate a big-bang replacement of working infrastructure.

children.text: What Is Information Blocking?

In 2016 Congress passed the 21st Century Cures Act with a deceptively simple goal: make health data flow freely. Section 4004 of that law created a legal prohibition against "information blocking" — defined in regulation at 45 CFR 171.103 as any practice by an "actor" that is likely to interfere with, prevent, or materially discourage the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI), unless required by law or covered by one of the enumerated regulatory exceptions. The definition is intentionally broad. Congress wanted to capture the full spectrum of behaviors — technical, contractual, and cultural — that had historically kept data siloed inside individual systems.

Three categories of entities qualify as "actors" under the rule: (1) health IT developers of certified health IT, (2) health information exchanges and health information networks (HIEs/HINs), and (3) healthcare providers. The law applies a slightly different knowledge standard to each group. For health IT developers and HIEs/HINs, information blocking occurs when the actor knows, or should know, that a practice is likely to interfere with EHI access. For healthcare providers, the standard is higher — the provider must actually know that the practice is unreasonable and likely to interfere. This asymmetry reflects Congress's view that technology vendors are more sophisticated market actors who should be held to a more demanding standard.

The scope of electronic health information covered by the rule has expanded since the regulation first took effect. From April 5, 2021 through October 5, 2022, EHI was limited to the data classes and elements defined in the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI) Version 1 — a relatively narrow set of clinical data including demographics, vital signs, laboratory results, and medications. Starting October 6, 2022, the definition expanded dramatically to encompass all information in a patient's HIPAA Designated Record Set (DRS) — every medical record, billing record, and other documentation used to make decisions about a patient, including images, wave files, and any other form of ePHI. This full-EHI expansion dramatically broadened the universe of data that actors must make available on request.

body.analogy: Think of information blocking like a toll bridge that was built with public funds but operated by a private company that then charges prohibitive tolls, only lets certain cars cross, and keeps the roadway in disrepair to discourage use. The 21st Century Cures Act is the law that says: the bridge must be open, the tolls must be reasonable, and the road must actually be drivable.
body.concept: Information blocking uses technical, contractual, or operational barriers to prevent the free flow of patient health data that patients and clinicians have a legal right to access.

children.text: The Eight Exceptions

The prohibition on information blocking is not absolute. ONC's 2020 rule finalized eight regulatory exceptions — codified at 45 CFR Part 171, Subparts B and C — that describe the circumstances under which an actor's practice of limiting EHI access does NOT constitute information blocking. Later rules added a TEFCA Manner exception (HTI-1, December 2023; Subpart D), renamed Content and Manner to Manner, and added a Protecting Care Access exception (December 2024); ASTP's HTI-5 proposed rule (December 2025) would eliminate TEFCA Manner. The original eight are divided into two categories: five exceptions describing reasons an actor might not fulfill a request for EHI, and three exceptions describing procedures actors may use when they do fulfill such requests. Critically, meeting an exception is voluntary — an actor is never required to invoke one. And satisfying an exception requires meeting all of the conditions specified in the regulation; partial compliance does not shield an actor from liability.

The five "not fulfilling" exceptions are: (1) the Preventing Harm Exception, which allows actors to limit EHI access when there is a reasonable belief that doing so would prevent substantial harm to a patient or another person; (2) the Privacy Exception, which covers situations where applicable state or federal privacy law prohibits the disclosure — this exception has multiple sub-conditions tied to specific HIPAA and state law scenarios; (3) the Security Exception, which permits practices directly related to safeguarding the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of EHI, tailored to specific security risks and implemented consistently and non-discriminatorily; (4) the Infeasibility Exception, which acknowledges that there are genuine technical, operational, or legal constraints that can make it infeasible to fulfill a particular request; and (5) the Health IT Performance Exception, which permits health IT systems to be taken offline or have performance temporarily degraded for maintenance, upgrades, and other routine operational activities.

The three "fulfilling requests" exceptions govern the manner in which actors respond to legitimate EHI requests: (6) the Content and Manner Exception allows actors to negotiate and maintain reasonable terms for the access, exchange, and use of EHI — but importantly, this exception requires that the actor first attempt to reach agreement using content and manner that meets the requestor's needs; (7) the Fees Exception permits actors to charge fees for providing EHI access, but those fees must be based on objective and verifiable cost-based criteria uniformly applied to all similarly situated requestors — a $50,000 fee for a connection that costs $500 to maintain would fall well outside this exception; and (8) the Licensing Exception allows health IT developers to require licensees to obtain licenses for interoperability elements, so long as the licensing terms are non-discriminatory and commercially reasonable.

children.text: Penalties and Enforcement

The enforcement architecture for information blocking is divided between two HHS agencies with distinct authorities over distinct actor categories. The HHS Office of Inspector General (OIG) holds primary enforcement authority over health IT developers, HIEs, and HINs. OIG finalized its civil monetary penalty (CMP) rule on June 27, 2023, with enforcement becoming effective September 1, 2023. Under this rule, OIG may impose penalties of up to $1 million per violation against covered health IT actors. OIG will consider the nature and extent of the practice, the harm or potential harm caused, the duration of the conduct, the actor's history of compliance, and whether financial loss to federal health care programs resulted.

Healthcare providers face a different enforcement mechanism — "disincentives" administered through existing Medicare payment programs rather than standalone fines. On June 24, 2024, HHS finalized the provider disincentives rule (published in the Federal Register at 89 FR 54662 on July 1, 2024, effective July 31, 2024). Under this rule, eligible hospitals found to have committed information blocking lose the ability to earn three-quarters of their annual market basket increase under the Inpatient Prospective Payment System (IPPS). Critical Access Hospitals see their Medicare reimbursement drop from 101% of reasonable costs to 100%. Individual clinicians in the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) face estimated median losses of $686, while the median group practice of six clinicians could lose about $4,116 (HHS estimates). Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) and ACO participants may be barred from the Medicare Shared Savings Program for at least one year — potentially worth millions in forgone shared savings payments.

The complaint and referral process runs through ONC (now rebranded as ASTP — the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy). Any person or entity may submit a complaint through the ONC Information Blocking Complaint Portal. By February 2026 nearly 1,600 complaints had been submitted; by July 31, 2026, ONC had logged 2,450 claims of possible information blocking, about 76 percent filed by patients or by third parties on their behalf and about 79 percent naming a healthcare provider as the potential actor. ONC reviews complaints and shares those with potential violations with OIG, which investigates all three actor types; when OIG finds that a healthcare provider committed information blocking, it refers the provider to CMS for the applicable Medicare disincentive. Enforcement escalated significantly in September 2025 when HHS Secretary Kennedy directed agency resources toward active information blocking enforcement — marking the most aggressive federal posture since the law took effect.

children.text: Common Scenarios: What Counts as Information Blocking

ONC has published extensive sub-regulatory guidance illustrating the types of practices that are likely — or unlikely — to constitute information blocking. One of the clearest categories involves unreasonable fees. The Fees Exception permits cost-based charges, but ONC guidance makes clear that fees must be objectively verifiable, uniformly applied, and proportionate to the actual cost of providing access. Charging a third-party app developer or competing health system dramatically inflated fees — while offering no-cost or nominal-cost connections to affiliated or non-competing partners — is a paradigmatic information blocking violation. The disparate treatment itself is the red flag, independent of the absolute dollar amount.

Requiring proprietary data formats when standardized FHIR APIs are available is another common scenario. The 21st Century Cures Act requires certified health IT to offer a standardized API "without special effort" for any individual patient or population of patients. An actor that makes data technically available only through a legacy HL7 v2 feed, a proprietary export format, or a cumbersome portal download — while refusing to enable the certified FHIR API — may be engaging in information blocking even if the data is theoretically accessible. Similarly, conditioning access on proprietary software licenses, requiring patients or clinicians to use specific applications, or building technical obstacles into the API workflow (such as excessive authentication steps applied only to competitors' apps) can all constitute information blocking.

Refusing to connect with competing health systems or vendor-neutral platforms is one of the most commercially significant patterns ONC has identified. A hospital system that shares discharge summaries, referral records, and care plans freely within its own affiliated network — but systematically delays, degrades, or refuses data exchange with providers at competing health systems — is likely engaging in information blocking, even if each individual refusal has a stated operational justification. ONC has specifically flagged "excessive delays" as a concern: a weeks-long processing time for a records request that could be fulfilled in minutes through existing technology is not a technical limitation; it is a practice that discourages access and may constitute information blocking absent a valid exception.

body.content: A regional HIE offers FHIR API connections to health system members at no charge. When a digital health startup applies for a connection to access de-identified population data for a public health analytics project, the HIE quotes $50,000 in upfront fees plus $10,000 per month in maintenance — terms offered to no other connection partner. The startup files a complaint with ONC. The HIE cannot satisfy the Fees Exception because the fees are not based on objective, verifiable, uniformly applied cost criteria. OIG would likely find this to be information blocking.
body.title: Scenario: The $50,000 API Connection Fee

body.content: A large EHR vendor's app marketplace approves hundreds of third-party applications. When a competing EHR vendor submits an app designed to help patients migrate their records to the new platform, the app is denied approval. The reason given is vague "security concerns" — but no security review was conducted and similar apps from non-competing developers were approved without review. This is a textbook Licensing Exception failure: the terms are discriminatory based on competitive status, not objective security criteria.
body.title: Scenario: Blocking a Competitor's App

children.text: Real Enforcement Cases and Industry Impact

As of early 2026, no entity has been publicly named as the subject of a completed enforcement action with a final penalty imposed — a reality that reflects both the complexity of information blocking investigations and the deliberate sequencing of the federal enforcement ramp-up. The enforcement machinery has been built in visible stages. OIG finalized its CMP rule in June 2023. Provider disincentives were finalized in June 2024. HHS Secretary Kennedy issued a high-profile enforcement directive in September 2025. In February 2026, ASTP/ONC announced it was issuing notices of investigation of potential nonconformity to certain certified health IT developers. The industry has been operating in an enforcement environment that was fully assembled only within the prior eighteen months.

The industry response to the information blocking framework has been substantial even in the absence of completed enforcement cases. Epic, the largest EHR vendor by U.S. market share, ran its App Orchard marketplace (since replaced by Epic Showroom) and has supported SMART on FHIR app authorization across its installed base. Oracle Health (formerly Cerner) upgraded its APIs to HL7 FHIR R4, the standard mandated by the ONC certification program. In a 2023 five-site test of the Bulk FHIR API (Jones et al., a medRxiv preprint from the SMART Cumulus Network), the Oracle Cerner platform exported 5 to 16 million resources at over 8,000 resources per minute, while three Epic sites exported at 1,555 to 2,500 resources per minute. These numbers reflect genuine technical investment in interoperability infrastructure — investment directly incentivized by the information blocking framework and the threat of CMP liability.

The population-level impact on data liquidity has been meaningful. The requirement that all certified health IT support standardized FHIR APIs has created the technical substrate for a new generation of interoperability use cases — from payer-to-provider data exchange under the CMS Interoperability Rule to patient-directed data aggregation through apps like Apple Health and CommonHealth. The ONC complaint portal data offers a revealing window into where friction remains: the fact that about 79 percent of claims name healthcare providers, not health IT developers, suggests that the cultural and organizational barriers to data sharing — not just the technical ones — remain the primary obstacle. Hospitals and clinician practices that have long treated patient data as an institutional asset are now being told, by federal law, that the patient's right to that data supersedes institutional convenience.

Industry Watch: In September 2025, the HHS-OIG and ASTP jointly issued an Enforcement Alert — a formal agency communication signaling that investigations are underway and that completed enforcement actions will be made public. Compliance officers at health IT companies and health systems should treat this alert as a direct warning that the years-long ramp-up period is ending.

points: Information blocking is defined at 45 CFR 171.103 as any practice by a health IT developer, HIE/HIN, or healthcare provider that is likely to interfere with the access, exchange, or use of EHI — unless required by law or covered by a regulatory exception.

Three actor categories are covered: health IT developers of certified health IT, health information exchanges and networks, and healthcare providers. Each faces a distinct knowledge standard under the law.

EHI expanded dramatically on October 6, 2022 — from USCDI Version 1 data elements to the full HIPAA Designated Record Set, covering essentially all patient medical and billing information held in any format.

ONC's 2020 rule finalized eight exceptions to information blocking (later rules added TEFCA Manner and Protecting Care Access), divided into five "not fulfilling" exceptions (Preventing Harm, Privacy, Security, Infeasibility, Health IT Performance) and three "fulfilling" exceptions (Content and Manner, Fees, Licensing). All conditions of an exception must be met for it to apply.

OIG can impose civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per violation against health IT developers and HIEs — effective September 1, 2023. Healthcare providers face Medicare payment disincentives under the June 2024 final rule, including loss of market basket increases and potential exclusion from the Medicare Shared Savings Program.

ONC had logged 2,450 claims of possible information blocking by July 31, 2026 — about 76 percent from patients or their representatives and 79 percent naming healthcare providers — revealing that cultural resistance to data sharing remains the dominant barrier.

As of early 2026, no completed enforcement actions with public penalty determinations have been announced, but investigations are active. ASTP/ONC began issuing notices of investigation of potential nonconformity to health IT developers in February 2026, and HHS Secretary Kennedy declared enforcement a department priority in September 2025.

The information blocking framework has already driven significant industry investment in FHIR APIs and interoperability infrastructure, with major EHR vendors like Epic and Oracle Health (Cerner) building out standardized API capabilities directly in response to the certification and enforcement requirements.

body.explanation: Charging dramatically different fees to competing versus non-competing developers fails the Fees Exception, which requires that fees be based on objective, verifiable, and uniformly applied cost criteria. Offering favorable terms to non-competitors while imposing punitive fees on competitors is a textbook discriminatory practice that ONC guidance explicitly identifies as likely information blocking. The other three options fall within recognized exceptions: the Security Exception covers ransomware incidents, the Privacy Exception covers state mental health privacy laws, and the Health IT Performance Exception covers scheduled maintenance.

A provider declines to share a patient's psychiatric notes because applicable state mental health privacy law prohibits disclosure without specific written consent.

title: Information Blocking: The Law, the Exceptions, and the Enforcement

children.text: Every time a patient is admitted to a hospital, an invisible machine swings into motion. The registration clerk's keystrokes in the admissions system must instantly reach the lab, the pharmacy, the radiology scheduling software, the billing engine, and the nursing floor's electronic whiteboard — all of which may be built by different vendors, running different software versions, and speaking subtly different dialects of the same messaging standard. The device that makes this happen is the interface engine, sometimes called an integration engine. It is among the least glamorous and most mission-critical pieces of infrastructure in healthcare IT.

Interface engines sit at the heart of hospital interoperability, acting as simultaneous translators, traffic directors, and circuit breakers for the flood of clinical data generated every second in a modern health system. Understanding how they work, who the major vendors are, and where the technology is heading is essential for anyone involved in health IT strategy, clinical informatics, or digital health product development.
What Interface Engines Do: The Translator and Router Function

At their core, interface engines perform three functions: they receive a message from a source system, transform it into the format the destination system expects, and route it to the right place at the right time. In a hospital without an interface engine, every system that needs to talk to every other system requires its own custom, hand-coded connection — what the industry calls a point-to-point interface. With ten systems, that means potentially 90 individual connections. Add a twentieth system and the number explodes to 380. This combinatorial nightmare is why the hub-and-spoke architecture that interface engines enable was such a transformative idea: each system connects once to the central engine, and the engine handles the rest.

The dominant message format flowing through these engines is HL7 version 2 (HL7 v2), a standard developed in the late 1980s that never quite standardized in practice. Each EHR vendor implements HL7 v2 slightly differently — different segment orderings, custom Z-segments carrying proprietary data, and varying interpretations of optional fields. An ADT (Admit-Discharge-Transfer) A01 message from Epic looks meaningfully different from one produced by Cerner or MEDITECH, even though all three claim compliance with the same specification. The interface engine's transformation layer — typically expressed as mapping logic written in a proprietary scripting language or JavaScript — handles these differences, reshaping the incoming message into exactly what the downstream system needs.

These messages travel between systems and engines using MLLP — the Minimal Lower Layer Protocol. MLLP is a lightweight TCP/IP wrapping protocol that solves a fundamental problem: TCP/IP delivers a continuous stream of bytes with no natural message boundaries. MLLP wraps each HL7 message in a start-block character (ASCII 0x0B) and an end-block character (ASCII 0x1C followed by a carriage return), allowing the receiving application to know precisely where one message ends and the next begins. Despite being technically simple, MLLP remains the backbone of clinical messaging in 2025 — it is reliable, low-overhead, and baked into decades of installed software that no one is eager to touch.

body.analogy: An interface engine is like an international airport hub. Passengers (messages) arrive from dozens of origin cities (source systems), speaking different languages and holding tickets in different formats. The hub translates their documents, routes them to the correct departure gate, and ensures they make their connecting flight — even when the rules change seasonally and new airlines keep arriving.

children.text: The Major Platforms: Rhapsody, Mirth Connect, Cloverleaf, and InterSystems

The commercial interface engine market is dominated by a handful of platforms that have each been battle-tested across thousands of hospital deployments. Rhapsody, now a standalone company after spinning out of Orion Health, is the most recognized name in the space. It has earned the Best in KLAS Integration Engine award for fifteen consecutive years as of 2024, a track record that reflects both its technical depth and its support quality. Rhapsody supports all major healthcare message standards — HL7 v2, HL7 v3, FHIR, DICOM, X12 — and is used by more than 1,900 healthcare teams across 31 countries. A 2024 Forrester Consulting Total Economic Impact study, commissioned by Rhapsody, found a 193% three-year return on investment for the health technology teams it interviewed.

Infor Cloverleaf, which has been in the healthcare integration market for over 20 years, occupies a similar enterprise tier. Its strengths lie in its mature HL7 v2 processing capabilities and its long track record in large academic medical centers and integrated delivery networks. InterSystems Health Connect (part of the HealthShare family) takes a different architectural approach, embedding the integration engine within a broader data platform built on the InterSystems IRIS data platform. One documented large health system deployment runs 1,000 interfaces, processes 104 million messages per weekday, and connects 136 systems — all through a single InterSystems installation built in under a year.

Mirth Connect, historically the go-to open-source option, powered roughly one-third of all public Health Information Exchanges in the U.S. and was deployed in over 40 countries. Owned and maintained by NextGen Healthcare, it offered a free community edition alongside a commercial support tier. However, with the release of version 4.6, NextGen has transitioned Mirth Connect from its dual open-source/commercial licensing model to a single proprietary license — meaning the source code for new versions is no longer publicly available. This shift prompted the community to fork the codebase into a project called Open Integration Engine, which aims to preserve the open-source option for organizations that built workflows around the free tier. The Mirth transition is a cautionary tale about the risks of building critical infrastructure on vendor-controlled open-source projects.

children.text: Modern iPaaS and API Management: The Cloud Era of Integration

Traditional interface engines were designed for an era of on-premises data centers, persistent TCP connections, and relatively stable message volumes. The shift to cloud computing, mobile applications, and consumer-facing health platforms has created demand for a different kind of integration tool: the Integration Platform as a Service, or iPaaS. These cloud-native platforms are built around RESTful APIs, event-driven architectures, and elastic scalability — properties that legacy MLLP-based engines were never designed to deliver. Federal FHIR API mandates and the expansion of telehealth have accelerated their adoption in healthcare.

MuleSoft, now part of Salesforce, is among the most widely deployed iPaaS platforms in healthcare. Its API-led connectivity model organizes integrations into three layers: System APIs that expose raw data from source systems (like an EHR), Process APIs that orchestrate business logic across multiple systems, and Experience APIs that deliver tailored data to specific consumers like mobile apps or patient portals. MuleSoft's healthcare accelerator includes pre-built assets for converting HL7 v2 messages, C-CDA documents, and X12 transactions into FHIR R4 resources, then ingesting them into data stores like AWS HealthLake. This FHIR facade pattern — where an API layer presents a modern FHIR interface over a legacy backend — is one of the most common architectural patterns in current healthcare integration projects.

Cloud providers have also entered the integration space with native healthcare services. AWS HealthLake provides a FHIR R4-compliant data store with built-in natural language processing for unstructured clinical data. Azure Health Data Services combines a FHIR server, DICOM service, and analytics capabilities into a single managed platform. Google Cloud's Healthcare API supports FHIR, HL7 v2, and DICOM natively. These services are not interface engines in the traditional sense — they do not perform the complex message transformation and routing that Rhapsody or Cloverleaf handle — but they serve as the destination and normalization layer that modern integration architectures route data toward. The practical result is a hybrid architecture: legacy interface engines handling v2 traffic on the hospital side, feeding cloud-native FHIR platforms that serve the analytics and application layers.

children.text: Building and Managing Interfaces: The Full Lifecycle

Building a new interface is rarely as simple as connecting two systems and pressing go. The lifecycle of a single interface — from initial requirements gathering to production monitoring — takes weeks for a straightforward feed and can stretch to months for complex multi-system integrations involving custom segment mapping, error handling logic, and compliance with specific data governance rules. A full enterprise implementation involving dozens of interfaces takes longer still. Every custom interface carries build and maintenance labor, which is why large health systems with hundreds of interfaces carry substantial annual integration budgets.

Interface management does not end at go-live. Every time a source system undergoes a version upgrade — a new EHR release, a lab analyzer software update, a billing system migration — every interface connected to that system must be reviewed, potentially retested, and possibly rewritten. This change management burden is one of the most underestimated costs in healthcare IT. A large hospital system might execute dozens of EHR upgrades and vendor changes per year, each touching multiple interfaces. Interface inventory management — maintaining an accurate, up-to-date catalog of every active interface including its business owner, message types, volume baseline, and dependencies — is considered a best practice but is poorly implemented at many organizations.

Modern interface engines provide monitoring dashboards that track message queue depth, throughput rates, error rates, and acknowledgment latency in real time. A sudden drop in message volume on an ADT feed can indicate that the sending system has crashed or lost network connectivity — catching this through monitoring is far preferable to discovering it when a nurse notices the patient board has stopped updating. Sophisticated engines support dead-letter queues, where messages that cannot be processed are held for human review rather than silently dropped, and reprocessing capabilities that allow a backlog of held messages to be replayed once an issue is resolved. These operational features are often the deciding factor when health systems choose between competing platforms.

steps.description: Define the business need, identify source and destination systems, document required data elements, message types (ADT, ORU, SIU, etc.), and trigger events. Agree on error handling and acknowledgment behavior.
steps.title: Requirements & Design

steps.description: Write transformation logic in the engine's scripting environment. Map source segments and fields to destination equivalents, handle Z-segments and custom fields, and implement any filtering or enrichment rules.
steps.title: Mapping & Build

steps.description: Test with synthetic and de-identified real messages. Validate that edge cases (empty fields, unusual character sets, high-volume bursts) are handled correctly. Coordinate with both source and destination system teams.
steps.title: Unit & Integration Testing

steps.description: Enable the interface in production with close monitoring for the first 48–72 hours. Watch queue depths, acknowledgment rates, and error logs. Keep rollback procedures ready if unexpected issues emerge.
steps.title: Go-Live & Hypercare

steps.description: Set up automated alerting on volume anomalies and error thresholds. Maintain the interface inventory record. Re-test and potentially remap when either connected system undergoes a version upgrade.
steps.title: Ongoing Monitoring & Change Management

body.message: Many health systems inherit hundreds of undocumented interfaces built over decades by staff who have since left. When a source system is decommissioned or upgraded, discovering what depends on it becomes an emergency archaeology project. Maintaining a living interface inventory — including business owners, downstream dependencies, and message volume baselines — is not glamorous work, but it dramatically reduces the cost and risk of every future system change.

children.text: The Transition to FHIR: Will Interface Engines Disappear?

FHIR has generated enormous enthusiasm in the interoperability world, and for good reason: it replaces the opaque, pipe-delimited structure of HL7 v2 with clean JSON resources accessible via standard RESTful APIs. ONC and CMS rules now require certified EHRs and payers to expose FHIR US Core APIs, and the UK's NHS, Australia's My Health Record, and health systems in dozens of other countries are embedding FHIR into national interoperability strategies.

Despite this momentum, HL7 v2 is not going away on any near-term horizon. HL7 International reports that 95% of U.S. healthcare organizations use HL7 v2. The reason is embedded infrastructure: laboratory instruments, medical devices, legacy pharmacy systems, and decades-old departmental applications speak HL7 v2 natively and will not be replaced simply because a superior standard exists. Replacing every HL7 v2 feed in a large health system would require years of parallel operation, enormous capital investment, and careful change management — resources most health systems are not in a position to commit simultaneously.

The realistic ten-year outlook is a hybrid architecture in which interface engines play a transformed but persistent role. Rather than disappearing, they evolve into v2-to-FHIR translation layers: receiving legacy HL7 v2 messages from clinical systems, converting them to FHIR R4 resources, and handing them off to cloud-based FHIR servers for storage and downstream consumption. Major vendors are already investing in exactly this capability — Rhapsody, InterSystems, and Cloverleaf all support FHIR natively alongside v2. The interface engine of 2030 will look less like a message broker and more like a universal translator standing between a legacy clinical world and a modern API ecosystem. The organizations that navigate this transition most successfully will be those that treat integration as a strategic competency rather than a back-office function.

FHIR is not replacing interface engines — it is giving them a new job. The engine of the future translates HL7 v2 messages from legacy systems into FHIR resources for cloud platforms, serving as the essential bridge between the clinical world that exists and the interoperability world we are building toward.

body.title: Traditional Interface Engines vs. FHIR-Native Integration

points: Interface engines are the hub-and-spoke backbone of hospital data exchange, replacing hundreds of point-to-point connections with a single, centralized translation and routing layer.
MLLP (Minimal Lower Layer Protocol) is the TCP/IP wrapping protocol that defines message boundaries for HL7 v2 traffic — it remains the clinical messaging transport standard in most hospitals.
HL7 v2 is used by 95% of U.S. healthcare organizations (HL7 International), despite being developed in the 1980s.

Leading commercial platforms — Rhapsody (Best in KLAS for 15 consecutive years), Infor Cloverleaf, and InterSystems Health Connect — each offer enterprise-scale integration with deep HL7 and FHIR support.
Mirth Connect, the dominant open-source option, transitioned to a proprietary license with version 4.6, prompting the community to fork it into the Open Integration Engine project.

Modern iPaaS platforms like MuleSoft use FHIR facade patterns — exposing clean FHIR APIs over legacy systems — while cloud providers like AWS HealthLake and Azure Health Data Services serve as FHIR-native storage destinations.
Building a single interface takes weeks to months, and every interface must be retested when a connected system is upgraded — the change-management burden that drives large integration budgets.

Interface engines will not disappear as FHIR adoption grows — they will evolve into v2-to-FHIR translation layers, bridging the legacy clinical world to modern cloud platforms for the foreseeable future.

body.explanation: TCP/IP is a continuous byte stream with no inherent message boundaries. MLLP solves this by wrapping each HL7 message in a start-block character (0x0B) and an end-block sequence (0x1C + carriage return), allowing the receiving application to parse individual messages reliably. Despite being technically simple, MLLP remains the dominant transport protocol for clinical HL7 v2 messaging in hospital environments today.

options.text: It encrypts HL7 messages to meet HIPAA security requirements.
It compresses large HL7 message files to reduce network bandwidth usage.
It wraps HL7 messages with start and end markers so receiving systems can identify message boundaries within a continuous TCP/IP byte stream.
It converts HL7 v2 messages into FHIR JSON resources for modern API consumption.

title: Interface Engines and Integration Platforms: The Plumbing of Healthcare Interoperability

children.text: Your health data tells a story that spans decades — every diagnosis, every medication, every lab value, every surgery. Yet for most of American healthcare history, patients have been passive observers of that story, unable to read it, let alone share it. Physicians held records in file cabinets. Hospitals locked data inside proprietary systems. Insurers sat on years of claims that patients never saw. The 21st century brought electronic health records, but digitizing a locked file cabinet does not make information free.

That reality is now changing — not because the industry chose transparency voluntarily, but because federal law now mandates it. A converging set of regulations — the 21st Century Cures Act, the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F), and the ONC Cures Act Final Rule — have created enforceable patient rights to electronic health data. APIs are the pipes. FHIR is the language. SMART on FHIR is the security handshake. Together, they are building the infrastructure for true health data portability. This lesson examines the legal foundations of those rights, the technical systems built to fulfill them, the real-world barriers that still limit access, and the road ahead.

children.text: The Original Foundation: HIPAA's Right of Access

Long before FHIR or APIs existed, patients already had a federal right to their health information. The HIPAA Privacy Rule, codified at 45 CFR §164.524, grants every patient the right to inspect and obtain a copy of their protected health information (PHI) maintained in a designated record set. This right covers medical records, billing records, and any other records used to make decisions about the individual.

The mechanics are straightforward on paper. A patient submits a written request to a covered entity — a hospital, physician practice, insurer, or their business associates — and the covered entity must act on that request within 30 calendar days of receipt. A single 30-day extension is permitted if the entity notifies the patient in writing of the reason for delay and provides a date by which it will complete the action. Covered entities may charge a reasonable, cost-based fee — but that fee can only cover labor for copying, supplies, and postage. They cannot charge for retrieving or reviewing the records, a distinction the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) at HHS has repeatedly emphasized in enforcement actions. When a patient uses a patient portal's View, Download, and Transmit functionality, no fee may be charged at all.

Despite this longstanding right, compliance was historically poor. Providers routinely imposed excessive fees, demanded notarized requests, required patients to appear in person, or simply failed to respond within the legally required window. OCR launched a Right of Access Initiative in 2019, specifically targeting providers who delayed, denied, or overcharged patients for their records. The initiative has resulted in dozens of settlements and civil monetary penalties. In December 2024, OCR finalized a $200,000 civil monetary penalty against OHSU — its 53rd Right of Access enforcement action — and in January 2025 it announced a $60,000 settlement with South Broward Hospital District (Memorial Healthcare System). These enforcement actions signal that HHS treats patient access as a genuine legal obligation — not a courtesy.

Under HIPAA 45 CFR §164.524, patients have the right to direct their PHI to a third party of their choosing — including a health app, a caregiver, or another provider. Covered entities cannot refuse on the grounds that they do not trust the receiving app or question the patient's reason for sharing.

body.message: HIPAA's Right of Access applies to 'designated record sets' — not necessarily every record a clinician ever created. Psychotherapy notes, certain quality assurance records, and information compiled for legal proceedings may be excluded. The 21st Century Cures Act's information blocking rules extend further, covering all electronic health information (EHI) — a broader category than HIPAA's designated record set.

children.text: 21st Century Cures Act: The Information Blocking Prohibition

The 21st Century Cures Act, signed into law in December 2016, took the concept of patient access and reframed it as a prohibition framework. Rather than simply granting rights to patients, it made it illegal for 'actors' in the healthcare ecosystem — health IT developers, health information networks, and healthcare providers — to engage in practices that interfere with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI). This prohibition, codified in the ONC Cures Act Final Rule at 45 CFR Part 171, took effect April 5, 2021.

The statute defines information blocking broadly: any practice that a provider knows — or that a health IT developer or health information network knows or should know — is likely to interfere with, prevent, or materially discourage access, exchange, or use of EHI — unless the practice falls within a defined exception. ONC's 2020 rule codified eight exceptions — among them preventing harm, privacy, security, and infeasibility — and later rules added TEFCA Manner and Protecting Care Access; practices required by law fall outside the definition itself. A practice that misses every exception is not automatically information blocking: whether it meets the definition is decided case by case. The scope of EHI covered by the prohibition expanded in October 2022 from a subset of structured data to nearly all information in a patient's designated record set — including clinical notes, imaging reports, and behavioral health records.

Enforcement unfolded in stages. HHS-OIG began enforcing against health IT developers and health information exchanges and networks for conduct on or after September 1, 2023, with civil monetary penalties of up to $1,000,000 per violation. Disincentives for healthcare providers became effective July 31, 2024 — making the prohibition fully operational across all actor types. Providers found to have committed information blocking may lose meaningful EHR user status (for hospitals, three-quarters of the annual market-basket increase), receive a zero score in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category, or be excluded from the Medicare Shared Savings Program for at least one year. HHS's September 2025 announcement of a crackdown on health data blocking, with a joint OIG–ASTP enforcement alert, signals continued and intensifying enforcement.

body.content: A regional hospital system charges patients $1 per page plus a $25 administrative fee to retrieve records requested for care coordination with another provider. Under HIPAA, the $25 fee is impermissible — it covers retrieval, not copying. Under the Cures Act information blocking rules, any policy that systematically discourages patients from exercising their access rights, without a valid exception, could constitute information blocking — even if the fee would survive HIPAA scrutiny. The two frameworks overlap but are not identical; compliance with one does not guarantee compliance with the other.

children.text: CMS-9115-F: The Patient Access API Mandate for Payers

While the 21st Century Cures Act and the ONC Cures Act Final Rule primarily regulate providers and health IT developers, CMS took parallel action on the payer side with the Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F), finalized in May 2020. This rule targets a data trove that patients had almost never been able to access: their insurance claims and clinical data held by Medicare Advantage plans, Medicaid managed care organizations, CHIP plans, and Qualified Health Plan (QHP) issuers on the Federally Facilitated Exchanges.

CMS-9115-F requires affected payers to implement a Patient Access API — a FHIR R4-based interface that patients can use to retrieve their own data. The API must expose adjudicated claims and encounter data, clinical data (including laboratory results), and — for Medicare Advantage drug plans — formulary information; CMS-0057-F later added prior authorization information starting in 2027. Critically, the rule requires that payers make data available going back to January 1, 2016 — giving patients a multi-year view of their own insurance history, not just recent claims. CMS enforced compliance beginning July 1, 2021 after exercising enforcement discretion through the first half of that year.

The Patient Access API uses SMART on FHIR for authorization. When a patient wants to connect a third-party app to their insurance data, the app redirects the patient to the payer's authorization server. The patient logs in with their insurer credentials and grants the app specific permissions using OAuth 2.0 scopes. The payer's server then issues a time-limited access token — the patient's credentials are never shared with the third-party app. The app presents this token to the FHIR API and retrieves the patient's data. The patient can revoke access at any time through the payer's portal. This architecture brings health insurance data access into alignment with how consumers already authorize apps to access their bank accounts or email.

Subsequent rulemakings have layered additional requirements on top of CMS-9115-F. The 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F) added requirements for Prior Authorization APIs, mandating that payers expose prior authorization decisions and timelines via FHIR and publicly report prior authorization metrics beginning in 2026. Each new mandate extends the scope of payer data that patients can access programmatically, steadily dismantling the information asymmetry that has defined the payer-patient relationship for decades.
What Data Does the Patient Access API Expose?

steps.title: Adjudicated claims and encounter data — every service billed to the insurer, going back to January 1, 2016
Clinical data including laboratory results and diagnostic information the payer holds
Prior authorization requests, decisions, and denial reasons (added by CMS-0057-F, starting January 2027)
Formulary and prescription drug coverage information via a Drug Formulary API
Provider directory information — network status and specialty data via a separate Provider Directory API

children.text: Blue Button 2.0, Apple Health Records, and the Patient App Ecosystem

CMS's own implementation of the Patient Access API concept predates CMS-9115-F. Blue Button 2.0 — launched as a production API in 2018 — gives Medicare beneficiaries the ability to authorize third-party apps to access their Medicare Part A (hospital), Part B (outpatient), and Part D (prescription drug) claims and encounter data. At launch the API offered FHIR-formatted claims data for 53 million Medicare beneficiaries — one of the largest repositories of longitudinal health claims data in the world. Beneficiaries authorize apps through Medicare.gov, retaining full control over which applications can access their information and for how long.

Blue Button 2.0 demonstrated both the promise and the persistent challenge of patient-facing health data APIs. On the promise side, the program proved that a FHIR API could operate at Medicare's scale — hundreds of millions of claims records served to authorized apps on demand. It attracted dozens of registered production applications spanning personal health management, care coordination, research platforms, and benefits navigation services. On the challenge side, actual beneficiary uptake remained modest: despite the size of the eligible population, the fraction of Medicare beneficiaries who connected an app to Blue Button 2.0 was small. Access rights and technical capability do not automatically translate into patient engagement.

Apple Health Records represents perhaps the most visible consumer-facing implementation of FHIR-based patient access. Launched with 12 hospital partners in 2018, the feature uses the FHIR R4 standard and the SMART on FHIR authorization framework to pull clinical records directly into the iPhone Health app. Apple now reports more than 500 supporting institutions in the U.S. ONC data from 2024 found that 70% of U.S. hospitals enabled patient access via FHIR-configured apps — up from 57% in 2021 — and ONC's 2024 survey data showed 57% of individuals using an app to access their records, compared to 38% in 2020. The program demonstrates that patients will adopt health data apps when the user experience is genuinely frictionless.

The SMART on FHIR standard, developed originally at Boston Children's Hospital and HL7, provides the authorization layer that makes the app ecosystem interoperable. SMART App Launch version 2.2.0 layers OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect on top of FHIR, providing a standardized way for apps to request specific scopes of patient data, confirm patient identity via OpenID Connect claims, and receive time-limited access tokens. This framework is now required by the ONC Cures Act Final Rule for certified health IT — meaning any EHR vendor seeking ONC certification must support it. The result is a genuine ecosystem: any SMART-compatible patient app can, in principle, connect to any certified EHR, without custom integration work.

body.analogy: Think of SMART on FHIR like the 'Sign in with Google' button that thousands of apps use. You never give the third-party app your Google password — Google's servers verify your identity and issue a limited permission token. SMART on FHIR does the same thing for health data: your EHR or payer verifies who you are and hands the app a time-limited key to specific parts of your record — nothing more, nothing less. The result is consent-based, scoped, revocable access that puts the patient in control.

children.text: The Gap Between Rights and Reality: Persistent Barriers

Despite a robust legal framework and steadily improving technical infrastructure, patient access to health data remains far from universal in practice. ASTP's analysis of 2024 Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS) data found that 77% of individuals nationally were offered online access to their health information, and 65% were both offered access and used it — leaving a sizable group who were offered access but never logged in.

The barriers are both structural and sociodemographic. On the structural side, patients with care scattered across multiple health systems face fragmentation: a portal from each provider, each requiring separate login credentials, each showing only that system's data. Patients who have seen five specialists in three health systems may need five portals to assemble a complete picture of their care. CommonWell Health Alliance and Carequality — the two major nationwide health information exchange frameworks, with CommonWell now a designated TEFCA QHIN and Carequality aligning its framework with TEFCA — enable provider-to-provider data sharing across organizations. But patient-initiated cross-provider exchange, where a patient directs their records from one system to another without involving a clinician, remains technically complex and poorly supported in most consumer-facing applications.

On the sociodemographic side, ONC data consistently documents disparities in portal access and use by race, ethnicity, income, education, and geography. Patients with lower health literacy may struggle to interpret clinical notes and lab values even when they can access them. Non-English speakers face language barriers in portal interfaces designed primarily for English-language users. Rural patients may lack reliable broadband for app-based access. Lower-resourced hospitals — small, rural, and Critical Access facilities — lag significantly behind large academic medical centers in deploying FHIR-enabled app APIs, meaning patients at those facilities may not yet have the same technical access as patients at well-resourced systems.

There is also the question of what patients can do once they have their data. A FHIR bundle of clinical data is rich and machine-readable, but it was not designed for lay audiences. Allergy codes, procedure codes, SNOMED-coded diagnoses, and LOINC-coded lab values are meaningful to clinicians and software systems — but a patient staring at a raw FHIR JSON file is not meaningfully informed. The real frontier of patient access is not just getting data out of systems — it is translating that data into actionable insight for the person it belongs to.

In 2024, 70% of U.S. hospitals enabled patient access via FHIR app APIs — up from 57% in 2021. Progress is real, but 30% of hospitals still do not, and small (66%), rural (66%), and Critical Access (64%) hospitals lag behind.
The Road to True Portability: What Comes Next

The regulatory infrastructure built between 2016 and 2024 has established that patients have enforceable rights to their electronic health information. The technical infrastructure — FHIR R4, SMART on FHIR, Patient Access APIs, Blue Button 2.0, TEFCA — has created standardized pipes through which that data can flow. What the ecosystem now needs is the final layer: applications, data intermediaries, and user experiences that make portable health data genuinely useful to patients in the moments that matter.

TEFCA, the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement finalized by ONC in January 2022 and operationalized through Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) beginning in 2023, is building the nationwide backbone for patient-directed exchange at scale. CommonWell and Carequality have both committed to TEFCA connectivity, potentially unifying the major nationwide exchange frameworks under a single governance structure. Under TEFCA's Individual Access Services, patients will be able to direct the movement of their records from any TEFCA-connected organization to any other — regardless of which EHR or payer system those organizations use.

The longer-term vision — a single, patient-controlled longitudinal health record — aggregates data from every provider, payer, pharmacy, lab, and device the patient has ever interacted with. Several companies are building toward this model, pulling FHIR data from multiple sources simultaneously using SMART on FHIR and assembling it into a unified timeline. As AI-powered interpretation layers mature, patients may eventually receive not just a copy of their records, but a personalized, plain-language explanation of what those records mean — closing the loop between access and understanding.

Two risks deserve attention as patient access expands. First, privacy: when patients share data with apps via SMART on FHIR, those apps are not necessarily covered entities under HIPAA — they may be regulated only by the FTC, which applies a weaker standard. A patient who shares their Medicare claims with a wellness app may have significantly less protection than they realize. Second, equity: if the apps and platforms that make portable data useful are designed for the already-connected and already-literate patient, the information blocking prohibition will have succeeded technically while failing the patients who most need to benefit from it. True portability is not just a legal right — it is an equity imperative.
Patients should not have to fight for their own health information. Data blocking is a patient safety issue — when records do not follow the patient, care suffers.

points: HIPAA's Right of Access (45 CFR §164.524) gives patients the right to their records within 30 days; fees can only cover copying costs — not retrieval, search, or review.

The 21st Century Cures Act prohibits information blocking by providers, health IT developers, and health information networks under 45 CFR Part 171; full enforcement across all actor types has been active since July 2024.
CMS-9115-F requires Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, and QHP payers to expose adjudicated claims and clinical data via FHIR Patient Access APIs, with data going back to January 1, 2016.

Blue Button 2.0 delivers FHIR-formatted Medicare claims data (53 million beneficiaries at its 2018 launch); Apple Health Records connects to 500+ facilities — both use SMART on FHIR for patient-authorized app access.

SMART on FHIR (OAuth 2.0 + OpenID Connect) is the standard authorization layer for patient-facing health apps, required for ONC-certified health IT; it enables consent-based, scoped, revocable access.
As of 2024, 77% of individuals were offered online access and 65% were offered and used it — legal access rights and technical availability do not automatically produce patient engagement.
CommonWell, Carequality, and TEFCA are building nationwide exchange infrastructure; patient-directed exchange across system boundaries remains the hardest problem to solve at scale.
The equity frontier: low-resourced hospitals lag in FHIR API deployment; apps that make portable data useful must be designed for patients with low digital literacy and limited connectivity.

title: Patient Access to Health Data: Rights, APIs, and the Road to True Portability

children.text: Americans move between jobs, between states, and between life stages. When they do, their health coverage often moves with them or, more precisely, it disappears and reappears in a different form. A factory worker switches from employer-sponsored coverage to a Marketplace plan after a layoff. A retiree transitions from commercial insurance to Medicare Advantage. A young adult ages off a parent's plan and enrolls in a state Medicaid program. Each of these transitions is not just an administrative event. It is a potential rupture in the continuity of care. The new payer inherits a member but not a record. The patient's diagnosis history, prior authorization approvals, chronic medication regimen, and recent specialist consultations exist somewhere on a server operated by the previous plan but are invisible to the clinicians and care managers now responsible for that person's health.

This invisibility has real consequences. A care manager at the new plan who does not know about a patient's recent hospitalization cannot schedule appropriate follow-up. A prior authorization reviewer who cannot see a previously approved six-month course of specialty medication may deny continuation, creating an abrupt gap in treatment. A disease management program that does not know a member has diabetes cannot enroll them in population health outreach. Every one of these failures costs money in duplicated diagnostic tests, avoidable hospitalizations, and adverse drug events, and most importantly it costs health. The problem is structural: the health insurance system has historically treated membership data as proprietary, not portable.

Payer-to-payer data exchange is the regulatory and technical effort to fix this structural failure. The concept is straightforward: when a member changes health plans, the new payer should be able to request and receive relevant clinical and administrative data from the previous payer, so that care continues without interruption. The execution has proved far more complex. This lesson traces the regulatory journey from CMS-9115-F's original 2022 mandate through its supersession by CMS-0057-F's January 2027 deadline, explains the technical architecture built on HL7's Da Vinci PDex Implementation Guide, and examines the real-world challenges of member identity matching, consent management, and data operationalization that stand between the regulatory vision and clinical impact.
The Coverage Gap Problem: Who Actually Switches Plans and Why It Matters

The scale of health plan switching in the United States is large enough to constitute a persistent public health challenge in its own right. The problem is most acute in Medicaid, where administrative-driven disenrollment and re-enrollment, a phenomenon researchers call churning, affects millions of people each year. Before the COVID-19 public health emergency froze Medicaid eligibility redeterminations, studies found that among full-benefit Medicaid beneficiaries enrolled at any point in a given year, roughly 10% experienced a gap in coverage of less than one year. Approximately 4% were disenrolled and re-enrolled within three months, and nearly 7% within six months. Many of these are not people who became ineligible for coverage. They are people who lost coverage due to paperwork failures, outdated addresses, or administrative processing errors, and then regained it shortly after.

The Medicaid unwinding that followed the end of pandemic-era continuous enrollment protections in April 2023 provided a stark illustration of this dynamic at extreme scale. States resumed eligibility redeterminations after a pause of more than three years, and over the following two years, more than 25 million people were disenrolled from Medicaid. Studies found that 69% of disenrollments were procedural rather than eligibility-based, meaning the vast majority of people who lost coverage were likely still eligible. Many re-enrolled within weeks or months, but each gap represented a period during which the re-enrolling member was invisible to their plan. Any care coordination, disease management, or prior authorization history accumulated during years of prior enrollment was gone from the new plan's view.

In Medicare Advantage, KFF found that about one in ten enrollees (11% of those in MA drug plans in 2013) voluntarily switched to another plan for the following year. In the Affordable Care Act Marketplace, switching rates are substantially higher: 43% of enrollees switched plans between 2015 and 2016, driven by premium volatility, insurer exits, and annual re-evaluation of cost-sharing structures. Each of these transitions creates a potential data gap. And unlike Medicaid churning where the member may return to the same plan, Marketplace switching typically involves entirely different payers who have no established data-sharing relationship.
