children.text: The Five Healthy People 2030 SDOH Domains

The US federal framework for organizing SDOH comes from Healthy People 2030, the decade-long set of national health objectives published by the Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion. Social determinants of health is one of its three overarching priority areas, alongside health equity and health literacy. Healthy People 2030 organizes SDOH into five domains, which have become the standard vocabulary for screening, measurement, and intervention.

The five domains are economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context. Each captures a cluster of conditions with strong, independent links to health — and each maps to specific, actionable interventions a health system or community organization can deploy.

Using a shared taxonomy matters more than it might seem. When a clinic, a payer, a community-based organization, and a public health department all describe social needs in the same five-domain language, they can screen consistently, share data, and coordinate referrals. The Healthy People 2030 framework is the connective tissue that lets those handoffs happen.

children.text: How Strong Are the Links? Two Well-Studied Examples

It is one thing to assert that social conditions matter; it is another to show the magnitude. Two of the most rigorously studied SDOH-to-health links — social connection and education — illustrate how large these effects are when measured carefully.

Social isolation is a striking case. A 2010 meta-analysis by Julianne Holt-Lunstad and colleagues benchmarked the mortality risk of weak social connection against established risk factors and found it comparable to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day — a comparison the US Surgeon General later cited in a formal advisory on loneliness. A follow-up 2015 meta-analysis covering over 3 million participants found social isolation associated with a 29% increase in mortality risk and living alone with a 32% increase. (Researchers caution the cigarette analogy can oversimplify, but the underlying mortality signal is robust.)

Education shows a similarly powerful gradient. People with more education live longer and healthier lives, and the relationship is graded — each additional level of attainment is associated with better outcomes. Education works through multiple channels: higher income, safer jobs, greater health literacy, and more control over one's circumstances, echoing the social-gradient findings of the Whitehall studies.

body.content:
Brigham Young University researcher Julianne Holt-Lunstad led meta-analyses establishing social connection as a major determinant of survival. The 2010 analysis benchmarked weak social ties against smoking, obesity, and physical inactivity, finding the mortality effect of social isolation comparable to smoking up to 15 cigarettes per day.
The 2015 follow-up, pooling over 3 million participants, found social isolation raised mortality risk by 29% and living alone by 32%. The work directly informed the 2023 US Surgeon General's Advisory on the epidemic of loneliness and isolation — moving social connection from a soft concern to a measured public health priority.
body.title: Social Connection as a Mortality Risk Factor (Holt-Lunstad)

children.text: Why This Reframes the Health System's Job

If 80% of health outcomes are driven by factors outside clinical care, then a health system that wants to improve outcomes — especially under value-based contracts that pay for results rather than visits — has to engage the social conditions of its population. This does not mean hospitals must become housing agencies or food banks. It means they must screen for social needs, connect patients to resources, and partner with the organizations that address those needs.

There is also an equity dimension. Social and economic disadvantage is not randomly distributed; it tracks race, income, and place because of the structural factors covered earlier in this course. That means SDOH burdens fall hardest on exactly the populations with the worst health outcomes. Addressing social needs is therefore not a separate agenda from equity — it is one of the most direct levers for reducing disparities.

The remaining lessons in this part of the course turn from evidence to practice: how clinical teams screen for social needs with validated tools, how they document them, and how specific interventions in housing and food security are showing measurable health and cost effects. The evidence in this lesson is the foundation; the next lessons are about acting on it.

body.message: The SDOH evidence justifies screening patients for social needs — but asking someone whether they are food insecure or about to be evicted, and then having nothing to offer, can erode trust and cause harm. Effective SDOH work pairs screening with a real referral pathway. The next lesson covers how to do this responsibly.
body.title: Screening without action can backfire

title: The Evidence on SDOH: What Drives Health More Than Health Care

children.text: From Knowing to Asking

The previous lesson established that social conditions drive most health outcomes. But a health system cannot act on a patient's housing instability or food insecurity if it does not know about it — and these needs are usually invisible in a standard clinical encounter. SDOH screening is the structured practice of asking patients directly about their social needs so that those needs can be documented and addressed.

A consistent finding across the literature is that patients are generally willing to answer these questions when they are asked respectfully, confidentially, and with a clear purpose. Screening surfaces needs clinicians would otherwise never learn about — a patient skipping medications to pay rent, a parent rationing food, an older adult who cannot get to appointments. None of these is visible on a lab panel.

But screening is only the first step, and doing it badly can cause harm. Asking someone whether they are food insecure and then offering nothing in response signals that the system sees the problem and does not care — eroding the trust screening was meant to build. Responsible SDOH screening is always designed as the front end of a pathway that ends in a referral and, ideally, a confirmed connection to help.

SDOH screening structures the question "what do you need outside the clinic?" Patients will generally answer when asked respectfully — but screening must be paired with a real response, or it erodes trust rather than building it.
The Major Validated Screening Tools

Several validated screening instruments are in wide use. They differ in length, setting, and the domains they emphasize, but they share the goal of standardizing how social needs are captured so that data can be aggregated, compared, and acted on. Two tools dominate US practice: PRAPARE and the CMS Accountable Health Communities tool.

PRAPARE — the Protocol for Responding to and Assessing Patients' Assets, Risks, and Experiences — was developed by the National Association of Community Health Centers (NACHC) together with AAPCHO and the Oregon Primary Care Association. It comprises 21 questions covering housing, food, employment, education, transportation, and social support. PRAPARE is the most widely used tool in Federally Qualified Health Centers and is designed to map to ICD-10 Z-codes for documentation.

The CMS Accountable Health Communities (AHC) Health-Related Social Needs (HRSN) Screening Tool is a shorter, 10-item instrument published by CMS in 2017. Its core covers five domains — housing instability, food insecurity, transportation problems, utility needs, and interpersonal safety — with optional supplemental questions on financial strain, employment, mental health, and more. It was built for the AHC model and has become a federal reference standard for health-related social needs.

children.text: Z-Codes: Documenting Social Needs in the Record

Identifying a social need is only useful if it is recorded in a way the system can use. ICD-10-CM Z-codes in the Z55-Z65 range are the standardized diagnosis codes for documenting social determinants of health. They let a clinician capture a social need as structured data that can be counted across a panel, reported for quality programs, and increasingly used by payers to understand and address population needs.

The categories map cleanly to the screening domains: Z55 covers education and literacy problems; Z56 employment and unemployment; Z57 occupational exposures; Z58 physical environment; Z59 housing and economic circumstances (Z59.0 is homelessness); Z60 the social environment; and Z62-Z65 various psychosocial circumstances. Per ICD-10 guidance, these are reported as secondary diagnoses, and notably they may be documented based on information from any clinician involved in the patient's care — not only the billing provider — which means social workers, nurses, and case managers can supply the documentation.

The central problem with Z-codes is not the codes themselves but how rarely they are used. CMS reported that Z-codes were documented for only about 1.6% of Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries in 2019, despite social needs being far more prevalent than that. The barriers are practical: many clinicians do not know the codes exist, lack a workflow for capturing them, or are unsure who is permitted to document them. Improving Z-code capture is a recurring target of health-system equity initiatives.

children.text: Closing the Loop: From Referral to Confirmed Help

Screening identifies a need and Z-codes document it, but neither solves anything on its own. The decisive step is the referral — connecting the patient to a community resource that can actually address the need — and, ideally, confirming the connection happened. The quality of this handoff is what separates SDOH programs that improve outcomes from those that simply generate data.

Referrals exist on a spectrum. A paper pamphlet listing food banks is the weakest form — the patient is left to navigate alone. A "warm" referral, where a staff member helps make the connection during the visit, is stronger. The strongest is a closed-loop referral: the receiving organization confirms the patient connected with services and reports that outcome back to the care team, so the loop is closed and the system knows whether the need was met.

A set of community resource and referral platforms has emerged to enable closed-loop referrals at scale, building shared directories and digital handoffs between health care and community-based organizations. The best known are findhelp (formerly Aunt Bertha) and Unite Us. These platforms let a clinic send an electronic referral, track its status, and receive confirmation — turning a vague suggestion into an accountable transaction.

body.content:
findhelp (formerly Aunt Bertha) operates a searchable national directory of social-service programs that lets clinical teams and patients find and connect to local resources, with referral tracking.
Unite Us builds coordinated-care networks that link health care organizations with community-based organizations and provide closed-loop referral tracking — the referring team is notified when a patient is served. Both are used by health systems, payers, and Medicaid programs to make social-needs referrals accountable rather than aspirational.

children.text: Designing Screening That Helps Rather Than Harms

Putting the pieces together, an effective SDOH screening program has four linked components: a validated tool appropriate to the setting, a respectful workflow for asking, structured documentation (including Z-codes), and a referral pathway capable of closing the loop. Missing any one of these undermines the others. A great tool with no referral pathway just catalogs suffering; a great referral network with no screening never finds the patients who need it.

Workflow and trust matter as much as instrument choice. Who asks the questions, how they are framed, whether the patient understands why, and whether the encounter feels safe all shape whether screening yields honest answers. Embedding community health workers or trained staff to conduct screening and follow up on referrals consistently produces better engagement than handing patients a form in a waiting room.

Finally, screening should be designed with the populations it serves, not just for them. Tools and workflows that are language-concordant, culturally appropriate, and sensitive to the stigma around needs like food insecurity or interpersonal safety will capture far more than a generic checklist. The goal is not a completed questionnaire — it is a patient whose unmet need was identified and actually addressed.

body.message: Requiring clinicians to screen without giving them time, training, documentation tools, or a referral network sets the program up to fail — and can damage patient trust. Before scaling screening, ensure the downstream referral pathway and the staff capacity to act on findings are genuinely in place.
body.title: Do not let screening become an unfunded mandate

title: SDOH Screening in Clinical Settings: Tools, Z-Codes & Referrals

children.text: The Authority That Lets States Reinvent Medicaid

Medicaid is governed by detailed federal rules — who must be covered, what services must be offered, how programs must operate. These rules create consistency, but they also constrain experimentation. So how do states test bold new approaches, like covering housing as a health benefit or running an all-payer global budget, when the standard rules would not allow it? The answer is the Section 1115 demonstration waiver — the single most powerful tool states have to reinvent their Medicaid programs, and the engine behind most major Medicaid managed care innovation.

Section 1115 of the Social Security Act gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to approve experimental, pilot, or demonstration projects likely to promote the objectives of the Medicaid program. What makes Section 1115 uniquely powerful is its breadth: it combines extensive waiver authority with a broadly defined purpose. The Secretary can waive almost any Medicaid state plan requirement and can permit federal matching funds for costs not otherwise matchable — letting states cover services and populations Medicaid normally would not. In effect, Section 1115 is a license to experiment with the program’s core rules.

For Medicaid managed care, 1115 waivers are foundational. Many states’ entire managed care programs operate under 1115 authority, and the boldest delivery and payment innovations — from value-based reforms to addressing social needs — are tested through these demonstrations. Understanding Section 1115 is understanding how Medicaid changes and how the most ambitious managed care experiments become possible.

Key Concept: A Section 1115 demonstration waiver lets the HHS Secretary waive most Medicaid rules and authorize federal funding for normally non-matchable costs, so states can test experimental approaches. Demonstrations must be "budget neutral" to the federal government and are generally approved for five years, then renewable.

children.text: How Section 1115 Works

A Section 1115 demonstration is, formally, a research and demonstration project: states must have an approved, publicly available evaluation strategy, because the authority is meant to test and evaluate new policy approaches, not simply to expand programs. The breadth is remarkable — under Section 1115, the Secretary can waive almost any state plan requirement under §1902 (with narrow exceptions like citizenship rules), to the extent necessary to carry out the demonstration. This lets states restructure eligibility, benefits, delivery systems, and payment in ways the standard rules would forbid.

Equally important is the "expenditure authority" that comes with 1115: the Secretary can permit federal financial participation for costs not otherwise matchable (CNOM) — federal dollars for services and populations not included in the regular Medicaid state plan. CNOM authority is how a state can use Medicaid funds for things like housing supports or services for populations Medicaid does not normally cover. Without it, the boldest innovations would have no funding mechanism; with it, states can finance genuinely new approaches with federal matching dollars.

The approval process is rigorous and often slow. A state submits a detailed application — describing the demonstration, enrollment estimates, requested authorities, research hypotheses, and documentation of public comment — and CMS reviews it case by case to determine whether the objectives align with Medicaid’s. There is a federal 30-day public comment period, and CMS must consider all comments. Negotiation typically takes anywhere from six months to two years, longer for comprehensive waivers that may encompass most of a state’s Medicaid spending, because each program element must be separately negotiated.

body.title: The 1115 Waiver Process

children.text: Budget Neutrality: The Central Constraint

The most important limit on Section 1115 is budget neutrality: a demonstration must not cost the federal government more than it would have spent without the waiver. Federal Medicaid expenditures under the demonstration cannot exceed what federal spending would have been without it, over the course of the project. This single rule shapes nearly every 1115 design, because it means a state cannot simply ask the federal government to pay for new things — it must show that, on net, the demonstration stays within the federal spending it would have incurred anyway.

Budget neutrality is typically calculated on a per-enrollee basis: per-enrollee spending under the demonstration cannot exceed the projected per-enrollee spending in the "without-waiver baseline." This creates a powerful dynamic. If a state spends below that baseline, the difference counts as savings — and the state can use accumulated savings to finance the costs-not-otherwise-matchable spending on populations or services Medicaid does not normally cover. In other words, a state that manages care efficiently enough to come in under its baseline can reinvest the savings into innovative services. Budget neutrality is both a constraint and, paradoxically, the funding source for innovation.

body.message: Budget neutrality means an 1115 demonstration cannot simply add federal cost — new services and populations must generally be financed from savings the demonstration itself generates against the without-waiver baseline. This is why 1115 innovations are framed as investments expected to reduce other spending, not as straightforward expansions.
body.title: Innovation Must Pay for Itself

children.text: What States Are Testing

Section 1115 has become the primary vehicle for the most ambitious Medicaid innovations, and recent years have seen a wave of demonstrations addressing health-related social needs (HRSN) — the social factors like housing and food that drive health outcomes. In 2022 CMS announced a demonstration opportunity to expand states’ tools to address enrollees’ health-related social needs, and by February 2024 had approved eight states under the HRSN framework — Arizona, Arkansas, California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, and Washington. These waivers authorize evidence-based housing and nutrition services for high-need populations, including coverage of rent or temporary housing and utilities for up to six months and meal support for up to six months.

The specific demonstrations are striking in scope. New York’s January 2024 waiver amendment included up to $3.673 billion to build HRSN infrastructure, including new "Social Care Networks," and to reimburse for HRSN services through Medicaid. Massachusetts’s MassHealth waiver supports housing (security deposits, rent, relocation, home modifications, housing case management), food security, and transportation. Arkansas’s supports housing deposits, moving costs, and tenancy-sustaining services. A separate 1115 opportunity addressed reentry for justice-involved individuals — partially waiving the Medicaid "inmate exclusion" so states can provide pre-release services — with the Biden administration approving 19 state reentry waivers.

These innovations are politically contingent, which is itself a defining feature of 1115. Because demonstrations are approved at the Secretary’s discretion, their direction shifts with administrations. In March 2025, the Trump administration rescinded the Biden administration’s HRSN guidance; CMS indicated this does not nullify existing HRSN approvals, but that it will consider HRSN and social-determinant requests on a case-by-case basis going forward. This illustrates a core truth about 1115: it is a powerful tool for innovation precisely because it is discretionary, which also means the innovations it enables can be expanded or curtailed as federal priorities change.
Why 1115 Is the Engine of Medicaid Innovation

Section 1115 occupies a unique place in Medicaid: it is the mechanism through which the program evolves. Almost every major delivery and payment innovation — including the all-payer and global-budget models discussed in the value-based-care course, comprehensive managed care expansions, and the social-needs demonstrations above — runs through 1115 authority. When a state wants to do something genuinely new with Medicaid, the path almost always leads to a Section 1115 waiver. It is, in a real sense, where the future of Medicaid is tested before it becomes standard.

body.analogy: Section 1115 is like a sanctioned "sandbox" or pilot program within a heavily regulated system. The standard Medicaid rules are the building code everyone must follow; an 1115 waiver is special permission to construct an experimental building that breaks some of those rules — but only if you can prove it won’t cost the city more than a normal building (budget neutrality), you document what you’re testing (evaluation), and you get the regulator’s sign-off (case-by-case approval). The sandbox is where new designs get proven before, sometimes, becoming the new code.
body.concept: How Section 1115 enables Medicaid innovation

children.text: The tension at the heart of 1115 is between flexibility and accountability. Its flexibility is what makes innovation possible — without it, Medicaid would be frozen in its statutory form. But that same discretionary flexibility means demonstrations can advance one administration’s priorities and be unwound by the next, that budget-neutrality calculations can be contested, and that "demonstrations" sometimes operate for decades without ever conclusively demonstrating anything. The required evaluations are meant to provide accountability, but the political nature of approval means 1115 is as much a policy instrument as a research tool.

This lesson sets up the course’s conclusion. The next and final lesson looks at where Medicaid managed care is heading — toward social determinants of health and whole-person care — and Section 1115 is precisely the authority making that direction possible. The HRSN demonstrations covered here are the leading edge of that future. Understanding 1115 means understanding not just a regulatory mechanism, but the very channel through which Medicaid managed care reaches beyond medical care toward the social factors that shape health, and through which the program will continue to transform in the years ahead.

points: A Section 1115 demonstration waiver lets the HHS Secretary waive almost any Medicaid state plan requirement (§1902) and authorize federal funding for normally non-matchable costs, so states can test experimental approaches — the most powerful tool for Medicaid innovation.
Section 1115 is uniquely broad, combining extensive waiver authority with a broadly defined purpose, and many states run their entire managed care programs and boldest reforms under 1115 authority.

1115 demonstrations are formally research projects requiring a public evaluation strategy, and expenditure authority (costs not otherwise matchable, CNOM) is what lets states fund services and populations outside the regular state plan.

The approval process is rigorous and slow — a detailed application, a 30-day federal comment period, and case-by-case CMS review — typically taking six months to two years, longer for comprehensive waivers.

Budget neutrality is the central constraint: federal spending under the demonstration cannot exceed without-waiver spending (usually per-enrollee), and savings below the baseline can finance innovative CNOM services — making innovation largely self-funded.

A wave of recent 1115s address health-related social needs (HRSN): eight states (AZ, AR, CA, MA, NJ, NY, OR, WA) approved by February 2024 for housing and nutrition services, including New York’s $3.673 billion Social Care Networks; a separate opportunity approved 19 state reentry waivers partially waiving the inmate-exclusion policy.

1115 innovations are politically contingent — in March 2025 the Trump administration rescinded the Biden HRSN guidance (without nullifying existing approvals), shifting to case-by-case review — reflecting that discretionary approval enables both expansion and curtailment.

Section 1115 is the engine through which Medicaid evolves, including the all-payer/global-budget and social-needs innovations, balancing flexibility (enabling innovation) against accountability (evaluation requirements amid political discretion).

title: Section 1115 Waivers and Managed Care Innovation

children.text: A Spectrum, Not a Switch

The previous lesson described the painful straddle between fee-for-service and value-based care. This lesson maps the destination side of that straddle in detail, because "value-based payment" is not one thing — it is a continuum of arrangements that transfer progressively more financial risk from the payer to the provider. At one end, a provider can earn a bonus for good performance while bearing no real downside. At the other, a provider receives a fixed payment to cover all of a population’s care and bears the full financial consequence if costs run high. Understanding where a contract sits on this continuum is the single most important thing to know about it.

The reason the continuum matters so much is that risk and reward move together. Arrangements with little downside risk are safe but offer modest upside; arrangements with full risk offer the largest rewards but can bankrupt a provider that miscalculates. Hospitals and physician groups generally move along this continuum over time — starting cautiously and taking on more risk as they build the capabilities to manage it. This lesson walks the spectrum from the gentlest to the most aggressive forms of risk-bearing.

Key Concept: Value-based payment is a continuum of risk transfer: from upside-only shared savings (bonus, no penalty), to two-sided risk (share savings and losses), to risk corridors (capped sharing), to capitation (a fixed payment covering all care, full provider risk). More risk means more potential reward — and more potential loss.

stats.context: Capitation is paid "per member per month" — a fixed amount per attributed patient regardless of services used (American College of Physicians)
stats.label: The Capitation Unit

stats.label: Capitation’s Risk Level

children.text: Upside-Only: The Gentle On-Ramp

The first step onto the risk continuum is upside risk, also called one-sided risk or shared savings. The provider is measured against a predetermined financial benchmark — typically the expected total cost of care for its attributed population. If the provider keeps actual costs below that target while meeting quality standards, it shares in the savings, earning a portion of the difference. Crucially, if costs exceed the target, the provider is not penalized: there is upside but no downside.

This asymmetry makes upside-only the natural starting point. It lets a provider learn to manage cost and quality, build the necessary data and care-coordination infrastructure, and earn rewards — all without risking a loss. The Medicare Shared Savings Program’s entry-level tracks work this way. The trade-off is that the rewards are modest precisely because the risk is low; payers do not pay large bonuses to providers who share none of the downside. Upside-only is a training ground, not a permanent home.

Indeed, the entire system is designed to push providers off the on-ramp over time. Because organizations typically grow into downside risk after starting upside-only — either pulled by larger financial incentives or pushed by contract mandates and program rules — two-sided arrangements are described as the more mature or advanced form of risk sharing. The gentle on-ramp exists to get providers ready for the road ahead.
Two-Sided Risk and Risk Corridors

The next step is two-sided risk, where the provider shares both savings and losses. If total cost of care comes in under the benchmark, the provider shares the savings as before; but if costs exceed the benchmark, the provider must share the loss — facing reimbursement cuts or owing money back to the payer. This is a fundamentally different proposition: the provider now has real money at stake in both directions, which sharpens the incentive to control costs but also exposes it to genuine financial danger.

To make two-sided risk survivable, contracts use risk corridors. A risk corridor caps the shared savings or losses using "risk bands": as actual results deviate further from the benchmark, the provider moves into bands where it shares a smaller percentage of the gains or losses. The effect is to limit how much a provider can win or lose in any period, protecting both sides from catastrophic swings. Risk corridors are the shock absorbers that let providers take on downside risk without betting the entire organization on a single bad year.

body.title: One-Sided vs. Two-Sided Risk

children.text: Capitation: Taking on the Full Risk

At the far end of the continuum sits capitation — the most complete transfer of financial risk to the provider. Under capitation, a provider receives a fixed payment per attributed patient, paid per member per month (PMPM), to cover a defined scope of care regardless of how many services that patient actually uses. The PMPM amount represents the expected cost of providing those services. If the provider’s actual costs for its patient panel come in below the capitation budget, it keeps the difference as surplus; if costs exceed the budget, the provider absorbs the loss.

Capitation comes in degrees of breadth. Primary care capitation pays a fixed PMPM for routine primary care and care coordination — a relatively contained risk. Specialty capitation pays specialists a fixed amount for a defined service area like oncology or behavioral health. Global capitation is the most sweeping: a provider or group takes full financial responsibility for all of a population’s care — hospital, specialist, and ancillary services alike. Global capitation makes the provider function almost like an insurer, which is why it represents one of the highest degrees of risk transfer short of starting an insurance plan.

body.title: The Risk Continuum, From Lowest to Highest

children.text: Because capitation transfers so much risk, it requires sophisticated protective machinery. Risk adjustment is essential: PMPM rates must be adjusted upward for sicker patients, or providers would be paid too little to care for high-need populations (and would be tempted to avoid them). Risk pools — a portion of the capitation withheld and paid out only if costs stay controlled — align incentives within physician groups. And stop-loss or reinsurance protects the provider against catastrophic individual cases, capping the loss any single very-sick patient can impose. Without these mechanisms, capitation would be a reckless bet rather than a managed risk.
Choosing Where to Stand on the Continuum

The central strategic question for any provider is not whether to take risk, but how much, how fast, and with what protections. Moving up the continuum increases both the potential reward and the required capability. Upside-only demands basic cost and quality reporting. Two-sided risk demands genuine ability to manage total cost of care. Capitation demands actuarial sophistication, robust data, deep care-management infrastructure, and enough scale to spread risk across a population — capabilities a small or unprepared provider simply will not have.

body.analogy: The risk continuum is like levels of investing. Upside-only shared savings is a savings account with a bonus — safe, modest returns, no chance of loss. Two-sided risk is a diversified portfolio with stop-loss orders — real gains and losses, but bounded. Capitation is running your own fund where you keep all the profit but cover all the losses. You move to higher-risk levels only as your knowledge, reserves, and tools grow — and you use protections (risk corridors, reinsurance) the same way an investor uses hedges.
body.concept: The value-based risk continuum

children.text: The mismatch between risk and capability is where providers get hurt. A group that jumps to capitation without the infrastructure to manage utilization, or without adequate risk adjustment for a sick population, can be financially destroyed by costs it cannot control. Conversely, a sophisticated, well-capitalized system that stays in upside-only leaves substantial reward on the table and signals it is not serious about value. Matching the level of risk to the organization’s real capabilities — and building those capabilities deliberately before advancing — is the essence of value-based financial strategy.

This continuum connects directly to the models covered in the value-based-care course: accountable care organizations typically operate in the shared-savings-to-two-sided-risk range, while Medicare Advantage and advanced primary care models push toward capitation. The same logic governs all of them. As payers and federal policy increasingly favor downside risk and full accountability, providers across the country are being pushed steadily rightward along this continuum. Knowing exactly what each arrangement transfers — and what capabilities and protections each demands — is what separates organizations that thrive under value-based payment from those that merely survive it.

points: Value-based payment is a continuum of increasing risk transfer from payer to provider: upside-only shared savings, two-sided risk, risk corridors, and capitation — with reward and danger rising together.
Upside-only (one-sided) risk lets providers share savings if they beat a cost benchmark with no penalty for overspending; it is the low-reward training ground for building value-based capabilities.
Two-sided risk requires providers to share both savings and losses, exposing them to real financial danger and marking the more mature, advanced stage of risk sharing.
Risk corridors cap shared savings and losses using risk bands, acting as shock absorbers that make two-sided risk survivable by limiting how much a provider can win or lose.

Capitation pays a fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) amount to cover a defined scope of care regardless of utilization; it ranges from primary care to specialty to global capitation, the broadest and riskiest.
Global capitation transfers full financial risk for all of a population’s care, making the provider function almost like an insurer — one of the highest degrees of risk transfer possible.
Capitation requires protective machinery: risk adjustment (higher PMPM for sicker patients), risk pools (withheld payments tied to performance), and stop-loss/reinsurance against catastrophic cases.

The strategic key is matching the level of risk to the organization’s real capabilities and building those capabilities before advancing; ACOs sit in the shared-savings-to-two-sided range while Medicare Advantage and advanced primary care push toward capitation.

title: Shared Savings, Risk Corridors, and Capitation: The Risk Continuum

children.text: The Question at the Heart of the Debate

Should a hospital be held to the same quality standard if half its patients live in poverty as a hospital whose patients are predominantly middle-class? Should a primary care practice treating a community with high rates of food insecurity, unstable housing, and limited transportation be judged on the same readmission rate curve as a practice in a wealthy suburb? These are not rhetorical questions. They are policy choices embedded in every value-based payment program — and the answer determines whether those programs help or harm the safety-net providers that serve America's most vulnerable patients.

Social risk adjustment refers to the practice of modifying quality and cost benchmarks — or risk scores — to account for patients' social and economic circumstances that are unrelated to the quality of clinical care. When a patient is readmitted to the hospital partly because she has no transportation to her follow-up appointment, no refrigerator for her medications, and no one at home to monitor her condition, that readmission reflects her social circumstances — not her provider's clinical competence. The debate is whether the payment system should account for that reality.

The stakes are enormous. The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), the Hospital Value-Based Purchasing Program, the Merit-Based Incentive Payment System, and the Shared Savings Program all use outcome and quality metrics that are sensitive to patients' socioeconomic status. Safety-net hospitals and practices that disproportionately serve low-income and disabled populations have argued for years that these programs systematically penalize them — not for delivering poor care, but for serving poor patients.

Social risk factors — including income level, housing stability, food security, education, transportation access, and social support — are estimated to influence up to 80 percent of health outcomes. Yet most value-based payment programs historically adjusted only for clinical diagnoses, not for these upstream determinants.
The NQF and the Evidence Base

The National Quality Forum (NQF) established an expert panel in 2014 to examine whether quality measures should be adjusted for social risk factors. The panel's report called for adjustment "under a defined set of circumstances," concluding that failing to adjust might worsen health disparities by creating systematic financial pressure on providers who serve disadvantaged populations. This finding sparked a multi-year policy debate involving CMS, MedPAC, the National Academy of Medicine, and Congress.

In 2017, the NQF completed a multi-stakeholder trial that tested social risk adjustment across multiple quality measures. The trial found that incorporating social risk factors into performance measurement was feasible — though challenging — and that social risk factors were statistically significant predictors of outcomes on many measures. The study documented clear performance disparities between providers serving high-social-risk versus low-social-risk populations, validating concerns that unadjusted comparisons were systematically misleading.

Research has consistently shown that dual-eligible beneficiaries (those who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid) and low-income subsidy recipients in Medicare Advantage perform worse on clinical quality measures, have higher readmission rates, and score lower on patient experience surveys — even when controlling for clinical diagnoses. These patterns persist across different geographic regions, health systems, and care settings, suggesting that the disparity is driven by social circumstances rather than differences in clinical care quality.

body.content:
The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), created by the ACA in 2010 with penalties beginning in fiscal year 2013, penalizes hospitals with higher-than-expected 30-day readmissions for conditions including heart failure, pneumonia, and hip/knee replacement. Safety-net hospitals — which serve disproportionately high shares of low-income and uninsured patients — have consistently received higher penalties under HRRP.
Critics argued that much of the gap reflected patients' social circumstances rather than poor hospital care. Congress partially addressed this in the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016, which required a peer-grouping system — applied from fiscal year 2019 — that compares hospitals to others with similar shares of low-income patients — a form of social risk adjustment for HRRP.
body.title: Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program and Safety-Net Hospitals

children.text: The Two Sides of the Policy Debate

The case for social risk adjustment rests on fairness and access. If safety-net providers are systematically penalized in value-based programs because of who their patients are rather than how well they perform clinically, the programs create a perverse incentive to avoid serving vulnerable populations. Over time, financial penalties can reduce resources available for quality improvement, drive providers to exit the market, or create pressure to limit services to high-risk patients. The ultimate losers are the patients who most depend on those providers.

The case against social risk adjustment is also grounded in legitimate policy concerns. Critics argue that adjusting outcome measures for patients' social circumstances could mask genuine disparities in the quality of care delivered to low-income patients. If a hospital serving mostly poor patients actually does deliver inferior care, adjusting the benchmark to account for poverty could obscure that reality and remove the accountability pressure that drives improvement. From this perspective, social risk adjustment could become a tool for excusing poor performance rather than addressing its root causes.

A third position — increasingly adopted by CMS — attempts to split the difference. Rather than adjusting outcome benchmarks for social risk, this approach focuses on measuring and rewarding active interventions to address social needs: screening patients for SDOH, connecting them to community resources, reducing disparities in performance within a provider's own patient population. This "stratification and accountability" approach holds that providers should not be rewarded merely for serving a disadvantaged population, but should be rewarded for actively reducing disparities within that population.

left.label: Arguments For Adjustment
points: Prevents systematic financial penalties on safety-net providers
Removes incentive to avoid enrolling or treating vulnerable patients
Reflects reality that social factors drive outcomes beyond providers' control
Supported by NQF, National Academy of Medicine, and safety-net advocates

right.label: Arguments Against Adjustment
points: Could mask genuine disparities in care quality for low-income patients
Removes accountability pressure to improve outcomes for disadvantaged populations
May create perverse incentive to label patients as socially disadvantaged
Difficult to implement consistently without reliable standardized SDOH data

body.title: Social Risk Adjustment: The Core Policy Debate

children.text: What CMS Has Actually Done

CMS has moved incrementally toward incorporating social risk into payment programs, though it has not adopted comprehensive social risk adjustment for most quality measures. The most significant step was the peer-grouping adjustment for HRRP, enacted in the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016 and applied from fiscal year 2019, which compares hospitals' readmission rates to peers with similar socioeconomic patient mixes rather than to the national average. This approach acknowledges that different hospitals operate in structurally different environments without fully excusing poor performance.

In 2024, CMS issued regulations requiring hospitals participating in federal payment programs to screen all patients for five social determinants: food insecurity, housing instability, transportation needs, utility difficulties, and interpersonal safety. These screening requirements create a standardized data foundation that could eventually support more rigorous social risk adjustment. CMS also established billing codes for Social Determinants of Health Risk Assessments, Community Health Integration services, and Principal Illness Navigation — creating reimbursement pathways for directly addressing social needs.

For Medicare Advantage, CMS introduced the Health Equity Index (HEI) as part of the Star Ratings system, taking effect for 2027 star ratings based on 2024–2025 performance data. The HEI rewards plans that achieve high performance specifically among enrollees with social risk factors — dual-eligible beneficiaries, low-income subsidy recipients, and disability-status enrollees. Rather than adjusting benchmarks downward, the HEI adds bonus points for demonstrating equitable outcomes across all enrolled populations.

children.text: The Data Problem and the Path Forward

The most practical obstacle to comprehensive social risk adjustment is data. Unlike clinical diagnoses, which are captured through standardized ICD-10 codes in medical claims, social risk factors are inconsistently documented across health systems, insurers, and geographic regions. Poverty is not an ICD-10 code. Housing instability, food insecurity, and transportation barriers are documented in some EHR systems but not others, and the definitions and screening tools vary widely.

The 2024 SDOH screening mandates represent an attempt to solve this data problem at the population level by requiring consistent, standardized screening across all Medicare- and Medicaid-participating hospitals. Over time, if these requirements are enforced and data is aggregated at the CMS level, it becomes possible to construct reliable patient-level social risk profiles that could support more refined payment adjustments. Several states — including Massachusetts, New York, and California — have moved faster than federal policy by requiring SDOH documentation in Medicaid managed care contracts.

The Vermont Blueprint for Health offers an instructive model. Vermont has integrated social risk data collection into its community health team model, including social-needs screening in participating practices. This data informs both population health interventions and, increasingly, payment arrangements that account for the social complexity of a practice's attributed population. Vermont's approach suggests that social risk adjustment is not just technically feasible but operationally achievable when built systematically into care delivery infrastructure from the ground up.

The emerging CMS framework distinguishes between "adjusting for" social risk (lowering benchmarks for disadvantaged populations) and "rewarding action on" social risk (paying for SDOH screening, community health integration, and demonstrated disparity reduction). Both approaches are moving forward simultaneously in different programs.

points: Social risk adjustment modifies quality and cost benchmarks to account for patients' social and economic circumstances — income, housing, food security — that drive outcomes beyond providers' clinical control.

The NQF's 2014 expert panel endorsed social risk adjustment under defined circumstances, and a 2017 multi-stakeholder trial confirmed it is feasible and that social factors are significant predictors of outcomes.

The core policy debate pits fairness concerns (safety-net providers are unfairly penalized) against accountability concerns (adjustment could mask genuine care quality disparities for low-income patients).

Congress partially adopted social risk adjustment for the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program in the 21st Century Cures Act (2016) by creating socioeconomic peer groups rather than comparing all hospitals to a single national benchmark.
CMS's 2024 SDOH screening mandate requires hospitals to screen patients for five social domains, building the data infrastructure needed for more systematic social risk adjustment in the future.

The CMS Health Equity Index, effective for 2027 Star Ratings, rewards Medicare Advantage plans for achieving equitable outcomes across social risk subgroups — an "accountability for equity" approach rather than benchmark adjustment.
The absence of standardized, reliable social risk data remains the primary technical barrier to comprehensive social risk adjustment in federal value-based payment programs.

This is a form of social risk adjustment that acknowledges structural differences in operating environments without fully eliminating accountability for readmission performance.

title: Social Risk in Risk Adjustment: Should We Adjust for Poverty?

children.text: The Low-Income Subsidy and Who It Represents

Within Medicare Advantage, no group of beneficiaries is more politically and programmatically complex than those who receive the Low-Income Subsidy (LIS) — also called Extra Help. The LIS program subsidizes Part D prescription drug costs for Medicare beneficiaries with limited income and resources, reducing or eliminating premiums, deductibles, and copayments for eligible enrollees. In 2024, about 13.7 million Medicare beneficiaries received the low-income subsidy — roughly a quarter of the 53 million Part D enrollees.

LIS beneficiaries are disproportionately represented in certain Medicare Advantage plans — particularly dual-eligible special needs plans (D-SNPs) that specialize in serving people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid. These beneficiaries carry significant social complexity: they are more likely to have multiple chronic conditions, unstable housing, food insecurity, limited health literacy, and barriers to transportation. They are also more likely to miss appointments, have lower medication adherence rates, and score lower on patient experience surveys — through no fault of the plans that serve them.

The Star Ratings system was designed when Medicare Advantage enrollment was dominated by relatively affluent, healthy seniors. As D-SNPs and LIS-serving plans have grown — driven by CMS policy and market dynamics — the system has had to grapple with a fundamental design tension: should plans serving the most complex, socially disadvantaged populations be held to identical performance standards as plans serving predominantly healthy, high-income beneficiaries?

Low-Income Subsidy (LIS) beneficiaries — also called Extra Help recipients — are Medicare Part D enrollees with limited income and resources who receive federal subsidies for prescription drug costs. Plans serving high LIS concentrations consistently face structural performance disadvantages in the Star Ratings system that are only partially offset by existing adjustments.
How the Star Ratings System Disadvantages LIS-Heavy Plans

The Star Ratings system measures performance on approximately 42 metrics, and LIS status correlates negatively with performance on a wide range of them. Medication adherence measures — which are triple-weighted in the Part D domain — show consistent LIS gaps. Research across multiple years of CMS data shows that LIS beneficiaries are significantly less likely to adhere to statins, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and oral diabetic medications, even when controlling for demographics and clinical diagnoses. The reasons are structural: cost-sharing (even if subsidized), transportation barriers, social instability, and limited pharmacy access in low-income neighborhoods.

CAHPS patient experience scores — weighted four times as heavily as process measures in the 2023–2025 Star Ratings, and twice as heavily from 2026 — also show systematic LIS disadvantages. LIS beneficiaries report lower satisfaction with their health plan and care experience across multiple CAHPS domains, including communication with providers, coordination of care, and plan responsiveness. Research has found that these lower CAHPS scores reflect real experience differences driven by factors including neighborhood poverty, language barriers, and concentration of LIS beneficiaries in plans with less administrative capacity — but they are partially attributable to social circumstances rather than plan performance.

The cumulative effect is that plans serving high concentrations of LIS beneficiaries face a structural performance headwind on multiple high-weight measures simultaneously. A plan serving 60 percent LIS beneficiaries competing against a plan serving 15 percent LIS beneficiaries for the same star rating faces a mathematically different challenge. This creates an equity paradox: the plans most committed to serving America's most vulnerable Medicare beneficiaries are the plans most financially penalized by the quality measurement system.

body.content:
Dual Eligible Special Needs Plans (D-SNPs) enroll beneficiaries who are simultaneously eligible for Medicare and Medicaid — the highest-complexity, most socially disadvantaged subset of Medicare beneficiaries. D-SNPs typically report lower star ratings than non-SNP Medicare Advantage plans, even when delivering care that health equity advocates consider high quality.
D-SNPs disproportionately serve beneficiaries with mental illness, substance use disorders, housing instability, and multiple chronic conditions — all characteristics associated with lower measured performance on star rating metrics. Despite serving arguably the most important population in Medicare, D-SNPs are persistently disadvantaged in the quality bonus payment system.
body.title: D-SNPs and the LIS Performance Gap

children.text: The Categorical Adjustment Index: A Partial Solution

CMS has been aware of the LIS performance gap for years and has responded with the Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI). The CAI adds points to a contract's overall star rating to adjust for the mean within-contract performance disparity associated with its percentage of enrollees receiving the Part D low-income subsidy or dual eligibility and those who are disabled. The adjustment is applied at the contract level, not the measure level, and it primarily benefits contracts with high LIS/dual-eligible enrollment.

The CAI works by estimating, across all contracts, the average within-contract gap between LIS/dual-eligible or disabled beneficiaries and other beneficiaries on selected measures. Each contract is then placed in an adjustment category by its share of LIS/dual-eligible and disabled enrollees, and a factor is added to (or subtracted from) its rating; contracts with larger shares receive larger positive adjustments. The goal is to ensure that such contracts' performance is not understated solely because of the composition of their enrolled population.

The CAI has limitations, however. Critics argue that it is insufficiently generous to fully offset the performance disadvantage facing heavily LIS-concentrated plans, and that the within-contract comparison methodology misses much of the structural disadvantage these plans face. Plans serving 80 percent LIS beneficiaries cannot simply be compared to themselves — they need comparison against the very different standard that applies to plans serving mostly healthy, wealthy seniors. The CAI represents an incremental accommodation rather than a fundamental redesign of the measurement framework.

body.title: Star Ratings Equity Mechanisms: Existing vs. Proposed

children.text: The Health Equity Index: A Framework Withdrawn

CMS introduced a new mechanism — the Health Equity Index (HEI) — as part of a broader effort to align Medicare Advantage incentives with health equity goals. Unlike the CAI, which adjusts for the penalty associated with having many LIS beneficiaries, the HEI is designed to reward plans that actively improve outcomes specifically for their most disadvantaged enrollees. CMS finalized the HEI in April 2023 to take effect for 2027 Star Ratings, using 2024 and 2025 performance data. In its CY2027 final rule (April 2026), CMS removed the HEI reward — by then renamed Excellent Health Outcomes for All — before it ever took effect, and kept the historical reward factor instead.

As designed, the HEI would have replaced the existing reward factor in the star ratings program. Plans would have earned HEI points based on their performance on specific quality measures among their Social Risk Factor (SRF) population — defined as enrollees receiving Extra Help/LIS, dual-eligible beneficiaries, and disability-status enrollees. Contracts meeting minimum SRF enrollment thresholds could have earned up to 0.4 points added to their unrounded star rating.

The HEI would have marked a philosophical shift from the CAI. Rather than simply adjusting for the negative performance effect of having many LIS beneficiaries, the HEI was designed to create a positive incentive for achieving high quality specifically among LIS and dual-eligible beneficiaries. A plan that served many LIS enrollees but did not improve their outcomes would have received no HEI reward. A plan that actively closed care gaps, improved medication adherence, and achieved high CAHPS scores among its LIS population would have earned a meaningful star rating bonus. It would have shifted the frame from "compensation for disadvantage" to "reward for demonstrated equity."

body.title: The Evolution of Equity Adjustments in Star Ratings

children.text: What These Changes Mean for Policy and Practice

The CAI represents genuine but partial progress toward a more equitable Medicare Advantage quality measurement system, and with the HEI withdrawn it remains the main equity mechanism — substantial structural problems remain. The core measurement framework still compares all plans on the same absolute performance thresholds using annually-shifted cut points that do not distinguish between plans serving 10 percent LIS beneficiaries and plans serving 80 percent LIS beneficiaries. Until CMS adopts either separate rating tracks for D-SNPs or individual measure-level social risk adjustment, the most vulnerable beneficiaries will continue to be served by plans that are disproportionately penalized in the quality bonus payment system.

Even without the HEI, the strategic lesson for plans holds. Plans need to identify their SRF population, track measure performance specifically within that subgroup, and build targeted interventions to close equity gaps — not just overall performance gaps. This requires more granular data infrastructure than most plans have historically maintained, and it requires care management programs that are designed specifically for the social complexity of LIS and dual-eligible beneficiaries rather than programs designed for the general MA population and then applied to SRF members by default.

The broader policy implication is that the link between health equity and Medicare Advantage financial performance remains politically contingent. The HEI would have stopped rewarding a plan that achieves high average star ratings by serving predominantly healthy, wealthy seniors while its LIS minority underperforms on the same terms as a plan with equitable outcomes across its full enrolled population. With the HEI withdrawn before its first ratings, whether a dedicated equity reward could have offset the structural disadvantages of the most LIS-concentrated plans remains untested.

CMS removed the Health Equity Index in its CY2027 final rule (April 2026), before its first ratings, and kept the historical reward factor. Plans still benefit from care management programs designed for their Social Risk Factor population — LIS recipients, dual-eligible beneficiaries, and disabled enrollees — because gaps among those members still pull down heavily weighted adherence and patient-experience measures.

points: Low-Income Subsidy (LIS) beneficiaries — about 13.7 million enrollees in 2024 — consistently score lower on Medicare Advantage star rating measures due to social and economic barriers that are structurally distinct from clinical care quality.

Plans serving high concentrations of LIS and dual-eligible beneficiaries face systematic performance disadvantages on the most heavily weighted star rating measures, including medication adherence (triple-weighted) and CAHPS patient experience surveys (weighted 4x in 2023–2025, 2x from 2026).

The Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI) partially offsets this disadvantage by adjusting final star ratings according to each contract's share of LIS/dual-eligible and disabled enrollees — but critics argue it is insufficient.

The Health Equity Index (HEI), finalized in 2023 for 2027 Star Ratings, would have replaced the old reward factor with a reward for high performance among each plan's Social Risk Factor population — but CMS removed it in its CY2027 final rule (April 2026) and kept the historical reward factor.

The HEI would have marked a philosophical shift from compensating for having disadvantaged enrollees to rewarding actively improving outcomes for them — changing the incentive from enrollment composition to care delivery equity.
As designed, contracts meeting minimum SRF enrollment thresholds could have earned up to 0.4 additional star rating points from the HEI for high SRF-specific performance.

Comprehensive reform of the star ratings system for equity — including separate D-SNP rating tracks or individual measure-level social risk adjustment — remains a pending policy challenge, and the HEI's withdrawal leaves the CAI as the only equity-specific adjustment.

body.explanation: The CAI is a defensive adjustment that partially compensates plans for the performance penalty associated with enrolling many LIS/dual-eligible beneficiaries — it adjusts ratings according to the contract's share of LIS/dual-eligible and disabled enrollees. The HEI, as designed, was an offensive reward that would have required plans to demonstrate high performance specifically among their SRF population to earn bonus points (CMS withdrew it in April 2026 before it took effect). One adjusts for disadvantage; the other would have rewarded demonstrated equity in care delivery.

It answers questions about healthcare policy, payment, technology, clinical care and operations, and it shows you the sources it drew on for each answer. Used well, it is the fastest way to get from a question to the right chapter, tool or document. Used carelessly, it is a confident voice you have no reason to trust.

This lesson covers what the Analyst is and how it finds its answers, how to set it up for your role, how to ask questions that produce useful answers, how to read and check what comes back, and where its limits are. The Analyst is available on Subscriber plans and above; the plans are listed at /pricing.

The difference between those two outcomes is mostly in how you ask and how you read. Neither takes long to learn, and both are the same skills you would use with a human research assistant: give a clear brief, and check the work before you rely on it.
How the Analyst Finds Its Answers

The Analyst does not answer from memory alone. When you send a question, it first rewrites it into a standalone search query, using your earlier messages for context, so that a follow-up such as "what about Medicaid?" is searched as a complete question. It then searches the platform's document library using both keyword and meaning-based matching, re-ranks the best matches, and writes its answer from the passages it found.

After the answer, it lists those passages as Sources. This is the most important design choice for you as a reader: every answer comes with the evidence it was built from, so you can check it. An answer whose sources do not support it is a signal to rephrase, narrow the question, or go to the document yourself.

The document library is broad. It holds federal and state policy documents, research reports, reference works, and the platform's own published analysis, tagged by pillar so the Analyst can tell you which part of the framework each source belongs to. It is not the open internet, and it is not updated the moment a rule changes, which is one more reason to check the date of any source an answer relies on.

Retrieval-based means grounded, not infallible. The Analyst answers from the passages it retrieves. If the right document is not in its library, or the question is phrased so the search misses it, the answer will be weaker, and the Sources list is how you will notice.

children.text: Set It Up for Your Role

The first time you open /chat you can pick a topic card or type your own question. If you tell the platform your role, at /welcome, the opening screen changes to four starting points chosen for that role, and your role is passed to the Analyst with each question so it can pitch the answer at the right level. The roles offered are Hospital / Health System Executive, Policy Analyst / Government Official, Clinician (MD, NP, PA), Health Economist / Actuary, Health Tech Professional, Medicaid / Compliance Officer, Student / Researcher, and Investor / Consultant.

You can change your role at any time with Change my role on the chat screen. If your work spans two roles, pick the one whose questions you ask most often; the role shapes the starting suggestions and the framing of answers, not what the Analyst is allowed to tell you.

The role does not lock you out of anything. A clinician can ask about actuarial methods and an investor about clinical quality measures; the Analyst answers both. What the role changes is the default level and framing, for example whether an answer about a payment model leads with its effect on hospital margins or on patient care.

children.text: Ask Questions That Produce Useful Answers

The Analyst's search works best on specific questions. Name the state, the program, the year and the decision you are facing. "How do global budgets work?" returns a textbook answer. "What would a hospital global budget under Vermont's Act 68 mean for a critical access hospital's commercial revenue, and which chapter of the book covers it?" returns an answer anchored in the right documents, with a pointer back into the book.

Use follow-ups rather than starting again. Because each question is rewritten with the conversation in mind, you can narrow step by step: ask for the overview, then the evidence, then the counterargument, then the tool that tests it. Ask it to compare two named options rather than to recommend one, and ask which source supports each part of its answer when the Sources list is long.

Ask the Analyst to point you onward. It knows the platform's structure, so questions such as which Research Lab tool models this, or which Academy course covers it, usually return a specific link. Its answers can also include a Try it in the HTR Lab link that opens the relevant tool directly. This is often the most valuable thing it does: not answering the question itself, but routing you to the place where you can work it out properly.

children.text: Read the Answer Like an Analyst

Treat every answer as a draft from a well-read colleague. Check that the claims you intend to rely on appear in the listed Sources, that the sources are current enough for the decision (a 2023 rule may have been replaced), and that numbers carry their year and their scope, national or state, Medicare or commercial. Where an answer points to a chapter, open it in the web reader; where it points to a tool, run it.

When an answer is useful, save the conversation with the Save button (Download transcript). The text file keeps the question, the answer and the attribution together, which is what you need when you bring the finding to a meeting. When an answer is weak, the fix is usually in the question: narrow it, name the source type you want, or ask what the Analyst does not know.

Be especially careful with three kinds of claim: numbers, dates and legal status. A figure can be right for one year and wrong for the next; a rule can be proposed, finalized, delayed or vacated; a program can be announced and then withdrawn. The Sources list tells you which document a claim came from, and the document tells you its date.

body.message: The Analyst is a research assistant. Its answers are not legal, financial, actuarial or clinical advice, and they can be wrong or out of date. Verify anything you will act on against the cited source and, where the stakes warrant it, with a qualified professional.
body.title: Not professional advice

children.text: The habit that matters most: before you repeat a number from the Analyst, find it in a listed source. If you cannot, do not repeat it.
Where the Analyst Fits in Your Routine

The Analyst is the Ask step in the read, run, ask, learn routine from the previous lessons. Its best uses are explaining a Research Lab result you did not expect, finding which chapter or Academy lesson covers a topic, comparing named policies or programs, and drafting a summary of evidence you will then check. Its weakest use is replacing the book's argument or the tool's calculation: it can explain both, but it should not stand in for either.

A good test of a session is whether it ended somewhere concrete: a chapter section you will read, a tool you will run with your own inputs, or a source you will cite. If a conversation ends with only the Analyst's own words, ask one more question: which document should I read to confirm this?

Used this way, the Analyst makes the rest of the platform faster rather than replacing it. Most readers find that their best sessions are short: a few precise questions that end with a chapter section to read and a tool to run, rather than a long conversation that ends with a long answer.

title: Getting Good Answers From the AI Analyst

children.text: The book's central claim is that the five pillars must be built in order, Policy, Technology, Economics, Clinical, Operations, because each one depends on the ones before it. A claim like that is easy to agree with and hard to feel. The Research Lab exists so you can feel it: you set the inputs, and the platform shows you what the dependency logic does to them.

In this lesson you will run the HTR Simulator on the three scenarios it ships with, learn to read its output, see the same logic applied to money in the Investment Tracker and to friction in the Friction Index, and then run a version of your own. Allow thirty minutes and keep /htr-simulator open as you read.

You need no data and no account to follow along. The simulator runs entirely in your browser on the scores you enter, and nothing you enter is saved. That makes it a safe place to try extreme settings and see what breaks.
What the Research Lab Is

The Research Lab is the platform's working environment: 35 interactive tools, grouped into benches that follow the book's structure. The benches are Policy & Quality, Payment Models, Technology & AI, Interoperability, VBC, Clinical & Quality, Population & Equity, and Knowledge & Workspace, each at its own address under /research-lab. The hub at /research-lab lists every tool with a one-line description.

Alongside the benches sit three tools that apply the book's framework directly and are the best place to start: the HTR Simulator (/htr-simulator), the Transformation Friction Index (/transformation-friction-index) and the Investment Tracker (/investment-tracker). All three read from the same dependency engine, so they never disagree about which pillar is holding another back.

Start with the framework tools even if your interest is specialist. They take minutes, they show you the dependency logic every other tool assumes, and they tell you which bench to visit next: if the simulator names Technology as your binding constraint, the Interoperability and Technology & AI benches are where the detailed work is.

The Research Lab tools are working environments for modeling and scenario planning, not reference pages. The book's Appendix F describes them that way, and the useful habit follows from it: change an input and watch what moves.
The HTR Simulator: Score Five Pillars, Watch the Sequence

Open /htr-simulator. You set a readiness score from 0 to 100 for each of the five pillars. The simulator then runs those scores through the book's dependency graph. Each pillar can only deliver what its upstream gates allow: if the pillar it depends on is weak, part of the capability you scored is paid for but not delivered. The simulator shows each pillar's score as a ghost bar with the delivered portion drawn solid on top, and states the points lost.

A gate's status depends on the delivered strength of the pillar upstream of it. At 70 or above the gate is open; between 40 and 69 it is partial; below 40 it is closed. Because each pillar reads its upstream pillars' delivered values rather than their nominal ones, damage cascades: weak Policy caps Technology, and the capped Technology, not the score you entered, is what Economics is then gated on.

The three scenarios are worth loading in order. The first reproduces the profile the book opens with, OneCare Vermont in 2013. The second keeps OneCare's ambition and changes only the order in which it was built. The third is the book's reading of Vermont in the fall of 2026, sourced to Acts 167, 51 and 68 and to the developments of July 2026, when the AHEAD agreement was withdrawn and the Medicaid hospital global budget was halted.

children.text: In the OneCare scenario, Economics is scored at 85 but delivers about 26.5. The money was real; the data infrastructure it depended on was not. That gap between what was paid for and what was delivered is the book's argument in one number.
Reading the Output

The simulator reports two composites. On paper is the average of the five scores you entered, what the investment looks like in a budget document. Delivered is the average of what each pillar can actually deliver behind its gates. The difference is the readiness lost to building out of order. In the OneCare scenario nearly half the paper value disappears; in the reordered scenario, where only Policy and Technology were raised, the loss falls from 22.7 points to 8.7.

Below the composites the simulator names the binding constraint: the pillar whose improvement would lift delivered readiness more than raising any other. In all three built-in scenarios it is Technology. For Vermont in Fall 2026, that matches the book's own reading in Chapter 1, §1.14: the Policy gate is open on state authority, but Technology is only partly built and is still the bottleneck, with Economics staged behind it. Finally, the simulator asks the Equity Imperative's question of each pillar and reports whether the design passes on all five.

Each pillar's row also tells you which upstream gate is holding it back and by how much. In the Vermont scenario, Clinical is scored at 65 but delivers about 28, because the Economics pillar it depends on is itself held back by Technology. The row-by-row view is where you see the cascade: one weak pillar early in the sequence shows up as lost capability in every pillar after it.

body.content:
The book's Chapter 1 opens with OneCare Vermont, the all-payer ACO that launched with high economic ambition on a voluntary mandate and without integrated real-time data. Load the OneCare Vermont (2013) preset and the simulator reproduces that profile: Economics at 85, Policy at 25, Technology at 20, delivered readiness 24.3.
Now load The same ambition, in order. The Economics, Clinical and Operations inputs are identical; only Policy (90) and Technology (80) move. Delivered readiness rises to 63.3. Nothing about the payment model changed. The upstream gates opened, and the same spending finally delivered.
body.title: OneCare, reordered

children.text: The Same Logic, Applied to Money and to Friction

The Investment Tracker (/investment-tracker) applies the dependency engine to capital. Its Sequencing check panel totals the disclosed value of the deals on the page for each pillar and checks each total against Vermont's Fall 2026 gate status, labelling a pillar Ahead of sequence when money is flowing into it behind a gate that is not yet open. A second panel does the same for your own initiatives: enter each one's pillar and committed capital, adjust the pillar scores if your situation differs from Vermont's, and see which initiatives are funded ahead of their upstream gate. Nothing you enter there is stored; it is a worksheet.

The Transformation Friction Index (/transformation-friction-index) asks a related question from the other side: where is the friction in a transformation, and what is binding? It scores the inputs it uses, shows whether friction is rising, and reports equity measures separately rather than averaging them into the index, so a worsening gap cannot be hidden by an improving average.

Using the three tools together gives you three views of the same problem. The simulator shows where readiness is lost. The Investment Tracker shows whether money is flowing into the pillars that can use it. The Friction Index shows where the effort is meeting resistance. When all three point at the same pillar, you have found the place to act.

body.message: The simulator and its companions apply the book's dependency logic to the scores you give them. They do not predict a state's budget or a hospital's margin. The value is in the comparison: the same inputs in a different order, or one pillar raised while the others hold still.
body.title: These are reasoning tools, not forecasts

children.text: Your Turn: A Fifteen-Minute Session

Now run the simulator on a system you know: your state, your hospital, or a program you have studied. You do not need precise numbers. A rough score for each pillar is enough, because the lesson is in what the dependency logic does to your scores, not in the scores themselves.

When you are done, write down two things in your own notes: the binding constraint the simulator named, and the single change that recovered the most delivered readiness. Those are the two facts a board, a legislature or a funder most needs to hear, and you now have a way to produce them in minutes.

If you are working with a team, run the session together and score the pillars independently first. Disagreements about the scores are often more revealing than the result: a team that cannot agree whether its data infrastructure is a 40 or a 70 has found the conversation it most needs to have.
