title: Building the PMO: Portfolio Governance for a Multi-Year Transformation

children.text: A Corporate Model With a Healthcare Track Record

John Kotter published his eight-step change model in "Leading Change" (Harvard Business School Press, 1996) after studying more than 100 corporate transformation efforts and finding a consistent pattern in why most of them fell short. The steps are: create urgency, form a guiding coalition, develop a vision, communicate the vision, remove obstacles, create short-term wins, sustain acceleration, and institute the change in culture and systems.

Nearly thirty years after publication, the model has moved well beyond its corporate origins and now has a real healthcare research literature behind it — not case studies written by consultants, but independently designed and published quality-improvement and health-services research. This lesson uses two of those published applications directly, rather than treating the framework as a piece of management theory imported without evidence.

Kotter's Eight Steps: (1) create urgency, (2) form a guiding coalition, (3) develop a vision, (4) communicate the vision, (5) remove obstacles, (6) create short-term wins, (7) sustain acceleration, (8) institute the change in culture and systems.
Steps 1–4: What Changes Under a Mandatory Deadline

Mandatory reform changes what several of the early steps mean in practice. Step 1, create urgency, is not a persuasion exercise when a legislature has already set a statutory deadline — the urgency exists whether or not leadership manufactures it. The analytical task shifts from creating urgency to presenting already-real urgency in terms specific and credible enough to produce organizational action rather than paralysis or denial. A public, well-documented financial presentation showing exactly how fragile a hospital system's finances are tends to do this far better than a general appeal to the importance of change.

Step 2, form a guiding coalition, is where the most consequential healthcare-specific risk concentrates. A coalition built only from administrative and financial leadership will produce a transformation plan that clinical staff can quietly decline to implement, regardless of how legally binding the underlying mandate is — because clinical decision-making authority in a hospital sits with medical staff governance, not the administrative org chart. Step 3, develop a vision, has to be specific enough to guide real decisions: an aspiration like "high-quality, affordable, equitable care for everyone" cannot be operationalized, while a specific target — a named percentage of patients in a coordinated-care model, a specific quality-measure benchmark, a specific network design — can be. Step 4, communicate the vision, has to reach several genuinely distinct audiences — clinical staff, administrators, the community, legislators, payers — each of whom needs the message calibrated to what they actually decide.

body.content: Researchers studying a federally qualified health center in rural Kentucky applied Kotter's eight-step framework to understand how the clinic implemented a proactive-office-encounter model aimed at closing preventive-care gaps and reducing health disparities, and published the analysis in a peer-reviewed case study. The study found clear evidence of Steps 1 through 7 in the clinic's actual implementation process — urgency was established, a coalition formed, a vision developed and communicated, obstacles removed, and short-term wins produced and sustained. Step 8, institutionalizing the change in the clinic's permanent culture and systems, was the one area the researchers identified as still needing work at the time of publication — a finding that previews this lesson's later point about which step healthcare change efforts most often fail to complete.
body.title: A Rural Kentucky Federally Qualified Health Center

children.text: Steps 5–8: Where Reform Efforts Actually Break

Step 5, remove obstacles, means clearing the barriers within the coalition's actual control — administrative complexity like prior-authorization requirements or certificate-of-need processes, organizational silos between departments that never share data, and contracting structures that still financially reward volume even after a value-based strategy has been announced on paper. Step 6, create short-term wins, requires results that are genuine, visible, and clearly attributable to the transformation effort — not cherry-picked metrics or coincidental improvements that would have happened anyway. Step 7, sustain acceleration, is specifically about surviving the multi-year span most healthcare reforms require, across multiple budget cycles, at least one election cycle, and the inevitable setbacks that occur along the way.

body.content: A prospective, longitudinal quality-improvement study applied Kotter's eight-step model to hand-hygiene compliance in an intensive care unit over 41 months and published the results. Compliance rose from 35.71% at baseline to 87.75% by the end of the study period — an increase of roughly 146%. The researchers attributed the result specifically to the model's systematic structure: it changed how ICU staff perceived hand hygiene as a practice and built an environment that both advocated for and sustained the improved behavior over more than three years, rather than producing a short-lived spike immediately after a training session.
body.title: A 41-Month ICU Hand-Hygiene Improvement Study

body.message: Announcing a metric as a transformation success when it was not actually caused by the transformation — or when it reflects a small, favorable subgroup rather than the whole population — tends to be noticed by exactly the staff whose buy-in the win was meant to build, and it damages trust in every subsequent claim of progress.
body.title: A "Short-Term Win" That Is Not Genuine Backfires

children.text: The Step Healthcare Skips

body.analogy: Institutionalizing a change is like converting a temporary detour into the new permanent road. The detour sign, the barriers, and the construction crew are all Steps 1 through 7 — visible, attention-getting, and clearly temporary. Institutionalization is quietly repaving the detour into the map itself, so that ten years later a new driver has no idea a different road ever existed. Most organizations tear down the detour signs the moment traffic starts flowing smoothly, long before the new route has actually become "just how people get there."
body.concept: Kotter's Step 8 — instituting change in organizational culture and systems

children.text: Step 8 is the step with no natural finish line to celebrate. Steps 1 through 7 each have a visible event attached — a launch, an early win, a period of acceleration. Institutionalization is instead the absence of an event: the new behavior simply continuing to be normal long after the program that created it has stopped being anyone's active, named project. Both the Kentucky FQHC study and the general pattern in healthcare change-management research point to this as the step most often left incomplete, which is why Lesson 6 of this course returns to it directly under the heading of benefits realization and sustainment.
Applying the Framework to Your Own Organization

The eight steps translate into a diagnostic an organization can run on itself at any point in a transformation, not only at the beginning. The questions below are ordered to match the framework and are deliberately specific enough to have a real yes-or-no answer, rather than an aspirational one.

steps.description: Is there a specific, credible, publicly presented case for why change is needed now — not a general appeal to importance?
steps.title: Urgency

steps.description: Does the guiding coalition include clinical leadership with real influence over medical staff, not only administrative and financial leaders?
steps.title: Coalition

steps.description: Is the vision specific enough that two people could independently evaluate whether a given decision is consistent with it?
steps.title: Vision

steps.description: Has the vision been communicated in language calibrated to each distinct audience — clinical staff, administrators, community, legislators, payers?
steps.title: Communication

steps.description: Have at least one administrative, one organizational, and one contracting obstacle been identified and actually removed?
steps.title: Obstacle removal

steps.description: Is there a genuine, attributable, visible result to point to yet — not a projection of a future result?
steps.title: Short-term wins

steps.description: Is there a plan for maintaining momentum across the next budget cycle and the next election cycle, not just the next quarter?
steps.title: Sustained acceleration

steps.description: If the transformation's named leader left tomorrow, would the new behavior continue without them?
steps.title: Institutionalization

body.title: An Eight-Step Diagnostic

points: Kotter's eight-step model — urgency, coalition, vision, communication, obstacle removal, short-term wins, sustained acceleration, institutionalization — was developed from more than 100 corporate cases and has since been applied in independently published healthcare studies (a case study and a quality-improvement study, not controlled trials).
Under a mandatory reform, Step 1 (urgency) already exists by statute; the task shifts to presenting it credibly rather than manufacturing it.
Step 2 (coalition) carries the highest healthcare-specific risk: a coalition without real clinical leadership will not produce implementation, regardless of legal mandate.
A published Kentucky FQHC case study found evidence of Steps 1–7 in a real preventive-care transformation, with Step 8 identified as the remaining gap.
A 41-month ICU study found Kotter's model raised hand-hygiene compliance from 35.71% to 87.75%, evidence specifically for the model's ability to sustain change, not just launch it.
Step 8, institutionalization, is the step most healthcare change efforts skip, because unlike the other seven it has no visible launch event to mark its completion.
The eight steps convert into a concrete diagnostic that can be run on any transformation at any point, not only at its start.

body.explanation: A durable, multi-year compliance gain — rather than a short-lived spike right after training — is exactly what Step 8 is meant to produce: the new behavior becoming the sustained default rather than a temporary intervention effect.

title: Kotter's Eight-Step Framework Applied to Mandatory Payment Reform

children.text: Why This Reform Type Is Different

A payment reform that adds a bonus on top of existing fee-for-service revenue asks an organization to do something extra for more money — a relatively easy sell. A global budget or a mandatory bundle asks an organization to accept that growing volume no longer grows revenue at all. That is a zero-sum reframing of every department's underlying incentive to do more, and it is why fixed-revenue reforms produce a resistance pattern that milder value-based arrangements typically do not: the threat to an individual department, service line, or physician group's existing model is not hypothetical or marginal. It is structural and immediate.

Resistance under this specific reform type tends to follow a small number of predictable patterns rather than a diffuse, unstructured objection to change in general. Naming those patterns in advance — rather than discovering them in the first year's performance data — is the difference between managing resistance proactively and reacting to it after it has already produced a measurable result.
Pattern One: Gaming the Boundary

CMS's Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement model made a 90-day bundled payment mandatory for lower-extremity joint replacement in a defined set of metropolitan statistical areas, launching in April 2016. It is one of the most directly documented examples in Medicare policy of how organizations respond, in practice, to a hard payment boundary imposed on them rather than one they chose.

body.content: Research on hospital behavior under CJR found that in the metropolitan areas where participation was mandatory, hospitals tended to treat healthier patients on average than in areas without the mandate, and were more likely to perform knee replacements in the inpatient setting — which the bundle covered — even when the same procedure performed outpatient, which the bundle did not cover, would have been the less costly option. Roughly 77% of CJR participant hospitals earned reconciliation payments in one or both of the model's first two performance years. When CMS made participation voluntary in half the areas and let outpatient knee replacements be billed outside the bundle in the model's third year, hospitals responded to the new boundary: the highest-spending hospitals dropped out where they could, and hospitals still in the mandatory bundle kept healthier knee patients in the covered inpatient setting rather than shifting them outpatient. A 2021 JAMA Internal Medicine study found savings fell from about $976 per episode in year two to $331 in year four — no longer statistically significant — with patient and site-of-care selection explaining three-quarters of the decline.
body.title: CMS's Mandatory CJR Bundle

children.text: The CJR pattern is not evidence of bad faith. It is evidence that organizations respond rationally to whatever boundary a payment reform draws. A fixed-revenue or fixed-bundle boundary will be optimized around unless the reform's design anticipates that response — which is why monitoring for boundary-shifting behavior has to be built into a transformation from its first year, not added after the data has already revealed a problem.
Pattern Two: Autonomy Anxiety

The second predictable pattern is resistance driven not by the financial mechanics of the reform but by the perceived loss of institutional independence — a hospital board or leadership team's anxiety about ceding operational control to an outside regulator, even when the regulator has no intention of dictating day-to-day decisions.

Maryland's own governance design, discussed in the previous lesson, treated this directly: "protecting hospital autonomy" was named explicitly, alongside close communication and calibrated budgets, as one of the specific themes leaders identified as necessary to manage the shift to global budgets. The lesson generalizes: a regulator or state agency that can credibly demonstrate it is not seeking to control operational decisions beyond the budget itself will face measurably less resistance than one whose intentions on that point remain ambiguous to the organizations being regulated.
Pattern Three: The Missing Coalition Seat

The third pattern connects directly back to Kotter's Step 2. Clinical staff who have no real seat in the guiding coalition — who experience the reform as something decided about them rather than with them — will disengage from implementation even when they have no legal ability to block the mandate itself. Disengagement is quieter than open opposition and correspondingly harder to detect: a clinician who simply does not change documentation habits, does not refer into a new care-management program, or does not flag early warning signs of a process breaking down produces exactly the kind of silent underperformance that shows up in outcome data a year later with no obvious single cause.

body.message: Transformation that clinical leaders oppose will fail regardless of administrative mandate, because clinical decision-making authority in a hospital sits with medical staff governance, not the administrative org chart that issued the mandate.
body.title: A Mandate Cannot Substitute for Coalition Membership

children.text: A Resistance-Management Playbook

The three patterns above point toward a common structural response: name the zero-sum trade-off explicitly rather than letting departments discover it on their own, build a data-informed reallocation process instead of an opaque top-down cut, create a visible pipeline of genuine early wins, monitor for boundary-shifting behavior from the reform's first year rather than its third, and formalize clinical leadership's coalition seat rather than treating clinical input as optional consultation.

Board delays or repeatedly requests more information before approving next steps

right.label: Underlying Driver

Autonomy anxiety — perceived loss of institutional independence, not necessarily disagreement with the reform's goals
No genuine coalition seat — the change was decided about them, not with them

title: Managing Organizational Resistance in a Fixed-Revenue-Envelope Transition

children.text: Start With the Register

The previous lesson made the case for a portfolio office. This one is the first thing that office should do in its first month: build the register and run the sequencing test against it. Neither step needs software, a consultant, or a budget line. Both need someone with the standing to ask every department what it is running, and the discipline to write the answers down in one place.

PMI's Standard for Portfolio Management treats portfolio definition as the foundational act: every component identified, classified, and assigned governance. Vermont has never published such a definition, so the book's Chapter 15 assembled one by reading Act 68, the AHEAD State Agreement, the Rural Health Transformation Program application, and the AHS transformation reports for every initiative carrying a named owner and a dated obligation. The exercise produced nineteen components across the five pillars. That number is not the point; the method is.

A register entry needs five fields, and each one does work. The pillar tells you which gate the component sits behind. The owner tells you who answers for it. The type separates compliance projects from strategic programs. The status says whether it is not started, in design, implementing, or done. And the calendar target records the statutory or contractual date — which, as the rest of this lesson shows, is the field you should trust least when deciding what to work on next.

Expect the register to move. Vermont withdrew from the AHEAD State Agreement in July 2026, which turned one component from a live program into a closeout obligation, and hospital transformation plans moved from submission to implementation after final plans were due in March 2026. A register that is not revisited at every governance review quietly becomes a record of last year's portfolio.

A portfolio register is not a status report. A status report lists what is happening. A register lists everything that has to happen, who owns it, and which pillar it depends on — so that the question "what should we work on next?" can be answered by dependency rather than by deadline.

steps.description: List every statute, grant, model agreement, and funded initiative that carries a named owner and a dated obligation. Read the source documents; do not rely on memory.
steps.title: Inventory the obligations

steps.description: Place each component in the pillar whose function it serves — Policy, Technology, Economics, Clinical, or Operations.
steps.title: Assign each a pillar

steps.description: One accountable lead per component. Components with no owner are a finding in themselves.
steps.title: Name an owner

steps.description: Not started, design, implementing, or done. "Design" and "implementing" are different statuses, and the difference decides the test.
steps.title: Record status honestly

steps.description: Keep the deadline, but treat it as context — it never decides whether a component should be running.
steps.title: Note the calendar target last

body.title: Building the register in one pass

children.text: The Four Steps, Turned Into Verdicts

The book's sequencing test asks four questions of every component, in order. Which pillar does it belong to? Is that pillar's upstream gate open? If the gate is closed, what is gating it, and is that resourced? If the gate is open, is this component actually running? The definition of an open gate comes from Chapter 1: open means the enabling work is finished, not that a milestone was declared.

Run against a register, those four questions produce a small set of verdicts, and the vocabulary matters because it changes the conversation. A component behind a closed gate that has not started is not "behind schedule" — it is correctly waiting. A component with nothing upstream holding it that has not started is late, even if its deadline is two years away. A component implementing while its gate is closed is spending money on output nobody can use yet.

Two qualifications come from Chapter 1 and keep the test from becoming a blunt instrument. First, design never waits for a gate: specifying what a payment model must measure is precisely what tells the technology build what to deliver, so Economics-as-design runs in parallel with the Technology stage. Second, some components produce value on their own. The book says Blueprint PCMH expansion, CCBHC certification, and Collaborative Care deployment proceed in parallel with Technology work — correctly — because they deliver value whether or not the downstream gates have opened.

Notice what the test does not use: the deadline. Calendar targets stay in the register because statutes and grants impose them, and a portfolio office has to report against them. But a verdict that changed with the deadline would just be the old status report under a new name. The test is useful precisely because two components with the same due date can receive opposite verdicts — one correctly waiting, one already late.
Only implementation waits for a gate. Design work, and care-model work that produces value on its own, should be running now.

code.Meaning: Not behind schedule; pressure belongs upstream
Budget spent on output nobody can use yet
Late even if early by calendar

body.title: The seven verdicts the test produces

children.text: Worked Example: Vermont, Fall 2026

Load the book's nineteen components with their Fall 2026 statuses into the platform's Portfolio Sequencing Test and use the same gate profile the HTR Simulator uses for Vermont: the Policy gate open on the strength of Acts 167, 51, and 68, and Technology only partly delivered. The Economics gate is therefore not open. The AHS-GMCB analytics vendor, which the book records as in procurement with a January 2027 operational target, is not yet running — and AHS reported in March 2026 that an analytics contract for regional planning was still under negotiation.

The test then sorts the portfolio. Thirteen components are on track. Two Economics components — RBP implementation and global-budget design and implementation — are in design, which is exactly what Chapter 1 says they should be doing while the Technology gate is closed. One, the Vermont CIN build-out, sits behind an open gate but is still only in design. Two are late by dependency order despite distant deadlines: the statewide AI-governance framework, which nothing upstream is holding, and — pointedly — the AHS PMO itself.

One component is flagged as running ahead of its gate: RHT Program deployment, which the book places in the Economics pillar and describes as active. That is not a verdict that the money is wasted. It is a prompt to ask which parts of the deployment depend on analytics that do not yet exist, and to hold those parts until they do. Finally, step three of the test names where schedule pressure belongs: the four unfinished Technology components, each of which holds the same three gated Economics components behind it.

children.text: What Happens When Nobody Owns the Sequence

The sequencing test assumes someone has the authority to act on its answers — to hold a component back, or to move resources to the one that gates everything else. The clearest public record of what happens without that authority comes from two health-insurance marketplace launches in 2013, each investigated afterward in detail.

The federal Office of Inspector General's case study of HealthCare.gov found that the most critical misstep was the absence of clear leadership, which delayed decisions, and that there was no entity serving formally as systems integrator to coordinate the separately contracted pieces of the build. It also documented poor coordination between policy and technical work and resistance to hearing bad news. Oregon, building its own exchange, made a structurally similar choice and did not recover.

body.content:
The HHS Office of Inspector General's February 2016 case study (OEI-06-14-00350) found that the "absence of clear leadership" delayed decisionmaking, and that no entity was formally serving as systems integrator to coordinate key functions built by different contractors.
After the failed October 2013 launch, CMS hired QSSI as technical systems integrator to coordinate technical tasks and resources, and the OIG reports that CMS recovered the website for high consumer use within two months — once one party owned the integration.
body.title: HealthCare.gov (federal marketplace, 2013)

body.content:
An independent review by First Data, commissioned by Governor John Kitzhaber and based on 67 interviews and more than 3,200 documents, found that Oracle had been hired on a time-and-materials basis, which contributed to a lack of scope control, delayed requirements, and unrealistic delivery expectations. "A system integrator with a stronger financial incentive for ensuring performance most likely would have pushed harder," the review said.
On April 25, 2014, Cover Oregon's board voted to abandon its own enrollment site and move to HealthCare.gov.
body.title: Cover Oregon (state marketplace, 2013–2014)

children.text: The lesson for a state portfolio is not that contractors are the problem. Vermont's own March 2026 Act 68 report lists contracted transformation support, a new hospital technical-assistance vendor, and an analytics contract under negotiation — sensible ways to add capacity. The question both marketplace reviews raise is different: when those contractors' deliverables depend on one another, who decides which one waits? A contractor delivers a defined scope. Only an owner with authority over the whole portfolio can hold one component back so that another can finish first.
Most critical was the absence of clear leadership, which caused delays in decisionmaking. — HHS Office of Inspector General, HealthCare.gov case study, 2016
Reading Risk Alongside Sequence

Chapter 15's risk register scores each risk as probability times impact. Two risks tie for the top score of 20: the analytics vendor not being operational by January 2027 (R-01), and portfolio-management infrastructure not being established before the 2027 deadlines (R-10). The sequencing test and the register point at the same place — the analytics gate — from two directions, which is a useful cross-check: if your pressure points and your highest risks disagree, one of the two is wrong.

The register also shows why a moderate risk score is not a licence to wait. Social-risk adjustment not being adopted before the FY2028 budgets (R-08) scores 12 — a medium probability times a high impact. Yet the sequencing test says this methodology has no upstream blocker and should already be running. Treating it as a FY2028 problem because that is when it is due is the scheduling error that leaves equity work perpetually late.

In practice, bring both artifacts to the same governance meeting. Start with the components that appear in both places — a pressure point in the sequencing test that also carries a top-scored risk. Those are the decisions the board should make first, and they are usually few. Then look for the opposite pattern: unblocked work with a middling risk score and a distant deadline. That is where equity and governance work tends to hide, because nothing on either list makes it feel urgent.

points: Sorts components by statutory or contractual date
Treats a waiting component as "behind schedule"
Leaves distant-deadline work (AI governance, social-risk adjustment) for later
Spreads pressure across every component with a near deadline

right.label: Dependency view
points: Sorts components by whether their upstream gate is open
Treats a waiting component as correctly waiting
Starts unblocked work now, whatever its deadline
Concentrates pressure on the few components holding closed gates

body.title: Two ways to read the same portfolio

children.text: Run It on Your Own Portfolio

The platform's Portfolio Sequencing Test takes either Vermont's register or yours. Start a blank register, enter your components with their pillar and status, and decide for each one whether its implementation genuinely depends on the upstream pillar — the "gated" flag. Then set how much of each pillar's enabling work is actually delivered. The tool uses the same dependency engine as the HTR Simulator and the Friction Index, so a gate opens at the same threshold everywhere on the platform.

Expect the first run to be uncomfortable. Most organizations find components with no owner, components running ahead of gates nobody had named, and at least one piece of unblocked work that has been parked because its deadline felt distant. The value is not the verdicts themselves but the conversation they force: who has the authority to act on them, and is that authority real?

A useful test of whether the review is working comes from the book's advice to legislators and board members. Ask one question: which component is currently the binding constraint on all the others, who owns it, and what would it take to accelerate it? An organization running a genuine portfolio answers in a sentence. An organization running a list answers with a status summary of everything — which is itself the finding.

body.analogy: A kitchen does not start plating the main course because the dinner reservation is at eight; it starts when the sauce it depends on is ready. A good expediter watches what each dish is waiting on, not the clock on the wall — and moves cooks to whatever is holding everything else up.

children.text: A Different Kind of Board Problem

A hospital governing board asked to approve a discretionary strategic initiative retains a real option: it can decline, delay, or scale it back. A board operating under mandatory payment reform — where an independent regulator has already set the rate methodology and a legislature has already set the deadline — is instead being asked to accept and implement a transformation it did not choose and cannot stop. That distinction changes what board management has to accomplish. The task is no longer persuasion toward a yes-or-no decision; it is education and engagement toward effective implementation of a decision that has already been made elsewhere.

Hospital community boards typically include members with genuine political relationships to local legislators, which means board management under mandatory reform is never purely an internal governance exercise — it is simultaneously a channel through which political and community sentiment about the reform reaches the legislature that mandated it. Three real transformation programs built three different governance designs to manage exactly this problem, and each offers a distinct, evidenced lesson.
Maryland: Naming the Sea Change Explicitly

Maryland's Health Services Cost Review Commission, an independent state agency, has held hospital rate-setting authority since a 1971 state statute, expanded to private payers in 1974 and to Medicare and Medicaid under a 1977 federal waiver. In 2014, working with CMS and the CMS Innovation Center, the state converted all acute-care hospitals to global budgets under the Maryland All-Payer Model — fixing each hospital's total annual revenue in advance rather than paying by volume of services delivered.

body.content: A 2022 qualitative study in JAMA Health Forum, based on interviews with 20 Maryland health care leaders, quotes one state regulator describing the global budget conversion as "a monumental change, a sea change, in the way that hospitals thought about raising revenue." The leaders interviewed identified a specific set of governance themes as necessary to manage that shift: setting achievable expectations rather than overpromising immediate results, protecting hospital autonomy rather than dictating operational decisions from the regulator, maintaining close and continuous communication between the commission and hospital leadership, using actionable data that hospitals could act on rather than only report, carefully calibrating each hospital's budget rather than applying a single formula uniformly, and building a shared commitment to the change across the state's hospital sector rather than treating compliance as adversarial. In 2019, Maryland and CMS extended the model into the Total Cost of Care Model, adding incentives for hospitals to help manage spending on services delivered by other, non-hospital providers — a sign the original governance approach had built enough durability to support expansion rather than retrenchment.
body.title: Maryland's Global Budget Conversion

children.text: Naming a change explicitly as a "sea change" rather than downplaying its magnitude — and then organizing governance specifically around not overpromising, protecting existing autonomy where possible, and communicating continuously — is itself a stakeholder-management strategy documented in Maryland's own case, not just a description of what the reform felt like from the outside.
Oregon: Building Community Governance Into the Structure

Oregon took a structurally different governance approach for its Medicaid Coordinated Care Organizations, launched under a 2012 state reform. Rather than a top-down regulator managing provider compliance, each CCO is governed as a required partnership among health care providers, community members, and other stakeholders in the health system who share in the financial risk of a single global budget covering physical, mental, and dental health care.

body.content: Each Oregon CCO is required to maintain a Community Advisory Committee, which produces a Community Health Assessment and a Community Health Improvement Plan for its region. Community stakeholders and Medicaid members themselves play a formal governance role that is substantially larger than in a traditional managed-care organization. The design deliberately trades some administrative simplicity for community legitimacy: a CCO's budget and priorities are shaped, in part, by the people who use the care it finances, not only by the providers and payers who deliver and fund it.
body.title: Oregon's Coordinated Care Organizations

children.text: Massachusetts: Co-Designing the Reform Before Launch

Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts took a third approach when it launched the Alternative Quality Contract in January 2009 — a global-budget-based commercial payment model combining a fixed per-patient payment, adjusted annually for health status and inflation, with substantial performance incentives tied to nationally accepted quality, effectiveness, and patient-experience measures.

body.content: Rather than designing the contract internally and then presenting it to providers as a finished product, BCBS Massachusetts built a team of physicians, finance experts, and measurement scientists and tested the contract concept directly with key hospital and physician leaders, local and national policy experts, employers, and other purchasers throughout the design process — before the contract was finalized. The framework explicitly linked payment reform, quality measurement, public engagement, legislative and regulatory strategy, organizational governance, and information technology as connected levers rather than treating the payment change in isolation. A Harvard Medical School study published in 2019 found the AQC slowed the growth rate of medical spending by up to 12% while improving patient care over eight years of operation, and the contract now covers more than 80% of the physicians and hospitals in the BCBS Massachusetts network.
body.title: The Massachusetts Alternative Quality Contract

children.text: A Stakeholder Management Framework for Mandatory Reform

The three cases point to a common structural lesson despite their different designs: each built a formal mechanism for a non-payer stakeholder group — hospital leadership in Maryland, community members in Oregon, physician and hospital leaders in Massachusetts — to shape the reform's design or governance, rather than only receiving it after the fact. The book's own account of Vermont's transformation coalition identifies exactly the gap this points to: Vermont's guiding coalition of AHS leadership, the state regulator, hospital CEOs, and the legislature's health reform oversight committee is missing systematic clinical leadership integration — the same gap Kotter's Step 2 identifies as fatal if left unaddressed.

body.message: This is not a hypothetical risk drawn from general change-management theory. The book's own analysis of Vermont's actual transformation coalition names clinical leadership engagement as its current, unresolved gap — precisely the coalition-composition risk Maryland, Oregon, and Massachusetts each built formal structures to avoid.
body.title: The Missing Coalition Seat Is a Named, Current Gap — Not a Hypothetical

children.text: The Step With No Finish Line

Kotter's eighth step — institute the change in culture and systems — is the step this course has now flagged twice as the one most transformation efforts skip, and it is worth being precise about why. Steps 1 through 7 each have a visible event attached: a public presentation that creates urgency, a coalition's first meeting, a launch, an early win, a period of visible acceleration. Institutionalization has no equivalent event to point to. It is the absence of an event — the new behavior simply continuing to be normal long after the program that created it has stopped being anyone's actively managed project.

That absence of a natural finish line is precisely why sustainment has to be planned and budgeted for deliberately, rather than assumed to happen automatically once a transformation has launched successfully. The Project Management Institute's Benefits Realization Management Framework (2016) gives this planning a formal structure.
PMI's Three-Part Discipline

Benefits realization management is the process of planning, tracking, realizing, and sustaining the strategic benefits a project, program, or portfolio is meant to produce. PMI's framework organizes it into three core elements: identify the benefits a program is meant to produce, execute the changes needed to produce them, and sustain those benefits after the program has formally concluded.

The third element — sustain — is the one most transformation plans never explicitly budget for. Most plans identify a target benefit clearly and execute a defined set of changes to reach it. Far fewer plans assign a named owner, a review cadence, and a monitoring mechanism to the period after the program has officially closed — which is exactly when a hard-won gain is most vulnerable to quietly reversing.

children.text: Case Study in Durability: Maryland's Five-Decade Run

Maryland's hospital rate-setting authority has operated continuously since a 1971 state statute — more than five decades, spanning multiple governors, legislatures, and federal administrations. The model has not been static across that period. It has been repeatedly revised: extended to private payers in 1974, to Medicare and Medicaid in 1977, converted to global budgets for all acute-care hospitals in 2014, and extended again into a Total Cost of Care model covering non-hospital spending in 2019. Each of those revisions was a course correction by the commission, CMS, and the hospitals — the model has never been a single design left to run unchanged.

body.content: The relevant lesson from Maryland is not that its original 1971 or 2014 design was perfect and therefore never needed to change. It is the opposite: the model survived and expanded specifically because it had a standing structure — the HSCRC as a permanent independent commission, with an ongoing relationship to CMS — that could keep making course corrections indefinitely, long after the original 1971 or 2014 launch events were no longer news. Durability came from a standing governance structure built to keep adjusting, not from getting the design right once and leaving it alone.
body.title: Maryland as the Institutionalization Benchmark

children.text: Case Study in Sustainment Infrastructure: CPC+'s Learning Collaboratives

CMS's Comprehensive Primary Care Plus model, a national advanced primary care medical home model that launched in 2017 across 14 regions and expanded to 18 by 2018, built its sustainment mechanism directly into the program's design rather than treating it as a follow-up activity after launch.

body.content: CPC+ included a standing national and regional learning system — in-person and web-based learning communities, national webinars, an annual national stakeholder meeting, cross-region collaboration, and individualized on-site coaching — organized around five core primary-care functions: access and continuity, care management, comprehensiveness and coordination, patient and caregiver engagement, and planned care and population health. The infrastructure did not end when a practice completed its initial transformation; it continued operating for the life of the model precisely so that gains made in year one did not depend on a single training event holding permanently.
body.title: CPC+'s Learning System

children.text: Case Study in Collapse: What Happens Without Sustainment Infrastructure

The NHS's National Programme for IT, examined in Lesson 3 for its governance-structure failure, offers a second, distinct lesson here about sustainment specifically. The UK's National Audit Office found not only that the programme itself failed, but that the lessons from its failure were not being captured or applied systematically — meaning the same structural risks remained live in the government's later digital transformation programmes. A program that has no mechanism for sustaining even its own institutional learning is unlikely to have a mechanism for sustaining the operational benefits it was originally built to produce.

children.text: Building a Sustainment Plan

A transformation's launch team should not be the same body responsible for its indefinite maintenance — the skills, incentives, and attention span required are different. A concrete sustainment plan names a benefit owner for each targeted gain, sets a review cadence that continues well past go-live, keeps the risk register open rather than closing the file at launch, and budgets ongoing resources for the kind of learning-collaborative-style support CPC+ built in, rather than treating training as a one-time event.

title: Sustaining the Change: Benefits Realization and Avoiding Reform Fatigue

children.text: The Execution Gap

Healthcare transformation programs rarely fail because the underlying analysis was wrong. The financial case for value-based payment, the clinical case for care coordination, and the equity case for closing measured disparities are each backed by decades of published evidence. Boards approve the strategy. Consultants deliver the report. Legislatures pass the statute. And then, in a large share of cases, very little actually changes in how the organization operates two years later.

What fails, far more often than the analysis, is the organizational change process: the sequencing, pacing, and management of the human and institutional change that structural reform actually requires. A hospital can have an airtight financial model for entering a global budget and still fail to execute it, because the model says nothing about how department heads will react when told that growing volume no longer grows revenue, or how a governing board will react to ceding rate-setting authority to an outside commission. This course is about that second problem — the one the analytical frameworks in a strategy deck do not solve.

Change management, project management, and portfolio management are related but distinct disciplines. Project management delivers a defined scope on schedule and budget. Program management coordinates related projects to produce benefits no single project could achieve alone. Portfolio management aligns the whole collection of programs and projects with organizational strategy. Change management is the layer underneath all three: the discipline of managing how people and institutions actually adopt the new state, regardless of how well the plan above them is built.

children.text: Two Failure Modes, Not One

It is useful to separate transformation failure into two distinct modes. An analytical failure means the underlying plan was wrong — the payment model does not actually align incentives, the clinical redesign does not actually improve outcomes, the technology does not actually do what the vendor promised. An execution failure means the plan was sound but the organization could not, or did not, actually carry it out: stakeholders were not brought along, governance never caught up with scope, or the change was announced but never institutionalized. Healthcare transformation research and practice consistently find the second failure mode is more common than the first.

The United Kingdom's National Programme for IT (NPfIT) is one of the most thoroughly studied examples of a pure execution failure in a health system context. Launched in the early 2000s to build a single national electronic health record and supporting IT infrastructure for the National Health Service, NPfIT was dismantled in 2011; in 2013 Parliament's Public Accounts Committee put its estimated cost at £9.8 billion and warned the final bill was likely to be higher. The core information-technology problem the programme set out to solve — clinicians across a national health system unable to share patient records — was a real and analytically sound problem to solve. What collapsed was execution.

body.content:
The UK's National Audit Office and Parliament's Public Accounts Committee both examined NPfIT's collapse in detail. Their findings center on governance, not technology: the programme's structure separated central decision-making authority from the local NHS organizations responsible for actually implementing the systems, creating a persistent gap between the people who designed the programme and the people who had to make it work in a hospital or clinic. Reviewers also found insufficient engagement with clinicians and other frontline stakeholders during design.
The National Audit Office's later assessment made a second finding that matters directly for this course: the lessons from NPfIT's failure were not being captured or applied systematically even in the UK government's subsequent digital transformation programmes — meaning the same governance gap was positioned to repeat itself elsewhere.
body.title: The NHS National Programme for IT (NPfIT)

children.text: What Makes Healthcare's Change Problem Specifically Harder

Every organization undergoing major change faces resistance, competing priorities, and limited bandwidth. Healthcare transformation adds structural features that a typical corporate change program does not have to manage. Clinical governance is legally and professionally separate from administrative governance — a hospital CEO cannot simply direct medical staff the way a corporate executive directs a business unit, because clinical decision-making authority sits with licensed professionals and medical staff bylaws, not the org chart. Patient safety obligations mean some changes cannot be piloted the way a retail company pilots a new store format; a clinical process change that fails silently can hurt someone before anyone notices the failure.

Authority is also unusually distributed. A single transformation initiative in a state like Vermont can simultaneously involve an independent state regulator, a federal agency, a state legislature, a hospital's own governing board — which typically includes community members with political relationships to local legislators — and, in many markets, organized labor. A corporate change leader answers to one board and one set of shareholders. A healthcare transformation leader is answering to several genuinely independent sources of authority at once, none of which can be overruled by the others.

points: Single governing board and shareholder base
Management has direct authority over most affected staff
Pilots can fail safely and be rolled back

right.label: Healthcare Transformation Under Mandatory Reform
points: Overlapping authority: regulator, legislature, board, medical staff
Clinical decision-making authority sits outside the org chart
A failed pilot can mean patient harm, not just a rollback
Statutory deadlines are set externally and cannot be renegotiated

body.title: Corporate Change vs. Healthcare Transformation

body.message: A statutory deadline changes the urgency calculation — the transformation is happening regardless — but it does not remove the need to build a coalition, communicate a vision, or manage resistance. Organizations that treat a legal mandate as a substitute for change leadership tend to produce exactly the compliance-only, minimally-adopted version of reform that shows up in the data years later as underperformance.
body.title: A Mandate Does Not Remove the Change-Management Problem

children.text: What This Course Covers

The five lessons that follow work through the change-leadership toolkit a healthcare transformation leader actually needs, in the order a real transformation program encounters them: first the framework for sequencing organizational change itself (Kotter's eight steps), then the governance infrastructure that keeps a multi-year, multi-component transformation from fragmenting into disconnected initiatives (the PMO and portfolio management), then the specific skill of managing governing boards and external stakeholders who did not choose the reform, then the specific and predictable resistance patterns that a fixed-revenue-envelope transition produces, and finally the discipline of making a transformation's gains durable instead of letting them erode once leadership attention moves elsewhere.

children.text: A statutory deadline is not negotiable, but the change-management work required to meet it well — rather than merely on paper — is exactly the same work described in this course, whether the reform is voluntary or mandatory.

points: Healthcare transformation programs more often fail from execution and change-management gaps than from flawed analysis.
Project, program, portfolio, and change management are related but distinct disciplines; change management is the layer that determines whether people and institutions actually adopt the new state.

PMI's research finds organizations with a strategy-aligned enterprise PMO see more projects meet their original goals, and organizations that treat project management as non-strategic see far higher outright failure rates.

The NHS's National Programme for IT is a canonical example of a pure execution failure: the underlying goal was sound, but centralized governance separated from local implementation authority caused the collapse.

Healthcare transformation is structurally harder to lead than typical corporate change because clinical governance sits outside the administrative org chart and authority is distributed across regulators, legislatures, boards, and medical staff.
A legal mandate changes the urgency calculation for a reform but does not remove the need for a guiding coalition, a communicated vision, or active resistance management.

This course builds the change-leadership toolkit in the order a real transformation encounters it: sequencing change, building governance, managing stakeholders, managing resistance, and sustaining the result.

title: Why Change Management Determines Transformation Success

children.text: The Number an ACO Lives or Dies By

The previous lesson showed that an ACO earns savings by keeping spending below a benchmark. This lesson is about the spending itself: total cost of care (TCOC), the single number that determines whether a value-based organization succeeds or fails financially. If population health is the method and the ACO is the contract, TCOC is the scoreboard.

Total cost of care is a holistic view of all healthcare spending for an entire population over a period — inpatient, outpatient, professional, pharmacy, and ancillary services, everything. It is typically expressed as a risk-adjusted per-member-per-month (PMPM) figure, so populations of different sizes and health profiles can be compared fairly. The HealthPartners TCOC framework is a widely used standard for measuring it.

The discipline of managing TCOC is different from managing a single disease or a single patient. It requires zooming out to the whole population's spending, finding where the money actually goes, and pulling the levers that reduce avoidable cost without harming care. This lesson covers where the cost concentrates and how to manage it down.

Total cost of care (TCOC) is all healthcare spending for a population over a period — inpatient, outpatient, professional, pharmacy, ancillary — usually expressed as a risk-adjusted per-member-per-month (PMPM) figure. It is the scoreboard for value-based success.
PMPM and Risk Adjustment

The standard unit of TCOC is per member per month (PMPM): total healthcare spending divided by the number of member-months in the population. PMPM normalizes cost to a comparable per-person, per-month figure, which is how value-based contracts, budgets, and benchmarks are expressed. A population's PMPM is the headline number leaders watch.

But raw PMPM is misleading without risk adjustment, because populations differ in how sick they are. A practice serving older, sicker patients will have a higher PMPM than one serving young, healthy patients — not because it is wasteful, but because its patients are genuinely more costly. Risk adjustment (the HCC/RAF methods from the risk-stratification lesson) corrects for this, so a risk-adjusted PMPM reflects efficiency rather than just patient mix.

This connects directly to the equity and risk-adjustment debates elsewhere in the curriculum: how you risk-adjust shapes whether comparisons are fair, and poorly done risk adjustment can either penalize those serving the sickest or mask real inefficiency. For TCOC management, the practical point is that you manage the risk-adjusted number — comparing your population's cost to what it "should" be given its risk, then attacking the gap.

body.title: How TCOC Is Measured

children.text: Where the Money Actually Goes

Managing TCOC starts with knowing where cost concentrates — and it concentrates dramatically, echoing the risk-stratification lesson. High-cost claimants (HiCCs) are a tiny fraction of the population but a huge share of spend: nationally, the top 5 percent of spenders account for roughly half of all health care spending, and the top 1 percent for about a fifth (AHRQ Medical Expenditure Panel Survey).

A second concentrated and fast-growing driver is specialty pharmacy. Specialty drugs are only about 2 percent of prescriptions but often drive 50 percent or more of total pharmacy spend. A small number of patients on high-cost specialty and infused medications can dominate a population's pharmacy budget, and this spend is growing rapidly — making pharmacy management a central TCOC concern, not an afterthought.

A third driver is avoidable acute utilization, especially emergency department visits. UnitedHealth Group estimated in 2019 that 18 million of the 27 million ED visits made each year by privately insured people are avoidable, costing about $32 billion — roughly $1,800 per visit — because treating the same problem in the ED costs far more than in urgent care, primary care, or telehealth (other researchers estimate a smaller avoidable share). Knowing this map — high-cost claimants, specialty pharmacy, avoidable acute care — tells you exactly where to aim TCOC management.

children.text: The Levers to Pull

With the cost map in hand, TCOC management deploys specific levers at each concentration. For high-cost claimants, the lever is intensive care management — the population health toolkit aimed at the highest tier of the pyramid, preventing the complications and acute events that drive their cost (often combined with case-by-case review of these expensive patients).

For specialty pharmacy, the levers are pharmacy-specific: prior authorization and step therapy to ensure appropriate use, biosimilar adoption (lower-cost versions of biologic drugs), rebate negotiation, and especially site-of-care steerage. Site-of-care steerage means directing where a patient receives an expensive infusion — a hospital outpatient setting can cost dramatically more than a physician's office or the patient's home for the identical drug. The savings depend on the drug and on the price gap between settings.

For avoidable acute utilization, the levers are the prevention and access strategies from across this course: strong primary care and same-day access so patients do not default to the ED, care management and chronic-disease programs to prevent the crises that lead to admissions, transitional care to prevent readmissions, and patient education on appropriate care settings. The throughline is that almost every TCOC lever is a population health activity from an earlier lesson, now aimed explicitly at the dollars.

body.content:
A patient needs a regular high-cost infused medication. Administered in a hospital outpatient department, it might cost several times more than the identical drug given in a physician's office or at home.
A TCOC program identifies these patients and works with the PBM/medical vendor to steer the infusions to the lower-cost site — saving the price difference between settings, with no change in the actual treatment the patient receives. Same drug, same dose, lower total cost of care.
body.title: Site-of-Care Steerage for an Infusion

children.text: Managing Cost Without Harming Care

The defining discipline of TCOC management is reducing cost without reducing necessary care — and the distinction is everything. The legitimate target is avoidable, low-value spending: the preventable admission, the duplicate test, the ED visit that should have been a primary care visit, the specialty drug given in a needlessly expensive setting. Cutting these improves value. Cutting necessary care to hit a number is both unethical and, in a value-based contract with a quality gate, financially self-defeating.

This is why TCOC is always managed alongside quality. An ACO that lowers its PMPM by skimping on care will fail its quality measures and forfeit savings (and harm patients). The right framing is efficiency: deliver the same or better outcomes at lower cost by eliminating waste, not by withholding value. Risk adjustment and quality gates are the guardrails that keep TCOC management honest.

TCOC ties the financial story of this course together. Population health's clinical activities — risk stratification, care management, chronic-disease programs, prevention — all ultimately express themselves in this one risk-adjusted PMPM number. Master where cost concentrates and which levers move it without harming care, and you have the financial discipline that makes value-based population health sustainable. The final module turns to ensuring all of this reaches everyone equitably, and to measuring whether it actually works.

body.message: The only legitimate way to reduce total cost of care is to eliminate avoidable, low-value spending — preventable admissions, duplicate tests, misplaced sites of care — never necessary care. In a value-based contract, skimping on care fails the quality gate and forfeits savings anyway. Risk adjustment and quality measures are the guardrails that keep TCOC management honest.
body.title: Lower Cost by Cutting Waste, Not Care

children.text: A portfolio exists to produce benefits, not deliverables. A completed analytics platform, a certified clinic or a new pricing rule matters only because of what it makes possible: affordable premiums, solvent hospitals, better access, a stronger workforce, narrower gaps. Benefits-realization management is the discipline of tracing each component to the benefits it serves and checking that those benefits actually arrive.

Chapter 15 makes this the Portfolio Manager's core purpose: ensure every component can trace its contribution to one or more of Act 167's five statutory goals, and that the portfolio as a whole produces the benefits that justify its cost. This lesson builds that trace, using the book's benefits-realization plan and PMI's practice guide.

The Transformation Leadership course covers how to sustain benefits after a reform launches. This lesson concentrates on the earlier step: designing the trace from components to goals, choosing the measures, and using it to make portfolio decisions.
Benefits, Not Deliverables

PMI's Benefits Realization Management: A Practice Guide describes benefits realization as the thread that runs from organizational strategy through project deliverables to the benefits they contribute, across portfolio, program and project management. It sets out shared terminology, core principles and a life cycle for identifying, planning, realizing and sustaining benefits.

PMI's own research suggests the discipline is rare. The guide cites the 2018 Pulse of the Profession finding that only one in three organizations report high benefits-realization maturity. Most organizations can say what they delivered; far fewer can say what it achieved.

For a transformation, the gap between delivery and benefit is where reforms quietly fail. A global budget can be implemented on time and still fail to slow cost growth. A medical-home program can reach full coverage and still leave access gaps unchanged. Without a benefits trace, the portfolio will report success on every component while the goals that justified it go unmet.

Benefits also take longer to appear than deliverables, and they are harder to attribute. Premiums respond to many forces besides one pricing rule; access gaps respond to staffing, transport and income as well as to clinical programs. A benefits plan does not need perfect attribution, but it does need agreed measures and agreed expectations about timing, set before results arrive, so that the portfolio is judged against a standard rather than a story.
A deliverable is something the portfolio produces. A benefit is a change in the world the deliverable makes possible. Portfolios are justified by benefits and should be judged by them.
Tracing to Act 167's Five Goals

Vermont's portfolio already has its goals in statute. Act 167 of 2022 set five: high-quality, accessible care; financial sustainability; affordability; a robust workforce; and health equity. Figure 15.8 of the book maps the portfolio's components to each goal, names a measurement metric and sets a 2028 target.

The mapping shows how benefits depend on combinations of components. High-quality, accessible care draws on the Blueprint medical homes, Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics, the HEROI equity methodology and the Care Integration Network. Affordability draws on reference-based pricing and global budgets. Health equity draws on HEROI, health-related social-need screening, social-risk adjustment and social-determinants data. No single component delivers any goal alone, which is why benefits have to be managed at portfolio level.

The targets are concrete enough to check. For accessible care, 90% or better follow-up within 30 days after behavioral-health hospitalization and readmissions below 12%. For affordability, commercial premium growth below 5% a year and total-cost-of-care growth below inflation plus one point. For the workforce, a primary-care staffing gap below 200 full-time equivalents, from 370.

children.text: Choosing Measures: Leading and Lagging

The 2028 targets in Figure 15.8 are lagging indicators: they show whether benefits arrived, but only after the fact. A portfolio office also needs leading indicators that show early whether benefits are on course. For affordability, a leading indicator might be the share of hospital revenue under the new pricing methodology; for equity, the share of hospitals using stratified quality data in their plans.

Leading indicators should be tied to the components that produce the benefit and measured on the portfolio's monthly or quarterly cadence. Lagging indicators are reviewed less often, typically quarterly against the Vermont Scorecard and annually at portfolio rebalancing, which is the cadence the book's roadmap sets.

Equity measures need special care. Chapter 10's principle, calibrate for the gap and not the average, applies here: a portfolio can raise an average while widening a gap. Benefits for equity should therefore be measured as gaps between groups or regions, as Figure 15.8 does with the BIPOC access target and Northeast Kingdom uninsurance, not as statewide averages.

children.text: Using Benefits to Make Portfolio Decisions

The benefits trace is a decision tool. It tells the Portfolio Manager which components are essential to which goals, so that when resources are short the portfolio protects the components on which the most benefit depends. It also reveals goals served by few components, which are more fragile: the workforce goal, for example, depends on a narrow set of investments.

Most importantly, it supports the hardest portfolio decision: stopping work. Chapter 15 gives the Portfolio Manager the duty of tracking benefits realization and recommending that a component be terminated when its benefits are no longer achievable. Without a benefits trace, that judgment cannot be made on evidence, and components continue on momentum.

The trace also connects the portfolio to its overseers. Legislators and boards care about the five goals, not the nineteen components. Reporting progress goal by goal, with the contributing components underneath, gives them the view they need and makes the portfolio's purpose visible in every report.

Benefits also guide sequencing at the margin. When two components compete for the same scarce resource and both are unblocked, the one contributing to more goals, or to a goal with fewer other contributors, usually has the stronger claim. The dependency logic decides what can run; the benefits trace helps decide what should run first among the things that can.

Financial sustainability, for instance, draws on reference-based pricing, global budgets, coding-gap closure and the portfolio office itself, and is measured by operating margin, deficit trajectory and administrative cost per discharge, with a 2028 target of no hospital in structural operating loss and the deficit trajectory reversed.
body.title: Chapter 15's benefits-realization plan

children.text: Build Your Own Benefits Trace

Start from your goals, not your components. Write down the outcomes your transformation exists to achieve, in the form your overseers would recognize: statutory goals, board-approved strategic aims or contractual targets. Then, for each goal, list the components that contribute to it and how.

Every component should appear under at least one goal. A component that serves no goal is a candidate for stopping. A goal with no contributing component is a gap in the portfolio. For each goal, choose one or two lagging measures with a target and date, and one or two leading measures you can track on the portfolio's regular cadence.

Review the trace at each quarterly performance review and at the annual rebalancing. When a benefit is drifting off course, the trace shows which components to examine first; when a component is no longer able to deliver its benefit, the trace supplies the evidence for a decision to stop or redesign it.

Share the trace with the people who run the components. Component leads who can see which goals their work serves make better day-to-day choices, and they are the first to notice when a deliverable is on track but its benefit is not.

children.text: The objection to building a portfolio office is almost always the same: we cannot afford it. Chapter 15 answers it directly with a cost-benefit table, and then makes a harder point: the table omits the most important number, the cost of failure. This lesson works through the book's business case, explains how to frame the cost of failure honestly, and gives you a structure for making the same case in your own organization.

A business case for management infrastructure is unusual because its benefits are mostly avoided losses. Nothing new appears when a portfolio office works; things simply stop going wrong. That makes the case easy to dismiss and important to make carefully.
The aim is a case that a budget office, a board or a legislature can test: costs that are explicit, benefits tied to specific risks, and a clear statement of what is assumed.
What the Portfolio Office Costs

Figure 15.9 of the book costs a staffed portfolio office for Vermont at about $0.85 million to $1.3 million a year, or roughly $4 million to $6.4 million over four to five years. The largest line is the five pillar program managers, shared across agencies and hospitals, at $500,000 to $850,000 a year. The senior Portfolio Manager, with the PfMP credential, is costed at $180,000 to $220,000 a year; two analysts at $120,000 to $160,000; and portfolio-management software at $50,000 to $100,000.

Each line is paired with the benefit it buys. The Portfolio Manager provides single accountability for the January 2028 deadline and directly avoids R-10, the risk that the transformation is managed as a collection of projects. The analysts maintain the master schedule, the risk register and the dashboard. The software provides real-time visibility, resource optimization and an audit trail for Act 68. The program managers carry delivery accountability and critical-path management within each pillar.

The book's comparison is with the money the office coordinates. At under 1% a year of the $195 million first-year Rural Health Transformation Program award alone, before counting any savings from reference-based pricing, the office is a small fraction of the investment it protects.

children.text: The Cost of Failure

The book's central argument is that the cost-benefit table leaves out the cost of failure. Without adequate portfolio infrastructure, Vermont risks delivering the January 2028 Strategic Plan as a descriptive document rather than a binding commitment, which the book's chapter on political sustainability identifies as the most dangerous failure mode. That outcome is not free. In the book's words, it is a multi-billion-dollar one: the continuation of the deficit trajectory Oliver Wyman projected, the failure of thirteen of fourteen hospitals to reach sustainability, and the loss of the political window that the mandatory architecture has opened.

Cross-industry evidence points the same way at smaller scale. PMI's 2017 Pulse of the Profession put the waste from poor project performance at about 9.7% of project spending. That is an average across industries and organizations, not a forecast for any Vermont program, so it should not be multiplied into a precise saving. Its use in a business case is to establish order of magnitude: typical waste from poor delivery is several times larger, as a share of spending, than the cost of the office proposed here.

There is also federal money at stake. The book notes in answering the third objection that Rural Health Transformation Program funds are contingent on demonstrated progress, so a portfolio that misses its components risks clawback. The office's cost, it argues, is less than 2% of a single year of the value it protects.

body.message: A business case for management infrastructure is most credible when it is conservative. State costs as ranges, tie benefits to named risks, use cross-industry figures for scale only, and say plainly which benefits are avoided losses rather than new savings.
body.title: Do not overclaim savings

children.text: Framing Avoided Losses

Because most of a portfolio office's value is avoided loss, the strongest framing ties each cost line to the specific risks it reduces. The risk register from Track 4 supplies this. The Portfolio Manager is costed against R-10 and, through the portfolio office, R-03. The Technology program manager is costed against R-01 and R-06, the two Technology risks that propagate into Economics and Clinical. The Economics program manager is costed against R-08, the risk that safety-net hospitals are penalized because social-risk adjustment arrives too late.

Linking costs to risks lets a decision-maker ask the right question. Not whether the office is affordable in the abstract, but whether paying for a given role is worth the reduction in a specific, scored risk. A $200,000 role that materially reduces a risk scored 20 on a portfolio worth hundreds of millions is an easy decision once the link is drawn.

The same logic answers the question of timing. A portfolio office hired after the critical gating decisions are made can only report on their consequences. Its value is highest before the gates it protects, which is why the book's roadmap puts the Portfolio Manager in seat by January 2027, nine months before FY2028 hospital budgets take effect.

children.text: Making the Case in a Hospital or Health System

The structure transfers directly to a hospital or health system. Inventory the transformation components and their combined budget. Build the risk register and identify the cross-component risks no single program owns. Cost the portfolio function at the scale your organization needs, which may be one portfolio lead and shared program leads rather than a full office. Then present the cost as a share of the investment it coordinates and tie each role to the risks it reduces.

Hospitals have one advantage in making the case: their financial exposure to transformation is direct and visible. Under a global budget, a hospital whose payment and clinical redesign are out of sequence feels the result in its operating margin, often within a year. Linking the portfolio function to protecting that margin is usually more persuasive to a board than any general argument about governance.

Whatever the setting, include the cost of doing nothing. A business case that only lists the cost of the office invites the answer 'not this year'. One that also states, with appropriate caution, what the organization stands to lose without it, invites a real decision.

children.text: Testing the Case Before You Present It

Before presenting, test the case the way a skeptical budget office would. Are the costs complete, including software, training and the time of people seconded to the office? Are the risks it claims to reduce on a real register with real scores? Are cross-industry figures used for scale only? Is the comparison base, the investment coordinated, stated accurately and current?

Then test it against the objections in the next lesson. The most common, that existing governance already covers this, is best answered inside the business case itself, by showing what the governance body cannot do without a portfolio office to supply it with data.

A case that survives these tests is short. It fits on one page: the investment coordinated, the cost of the office as a share of it, the three or four top risks it reduces, and the date by which it must exist to be useful.

The one-page version: the portfolio office costs under 1% a year of what it coordinates, directly reduces the portfolio's highest-scored risks, and is worth most if it exists before the gates it protects.

children.text: This capstone brings the course together into one exercise. You will define a transformation portfolio, sequence it by dependency, find its binding constraint, check its capital against its gates, model what a slip would do, build its risk register and benefits trace, and finish with a one-page portfolio brief that answers the oversight question from Lesson 14.

Use a real organization if you can: your hospital, your agency, your state or a program you know well. If you cannot, use Vermont's portfolio as Chapter 15 records it; the platform's tools load it as a preset. Allow three to four hours, in one or two sittings.

Every step uses a platform tool, and each tool corresponds to a row of Chapter 15's Work This Chapter on the Platform table. By the end you will have done, at small scale, the core work of a portfolio office.
Step 1: Define and Sequence the Portfolio

Begin with the inventory method from Lesson 3. List every component with a named owner and a dated obligation, assign each to one pillar, and record its type, priority, lead and next stage gate. Then open the Portfolio Sequencing Test at /portfolio-sequencing-test, replace the Vermont preset with your components, and set each component's status and whether its implementation needs the pillar's upstream gate.

Score the five pillars' current readiness and read the verdicts. Note which components are correctly waiting, which are late by dependency order, which are running ahead of a closed gate, and which unfinished components the test identifies as the places where schedule pressure belongs. Compare that list with where your organization's attention actually is today.

If you are using Vermont's portfolio with the Fall 2026 scores, you should find twelve components on track, the RHT Program deployment running ahead of its gate, three components late by dependency order, and the four Technology components as the pressure points. If your results differ, check the gate settings before the scores.
