children.text: Step 2: Find the Binding Constraint and Check the Capital

Open the Transformation Friction Index at /transformation-friction-index and score your organization or state on each pillar. Chapter 15 notes that the tool finds the binding constraint by sensitivity rather than by the highest bar: the pillar whose improvement would lift delivered readiness most is where the portfolio manager's attention belongs. Then list your three most urgent initiatives by deadline. If none sits in the binding-constraint pillar, your portfolio is being scheduled by calendar rather than by dependency.

Next, open the Investment Tracker at /investment-tracker and use the portfolio check to enter your components' committed capital by pillar. The tool checks each against its pillar's limiting gate and flags components funded ahead of their upstream gate. The book calls money moving faster than dependency order the early signal of premature investment.

Record three facts from this step: the binding-constraint pillar, whether your most urgent initiatives sit in it, and which components are funded ahead of their gate. These become the centre of your portfolio brief.

If the two tools disagree, for example the Friction Index names Technology while your capital is concentrated in Economics, that disagreement is the finding. It usually means money is following deadlines or sponsors rather than the dependency chain.
The binding constraint is found by sensitivity, not by the weakest score. Ask which pillar's improvement would lift delivered readiness most; that is where the next dollar and the next hour belong.
Step 3: Model a Slip and Score the Portfolio

Open the HTR Simulator at /htr-simulator, enter your pillar scores, and lower the binding-constraint pillar by fifteen points. Watch the downstream pillars fall with it. Then use the Impact Simulation at /impact-simulation to model what a single component slipping does to the rest of the portfolio and identify the components with no slack, the ones whose slip moves other pillars' outcomes.

Then score the portfolio the way an outside reviewer would, using the Transformation Scorecard at /research-lab/knowledge-workspace?tab=scorecard. Chapter 15 makes a pointed observation about this step: divergence between what the portfolio office reports and what the scorecard shows is itself a governance finding. If your own status reports describe the portfolio as healthier than the scorecard does, note where and why.

If you have a Subscriber plan, the HTI Dashboard at /hti-dashboard shows Vermont's five-pillar status moving over time rather than at a single date, which is the trend a monthly report cannot show. Use it to compare your portfolio's direction of travel with Vermont's.

children.text: Step 4: Register the Risks and Trace the Benefits

Build a risk register using Lesson 10's format. Start with the pressure points and the no-slack components from the first three steps: each is a risk to everything that depends on it. Add structural risks to the mandate, funding, capacity and engagement. Score each on a fixed probability and impact scale, choose a response, and name an owner. Then read the register as Lesson 11 does: plot it, group risks by shared cause, and check which can be reduced by work that is unblocked today.

Build the benefits trace from Lesson 12. List the goals your transformation serves, map every component to at least one, and choose a lagging measure with a target and a date, plus a leading measure, for each goal. Flag components that serve no goal and goals that no component serves.

Together, the register and the trace complete the picture: what the portfolio contains, in what order it must run, what threatens it, and what it is for. That is the information a governance body needs and rarely receives.

body.message: It is tempting to leave the most uncomfortable risks off a register you will show to others, especially risks about leadership, capacity or political will. Chapter 15's own register puts the absence of the portfolio function at the top. An honest register is the only useful one.
body.title: Keep the register honest

children.text: Step 5: Write the One-Page Portfolio Brief

Finish with a one-page brief for your governance body. Open with the answer to the oversight question: which component is the binding constraint, who owns it, and what would it take to accelerate it. Follow with the sequencing findings, components running ahead of their gate and components late by dependency, and the capital funded ahead of its gate.

Then give the two or three risks that need a decision now, each with options and the cost of not deciding, and a benefits summary showing whether each goal is on course. Close with the management infrastructure the portfolio needs, costed as a share of what it coordinates and tied to the risks it reduces, as in Lesson 13.

If you can write that page with confidence, you have done what Chapter 15 argues Vermont, and most organizations running a transformation, have not yet done: managed the transformation as a portfolio. Revisit the brief quarterly. The binding constraint will move, and the brief is how you will know.

Share the brief with the people who own the components as well as with the governance body. Component leads who see the whole portfolio, its binding constraint and its top risks understand why their own component is being accelerated, held back or resourced differently, and they become the first line of the portfolio's early-warning system. A portfolio brief that only travels upward manages the governance body; one that also travels outward manages the portfolio.

title: Capstone: Build and Run Your Own Transformation Portfolio

children.text: A portfolio that has not been defined cannot be managed. PMI's portfolio standard requires every component to be identified, classified and assigned governance before anything else is done with it. That sounds obvious, yet most organizations running a transformation have never written down the complete list of what they are running.

Chapter 15 does that work for Vermont, producing a 19-component inventory. This lesson shows how the inventory was built, how each component is classified, what the exercise typically reveals, and how to build the same inventory for your own organization or state.

The book calls this exercise often the single highest-value first step toward portfolio governance. It costs little, needs no new authority, and almost always changes how leaders understand the scale of what they are doing.
Why Definition Comes First

Every later portfolio decision depends on the inventory. You cannot schedule components by dependency if you have not listed them. You cannot resolve resource conflicts between components you do not know exist. You cannot trace benefits to goals, or score risks against components, without a complete list to work from.

Vermont, the book notes, has never published such a definition. Its transformation arrives through several channels at once: statutes, a federal model agreement and its closeout, a federal grant program, and a series of agency reports. Each channel carries its own obligations and deadlines, and each tends to be owned by a different unit. Without an inventory, nobody sees them as one body of work.

That is not unique to Vermont. Initiatives in large organizations are usually owned by different departments that do not otherwise compare notes, so the total is invisible from any single seat. Defining the portfolio is the act of making it visible from one seat.

Definition also protects against double counting and silent gaps. Two units can each believe the other owns a piece of work, or both can be doing it. Writing every component down, once, with one owner, is the simplest way to find both problems before they cost a deadline.
The portfolio inventory is the foundation document of portfolio management: every component, its pillar, its owner, its type, its priority and its next stage gate, in one place.
How Vermont's 19 Components Were Found

The inventory in Figure 15.3 is HTR's own, not an official state document. It was assembled by reading Act 68, the AHEAD State Agreement, Vermont's Rural Health Transformation Program application and the AHS transformation reports, and listing every initiative that carries a named owner and a dated obligation. Each was then assigned to the pillar whose function it serves.

Two rules made the exercise work. First, an initiative only counts if it has an owner and a date; aspirations without either are not components yet. Second, each component goes to exactly one pillar, chosen by function: a data platform is Technology even if it is funded through a payment program. Applied in early 2026, the exercise produced nineteen components.

The book is careful about what the number means. Nineteen is what the exercise produced at that date. It is not a number Vermont has adopted, and anyone repeating the exercise against later reports should expect it to move, as components finish, new obligations arrive or, as happened in July 2026, a federal agreement is withdrawn and becomes a closeout obligation instead.

children.text: Classifying the Components

Figure 15.3 classifies each component on five attributes. Type distinguishes compliance projects, strategic projects, operational programs, analytical projects and organizational projects; the type tells you how the component should be managed. Priority is critical, high or medium. Lead names the accountable organization. The status and stage-gate column records where the component is now and the next point at which it must demonstrate progress.

The pillar column matters most for scheduling. Because the components are grouped by pillar, each inherits that pillar's inbound dependencies from the five-pillar framework. An Economics component such as reference-based-pricing implementation cannot be productively implemented before the Technology components that make it measurable, however close its own deadline is. Track 3 of this course turns that observation into scheduling rules.

The sample below shows one component from each pillar as the book recorded it for 2026. The full inventory is in Figure 15.3, and the Portfolio Sequencing Test on the platform loads all nineteen as its Vermont preset.

children.text: What the Inventory Usually Reveals

The book's Implications section describes what organizations typically discover when they build their first inventory. They are running more simultaneous transformation components than they had counted. Several components have no named owner. And two or three components sit downstream of a dependency nobody is tracking.

Vermont's inventory carries one more lesson: the portfolio function itself is a component. AHS PMO establishment appears in the Operations pillar with a critical priority and a target of being operational in the second quarter of 2027. A portfolio can, and here does, contain the component responsible for managing the portfolio, and if that component slips, everything else is managed less well.

None of these findings requires new data or new authority to produce. They come from reading documents the organization already has and writing the results in one table. That is why the book recommends the inventory as the first step for any state or organization, wherever it is in its transformation.

The inventory also changes conversations with oversight bodies. A legislature or board that receives component-by-component reports sees activity; one that receives the inventory sees the shape of the whole, including which components carry critical priority, which share a deadline, and which have no owner. That shift from activity to shape is the first sign that a portfolio is being managed rather than merely reported.

The number of components will differ; the book's point is that most organizations underestimate their portfolio until they do this, because no single department sees the whole.

children.text: An initiative without a named owner is not a component; it is a risk. Record it, and make assigning an owner the first action against it.
Build Your Own Inventory

You can build a first inventory in an afternoon. Start from the documents that impose obligations on your organization: statutes and regulations, contracts and grant agreements, board-approved plans and any regulator's directives. For a hospital, that includes payer contracts with value-based terms, state reporting obligations, and capital projects tied to the transformation.

Then enter your components into the Portfolio Sequencing Test at /portfolio-sequencing-test. The tool starts with Vermont's nineteen components; you can remove them, add your own with the + Add component button, and set each one's pillar, status and calendar target. In Track 3 you will use the same tool to run the sequencing test on your inventory. For now, the goal is a complete list with an owner and a pillar for every line.

Keep the inventory dated and revisit it at a fixed interval. A portfolio is not static: components finish, new obligations arrive, and some components should be stopped. The inventory is the document in which those changes become visible.

children.text: Conventional scheduling orders work by deadline and by resource availability. Chapter 15 argues that a five-pillar portfolio has a third, overriding constraint: the dependency structure from Chapter 1. Each component inherits the inbound dependencies of its pillar, so an Economics component cannot be productively implemented before the Technology work that makes it measurable, however near its deadline.

This lesson explains why that constraint changes the portfolio manager's job, sets out the two decision rules the book derives from it, shows how gate status differs from a conventional critical path, and walks through what the platform's Portfolio Sequencing Test finds when it is run on Vermont's nineteen components.

The Transformation Leadership course includes a hands-on workshop that runs the same test step by step. This lesson concentrates on the scheduling logic behind it, which is what you need to apply the test to a portfolio the tool has never seen.
Why Deadlines Are the Wrong Organizing Principle

A statutory deadline tells you when something must be finished. It says nothing about whether the work it depends on will be ready in time. A portfolio scheduled by deadline alone will push hardest on whichever component is due soonest, even when that component cannot yet produce anything usable because its upstream pillar is still being built.

Chapter 15 ties this directly to the failure that opens the book. OneCare Vermont, the all-payer accountable care organization, advanced its payment model on a voluntary mandate without the integrated real-time data that would have made it manageable. In portfolio terms, an Economics component was implemented ahead of its Technology gate. The book's point is that a portfolio manager who schedules Vermont's current components by statutory date alone will reproduce exactly that failure.

The alternative is to schedule by dependency first and deadline second. The deadline still matters: it tells you how much time the dependency chain has. But the order of work comes from the chain, not from the calendar.

Design work is the important exception. Economics-as-design, the modeling and methodology that prepare a payment change, runs in parallel with Technology work. Only implementation waits for the gate (Chapter 1, §1.11.2).
Two Decision Rules a Gantt Chart Does Not Give You

The first rule: a component whose upstream pillar gate is still closed is not behind schedule. It is correctly waiting. Accelerating it consumes budget and political capital to produce output nobody can use. The book's clearest case is the AHS and Green Mountain Care Board analytics-vendor deployment, which carries the register's highest delivery-risk score, 20, tied only with the risk that the portfolio function itself is not established. It scores so high not because its own deadline is nearest, but because three downstream components converge on it.

The second rule is the inverse: a component with no unmet upstream dependency should be running now, however distant its deadline. Social-risk adjustment, the methodology that keeps global budgets from penalizing hospitals serving sicker and poorer populations, has a FY2028 target and no upstream blocker. Treating it as a FY2028 problem because that is when it is due is, in the book's words, the scheduling error that leaves equity work perpetually late.

Together the two rules reverse a common instinct. They tell the portfolio manager to relieve pressure on some components that look late and to add pressure to some that look early. Neither move makes sense on a deadline-ordered chart; both make sense once the dependencies are drawn.

Not yet started or still in design

right.label: Looks early, is late

Not yet running
Right action: start it now, whatever its deadline

body.title: Two components, two misleading calendars

children.text: Gates Versus the Critical Path

Conventional schedule analysis finds the critical path: the longest chain of linked activities, which sets the earliest possible finish. The five-pillar framework adds gates. A gate opens when the enabling work in an upstream pillar is actually finished, not when a milestone is declared (Chapter 1, §1.4). A component can sit on a schedule's critical path and still be the wrong thing to accelerate, if its gate is closed.

The book compresses this into the Portfolio Manager's Sequencing Test, four questions applied to every component in order. Which pillar does it belong to? Is that pillar's upstream gate open? If closed, what is the gating component, and is it resourced? If open, is this component running? Applied across all nineteen components, the test produces the portfolio's true critical path, which will not match the order of statutory deadlines.

The third question carries the managerial insight. When a component is waiting on a closed gate, schedule pressure belongs on the gating component, not on the waiting one. Moving pressure upstream to where the constraint actually sits is the most useful thing a portfolio manager does with a schedule.

body.title: The Portfolio Manager's Sequencing Test (Chapter 15, §15.7)

children.text: What the Test Finds in Vermont's Portfolio

The platform's Portfolio Sequencing Test at /portfolio-sequencing-test runs these four questions on Vermont's nineteen components, using the same dependency engine as the HTR Simulator and Vermont's Fall 2026 readiness scores. With those inputs the Policy and Technology gates are open, while Economics is blocked by a Technology pillar that is only partly built, and Clinical and Operations are blocked further down the chain.

The verdicts follow. Twelve components are on track. Reference-based-pricing implementation and global-budget design are doing design work in parallel under a closed gate, which the test marks as correct. The Care Integration Network build-out is ready to implement: its gate is open but it is still in design. RHT Program deployment is implementing ahead of its gate. And three components are late by dependency order because nothing upstream is holding them and they have not started: the statewide AI-governance framework, the AHS restructuring work and the portfolio office itself.

The test also names where schedule pressure belongs. The four unfinished Technology components, the analytics deployment, the Care Integration Network, the health information exchange expansion and the AI-governance framework, each hold three Economics components waiting behind them. Those four, not the Economics components with nearer deadlines, are where a portfolio manager's attention should go.

children.text: Applying the Logic to a Portfolio of Your Own

To run the test on your own portfolio, load your inventory from Lesson 3 into the Portfolio Sequencing Test, replacing Vermont's components. For each component set its pillar and status, and decide whether its implementation genuinely needs the pillar's upstream gate. Care-model programs that produce value on their own, and analytical methodologies with no upstream blocker, are usually not gated; the tool lets you mark them so.

Then score the five pillars' current readiness, or start from the Vermont preset and adjust it. Read the verdicts in two passes. First, look for components running ahead of their gate and decide whether each is a deliberate trade-off or a mistake. Second, look at the list of components where schedule pressure belongs and compare it with where your leadership's attention actually is. The gap between those two lists is the most useful finding the test produces.

Repeat the test whenever a gate status changes. A portfolio's critical path moves as upstream work finishes, and the components that were correctly waiting last quarter may be late this quarter if they did not start when their gate opened.

children.text: Chapter 15's first objection ends with a list of what the existing oversight arrangements do not provide, and earned-value tracking is on it. The book's point is that monthly reports track activities, not performance. They say what was done, not whether the work is delivering the value planned for the money and time spent.

Earned value management (EVM) is the standard technique for measuring performance in that sense. This lesson explains its three core quantities and four basic indicators, works through an illustrative example, sets out the federal standards that govern it, and then marks its limits: what EVM cannot tell a five-pillar portfolio manager, and what has to be read alongside it.
EVM is most useful for predictive components with a baseline. For adaptive components, Lesson 8's cycle-output measures fit better. A portfolio office uses each where it fits.
The Three Core Quantities

Earned value compares three numbers at any point in time. Planned value (PV) is the budgeted cost of the work scheduled to be done by now. Earned value (EV) is the budgeted cost of the work actually completed by now. Actual cost (AC) is what has really been spent to complete that work.

The insight of EVM is that progress is measured in the budget's own units. A component that has spent half its money has not necessarily done half its work; earned value asks how much of the planned work, valued at its planned cost, is genuinely complete. Comparing earned value with planned value shows whether the component is ahead of or behind schedule. Comparing earned value with actual cost shows whether it is over or under budget for the work done.

EVM depends on a baseline: a scope broken into measurable pieces, each with a planned cost and a planned date. That is why it fits predictive components and why the book's finding that no pillar has a formal work-breakdown structure (Lesson 6) matters. Without a baseline there is nothing to earn value against.

Planned value is what you said you would have done. Earned value is what you have actually done, valued at plan. Actual cost is what it really cost. Every EVM indicator is a comparison of two of these three numbers.
Four Basic Indicators

Schedule variance is earned value minus planned value: negative means less work is done than planned. Cost variance is earned value minus actual cost: negative means the work done cost more than planned. The two performance indices express the same comparisons as ratios. The schedule performance index (SPI) is earned value divided by planned value, and the cost performance index (CPI) is earned value divided by actual cost. A value of 1.0 means on plan; below 1.0 means behind schedule or over cost.

Ratios are useful at portfolio level because they let components of very different sizes be compared on one scale. A component with an SPI of 0.8 is delivering eighty percent of its planned work rate, whether its budget is two hundred thousand dollars or twenty million.

The indices also support forecasting. If a component's cost performance has been stable, dividing its total budget by its CPI gives a rough estimate at completion. Forecasts like this are only as good as the stability of past performance, but they are far more informative than a status of 'in progress'.

children.text: An Illustrative Calculation

Consider a hypothetical analytics deployment with a total budget of $2.0 million. These figures are invented to show the arithmetic; they are not Vermont's. Six months in, the plan said $1.0 million of work would be complete, so planned value is $1.0 million. Measured against the work breakdown, the work actually finished was budgeted at $0.8 million, so earned value is $0.8 million. Actual spending to date is $1.0 million.

Schedule variance is $0.8 million minus $1.0 million, or minus $0.2 million, and the SPI is 0.8: the component has delivered eighty percent of the work it planned to deliver by now. Cost variance is $0.8 million minus $1.0 million, also minus $0.2 million, and the CPI is 0.8: each dollar spent has bought eighty cents of planned work. If that cost performance holds, the simple estimate at completion is $2.0 million divided by 0.8, or $2.5 million.

A monthly activity report for the same component might read 'vendor onboarded, data feeds in testing, on track for go-live'. Both can be true at once. The earned-value view shows what the activity view hides: the component is behind and over cost, and the gap will grow unless something changes.

children.text: Federal Standards and Expectations

Earned value is not an exotic private-sector technique; it is embedded in federal practice. The Government Accountability Office's Cost Estimating and Assessment Guide (GAO-20-195G), issued in March 2020 as the first update to its 2009 guide, sets out best practices for managing program cost through earned value management, including how an EVM system is set up, executed and validated. Federal agencies implement EVM systems against the industry guidelines in the EIA-748 standard.

This matters for a state transformation funded partly by federal programs. Federal partners and auditors are used to performance measured this way, and a portfolio office that can report schedule and cost performance indices for its major components speaks their language. Chapter 15's second objection makes the related point that a time-bounded, outcome-specified, heavily financed portfolio with legally binding deadlines is exactly the kind of work that federal partners expect to be professionally managed.

A state need not adopt a full certified EVM system to benefit. Applying the core quantities to the handful of large predictive components, with a simple monthly calculation, captures most of the value at little cost.
Start small: the three or four largest predictive components, a baseline for each, and a monthly SPI and CPI. That alone turns an activity report into a performance report.
What Earned Value Cannot See

Earned value measures adherence to plan. It cannot tell whether the plan respects the portfolio's dependencies. A component can report an SPI of 1.0, perfectly on schedule, while it is running ahead of its upstream gate and producing output nobody can yet use. In the terms of Lesson 7, earned value would score such a component as healthy while the sequencing test flags it as a problem.

Nor does earned value measure benefits. A component can be delivered on time and on budget and still fail to produce the benefit that justified it, which is why Track 4 adds benefits-realization tracking. And for adaptive components, whose plans are meant to change, a fixed baseline is the wrong yardstick altogether.

The portfolio office therefore reads three things together each month: earned value for the predictive components, the sequencing verdicts for every component, and benefits indicators against the goals the portfolio serves. Each catches failures the others miss.

children.text: Proposals for a portfolio office meet the same objections in almost every public organization. Chapter 15 anticipates five and answers each. This lesson works through them, then turns to the implementation roadmap the book schedules backward from the January 2028 deadline, and ends with the single question the book recommends to legislators and board members who oversee a transformation.
Knowing the objections in advance matters because each contains a partial truth. A good answer acknowledges what is right in the objection before explaining why the conclusion does not follow.
The objections are written for Vermont, but each has an equivalent in a hospital boardroom or another state's agency, and the answers transfer with them.
Objections One and Two: 'We Already Manage This' and 'This Is Government'

The first objection is that existing arrangements already cover the work: the Health Care Advisory Committee and monthly reports. The partial truth is that these provide real oversight. The book's answer is that the HCAC is a governance body, not a portfolio office. It provides oversight, not an integrated master schedule, resource-conflict resolution, a maintained risk register or earned-value tracking, and the monthly reports track activities rather than performance. The HCAC is the right governance body; it needs a portfolio office to give it the data to govern.

The second objection is that government does not run projects like the private sector. The partial truth is that public programs have different accountabilities. The book's answer is that Vermont's transformation is a time-bounded, outcome-specified, heavily financed portfolio of interdependent programs with legally binding deadlines. The Rural Health Transformation Program is a federal grant with deliverables and reporting obligations; the withdrawn AHEAD agreement still carries federal closeout requirements; Act 68 has a statutory deliverable in January 2028. Federal partners expect professional management of exactly this kind of work.

Both answers share a pattern: they accept the premise and show that it does not reach the conclusion. Yes, there is oversight; no, oversight is not management. Yes, this is government; that is precisely why its obligations demand professional delivery.
Oversight asks whether the work is going well. Management makes it go well. A portfolio needs both, and one cannot substitute for the other.
Objections Three, Four and Five: Cost, Hospitals and Consultants

The third objection is cost in a year of budget cuts. Lesson 13 gave the full answer: Rural Health Transformation Program funds depend on demonstrated progress, the office costs a small fraction of the value it protects, and the alternative is a partial transformation that costs far more. The fourth is that hospitals will not accept being managed by AHS. The book's answer clarifies the role: the Portfolio Manager does not manage hospitals but manages AHS's contribution to the portfolio. Hospital plans are produced by hospitals, approved by AHS and monitored through the Green Mountain Care Board.

The fifth objection is the newest: AHS already has expert help. Its March 2026 Act 68 report lists contracted support from Manatt, Phelps & Phillips, a new hospital technical-assistance vendor and analytics support under negotiation. The book's answer is that a contractor delivers a defined scope. It cannot hold a state component back until its upstream gate opens, reassign agency staff between components, or answer to the Legislature for the portfolio as a whole. Contracted support adds capacity, not authority, and every new contract is another component that someone has to sequence.

Taken together, the five answers define the role by contrast. It is not oversight, not a private-sector import, not an unaffordable luxury, not control over hospitals and not something a contractor can supply. It is the integrating authority that none of the existing arrangements provides.

children.text: The Implementation Roadmap

The book anchors its roadmap to the one date that cannot move: the Statewide Strategic Plan, due January 15, 2028. Figure 15.10 schedules the portfolio office's build-out backward from that deadline and against the components it exists to sequence. A Portfolio Manager hired by January 2027 has nine months before FY2028 hospital budgets take effect in October 2027, which the book judges enough only if the office is running before the Technology gate it is meant to protect.

From mid-2027 the office runs on a fixed cadence: monthly governance reviews, quarterly performance reviews against the Vermont Scorecard, and annual portfolio rebalancing. The book's aim is that the January 2028 plan arrives with portfolio-management evidence, benefits tracked, risks managed and resources deployed in dependency order, after which the office carries the portfolio into the plan's three-year update cycle.

Scheduling backward from a fixed deadline is itself a portfolio technique. It exposes how little time remains for each step and makes the cost of delay concrete: every month the portfolio office is late is a month of gating decisions made without it.

children.text: The Question Oversight Should Ask

Chapter 15's advice to legislators and board members is a single question that separates a real portfolio from a reporting exercise: which component is currently the binding constraint on all the others, who owns it, and what would it take to accelerate it? An organization managing a genuine portfolio can answer in one sentence. An organization managing a list will answer with a status summary of all nineteen components.

The question works because it can only be answered by someone who sees the dependencies. Identifying the binding constraint requires knowing which upstream work is holding back the most downstream value. Naming its owner requires that ownership be assigned. Saying what would accelerate it requires having thought about resources across components. A reporting function cannot answer it; a portfolio function answers it routinely.

Oversight bodies can ask the question at every review and track whether the answer changes. If the binding constraint never moves, either the portfolio is not acting on it or the answer is not being given honestly. Both are findings an oversight body should want to know.
Which component is currently the binding constraint on all the others, who owns it, and what would it take to accelerate it? (Transforming Healthcare, Chapter 15)
Preparing for the Objections in Your Own Setting

Before proposing a portfolio function, write down the objections you expect, in the words your organization will use. In a hospital they may be that the executive team already coordinates, that service-line leaders own their own changes, or that the transformation office would duplicate finance and quality. Each usually maps to one of the book's five.

For each, prepare the partial truth and the answer, with evidence from your own inventory, sequencing results, risk register and benefits trace. Objections are answered most convincingly not by argument about governance but by showing a specific dependency nobody owns, a specific risk nobody manages, or a specific component running ahead of its gate.

Finally, prepare your own answer to the oversight question. If you cannot yet say which component is your portfolio's binding constraint, who owns it and what would accelerate it, that inability is the strongest argument for the function you are proposing.
The most persuasive answer to any objection is a concrete example from your own portfolio: an unowned dependency, an unmanaged cross-pillar risk, or a component running ahead of its gate.

children.text: Nineteen components, shared stage gates, one January 2028 deadline, three statutory predecessors and the closeout obligations of a withdrawn federal agreement. Chapter 15 concludes that this is not a problem component managers can solve by working harder or coordinating better among themselves. It needs a single designated authority with the mandate and the access to manage the transformation as a whole: a Portfolio Manager.

This lesson defines that role as the book does: what the Portfolio Manager does, the authority the role must carry to be useful, the credential that fits it, and where the role should sit. It also explains why contracted support, however expert, cannot fill it.

The central message is that the role is defined by its authority more than its tasks. Many people can maintain a register or chair a meeting. Only a role with the power to sequence work can change what the portfolio delivers.
Why One Integrator

Component managers optimize their components. That is their job, and they should do it well. But a portfolio's most important decisions are the ones no component manager can make: which component gets scarce staff this quarter, which one should wait for an upstream dependency, which one should be stopped because its benefits are no longer achievable. Left to negotiation among peers, those decisions default to whoever has the nearest deadline or the loudest sponsor.

Chapter 15's Implications section puts the point sharply for state leaders. Vermont does not lack oversight: it has the Health Care Advisory Committee (HCAC), monthly legislative reporting and federal review. What it lacks is an integrator, one role accountable for the portfolio as a whole, with authority to resolve resource conflicts between components that today are managed by different units against different deadlines.

The idea is not new to Vermont. Oliver Wyman's Act 167 report recommended a dedicated project-management function to manage the state's transformation portfolio, the November 2025 transformation report repeated the finding, and the AHS restructuring analysis in Chapter 16 identifies establishing a portfolio office as a critical organizational project. Chapter 15's contribution is a precise definition of the role.
The single most consequential decision is not whether to hire a Portfolio Manager but whether that role is given authority over sequencing. (Transforming Healthcare, Chapter 15)
What the Portfolio Manager Does

The book lists the role's responsibilities in summary. The Portfolio Manager chairs the monthly portfolio review board and maintains the portfolio register and the risk register. The role authorizes components being added to or removed from the portfolio, keeps every component aligned to Act 167's five statutory goals, and resolves resource conflicts between components.

The role also faces outward. It owns the Vermont Scorecard reporting to the HCAC and the AHS Secretary, manages portfolio-level relationships with the HCAC, the Green Mountain Care Board, hospital chief executives, the Legislature and CMS, and tracks benefits realization, recommending that a component be terminated when its benefits are no longer achievable.

Read the list for what is missing as much as what is present. The Portfolio Manager does not run components, write rules, design payment models or manage hospitals. Every duty concerns the portfolio as a whole: its composition, its alignment, its resources, its risks, its benefits and its story to the people who oversee it.

children.text: Authority Is the Job

A Portfolio Manager without authority becomes a reporting function: it documents the portfolio's problems without being able to fix them. The book specifies the authority the role needs. It reports directly to the AHS Secretary, with a co-reporting relationship to the Green Mountain Care Board. It holds budget authority over the transformation PMO. And it can require reporting from all nineteen component leads.

The most important power is over sequencing. The book is direct: a portfolio office that reports status without the power to hold a component back until its upstream gate opens will document the failure cascade rather than prevent it. Holding a component back is uncomfortable, because the component's sponsors will see it as a delay. It is also the single decision that most distinguishes a managed portfolio from a list of projects.

Authority also has limits, and the book draws them clearly when answering the objection that hospitals will not accept being managed by AHS. The Portfolio Manager does not manage the hospitals. It manages AHS's contribution to the portfolio. Hospital plans are produced by hospitals, approved by AHS and monitored through the Green Mountain Care Board. The role is an orchestrator, not a controller.

children.text: The Credential: PMI Portfolio Management Professional

The book names PMI's Portfolio Management Professional (PfMP) credential as the appropriate one for the role, together with substantial program or portfolio experience and experience in health systems or large-scale government programs. The PfMP is PMI's credential for practitioners who manage portfolios aligned to organizational strategy.

PMI's current eligibility rules offer three paths, all requiring 96 months (eight years) of professional business experience within the past fifteen years. With a secondary diploma, a candidate also needs 84 months of portfolio-management experience. With a bachelor's degree or higher, the requirement is 48 months. With a degree from a program accredited by PMI's Global Accreditation Center, it is 36 months. Requirements change, so check PMI's current exam content outline before relying on these figures.

A credential is evidence of method, not a substitute for judgment. For a state transformation, the book pairs it with health-system or government program experience, because the hardest parts of the job are political and institutional: persuading agencies to share resources, telling a sponsor that their component must wait, and explaining the portfolio's logic to a legislature.

children.text: Where the Role Sits, and What Contractors Cannot Do

For Vermont, the book places the role at the level of the AHS Secretary, or as a dedicated chief portfolio officer. For a hospital or health system, the equivalent sits close to the chief executive or chief strategy officer, above the individual program leads. In either case the test is the same: can the role move resources and change the order of work across organizational boundaries? If not, it is placed too low.

The fifth objection the book answers is that AHS already has expert help. Its March 2026 Act 68 report lists contracted transformation support from Manatt, Phelps & Phillips, a new hospital technical-assistance vendor, and analytics support under negotiation. The book's reply is that a contractor delivers a defined scope. It cannot hold a state component back until its upstream gate opens, reassign agency staff between components, or answer to the Legislature for the portfolio as a whole.

Contracted support adds capacity, not authority. Worse, every new contract is one more component, with its own deliverables and deadline, that someone has to sequence. The more expert help a transformation buys, the more it needs a portfolio manager to integrate it.

Timing matters as much as placement. The book's roadmap puts a Portfolio Manager in the seat by January 2027, nine months before FY2028 hospital budgets take effect in October 2027, so the role is running before the Technology gate it is meant to protect. A portfolio manager hired after the gating decisions have been made can only report on their consequences.

body.message: A coordinator who schedules meetings and compiles reports is useful, but it is not the role Chapter 15 describes. If the person cannot resolve a resource conflict or hold a component back, the portfolio still has no integrator.

Vermont has oversight bodies but no integrator: no role accountable for the whole with authority over resource conflicts between components.

The Portfolio Manager chairs the review board, maintains the portfolio and risk registers, keeps components aligned to Act 167's goals, resolves resource conflicts, owns Scorecard reporting and tracks benefits.
The role needs authority: a direct report to the AHS Secretary, a GMCB co-reporting line, budget authority over the PMO and power to require reporting from every component lead.
The decisive power is over sequencing: without it, a portfolio office documents the failure cascade instead of preventing it.
PMI's PfMP requires 96 months of business experience plus 84, 48 or 36 months of portfolio experience depending on education.
Contractors add capacity, not authority, and each new contract is another component someone has to sequence.

children.text: Not every component of a transformation should be managed the same way. Some have a fixed legal deadline and a well-defined deliverable; a detailed plan, followed carefully, is exactly right for them. Others are trying to hit a target that is still moving, where the best plan is a short cycle of building, testing and adjusting. Managing both kinds identically guarantees that one of them is managed badly.

Chapter 15 assigns each of Vermont's components to a predictive, adaptive or hybrid approach. This lesson explains the three approaches as PMI's guidance describes them, shows how the book classifies the components and why, and sets out how a portfolio office governs a portfolio that mixes all three.
The choice is not a matter of fashion. It follows from two properties of each component: how stable its requirements are, and how much is gained by learning quickly from early results.
Three Approaches

A predictive approach, often called waterfall, defines scope, schedule and cost early and manages change through formal control. It suits work whose requirements are well understood and whose deadline is fixed. An adaptive approach, which includes agile methods, plans in short cycles, delivers in increments and expects requirements to change as the team learns. It suits work whose requirements cannot be fully known in advance.

Between them lies the hybrid approach: a component with fixed deliverables at its boundary and adaptive work inside it, or a mostly predictive plan with some agile elements. PMI's Agile Practice Guide, developed with the Agile Alliance and published in 2017, treats hybrid life cycles as a legitimate fit-for-purpose choice rather than a compromise, and describes combinations ranging from predominantly predictive with some agile components to largely agile with a predictive component.

PMI's recent standards have moved further in the same direction. The PMBOK Guide's eighth edition presents its process guidance as reference material that applies to predictive, agile and hybrid work alike. The choice of approach is now treated as one of the first decisions in managing any piece of work, not a matter of organizational style.

children.text: How Chapter 15 Classifies Vermont's Components

The book assigns predictive management to components with fixed statutory deadlines and well-defined deliverables: the reference-based-pricing methodology rulemaking, the Statewide Strategic Plan (with adaptive elements), the analytics-vendor deployment, Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic certification, and AHS restructuring. Each has a defined end product and a date that cannot move.

Adaptive management goes to components where requirements evolve and rapid learning beats adherence to a fixed plan. The statewide AI-governance framework is the clearest case, because the regulatory landscape is changing faster than any fixed plan could anticipate. The Care Integration Network build-out depends on vendor outputs and an evolving FHIR ecosystem. Blueprint medical-home expansion proceeds practice by practice. And the HEROI equity-scoring methodology iterates as data quality improves.

The fourteen-hospital transformation planning effort is the book's hybrid example: fixed deliverables, because each hospital's plan is due on a schedule, with hospital-specific content developed iteratively inside that frame.

children.text: Why the Distinction Matters for the Portfolio

Using the wrong approach fails in predictable ways. Managing an adaptive component predictively produces a detailed plan that is out of date before it is approved, followed by a series of change requests that consume more effort than the work. Managing a predictive component adaptively risks missing a statutory deliverable while the team iterates on details that were never in question.

For the portfolio office, the approach also determines what progress looks like. A predictive component reports against its baseline: activities done, milestones met, earned value. An adaptive component reports learning and increments delivered: what was built this cycle, what was tested, what changed in the plan as a result. Holding an adaptive component to a baseline it was never meant to have will show it as permanently late; holding a predictive component only to increments will hide a slipping legal deadline.

The approach also interacts with the dependency logic from Lesson 7. Adaptive components upstream of a gate are especially important to watch, because their finish date is less certain by design. The Care Integration Network is adaptive and sits in the Technology pillar that gates Economics. A portfolio manager should track its increments closely, because the gate opens when enough of the network is genuinely usable, not when a planned date arrives.

Hybrid components need the most care, because they carry both risks. The fourteen hospital plans have fixed due dates, so the portfolio office must track them predictively at the boundary. Inside each plan, content is developed iteratively with each hospital, so the office should expect revisions and judge each plan by whether it is converging on a usable result rather than by whether it matches an early draft.

body.analogy: Building a bridge and designing a new clinical workflow are both projects, but nobody would manage them the same way. The bridge needs a complete design before the first pour, because changing it halfway is ruinous. The workflow is best tried with a few clinicians, adjusted and tried again, because no one can predict in advance how it will feel at 3 a.m. on a busy unit.
body.concept: Predictive and adaptive approaches

children.text: Governing a Mixed Portfolio

A portfolio that mixes approaches needs governance that respects both. The book's roadmap sets a fixed cadence for the whole portfolio: monthly governance reviews, quarterly performance reviews against the Vermont Scorecard, and annual portfolio rebalancing. Within that cadence, predictive components are reviewed against their baselines and stage gates, and adaptive components against their cycle outputs and the outcomes they are aiming at.

Two practices make the mix workable. First, every component, whatever its approach, states the outcome it exists to produce and the date by which the portfolio needs it, so adaptive work cannot drift indefinitely. Second, adaptive components declare in advance what evidence will show they are ready to open the next gate, so the decision is made on agreed criteria rather than on a plan date or a mood.

The book's credential mapping follows from the same distinction: PMP for the predictive components, PMI-ACP for the adaptive ones, which is why it recommends both for the Policy and Technology program managers whose pillars contain both kinds of work.

children.text: Classify Your Own Components

Take the inventory from Lesson 3 and add an approach column. For each component ask two questions: are its requirements stable enough to plan in detail now, and is there a fixed external deadline for a defined deliverable? Two yes answers point to predictive management. Two no answers point to adaptive. Mixed answers usually point to hybrid: fixed boundaries with iterative content inside them.

Then check your staffing against the classification. Teams experienced only in predictive delivery often struggle with adaptive components and vice versa. Where a pillar contains both, its program lead needs fluency in both, which is the logic behind the book's dual-credential recommendation for Policy and Technology.

Finally, check your reporting. If every component reports the same metrics in the same format, the portfolio office is probably holding some components to the wrong measure. Adjusting the report template to the approach is a small change that removes a large source of false alarms and false comfort.
A component reported as permanently late may simply be adaptive work held to a predictive baseline. Check the approach before you check the team.

PMI's Agile Practice Guide, developed with the Agile Alliance in 2017, treats hybrid life cycles as a legitimate fit-for-purpose choice.

The wrong approach fails predictably: stale plans and change-request overload, or missed legal deadlines.
A mixed portfolio shares one governance cadence but reports each component on the measure that fits its approach, with need-by dates and agreed gate evidence.
The book maps PMP to predictive work and PMI-ACP to adaptive work, which is why Policy and Technology leads need both.

children.text: A Portfolio Manager cannot manage nineteen components directly. Below the portfolio sits the program level, and in the five-pillar framework the programs are the pillars themselves. Each pillar needs a program manager who manages its components as a coherent whole and answers to the Portfolio Manager for them.

This lesson describes the five pillar program manager roles in Chapter 15, the credentials that fit them, and the three-tier governance structure PMI defines for a portfolio. It closes with what changes when the same structure is built inside a hospital rather than a state agency.

Structure is the part of portfolio management that organizations most often skip, because it feels like overhead. The book's argument is that it is the opposite: without it, the coordination work still has to happen, but it happens informally, inconsistently and invisibly.
Each Pillar Is a Program

In PMI's terms, a program is a group of related projects managed together for benefits no single project could deliver. Chapter 15 treats each pillar as exactly that. The Technology pillar's components, the analytics platform, the health information exchange, the Care Integration Network and the AI-governance framework, only produce a usable data substrate together. The Economics pillar's components only change hospital incentives together.

So each pillar needs a designated accountability point with the skills and authority to manage its components as one program. The book is careful that these roles are not exclusive to the state agency. For hospital-owned components, the program manager may sit in a hospital's project office; for state-administered components, in AHS. What matters is that every pillar has one.

The pillar program manager's distinctive job is managing interdependencies inside the pillar and reporting the pillar's readiness upward, because the pillar's readiness is what opens or closes the gate for the pillars downstream of it.
A pillar program manager owns two things a project manager does not: the dependencies between the pillar's own components, and the pillar's readiness as an input to every pillar downstream.
Five Roles, One Framework

Figure 15.4 of the book sets out the five roles. Each pairs a project-management credential with domain experience, names the key deliverables the role is accountable for, and specifies a dual reporting line: to the Portfolio Manager for the portfolio, and to the domain leader who owns the pillar's subject matter.

The dual reporting is deliberate. The Payment Reform Program Manager answers both to the Portfolio Manager and to the Green Mountain Care Board's executive director, because the board owns hospital budgets and pricing. The Clinical Transformation Program Manager answers to the Portfolio Manager and to the Blueprint director and Medicaid medical director, because clinical programs run through them. Dual reporting keeps the program manager connected to both the portfolio's logic and the domain's expertise.

Notice that the deliverables are dated and specific: analytics vendor operational by January 2027, reference-based-pricing rates in effect for FY2028, 100% patient-centered medical home coverage by FY2028, the portfolio office operational by the second quarter of 2027. A program manager is accountable for outcomes with dates, not for activity.

children.text: The Credentials: PMP and PMI-ACP

The book recommends PMI's Project Management Professional (PMP) credential for every pillar role, with PMI's Agile Certified Practitioner (PMI-ACP) credential added where a pillar's work is adaptive. The PMP is the general credential for leading projects. PMI's current eligibility rules offer three paths: a secondary diploma with 60 months of project-management experience; a bachelor's degree with 36 months; or a degree from a GAC-accredited program with 24 months. The first two also require 35 hours of project-management education, which a CAPM certification can satisfy, and experience counts within the past eight years.

The PMI-ACP covers agile methods. PMI requires 21 contact hours of formal training in agile practices together with agile project experience; published summaries of the exact experience rules differ, so candidates should check PMI's current handbook. Lesson 8 of this course explains why the book pairs PMI-ACP with the Technology and Policy roles in particular: the AI-governance framework, the Care Integration Network build-out and parts of rulemaking evolve faster than a fixed plan can anticipate.

As with the PfMP, the credential signals method rather than guaranteeing results. The book's pairing of each credential with specific domain experience, health policy, informatics, finance, clinical practice or hospital turnaround, reflects that pillar program managers have to understand the substance of their components well enough to judge when one is truly ready.

children.text: Three Governance Tiers

PMI defines three tiers of portfolio governance. The Portfolio Governance Body provides strategic oversight: it sets direction, approves the portfolio's composition and makes decisions above the Portfolio Manager's authority. For Vermont, the book identifies this body as the AHS Secretary together with the HCAC and the Green Mountain Care Board. The Portfolio Management Office provides operational coordination; in Vermont that is currently the under-resourced AHS Health Reform Office. The component level is the individual programs and projects.

The first of the five objections answered in Chapter 15 turns on this distinction. Asked whether the HCAC and monthly reports already provide portfolio management, the book replies that the HCAC is a governance body, not a portfolio office. It provides oversight, not an integrated master schedule, resource-conflict resolution, a maintained risk register or earned-value tracking. The HCAC is the governance tier; it needs a Portfolio Manager and an office to give it the data to govern.

The book lists the gaps that establishing the portfolio office must fill: a dedicated Portfolio Manager with the PfMP credential, two PMO analysts, portfolio-management software, standardized reporting, the five pillar program managers, and formal project leads for all nineteen components.

children.text: The Same Structure Inside a Hospital

A hospital or health system running its own transformation faces the same structural problem at smaller scale. Its governance body is the board or a board committee. Its portfolio office is the transformation or strategy office. Its programs may map to the five pillars, or to service lines with the pillars as a cross-check. What carries over is the principle: each level exists, is staffed, and knows which decisions belong to it.

The book's advice to hospital project-office leaders is to treat Figure 15.3 as a template. Build the inventory, assign each component a pillar, an owner, a type and a stage gate, and then assign each pillar an accountable program lead. Small organizations can combine roles, one person leading two pillars, but should not leave a pillar without a named lead.

Hospitals also sit inside the state's portfolio. Several of Vermont's components are hospital-owned, and the fourteen hospital transformation plans are a single Operations program at state level. A hospital whose own portfolio office maps cleanly onto the state's pillars makes coordination with the state far easier, because both sides then speak about the same components in the same terms.
Combining roles is acceptable in a small organization. Leaving a pillar with no named program lead is not; that pillar's dependencies will go unmanaged.

points: In the five-pillar framework each pillar is a program: its components only deliver their benefit together.
Every pillar needs a designated program manager, who may sit in the state agency or in a hospital project office depending on who owns the components.
The five roles in Figure 15.4 pair a PMP with domain experience, carry dated deliverables and report both to the Portfolio Manager and to a domain leader.
PMP eligibility requires 60, 36 or 24 months of project experience depending on education; PMI-ACP requires 21 hours of agile training plus agile experience.
PMI's three governance tiers are the governance body, the portfolio office and the component level; Vermont's governance body is the AHS Secretary with the HCAC and GMCB.
The HCAC is a governance body, not a portfolio office; it needs a Portfolio Manager and an office to supply the data it governs with.
Hospitals can mirror the same structure at smaller scale, combining roles if needed but never leaving a pillar without a named lead.

The book's answer is that the HCAC is the right governance body but needs a Portfolio Manager and an office to give it the data it needs to govern; it does not replace either.

children.text: Healthcare transformation is usually discussed as a problem of policy design: the right payment model, the right mandate, the right technology. Chapter 15 of Transforming Healthcare makes a different argument. Once the design is settled, transformation becomes a problem of delivery, and delivery at this scale is a discipline with its own standards, roles and tools. Most transformation efforts never adopt that discipline, and the gap shows up as missed deadlines, stranded investments and reforms that exist on paper but not in practice.

This opening lesson makes the case that the gap is real and costly. It shows how every concept in the five-pillar framework maps onto a project-management discipline, what the evidence says about the cost of poor delivery, what a well-documented federal health program failure looked like from the inside, and how the same gap appears in Vermont's transformation today.

The rest of the course then builds the discipline step by step: defining the portfolio, staffing and governing it, scheduling it by dependency, managing its risks, tracing its benefits, and making the case for paying for it.
Every Framework Concept Is a Management Discipline

Chapter 15 opens with an observation that reframes the whole book. Every concept introduced in the earlier chapters maps to an established project-management discipline, whether or not it was presented in those terms. Defining the five pillars is scope management: deciding what is in and out of each body of work. The execution sequence is schedule management with dependency logic. The failure cascade, in which a weak upstream pillar degrades everything downstream, is risk management. The implementation matrix is cost and resource management. The Vermont Scorecard is benefits-realization management.

Put those together and the five-pillar framework is, in its entirety, a portfolio-management architecture. The book's diagnosis of Vermont follows directly: the state has the analytical architecture but is not managing its transformation as a portfolio. The analysis exists; the operating machinery to act on it does not.

This matters because analysis and delivery fail differently. A flawed analysis can be corrected by better analysis. A delivery gap cannot: no amount of additional insight will coordinate nineteen components owned by different agencies against a single statutory deadline. That takes people with the authority and the tools to do it.

The five-pillar framework tells you what has to be built and in what order. Portfolio management is the discipline that makes sure it actually gets built in that order, by people accountable for the result.

children.text: What Poor Delivery Costs

The Project Management Institute (PMI) surveys organizations every year on how their projects perform, in a report called Pulse of the Profession. Its 2017 edition put the cost of poor project performance at about 9.7% of project spending: roughly $97 million wasted for every $1 billion invested. The 2018 edition put it at 9.9%. These are cross-industry averages, not healthcare-specific figures, but they set the order of magnitude: a meaningful share of every transformation budget is at risk from how the work is managed, not from what the work is.

The same research program has consistently found large differences between organizations that manage delivery well and those that do not. PMI's 2014 report, The High Cost of Low Performance, found that high-performing organizations completed 89% of their projects successfully against 36% for low performers, and that projects aligned to organizational strategy succeeded more often than misaligned ones. Alignment to strategy is precisely what portfolio management exists to provide.

Treat these figures with appropriate care. They are self-reported survey results, the definitions of success have shifted between editions, and none of them is a forecast for any particular program. Their value is directional: across thousands of organizations, the way work is governed shows up in whether it delivers.

children.text: A Health Case From the Inside: HealthCare.gov

The most thoroughly documented delivery failure in recent American health policy is the October 2013 launch of HealthCare.gov, the federal insurance marketplace created under the Affordable Care Act. Two federal reviews examined what went wrong, and both describe management failures rather than a flawed policy idea.

The Government Accountability Office's July 2014 report, GAO-14-694, found that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) began building the marketplace systems without effective planning or oversight. Task orders were issued while key requirements were still unknown, including how many states would use the federal marketplace and how many people might enroll. Unclear guidance left confusion over who had authority to approve contractor requests to spend funds. Key governance reviews were delayed, and the site launched without verification that it met its performance requirements. The HHS Office of Inspector General's 2016 case study, based on interviews with 86 officials, staff and contractors, reached a similar picture and also recorded the recovery: CMS restored the site for high consumer use within two months and adopted more effective organizational practices.

Every element of that list is a portfolio-management failure. Requirements were not defined before work began. Authority was not assigned. Governance checkpoints were skipped. Nobody verified that the component everything else depended on was ready before the date arrived. The recovery, equally, came from putting integrated management in place, not from changing the policy.

body.content:
GAO-14-694 found that CMS issued task orders before key technical requirements were known, that unclear guidance caused confusion over who could approve contractor spending, that key governance reviews were delayed, and that the site launched without verification that it met performance requirements.
The HHS Inspector General's case study (OEI-06-14-00350) found that CMS recovered the website for high consumer use within two months and adopted more effective organizational practices, and called on the agency to keep applying those lessons.

body.message: HealthCare.gov is often filed as an IT failure. The federal reviews describe something more general: a program with a fixed public deadline, many contractors and no single point of integrated accountability. That description fits most state health-transformation efforts, whatever their technology content.

children.text: Vermont's Version of the Gap

Chapter 15 applies the same lens to Vermont. The Agency of Human Services (AHS) is managing the state's transformation as a collection of projects without the program or portfolio infrastructure to coordinate them, so work is sequenced by who is available rather than by what the portfolio needs. The book is explicit that this is not a criticism of AHS staff, who are executing an extraordinary mandate with insufficient capacity. It is a structural observation: the capacity does not yet exist.

The need was identified early. Oliver Wyman's Act 167 report recommended in 2024 that AHS establish a dedicated project-management function, and the November 2025 transformation report repeated the finding. Chapter 15's contribution is to define that function precisely, using PMI's standards, and to schedule it against the January 15, 2028 deadline for the Statewide Health Care Delivery Strategic Plan.

The scale is what makes the gap dangerous. Chapter 15 counts 19 components in the transformation portfolio, ten scored risks in its register, and fourteen hospital transformation plans the portfolio must coordinate. No component manager, however capable, can see across all of that from inside one component.

children.text: What This Course Covers

The course follows the order in which a portfolio function is actually built. Track 1, which you are in now, establishes the levels of management and how to define a portfolio by inventorying its components. Track 2 staffs and governs it: the Portfolio Manager, the five pillar program managers, the governance tiers and the ten knowledge areas a portfolio office has to run.

Track 3 schedules the portfolio by dependency rather than by deadline, chooses predictive, adaptive or hybrid management for each component, and measures progress with earned value. Track 4 builds and reads the risk register and traces every component to the benefits that justify it. Track 5 makes the business case, answers the standard objections, and ends with a capstone in which you build and run a portfolio of your own on the platform's tools.

Two companion resources sit alongside this course. Five Pillars, One Imperative introduces the portfolio argument in a single Track 8 lesson, and the Transformation Leadership course includes a hands-on workshop on running the sequencing test. This course goes deeper on the management system itself; the workshop is the best place to practise one technique in isolation.

A useful test to carry through the course comes from the chapter's advice to legislators and boards: which component is currently the binding constraint on all the others, who owns it, and what would it take to accelerate it? An organization managing a real portfolio can answer in one sentence.

points: Every concept in the five-pillar framework maps to a project-management discipline: scope, schedule, risk, cost and resources, and benefits realization.
PMI's Pulse of the Profession put waste from poor project performance at about 9.7% of project spending in 2017 and 9.9% in 2018, across industries.
High-performing organizations complete far more projects successfully than low performers, and strategic alignment, the core job of portfolio management, is part of the difference.
GAO found that HealthCare.gov was built without effective planning or oversight: undefined requirements, unclear authority, delayed governance reviews and no verification before launch.
Vermont's transformation is being managed as a collection of projects; Oliver Wyman recommended a project-management function in 2024 and the November 2025 report repeated it.
Vermont's portfolio has 19 components, ten scored risks and fourteen hospital plans converging on the January 15, 2028 Strategic Plan.
The test of a real portfolio is whether its managers can name the binding constraint, its owner and what would accelerate it in one sentence.

These are the failures portfolio and program management exist to prevent, which is why the case is a lesson for any large health transformation.

title: The Project-Management Gap in Healthcare Transformation

children.text: The single most common error in managing a large transformation is managing it at the wrong level. A collection of interdependent programs gets run as a list of projects, each on time and on budget by its own measures, while the whole fails to produce what it was for. Avoiding that error starts with three words that are used loosely in everyday speech and precisely in professional practice: project, program and portfolio.

This lesson defines the three levels as PMI's standards define them, introduces the current editions of those standards, applies the hierarchy to Vermont's transformation, and gives you a quick diagnostic for the level at which your own work is being managed.

None of this is bureaucracy for its own sake. Each level answers a different question and is judged by a different measure of success, and choosing the wrong level means asking the wrong question of the work.
Three Levels, Three Questions

In PMI's hierarchy, a project is a temporary endeavor that creates a unique result, with a defined scope, schedule and budget. A program is a group of related projects managed together to produce benefits that none of them could produce alone. A portfolio is a collection of programs, projects and operations managed as a group to achieve an organization's strategy.

Each level asks a different question. A project asks whether the deliverable was produced as specified. A program asks whether the related projects together produced the intended benefit. A portfolio asks whether the organization is doing the right things, in the right order, with its resources, to achieve its strategy. A project can succeed while its program fails, and a program can succeed while the portfolio fails, if the program was the wrong one to run or was run at the wrong time.

The levels also differ in what they manage. Projects manage tasks and deliverables. Programs manage the interdependencies between projects and the benefits they produce together. Portfolios manage priorities, resource allocation and strategic alignment across everything, including the decision to start, pause or stop programs.

The levels are not ranks of importance. A brilliant project manager and a mediocre portfolio manager can coexist, and the transformation will still suffer, because each level does work the others cannot. What matters is that every level exists, is staffed, and knows which decisions belong to it.

body.analogy: Think of a hospital building program. Pouring the foundation is a project. Building, equipping and staffing the new emergency department is a program: several projects that only deliver value when all are done. Deciding whether the system builds the emergency department this year, or a primary-care network first, and moving capital between them as conditions change, is portfolio management.

children.text: The Standards Behind the Levels

PMI publishes a separate standard for each level, and each has moved on since the book's sources were first assembled. The PMBOK Guide, the project-level reference, reached its eighth edition in November 2025. That edition condenses the seventh edition's twelve principles into six, organizes practice into seven performance domains, and brings back process-level guidance as flexible reference material for predictive, agile and hybrid work.

The Standard for Program Management reached its fifth edition in 2024. It is principle-led, identifying eight principles that guide program management, and adds a Collaboration performance domain. The Standard for Portfolio Management is still in its fourth edition, published in November 2017; PMI has a fifth edition in development and ran public comment periods on drafts during 2026, but as of this lesson it has not been published.

Chapter 15 cites the fourth editions of the portfolio and program standards and the sixth through eighth editions of the PMBOK Guide. The definitions used in this course are stable across those editions; what has changed is mainly how the standards are organized, with recent editions moving from prescriptive processes toward principles and performance domains.

children.text: Standards give a shared vocabulary. When a state agency, a hospital PMO and a federal partner all mean the same thing by 'program' and 'benefit', coordination becomes much easier. That shared vocabulary is a large part of their value.
Vermont's Transformation at Three Levels

Figure 15.2 of the book applies the hierarchy to Vermont. At the project level are bounded pieces of work with a deliverable: deploying the analytics vendor that gives AHS and the Green Mountain Care Board access to VHCURES claims data, closing coding gaps at a single hospital, deploying the Collaborative Care Model at one Blueprint practice, or completing the rulemaking for reference-based pricing.

At the program level are groups of related projects that only deliver value together: the Technology pillar program, combining VHCURES analytics, the VITL health information exchange, the Care Integration Network and AI governance; the Blueprint patient-centered medical home expansion across thirteen health-service-area projects; and the design and implementation of hospital global budgets. At the portfolio level is the whole: all 19 components across the five pillars, aligned to Act 167's five goals and the January 2028 Strategic Plan.

The book's finding is that Vermont operates at all three levels but has management infrastructure only at the first. Projects have managers. Programs mostly do not have program managers. The portfolio has no portfolio manager. Work is therefore coordinated, where it is coordinated at all, through the goodwill and spare capacity of people whose formal job is a single project.
