children.text: The Level Error and Its Symptoms

Managing a portfolio as a set of projects produces recognizable symptoms. Status reports are long lists of green, amber and red projects with no view of which matters most. Two components compete for the same scarce staff and the conflict is settled by whoever escalates loudest. A component finishes on time but cannot be used because the work it depended on is not ready. Nobody has the authority to stop or pause a component, so the portfolio only ever grows.

The most dangerous symptom is that every individual manager can be doing well. When each project is measured only against its own scope, schedule and budget, a portfolio can be failing while every dashboard is green. The failure lives in the spaces between projects, where no one is measured.

The cure is not more reporting. It is assigning someone the job, and the authority, of managing the spaces between projects: first at the program level within each pillar, and then at the portfolio level across all five.

The level error is also expensive in a quieter way. Without a portfolio layer, nothing is ever stopped. Components that have lost their purpose, because a federal model was withdrawn or a better approach emerged, keep consuming staff and money because no one has the authority to end them. PMI's portfolio standard treats terminating components as a normal, healthy decision; Chapter 15 gives Vermont's Portfolio Manager the duty of recommending termination when a component's benefits are no longer achievable.

body.message: If every component in your status report is on track and the transformation as a whole is still slipping, you are almost certainly managing at the wrong level. The question to ask is not which project is late, but which dependency between projects nobody owns.
body.title: Green dashboards, failing portfolio

children.text: Diagnose the Level of Your Own Work

You can tell the level at which your organization is managing its transformation by asking a few direct questions. The answers usually reveal whether a program and portfolio layer exists in practice, regardless of what the organization chart says.

If the answers point to project-level management only, the next lesson's exercise, building a complete inventory of components, is the place to start. A portfolio cannot be managed until it has been defined.

title: Project, Program, Portfolio: Getting the Levels Right

children.text: A risk register is a list. A portfolio manager needs to see a shape: which risks cluster, which share a cause, which would trigger others, and which are scored modestly but still demand action now. Chapter 15 makes that shift by plotting the register by probability and impact, and by reading it against the dependency logic of the whole book.

This lesson reads Vermont's register the way the book does: as a heat map, as a set of risks with shared causes, and as a set of signals that should trigger escalation. It then shows how the platform's simulators turn the register's two Technology risks into something you can watch happen.
The aim is to move from asking how big each risk is to asking what the risks together say about where the portfolio is fragile.
The Heat Map

Figure 15.7 plots each risk on a grid, probability on one axis and impact on the other. The book's comment is that the register's shape is clearer than its rows. The two risks scored 20 share the critical corner of the map, high probability and critical impact, and one of them is the absence of the portfolio function itself.

That observation carries the chapter's whole argument. The single most dangerous condition in the portfolio is not a technical failure or a budget shortfall. It is the lack of anyone positioned to manage the other risks. A register whose top risk is 'nobody is managing this register' is telling its readers what to do first.

The map also shows what sits in the middle. Social-risk adjustment (R-08) scores 12, mid-map. The book's reminder is that a moderate score is not a licence to wait: the sequencing test says this component has no upstream blocker and should already be running. Risk score and dependency status answer different questions, and the portfolio manager needs both.

Risk score tells you how bad a risk would be. Dependency status tells you whether the work that prevents it can start now. A moderate risk whose prevention is unblocked deserves action before a severe risk whose prevention must wait.
Shared Causes and Correlated Risks

Risks on a register are often treated as independent, but in a five-pillar portfolio many share a cause. R-01, the analytics vendor not being operational, and R-06, persistent VITL connectivity gaps, are both failures of the Technology pillar. If Technology slips, both are likely to materialize together, and through the dependency chain they then degrade Economics and Clinical work at the same time.

Correlation changes how risks should be managed. Two risks that would each be survivable alone can be overwhelming together. A portfolio manager who mitigates R-01 and R-06 separately, with different owners and no shared plan, may miss that the most effective mitigation for both is the same: protecting and resourcing the Technology program as a whole.

Capacity risks correlate too. R-03, an overcommitted agency producing a non-binding Strategic Plan, and R-10, no portfolio infrastructure, both stem from the same shortage of management capacity. The book's response to R-03 includes establishing the portfolio office, the same action that avoids R-10. One well-chosen response can retire several risks.

Correlation also runs through external risks. Federal Medicaid cuts (R-05) and the loss of the EAST Fund backstop after the AHEAD withdrawal hit the same Clinical and Economics components at once. Scenario planning that assumes both happen together is more honest than planning for each separately and hoping they do not coincide.

children.text: Watching a Risk Happen in the Simulators

Chapter 15's platform guide suggests a direct way to see why the Technology risks dominate. Open the HTR Simulator at /htr-simulator, load the Vermont, Fall 2026 scenario, and lower the Technology score. Economics and Clinical fall with it. The book calls this the risk register's R-01 and R-06 in visual form.

The effect comes from how the simulator models dependency. Each pillar is gated on the delivered strength of the pillars upstream of it, not on their nominal scores, so a weaker Technology pillar caps Economics, and the capped Economics in turn caps Clinical. A risk that materializes in one pillar propagates down the chain, which is exactly why cross-pillar risks belong on the portfolio register.

The Impact Simulation at /impact-simulation lets you model what a single component slipping does to the rest of the portfolio, and shows which components have no slack: the ones whose slip moves other pillars' outcomes. Together the two tools turn an abstract score into a visible consequence, which is often what a governance body needs before it will fund a mitigation.

children.text: When to Escalate

Escalation is a response in its own right: referring a risk to a higher level when it exceeds the current owner's authority. In a portfolio, escalation paths follow the governance tiers from Track 2. A component lead escalates to the pillar program manager, the program manager to the Portfolio Manager, and the Portfolio Manager to the governance body, which for Vermont is the AHS Secretary with the HCAC and the Green Mountain Care Board.

Good escalation is triggered by rules agreed in advance, not by frustration. Typical triggers are a score crossing a threshold, a risk spanning pillars owned by different program managers, a response that needs resources the owner does not control, and a risk to a component on the portfolio's true critical path. Writing these triggers down protects owners from being blamed for escalating and protects the governance body from surprises.

R-10 shows the limit of escalation. Its owner in the register is the AHS Secretary, the top of the structure, because the risk concerns whether the structure exists at all. When the highest-scored risk is owned at the top, the governance body cannot delegate it; it has to act.

Escalation should also flow downward. When the governance body decides on an escalated risk, the decision and its reasoning need to return to the people who raised it, so the same risk is not escalated again next month and so owners learn what the governance body will and will not decide.

body.message: Escalating a risk moves the decision to someone with more authority. It does not remove the original owner's responsibility to supply the analysis, the options and the consequences of inaction. An escalation without those is just a complaint.
body.title: Escalation is not abdication

children.text: A Monthly Reading Routine

Each month, before the governance review, the portfolio office should read the register in three passes. First, the heat map: what has moved toward the critical corner, and why? Second, shared causes: which risks have the same root, and is there a single response that addresses several? Third, dependency status: which risks can be reduced by work that is unblocked today, regardless of score?

The output is short: the two or three risks that need a decision from the governance body this month, with options and consequences. That is what turns a register from a compliance artifact into the main agenda of portfolio governance.

Keep a record of how each month's top risks were handled. Over a year, that record is evidence for federal partners, legislators and auditors that the portfolio was actively managed, which is itself one of the benefits the book claims for a portfolio office.
The register's best monthly output is not the full table. It is two or three decisions the governance body must make now, each with options and the cost of not deciding.

children.text: Every chapter of Transforming Healthcare analyzes risk: what happens if a mandate is weakened, if data infrastructure is late, if federal funding falls. Chapter 15 observes that Vermont analyzes these risks but does not manage them operationally, because no maintained register exists. Analysis that lives in reports is not management. Management means a named owner, a chosen response, and a regular review.

This lesson builds the portfolio risk register the way Chapter 15 does: what goes in each column, how risks are scored, which response strategies are available, and how Vermont's ten risks look when written in that format. The next lesson reads the finished register for what it says about the portfolio as a whole.

A portfolio register differs from a project register in one important way. Its risks usually span more than one component and often more than one pillar, and the most serious ones concern the dependencies between pillars rather than the work inside any single component.
What a Portfolio Register Records

Figure 15.6 of the book uses a standard format with eight columns. Each risk has an identifier and a plain statement of what might happen and what it would cause. It records the pillars affected, the probability and the impact, a score combining the two, the response chosen, and the owner accountable for carrying out the response.

Writing the risk statement well matters more than it seems. Good statements name a cause and a consequence: the analytics vendor is not operational by January 2027, so hospitals enter Act 68 global budgets without financial-management capability. A vague statement such as 'data problems' cannot be owned, scored or responded to, because no one can tell when it has happened or what would prevent it.

The pillars column is what makes the register a portfolio register. Six of Vermont's ten risks touch two pillars, and one touches all five. Those cross-pillar risks are exactly the ones no single component manager would put on their own register, because no single component owns them.

The owner column deserves the same care as the risk statement. An owner must be a person or role with the authority to carry out the response, not a committee or an organization. Where the book names two owners, such as a program manager together with the Portfolio Manager, it is signalling that the response needs both the pillar's expertise and the portfolio's authority over resources.

children.text: Scoring: Probability Times Impact

Chapter 15 scores each risk as probability multiplied by impact. Probability is rated Low (1), Low to Medium (2.5), Medium (3), Medium to High (3.75) or High (4). Impact is rated Low (1), Medium (3), High (4) or Critical (5). Bands that straddle two levels are scored at the midpoint, which is why some scores are not whole numbers.

On that scale the highest possible score is 20: a high-probability risk with critical impact. Two of Vermont's risks reach it. R-01 is the analytics vendor not being operational by January 2027. R-10 is the portfolio-management infrastructure itself not being established before the 2027 deadlines, leaving the transformation managed as a collection of projects.

Scores rank risks for attention; they are not precise measurements. The value of a fixed scale is consistency: two people scoring the same risk should land close together, and a risk's score can be compared from month to month as conditions change.

children.text: Five Ways to Respond

PMI practice recognizes five responses to a threat. Avoid changes the plan so the risk cannot occur. Mitigate reduces its probability or its impact. Transfer shifts its consequences to another party, typically through a contract or insurance. Accept takes no proactive action beyond monitoring, sometimes with a contingency reserve. Escalate hands the risk to a higher level, such as the portfolio or the governance body, when it is beyond the current owner's authority.

Vermont's register uses several of these and pairs each with specific actions. R-10 is to be avoided by putting a Portfolio Manager in seat by January 2027 and the portfolio office in operation by the second quarter of 2027. R-04, a governor committed to modifying Act 68, is accepted and monitored, with actions to build irreversibility and maintain legislative relationships, because the portfolio cannot remove a political risk. Most other risks are mitigated.

The register also uses accelerate as a response for two risks, R-01 and R-08. Acceleration is a form of mitigation aimed at time: for R-01, a parallel route to claims data and compensating investment in coding accuracy; for R-08, making the Economics program manager lead social-risk adjustment as co-equal with global-budget design.

A response is only real if it has actions, an owner and a date. 'Mitigate' written alone in the response column is a label, not a plan. Each of Vermont's responses lists concrete actions, such as scenario planning for a 30% reduction in Medicaid-funded investment under R-05, which is what allows the monthly review to check whether the response is actually under way.

children.text: Vermont's Ten Risks

Read as a whole, Vermont's register is dominated by dependency and capacity. Two risks concern Technology readiness: the analytics vendor (R-01) and persistent gaps in connectivity through VITL, the state's health information exchange (R-06). Two concern capacity to manage the transformation: an overcommitted agency producing a non-binding Strategic Plan (R-03) and the absence of portfolio infrastructure (R-10). Others concern the payment design itself, the external environment and clinical ownership.

The external risks are worth noting because they cannot be managed away. Federal Medicaid cuts under H.R. 1 constrain Medicaid-funded clinical investments, with no EAST Fund backstop after Vermont's withdrawal from the AHEAD model (R-05). A change of governor could put the mandatory architecture at risk (R-04). For risks like these, the portfolio's job is to plan scenarios and build resilience, not to promise prevention.

Every risk has a named owner, and the owners are mostly program managers and the Portfolio Manager. That is not an accident: a risk whose owner does not yet exist cannot be managed, which is one more reason R-10, the missing portfolio function, sits at the top of the register.

children.text: Build Your Own Register

Start from the inventory and the sequencing results from earlier lessons. The richest source of portfolio risks is the list of components where schedule pressure belongs: each gating component that might be late is a risk to everything waiting behind it. Add risks to the mandate, to funding, to capacity and to engagement, and write each as cause and consequence.

Score with a fixed scale, such as the one in Figure 15.6, and agree it in advance so scores are comparable. Then choose a response and a named owner for every risk scoring above a threshold you set. A risk without an owner should itself be escalated to the governance body, since an unowned risk is a governance failure.

Finally, set the cadence. The book's portfolio runs monthly governance reviews, and the register should be reviewed at each one: new risks added, scores updated, responses checked for whether they are actually happening. A register updated once a year is a document; one reviewed monthly is a management tool.

children.text: What does a portfolio office actually have to run? The PMBOK Guide's sixth edition, published in 2017, organized project management into ten knowledge areas. Later editions reorganized the same ground into principles and performance domains, but Chapter 15 argues that the ten areas remain the clearest checklist of the machinery a portfolio office has to operate.

This lesson walks the ten areas against Vermont's operational capacity, as Figure 15.5 of the book does. The pattern is consistent: the book addresses every area analytically, but the state lacks the operating machinery to manage it. The lesson then looks closely at integration and scheduling, where federal guidance offers practical standards, and closes with a way to use the checklist on your own organization.

Use the ten areas as an audit, not as a curriculum. The question for each is not whether your organization understands it but whether someone is actually running it, every month, across the whole portfolio.
From Knowledge Areas to Principles

The ten knowledge areas of the PMBOK Guide's sixth edition are integration, scope, schedule, cost, quality, resource, communications, risk, procurement and stakeholder management. Each describes a body of practice a project or portfolio needs. The seventh edition, published in 2021, moved away from that structure toward principles and performance domains. The eighth edition, published in November 2025, condensed the seventh edition's twelve principles into six, organized practice into seven performance domains, and restored process-level guidance as flexible reference material.

The book acknowledges the change and keeps the ten areas for a practical reason. As a checklist, they are concrete. A portfolio office either maintains an integrated master schedule or it does not; it either has a portfolio-level procurement strategy or it lets contracts one at a time. The principles-based editions are better guides to judgment, but the ten areas are a better audit of capacity.

Nothing in the later editions makes the ten areas wrong. They describe the same work organized differently. Using the older list as a checklist while reading the newer editions for method is a sensible way to combine the two.
A knowledge area is covered only when someone runs it across the whole portfolio on a regular cadence. Understanding it, or running it component by component, does not count.
Vermont's Gap, Area by Area

Figure 15.5 reads each area against Vermont's operational capacity. In integration, the dependency map, execution sequence and scorecard exist on paper, but operational integration does not. In scope, no pillar has a formal work-breakdown structure. In schedule, statutory deadlines are tracked in isolation rather than as an integrated master schedule. In cost, Rural Health Transformation Program spending is tracked for federal compliance, not for portfolio performance.

The remaining six follow the same pattern. Quality is measured program by program, with no portfolio aggregation. Resources are overcommitted, with no formal leveling across components. Communications and stakeholder engagement run component by component, with no portfolio-level strategy for hospitals, the Green Mountain Care Board, the HCAC, the Legislature or CMS. Risk is analyzed in the book but not managed operationally through a maintained register. Procurement lets contracts for analytics and technical assistance one component at a time.

The common thread is the absence of a portfolio layer. Each area is handled, if at all, inside individual components, and so the interactions between components, where the portfolio's real risks live, go unmanaged in all ten.

children.text: Integration and Schedule: The Master Schedule

Of the ten areas, integration and schedule matter most for a transformation with a single statutory deadline, and both converge on one artifact: the integrated master schedule. It brings every component's activities into one schedule, with the dependencies between them, so that the effect of one slip on everything downstream can be seen and managed.

The U.S. Government Accountability Office publishes the most widely used public standard for judging a schedule. Its Schedule Assessment Guide (GAO-16-89G), issued in December 2015, sets out ten best practices and four characteristics of a reliable schedule: comprehensive, well-constructed, credible and controlled. The practices include capturing and sequencing all activities, assigning resources, confirming that the critical path is valid, conducting a schedule risk analysis, updating the schedule with actual progress, and maintaining a baseline.

For a five-pillar portfolio, one addition matters: the schedule's logic must include the dependencies between pillars, not just between activities inside a component. A master schedule that links tasks within each component but treats the pillars as independent will produce a critical path that looks valid and is wrong, because it misses the gates. Track 3 returns to this point in detail.

children.text: Resources, Procurement and Stakeholders

Three of the ten areas are where portfolios most often fail quietly. Resource management at portfolio level means knowing that the same few analysts at the state agency are assigned to five components at once, and leveling that load deliberately rather than letting each component assume it has them. Without leveling, every component's schedule is optimistic, because each counts on people who are also counted elsewhere.

Procurement at portfolio level means designing contracts so that they fit the dependency structure: not letting a technical-assistance contract whose work depends on analytics capability before the analytics contract is in place, and avoiding several overlapping contracts each delivering part of the same capability. Stakeholder management at portfolio level means hospitals, regulators, the Legislature and federal partners hear one coherent account of the transformation rather than nineteen separate ones.

All three are invisible from inside a component. A component manager sees their own staff, their own contract and their own stakeholders. Only a portfolio view shows the double-booked analyst, the contract sequenced ahead of its dependency, or the hospital chief executive receiving conflicting messages from three state programs in the same week.

body.message: Buying external help without portfolio-level procurement adds work to the portfolio. Every contract has deliverables, deadlines and dependencies that must be sequenced, which is why the book warns that contracted support adds capacity but not authority.

children.text: Use the Checklist on Your Own Organization

The ten areas make a fast, honest audit of portfolio capacity. For each area, ask the same two questions: is it being run across the whole portfolio, and on what cadence? An area run inside each component but not across them counts as a gap, because that is where the portfolio's interactions are unmanaged.

Most organizations will find, as Vermont did, that they understand all ten and run few of them at portfolio level. That is not a failure of knowledge. It is the predictable result of having no portfolio layer, and it points directly at what a portfolio office has to take on first: usually integration, schedule, resource and risk, because those are where dependency failures show up earliest.

Record the audit alongside your component inventory from Lesson 3. Together they describe both what the portfolio contains and how well it is managed, and they form the baseline against which the portfolio office's progress can be measured.

children.text: Two Questions: What and Why

Cheap sequencing made genetic testing feasible, but "a genetic test" is not one thing. To use genetics in medicine you must understand two distinct dimensions: WHAT the test looks at (how much of the genome, examined how) and WHY it is being done (the clinical purpose). Confusing these is a common source of error — the right test depends on both.

This lesson maps both dimensions: the technical methods (from a single gene up to the whole genome) and the clinical purposes (diagnostic, predictive, carrier, pharmacogenomic). And it addresses the increasingly important question of direct-to-consumer testing versus clinical-grade testing, which differ in ways that matter enormously for patients.

The practical goal is to be able to reason about which test fits a clinical situation, what it can and cannot tell you, and how to interpret what comes back. A genetic test ordered or interpreted incorrectly can mislead a patient about their health, their cancer treatment, or their family — so understanding the test landscape is foundational clinical knowledge.

A genetic test has two dimensions: WHAT it examines (single gene up to whole genome) and WHY (diagnostic, predictive, carrier, or pharmacogenomic). The right test depends on both, and clinical-grade testing differs importantly from direct-to-consumer tests.
How Much of the Genome: The Methods

Tests differ in how much DNA they examine, trading focus for breadth. Single-gene testing looks at one specific gene — ideal when a condition has distinctive features and a known causative gene (e.g., testing the HBB gene for sickle cell disease, or testing a relative for a known familial variant). It is precise and inexpensive but blind to everything else.

Gene panels examine a defined set of genes — from a few to many hundreds — chosen because they could all explain a particular presentation (e.g., a hereditary-cancer panel, or a cardiomyopathy panel). Panels are the workhorse for conditions that can be caused by many genes. Going broader, whole exome sequencing (WES) reads the exome — only about 1 to 2 percent of the genome, but the protein-coding portion that harbors roughly 85 percent of known disease-causing variants — making it an efficient catch-all when the causative gene is unknown.

Whole genome sequencing (WGS) reads essentially all the DNA, coding and non-coding, providing the most complete picture; it is used when a strong genetic suspicion remains unexplained by WES. Separately, chromosomal microarray (CMA) detects large deletions, duplications, and copy-number changes (with higher detection than the older karyotype), and karyotyping visualizes whole-chromosome abnormalities. CMA and karyotype are mainstays of prenatal and developmental diagnosis. The general principle: start as targeted as the clinical question allows, and broaden only as needed.

children.text: Why the Test: The Clinical Purposes

The same sequencing technology serves very different clinical purposes, and the purpose shapes interpretation and counseling. Diagnostic testing seeks to confirm or rule out a suspected genetic condition in a symptomatic patient — answering "what does this person have?" Predictive (or presymptomatic) testing assesses future risk in a currently healthy person — for example, testing for a BRCA variant to gauge future cancer risk, or for a known familial condition.

Carrier testing identifies whether a healthy person carries a recessive variant they could pass to children even though they are unaffected themselves (relevant to cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, Tay-Sachs, and others) — central to reproductive planning. And pharmacogenomic testing examines genes affecting drug metabolism to guide medication choice and dosing (the subject of the next lesson).

These purposes carry different stakes and counseling needs. A diagnostic result explains current illness; a predictive result delivers risk information about a future that may never come, with profound psychological and family implications; a carrier result matters mainly for reproduction; a pharmacogenomic result guides prescribing. The same BRCA variant means different things tested diagnostically in a cancer patient versus predictively in their healthy sibling. Matching the purpose to the situation — and counseling appropriately — is as important as choosing the right method.

children.text: Clinical-Grade vs. Direct-to-Consumer

A patient may arrive with results from a direct-to-consumer (DTC) test like 23andMe, and understanding how these differ from clinical testing is essential. DTC tests are ordered by the consumer without a clinician, and report a mix of ancestry, traits, and FDA-authorized health information (some disease-risk variants, carrier status, and pharmacogenomic findings). In 2017, 23andMe became the first company to receive FDA marketing authorization for direct-to-consumer genetic health risk reports (following a 2015 authorization for a carrier-screening test), and in 2018 the FDA authorized its BRCA1/BRCA2 report, which covers just three variants.

But DTC tests have critical limitations that patients often misunderstand. They do not diagnose conditions — they identify predispositions, not certainties. They examine only specific, pre-selected variants, so they miss rare or novel variants in the same genes (a DTC BRCA test checks only a few variants and can give false reassurance to someone who actually carries a different pathogenic BRCA variant). And their accuracy and relevance vary by ancestry, because the variants tested were studied largely in particular populations.

The practical guidance: DTC results should not be acted on clinically without confirmation by a clinical-grade test and professional interpretation. A reassuring DTC result does not rule out a condition, and a concerning one must be verified before any medical decision. Clinical-grade testing — ordered and interpreted by professionals, often with genetic counseling — is the standard for any result that will drive care.

body.message: DTC tests check only a few pre-selected variants, so a "negative" result can falsely reassure someone who carries a different pathogenic variant the test did not look for. DTC results identify predispositions, not diagnoses, and vary in accuracy by ancestry. Never act clinically on a DTC result without confirmation by clinical-grade testing and professional interpretation.
body.title: A "Negative" Direct-to-Consumer Test Is Not Clinical Clearance

children.text: Choosing and Interpreting Tests Well

Putting the dimensions together, choosing a genetic test is a clinical reasoning exercise: define the question (diagnostic, predictive, carrier, pharmacogenomic), then pick the narrowest method that can answer it (single gene or panel if the candidates are known; WES or WGS if not). Broader is not always better — a whole genome generates far more variants of uncertain significance and incidental findings to interpret and counsel about.

Interpretation is where the difficulty lies, as the previous lessons established. Every test result must be read through the ACMG classification lens, and the broader the test, the more uncertain findings (VUS) and unexpected secondary findings it will surface — each requiring careful interpretation and, often, genetic counseling. The test is only the first step; making sense of the result, in the context of the patient and their family, is the harder work.

The throughline is that genetic testing is powerful but must be matched to purpose, chosen at the right breadth, distinguished from consumer testing, and interpreted carefully. With this map of the testing landscape established, the next lessons dive into the major clinical applications — pharmacogenomics, oncology, and hereditary conditions — where these tests are actually put to use to change care.

body.content:
A child presents with unexplained developmental delay and no clear diagnosis. A single-gene test would be a shot in the dark; a clinician might start with chromosomal microarray (to catch copy-number causes) and, if negative, proceed to whole exome sequencing to search broadly for a causative variant.
Contrast this with a healthy adult whose mother carries a known BRCA1 variant: here a targeted single-variant test for that specific familial variant is exactly right — precise, inexpensive, and definitive. Same toolkit, different question, different correct test.

children.text: Pushing Value Down to the Provider

A subtle but important point runs through this entire course: capitating an MCO transfers risk to the plan, but it does not automatically change how that plan pays the doctors and hospitals delivering care. An MCO can receive a capitated, value-oriented payment from the state and then turn around and pay its providers on straight fee-for-service — recreating the very volume incentives managed care was supposed to escape, just one layer down. Value-based purchasing (VBP) in Medicaid managed care is the effort to close that gap: to push value-based payment all the way down from the state, through the MCO, to the providers who actually deliver care.

This matters because the state’s ultimate goal is better care at sustainable cost, and that depends on the incentives facing the people at the bedside, not just the plan’s balance sheet. So states increasingly use their contracts with MCOs to require or encourage the plans to adopt value-based arrangements with their providers — shared savings, bundled payments, capitation, pay-for-performance, and the like. VBP in Medicaid is, in essence, the state using its leverage over MCOs to spread value-based payment throughout the delivery system.

This lesson examines how states drive provider-level value-based payment through their MCOs, the frameworks they use to define it, the targets they set, and the powerful financial mechanism — state directed payments — that increasingly carries these efforts. It connects the risk continuum from the hospital-finance course directly to the Medicaid managed care machinery built throughout this one.

Key Concept: Value-based purchasing (VBP) in Medicaid managed care is the state’s use of its MCO contracts to require or encourage plans to pay their providers through value-based arrangements (shared savings, bundles, capitation, pay-for-performance) — pushing value-based payment from the state, through the plan, to the provider level.

children.text: How States Drive VBP Through MCOs

States generally use two approaches to drive value-based payment through their Medicaid MCOs. The first is setting value-based payment targets — requiring that a certain percentage of an MCO’s provider payments flow through value-based arrangements, without dictating exactly which models. The second is prescriptively directing MCOs to adopt specific payment models — telling plans precisely what kind of value-based arrangement to use. Many states blend the two: setting an overall target while specifying acceptable model types.

The trend is unmistakably toward more requirements. More states are requiring the use of VBP or alternative payment models in the contracts between their MCOs and providers, with roughly 26 states defining the types of VBP model that MCOs must use. This reflects a recognition that simply capitating the MCO is not enough — the state must affirmatively require the plan to transmit value-based incentives to providers, or the plan may default to paying providers in ways that perpetuate volume-driven care.

To make targets concrete, states set saturation targets — the share of MCO payments that must be value-based — and often ramp them up over time. About 19 states have set required minimum saturation targets, and a classic example is Arizona, where the required proportion of MCO revenues in value-based arrangements started at 5% in 2013, rose to 10% in 2014, and climbed to 20% in 2015 and 2016. This gradual ramp gives plans and providers time to build the capabilities value-based payment requires while steadily increasing the pressure to adopt it.

children.text: The HCP-LAN Framework: A Common Language

A challenge in requiring VBP is defining what actually counts as "value-based." Without a common standard, every state and plan might define it differently, making targets meaningless and comparison impossible. To solve this, many states adopt the Health Care Payment Learning & Action Network (HCP-LAN) framework, a widely used classification that sorts payment arrangements into categories by how much they tie payment to value and risk — from pure fee-for-service (Category 1), to fee-for-service linked to quality (Category 2), to alternative payment models built on fee-for-service architecture (Category 3), to population-based payment (Category 4).

The framework gives states a precise vocabulary for their requirements. About 17 states specifically reference the HCP-LAN framework in defining acceptable VBP arrangements, and of those, 10 specify the categories MCOs should use — usually HCP-LAN Category 2C or higher, meaning at least fee-for-service tied to quality and ideally more advanced models. Even states that do not explicitly cite HCP-LAN typically use definitions that align with or overlap its categories. The framework has become the de facto common language for Medicaid VBP, letting a state say exactly how far up the value ladder it expects its plans to push.

This connects directly to the risk continuum from earlier study. HCP-LAN’s categories essentially map the same spectrum — from no risk (fee-for-service) through pay-for-performance and shared savings up to full population-based capitation. When a state requires its MCOs to move providers to "Category 3 or higher," it is requiring them to move providers up the risk continuum into shared savings and beyond. The framework is how that abstract continuum becomes a concrete, measurable contract requirement.
State Directed Payments: The Growing Mechanism

The most consequential and fastest-growing tool for VBP in Medicaid managed care is the state directed payment (SDP). Created when CMS updated the managed care regulations in 2016, SDPs allow a state to direct how its MCOs pay providers — overriding the normal rule that plans set their own provider rates. Through SDPs, a state can require MCOs to use minimum or maximum fee schedules, make uniform rate increases for selected providers, require participation in multi-payer models, or require providers to participate in value-based purchasing arrangements. SDPs are how a state reaches through the MCO to shape provider payment directly.

SDPs have exploded in scale. Between February 2023 and August 2024, CMS approved 302 state directed payment arrangements across 40 states and Puerto Rico, and the arrangements approved as of August 2024 are projected to spend $110.2 billion a year — nearly a 60% increase over the $69.3 billion projected just eighteen months earlier. This staggering growth reflects how central SDPs have become to state Medicaid strategy, both for raising provider payment (often toward Medicare levels) and for advancing value-based and quality goals. The VBP-oriented SDPs tie payments to metrics like patient satisfaction, reduced readmissions, and improved chronic-disease management.

This rapid growth drew regulatory attention. In 2024, CMS released a managed care rule with additional updates intended to improve the oversight and transparency of directed payments — a response to concerns that SDPs were growing so fast, and channeling so much money, that they needed tighter guardrails. States now report a range of evaluation measures for their SDPs, such as hospitalization and readmission rates, utilization and timeliness of preventive and specialty care, and outcomes for common chronic conditions, so the billions flowing through SDPs can be tied to demonstrable results rather than simply raising payments.

body.message: State directed payments let states reach through MCOs to shape provider payment and advance value-based goals, but their explosive growth to $110+ billion a year prompted CMS to tighten oversight and transparency in 2024. The same mechanism that can drive value-based purchasing can also simply inflate payments, which is why CMS is demanding clearer evaluation of what SDPs actually achieve.
body.title: SDPs Are Powerful — and Under Scrutiny

children.text: Why VBP Ties the Course Together

Value-based purchasing is where Medicaid managed care reconnects with the broader value-based-care movement that this body of study began with. Everything earlier in this course built the machinery of managed care — selecting plans, setting rates, ensuring networks and quality, overseeing performance. VBP is the layer that aims that machinery at the ultimate goal: not just transferring risk to plans, but actually changing how care is paid for and delivered all the way to the provider, so that value, not volume, drives the system from top to bottom.

body.analogy: A state requiring VBP through its MCOs is like a parent company that pays its regional managers (the MCOs) a fixed budget and then insists those managers also pay their store employees (providers) based on customer satisfaction and results, not just hours worked. Without that insistence, a regional manager might pocket the efficiency and still pay employees the old way — so the incentive to improve never reaches the front line. VBP requirements, HCP-LAN categories, and state directed payments are the parent company’s way of making sure the new incentives flow all the way down to where the work actually happens.
body.concept: Pushing value-based payment to the provider level

children.text: The honest caveat is that requiring VBP does not guarantee it works. As the hospital-finance course showed, value-based payment’s benefits depend on execution — providers must have the data, scale, and capabilities to manage risk, and shared savings must actually offset lost volume. A state can mandate that 50% of MCO payments be "value-based" and still see little change if the underlying arrangements are weak (mere pay-for-performance bonuses rather than real risk) or if providers lack the infrastructure to respond. The targets and frameworks are necessary scaffolding, but the building still depends on genuine capability beneath them.

This lesson opens the final module by showing Medicaid managed care reaching toward value. The next lesson, on Section 1115 waivers, examines the federal authority that lets states innovate beyond standard rules — including many of the boldest VBP and delivery-reform experiments. And the closing lesson looks at where the whole field is heading, toward social determinants and whole-person care. Value-based purchasing is the bridge: it takes the managed care structure built across this course and points it at the same destination the entire value-based-care movement is pursuing — paying for health and outcomes rather than volume of services.

points: Value-based purchasing (VBP) in Medicaid managed care is the state’s use of MCO contracts to require or encourage plans to pay their providers through value-based arrangements, pushing value-based payment from the state through the plan to the provider level.

It matters because capitating an MCO does not change how the MCO pays providers; without VBP requirements, plans may keep paying providers fee-for-service and recreate volume incentives one layer down.
States drive VBP two ways: setting value-based payment targets (a minimum share of payments that must be value-based) and prescriptively directing MCOs to adopt specific models, often combined.

About 26 states define required VBP model types and 19 set minimum saturation targets, frequently ramped over time — Arizona moved from 5% of MCO revenues in value-based arrangements in 2013 to 20% by 2015–2016.

Many states use the HCP-LAN framework to define "value-based," with ~17 referencing it and 10 specifying categories (usually Category 2C or higher); the framework maps the same risk continuum from fee-for-service to population-based payment.

State directed payments (SDPs), created by CMS in 2016, let states direct how MCOs pay providers — including requiring VBP participation — and have grown explosively to a projected $110.2 billion a year as of August 2024 (302 arrangements in 40 states), up ~60% in 18 months.

The rapid SDP growth prompted CMS to tighten oversight and transparency in 2024 and to require evaluation measures (readmissions, preventive care, chronic-disease outcomes), since SDPs can either advance value or simply inflate payments.

Requiring VBP does not guarantee results — benefits depend on execution, provider capability, and whether the arrangements involve real risk — so targets and frameworks are necessary scaffolding but not sufficient on their own.

title: Value-Based Purchasing in Medicaid Managed Care

children.text: The Equity Gap That Value-Based Care Must Confront

Value-based care was designed to improve quality while reducing costs — a goal that sounds universal but has been implemented in ways that systematically exclude or disadvantage the people who most need better care. The promise of VBC is that if we pay for outcomes rather than volume, the entire health system will orient toward keeping people healthy and intervening effectively when they get sick. But that promise breaks down when the populations most likely to get sick are also the populations whose providers are most financially penalized for serving them, and whose social circumstances make achieving measured outcomes hardest.

Health disparities in the United States are pervasive, well-documented, and stubbornly persistent. Black Americans have shorter life expectancies than white Americans, higher rates of preventable hospitalizations, worse outcomes for nearly every major chronic disease, and less access to high-quality specialty care. Hispanic Americans face systematic barriers to accessing care due to language, immigration status, and geographic concentration in underserved communities. Rural Americans — regardless of race — face provider shortages, longer travel distances to specialists, and hospital closures that have accelerated over the past decade. These are not statistical abstractions; they are the lived experiences of tens of millions of Americans who depend on a healthcare system that was not designed with them in mind.

An analysis of U.S. county data (Hood et al., American Journal of Preventive Medicine, 2016) estimated that socioeconomic factors — income, education, employment, family and social support, community safety — account for about 47 percent of modifiable health outcomes, health behaviors for 34 percent, and clinical care for only 16 percent. This means that value-based programs focused exclusively on clinical quality metrics are, at best, optimizing a minority of the drivers of health. A VBC system that ignores social determinants is like a building code that focuses only on the foundation while ignoring whether the occupants have heat, water, and a safe neighborhood.

Social determinants of health — income, housing, education, food security, transportation, and neighborhood safety — together with health behaviors, account for roughly 80% of modifiable health outcomes, while clinical care accounts for about 16% (Hood et al., 2016). A value-based care system that ignores these upstream factors cannot achieve equitable health improvement, regardless of how well it optimizes clinical delivery.

children.text: How Current VBC Design Can Worsen Disparities

The architecture of most value-based payment programs contains features that can actively worsen health disparities, even when the programs' intentions are positive. The clearest example is financial benchmarking based on historical costs. When ACOs or hospitals have their savings targets set relative to their own historical spending, providers who historically underserved low-income populations — spending less not because of efficiency but because patients couldn't afford care — will have lower baselines and therefore must improve more to earn bonuses. Conversely, providers who historically overspent may generate "savings" simply by stopping unnecessary high-cost care, even without improving outcomes.

Quality metrics in VBC programs are similarly biased by the populations they measure. Preventive care rates, disease management outcomes, and patient experience scores are all sensitive to social determinants that providers cannot control. A physician practicing in a food desert who consistently struggles to improve her patients' HbA1c levels despite excellent clinical care faces the same performance benchmark as a physician in an affluent community where patients can afford fresh food, have stable employment, and can take time off to manage their chronic conditions. Without social risk adjustment, the quality measurement system punishes the former and rewards the latter.

Provider network and geographic access issues compound these problems. VBC programs are most effective when patients have consistent, ongoing relationships with their primary care providers — the foundation of care coordination and preventive care. But underserved communities have higher rates of safety-net provider dependence, federally qualified health center (FQHC) utilization, and emergency department use as primary care. These non-standard care patterns make attribution difficult in ACO models and reduce the effectiveness of care coordination interventions designed around assumptions of regular primary care visits.

body.message: Value-based care programs that penalize providers for serving disadvantaged populations create incentives for "cream skimming" — the strategic avoidance of high-risk, high-complexity, socially disadvantaged patients in favor of healthier, wealthier ones. When financial models reward efficiency over equity, providers who serve the most vulnerable patients can face the steepest penalties, creating pressure to deprioritize or exclude these populations from VBC arrangements.
body.title: The "Cream Skimming" Risk

children.text: The Social Determinants Framework in Practice

Addressing social determinants within a VBC framework requires moving beyond clinical-only interventions. Several models have demonstrated that systematic SDOH screening and community-based intervention — when integrated with clinical care delivery — can improve both health outcomes and financial performance. The logic is compelling: a patient who loses her apartment will generate emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and uncontrolled chronic disease management costs that dwarf the cost of housing support. If the VBC arrangement captures the savings from those avoided costs, investing in housing support can be financially rational, not just compassionate.

The Camden Coalition of Healthcare Providers in Camden, New Jersey pioneered the concept of "hotspotting" — identifying the highest-cost, most frequently hospitalized patients and providing intensive community-based support to address both clinical and social needs. Its wraparound services included housing assistance, transportation, medication management, and care coordination. When the approach was tested rigorously, however, the result was sobering: a randomized trial of the Coalition's care-transitions program (Finkelstein et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2020) found 180-day readmission rates of 62.3 percent among enrolled patients versus 61.7 percent under usual care — no significant difference. The model still shaped complex care management nationally, and the trial is a standing lesson that promising before-and-after results need controlled evaluation.

The Vermont Blueprint for Health, whose multi-payer community health teams began in pilot communities in 2008, integrates community health teams — social workers, care coordinators, community health workers — with primary care practices. These teams address social needs alongside clinical needs. A peer-reviewed analysis of six years of Vermont all-payer claims (Jones et al., Population Health Management, 2016) associated the Blueprint's community-oriented medical-home model with lower expenditures and utilization while maintaining quality — one of the longest-running statewide examples of linking community supports to primary care.

body.content:
The Accountable Health Communities (AHC) Model, launched by CMMI in 2017, tested whether systematically identifying and addressing health-related social needs — through screening, referral, and community navigation — could reduce Medicare and Medicaid utilization and costs.
Twenty-eight bridge organizations screened more than 1 million Medicaid and Medicare beneficiaries for five core needs: housing instability, food insecurity, transportation problems, utility difficulties, and interpersonal violence. In the Assistance Track, navigation-eligible beneficiaries (at least one need plus two or more ED visits in the prior year) were randomized to referral information alone or referral plus an offer of navigation; the Alignment Track was not randomized. CMS's final evaluation found that navigation lowered total health care expenditures — with fewer inpatient admissions and readmissions among Medicaid beneficiaries and fewer ED visits and ambulatory-care-sensitive admissions among fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries — even though rates of need resolution were similar to the control group.
body.title: CMS Accountable Health Communities Model

children.text: What an Equity-Centered VBC System Looks Like

Building a VBC system that works for everyone requires changes at multiple levels: the data infrastructure for measuring equity, the payment architecture that removes penalties for serving disadvantaged populations, the workforce that can address social and clinical needs together, and the community partnerships that connect healthcare systems to social services. None of these changes is simple, and all of them require sustained policy commitment across multiple administrations.

On measurement, equity-centered VBC requires stratifying all quality measures by race, ethnicity, income, disability status, and social risk factor status — and holding providers accountable for reducing within-panel disparities, not just improving average performance. CMS moved in this direction in 2023, finalizing a Health Equity Index reward for Medicare Advantage Star Ratings and a health equity adjustment for the Hospital Value-Based Purchasing program, but reversed both in 2025: the FY2026 inpatient rule removed the hospital adjustment, and the CY2027 Medicare Advantage rule did not implement the reward. But the data infrastructure for consistent race and ethnicity reporting in healthcare claims remains incomplete, and many providers cannot accurately stratify their own quality data by social characteristics.

On workforce, community health workers (CHWs) have emerged as one of the highest-value tools for bridging clinical care and social needs. CHWs are trusted community members who provide health education, navigation, care coordination, and social support — often in patients' homes and in community settings rather than clinical offices. In the CY2024 Physician Fee Schedule, CMS created Medicare's first Community Health Integration codes (G0019, G0022) for CHW services furnished under a billing practitioner's supervision; Medicaid coverage of CHW services remains a state option; in KFF's 2022 survey, 29 of 48 responding states reported allowing Medicaid payment for CHW services. This represents a significant structural change that could enable systematic SDOH intervention at scale.

children.text: The Policy Landscape and What Remains Unresolved

CMS has articulated a health equity commitment across multiple programs and policy documents, but translating that commitment into payment design that meaningfully advances equity is a work in progress. The Innovation Center's October 2021 Strategy Refresh named health equity a strategic objective, committing to embed it in every model. The AHC model, the Making Care Primary model, and ACO REACH all included equity-specific requirements or payment adjustments. Yet in March 2025 CMMI announced the early termination of four models — Making Care Primary among them — raising uncertainty about the long-term trajectory of equity-focused innovation.

Medicaid is potentially a more powerful lever for health equity in VBC than Medicare, because Medicaid disproportionately serves the populations with the most pronounced health disparities — low-income adults, children, people with disabilities, and pregnant women. Several states have moved aggressively to incorporate SDOH into Medicaid managed care contracts: North Carolina's Healthy Opportunities Pilots — described by the state as the nation's first comprehensive program to test evidence-based non-medical interventions for high-needs Medicaid enrollees — tested whether braiding healthcare and social service funding could improve outcomes for the most complex enrollees; services stopped on July 1, 2025, when state funding lapsed. Massachusetts, Oregon, and California have implemented similar Medicaid innovations.

The fundamental unresolved tension is between universalism and targeting. A truly equitable VBC system would require different standards, different investments, and different timelines for providers and populations at different starting points — a form of affirmative payment design that explicitly prioritizes closing gaps rather than maximizing average performance. American health policy has historically struggled with this kind of targeted approach, preferring universal standards that appear fair on paper but embed structural inequities in practice. Resolving that tension — acknowledging that equity sometimes requires differential treatment — is the defining political and policy challenge for the next generation of value-based care design.

body.analogy: A school system that grades every student on the same curve regardless of whether they had tutors, stable housing, and enough food is not measuring academic achievement — it is measuring socioeconomic advantage. Value-based care faces the same problem: measuring health outcomes on a single universal scale when the determinants of those outcomes are profoundly unequal.
body.concept: Health Equity and VBC Performance Measurement

points: Social determinants of health — income, housing, education, food security, and transportation — together with health behaviors, drive roughly 80 percent of modifiable health outcomes, meaning VBC programs focused only on clinical quality metrics are optimizing a minority of what actually drives health.

Current VBC program design can worsen disparities through historical cost benchmarking, unadjusted quality metrics, and financial penalties that disproportionately fall on safety-net providers serving the most disadvantaged populations.

The "cream skimming" risk — providers strategically avoiding high-complexity, socially disadvantaged patients — is a real consequence of VBC financial models that penalize rather than reward serving vulnerable populations.

Community health workers, SDOH screening programs, and cross-sector partnerships between healthcare and social services represent promising operational strategies for addressing social determinants within VBC arrangements.

The Vermont Blueprint for Health and CMS Accountable Health Communities Model provide real-world evidence that linking community supports to primary care, and social-needs screening to navigation, can lower spending and hospital-based use.

CMS made health equity a design objective for Innovation Center models in 2021 and created Medicare billing codes for community health integration and SDOH risk assessment in 2024 — but in 2025 it rolled back several equity provisions, so equity-adjusted payment design remains unsettled.

Building a VBC system that works for everyone requires stratified quality measurement, social risk adjustment, universal SDOH screening, community health integration, and outcome accountability for demonstrated disparity reduction — not just average performance improvement.

body.explanation: The AHC Model specifically tested the clinical and financial impact of screening beneficiaries for five health-related social needs — housing instability, food insecurity, transportation, utilities, and interpersonal safety — and then providing community navigation to connect them with social services. CMS's final evaluation found that navigation lowered total health care expenditures and hospital-based use among navigation-eligible beneficiaries (fewer inpatient admissions for Medicaid enrollees, fewer ED visits for fee-for-service Medicare enrollees), supporting the premise that addressing social needs can reduce utilization and cost.

title: Who Gets Left Behind: Health Equity, Social Determinants, and Building a VBC System That Works for Everyone

children.text: The Fundamental Problem: A System That Pays for Sickness, Not Health

The United States spends more on healthcare than any other nation in the world — $5.3 trillion in 2024, or $15,474 per person (CMS). And yet, by nearly every measure of population health, the country performs below its peer nations. Life expectancy in the U.S. was 78.4 years in 2023, 4.1 years shorter than the average among comparable wealthy countries. Rates of chronic disease, preventable hospitalizations, and avoidable deaths are persistently higher in the U.S. than in nations that spend far less. The paradox is stark: more spending, worse outcomes.

This paradox is not the result of incompetent physicians, inferior technology, or inadequate hospitals. On most measures of technical medical capability — cancer survival rates, cardiac intervention outcomes, cutting-edge diagnostic tools — American medicine is among the best in the world. The problem is structural. The way the United States pays for healthcare systematically rewards the wrong things: it rewards treating illness rather than preventing it, rewards individual services rather than coordinated care, and rewards volume rather than value. The payment architecture shapes the behavior of every actor in the system, and the current architecture is pointing almost everyone in the wrong direction.

Value-based care (VBC) is the policy response to this misalignment. It is a broad umbrella term for payment and care delivery approaches that tie financial incentives to quality outcomes, patient experience, and cost-efficiency — rather than to the raw count of services delivered. Understanding value-based care requires first understanding the problem it is designed to solve: the incentive structure of fee-for-service medicine and the consequences that structure produces.

Key Concept: Value-based care is a healthcare payment and delivery model in which providers are compensated based on patient health outcomes and the efficiency of care delivery — rather than on the volume of services provided. The central idea is to align financial incentives with the goal of keeping patients healthy.

children.text: The Triple Aim: The Framework Behind Value-Based Care

The intellectual foundation of the value-based care movement is the Triple Aim, a framework articulated by the Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI) in 2008. The Triple Aim holds that health system improvement requires simultaneously pursuing three goals: improving the patient experience of care (including quality and satisfaction), improving the health of populations, and reducing the per-capita cost of healthcare. These three dimensions are not naturally in tension — indeed, the Triple Aim's central insight is that addressing all three together is both possible and necessary.

Fee-for-service medicine is structurally incapable of pursuing the Triple Aim because it optimizes only for volume — which is a proxy for neither quality nor health. A system that pays for more services will generate more services, regardless of whether those services improve the patient experience, improve population health, or reduce cost. The Triple Aim requires payment mechanisms that can reward coordination, prevention, and efficiency rather than activity.

In 2014, Thomas Bodenheimer and Christine Sinsky (Annals of Family Medicine) proposed expanding the framework to a "Quadruple Aim" that adds a fourth dimension: improving the health and well-being of the healthcare workforce. This addition acknowledges that provider burnout — driven in part by the administrative burden of documentation-heavy FFS billing and compliance programs like MIPS — is itself a systemic problem that undermines care quality. A truly value-based system should improve the experience of care for clinicians, not just patients.

The problem is not that American medicine lacks quality. The problem is that the payment system rewards the wrong quality — the quality of filling out a claim, not the quality of keeping a patient well.
The Spectrum of Value-Based Payment Models

Value-based care is not a single payment model — it is a spectrum of approaches that shift incentives away from pure volume and toward quality, efficiency, and outcomes. These models vary in the degree of financial risk they impose on providers, the scope of services they cover, and the populations they address. Understanding the landscape of models is essential for anyone navigating healthcare finance and policy.

At one end of the spectrum are pay-for-performance (P4P) programs, which layer quality bonuses or penalties on top of existing FFS payments. MIPS is a prominent example: it preserves fee-for-service billing while adjusting final payments up or down based on a quality and cost score. P4P models represent the lowest-risk entry point into value-based care — they do not require providers to change their fundamental revenue model — but they also generate the least structural change in care delivery because the FFS volume incentive remains intact.

Moving up the risk spectrum, bundled payment models establish a single fixed payment for an entire episode of care — for example, a total knee replacement including surgery, inpatient stay, rehabilitation, and follow-up visits over a defined period. Providers who manage the episode below the target price retain the savings; those who exceed it share in the loss. Bundled payments create powerful incentives for care coordination across the inpatient and post-acute continuum, but they apply only to defined episodes and do not address population health or primary prevention.

children.text: Accountable Care Organizations: The Flagship VBC Model

Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) are the most widely deployed model of value-based care in the United States. An ACO is a group of doctors, hospitals, and other healthcare providers who agree to share accountability for the quality and total cost of care for an assigned population of patients. Rather than being paid for each individual service, ACO participants receive their FFS payments as usual — but at year's end, if the ACO's total spending for its attributed beneficiaries is below a risk-adjusted benchmark, the ACO earns a share of those savings. If spending exceeds the benchmark, the ACO may owe losses back, depending on its risk track.

The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) is the largest ACO program in the United States. As of January 2024, 480 MSSP ACOs include more than 608,000 clinicians providing care to nearly 11 million Medicare beneficiaries. In 2023, MSSP ACOs generated $2.1 billion in net savings for Medicare — a record at the time, surpassed in 2024 at about $2.5 billion — while also demonstrating quality improvements in diabetes management, blood pressure control, cancer screening, and depression care.

The ACO REACH (Realizing Equity, Access, and Community Health) model, administered by CMMI, tests deeper accountable care, including a Global option in which ACOs take on 100% of shared savings and losses and may elect capitated payments. In 2023, the 132 ACO REACH participants managed care for more than 2 million Medicare beneficiaries, generating $695 million in net savings. The model explicitly incorporates health equity requirements — ACOs must develop health equity plans and report on disparities for high-need populations — marking a significant expansion of the VBC framework beyond cost and quality to address systemic disparities in care access and outcomes.

body.content:
In 2023, the MSSP achieved its seventh consecutive year of program-wide savings, with $2.1 billion returned to Medicare; 2024 then set a new record of about $2.5 billion across 476 ACOs (CMS). ACOs in the program earned shared savings payments totaling $3.1 billion — also a record. Performance also improved on quality measures related to diabetes care, blood pressure control, colorectal and breast cancer screening, statin therapy, and depression screening.
As of January 2024, 480 ACOs participated, covering nearly 11 million beneficiaries through the work of more than 608,000 clinicians. The program demonstrates that large-scale ACO participation can simultaneously reduce Medicare spending and improve measured quality — the core promise of the Triple Aim.

children.text: Capitation and Global Budgets: The Deepest Form of VBC

At the far end of the value-based care spectrum are capitation and global budget models, which represent the most complete structural departure from fee-for-service. Under full capitation, a provider organization receives a fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) payment from a payer to cover all covered services for an assigned population — regardless of how many services are actually used. The provider keeps the margin if it delivers care efficiently; it absorbs the loss if it does not. Capitation fully inverts the FFS incentive: instead of more services = more revenue, the logic becomes appropriate care = retained margin.

Global budgets extend this logic to entire health systems or regions. Rather than paying on a per-patient basis, a global budget model sets an annual spending total for a defined population and gives a delivery system or state accountability for staying within that budget while meeting quality standards. Global budgets are common in other countries — the UK's NHS operates largely on a global budget basis — but they are rare in the United States, where Maryland's hospital global budgets and Pennsylvania's Rural Health Model have been the most prominent examples.

Vermont's All-Payer ACO Model, which ran from 2017 (performance years from 2018) through December 31, 2025, is particularly noteworthy because it aligned Medicare, Medicaid, and major commercial insurers under a single, statewide value-based payment framework — the first all-payer ACO model in the U.S. The model drove significant investment in primary care infrastructure and care coordination in Vermont, and its record offers lessons for other states seeking to address both cost and health equity through payment reform.

children.text: Why the Transition Is Hard — and Why It Is Happening Anyway

The case for value-based care is compelling in theory, and the evidence from programs like MSSP and ACO REACH is increasingly convincing in practice. Yet the transition from fee-for-service to value-based payment has been slower and more contested than reformers hoped when the ACA established CMMI in 2010. The reasons are structural, financial, and cultural. Provider organizations that built their facilities, staffed their teams, and financed their operations around FFS revenue cannot rapidly restructure without risk. A hospital that derives 40% of its margin from high-volume elective procedures does not easily absorb the shift to a model that rewards reducing utilization.

There is also the challenge of measurement. Value-based payment requires robust quality metrics, reliable patient attribution, risk adjustment that does not penalize providers caring for sicker or more complex populations, and data infrastructure that can track patients across settings and over time. Building these systems is expensive, slow, and contentious. Disputes over which quality measures are clinically meaningful, how to attribute patients to providers in a fragmented system, and how to adjust benchmarks for social determinants of health have occupied policy debates for more than a decade without full resolution.

Despite these barriers, the direction of travel is clear. CMS has set explicit goals for moving Medicare toward value-based payment, and commercial payers have followed. The combination of rising healthcare costs, aging demographics, and the documented failure of FFS to produce commensurate health outcomes has created irreversible pressure for payment reform. For healthcare professionals, administrators, and policymakers, understanding the architecture of value-based care — its models, its incentives, its measurement systems, and its limitations — is no longer optional. It is the vocabulary of the field.

body.message: Value-based care programs have documented early successes in reducing cost and improving quality metrics for defined populations — but evidence on long-term population health impact and equity outcomes is still developing. Not all VBC models reduce health disparities; some early evidence suggests that ACOs serving more advantaged populations outperform those serving high-need, low-income populations, raising important questions about how VBC design can be improved to reduce — rather than widen — health equity gaps.
body.title: Key Limitation of VBC

points: The U.S. spends $5.3 trillion on healthcare annually — about 2.5 times the OECD per-capita average — yet achieves below-average outcomes on most population health indicators, including life expectancy.

The core cause of this paradox is a fee-for-service payment architecture that rewards volume over value, fragmenting care and incentivizing overtreatment while under-incentivizing prevention and coordination.
Value-based care (VBC) is a broad umbrella for payment models that tie financial incentives to quality, outcomes, and cost-efficiency — the central mechanism for realigning the payment system.
The Triple Aim framework — improving patient experience, improving population health, and reducing per-capita cost — provides the conceptual foundation for VBC design.

VBC models exist on a spectrum from low-risk pay-for-performance programs (like MIPS) to full capitation and global budgets; each point on the spectrum involves different degrees of financial risk and structural change.
ACOs are the flagship VBC model in Medicare; the MSSP generated a record $2.1 billion in net savings in 2023 while improving quality metrics — the seventh consecutive year of program-wide savings.

The transition to VBC faces structural, financial, and measurement barriers — but the policy and market direction is clear, making VBC literacy an essential competency for all healthcare professionals.

body.explanation: Pay-for-performance programs like MIPS preserve the fee-for-service billing structure and layer quality adjustments on top — providers still earn more by delivering more services, but their final payment is modified upward or downward by a quality and cost score. Capitation replaces the per-service payment with a fixed per-member-per-month amount, fully inverting the FFS incentive: efficient, high-quality care generates margin, while unnecessary utilization erodes it.

title: Why the Way We Pay for Healthcare Is Breaking the System — And How Paying for Value Could Fix It

children.text: A Field at an Inflection Point

Value-based care is no longer an experiment at the margins of American healthcare — it is the explicit direction of federal policy. But "the future of VBC" is not a smooth, predictable curve. The years 2025 and 2026 brought one of the sharpest strategic pivots in the history of the CMS Innovation Center (CMMI), the federal body that designs and tests new payment models. Understanding where VBC is heading means understanding both the durable trends and the recent reset that reshaped them.

On May 13, 2025, CMMI launched a new strategy organized around three pillars: promoting evidence-based prevention, empowering people to achieve their health goals, and driving choice and competition. All three sit on a single foundational principle the Center repeated insistently — protecting the federal taxpayer. The Innovation Center declared it would focus on the models that show the greatest promise for generating savings while improving quality, signaling a smaller, more demanding portfolio than the sprawling set of demonstrations that came before.

This matters because it changes what "value" is being optimized for. The previous era emphasized broad participation and equity-focused expansion. The current era emphasizes demonstrable financial performance, downside risk, prevention built into every model, and competition among providers. The destination — paying for outcomes instead of volume — is unchanged. The route, the guardrails, and the rhetoric have shifted considerably.

Key Concept: The CMS Innovation Center (CMMI) is the federal "laboratory" for payment reform. Its strategy determines which value-based models exist, who can join them, and how much financial risk providers must bear — making CMMI’s direction the single best predictor of where VBC is heading.

stats.label: CMMI 2025 Strategy
