children.text: The Portfolio Reset: What Ended and Why

The clearest signal of the new direction was what CMMI chose to stop doing. In 2025 the Innovation Center terminated several models before their originally scheduled end dates — most notably Primary Care First (PCF) and Making Care Primary (MCP). On its face, ending primary-care models looks like a retreat from primary care. CMMI framed it as the opposite: a way to move beneficiaries into more permanent, scalable programs — above all the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP), the agency’s flagship and permanent accountable care initiative.

The logic of the reset is that CMMI will narrow its portfolio to models with clearer savings logic, more defined provider obligations, and cleaner policy goals, while keeping primary care and accountable care as the foundation. Future models will place greater weight on downside financial risk — meaning providers can lose money, not just share in savings — and on measurable reductions in unnecessary utilization. The result is a smaller portfolio that asks more of the participants who remain.

body.message: The earlier ambition to place essentially all Traditional Medicare beneficiaries (and the vast majority of Medicaid beneficiaries) in accountable care relationships by 2030 has not been restated under the 2025 strategy. The emphasis shifted from maximizing participation to demonstrating savings — a meaningful change in how success is defined.
body.title: A Notable Absence: The 2030 Goal

children.text: For providers, the reset created real disruption. Organizations built around models that were terminated early had to find a new home, typically MSSP or a successor demonstration. This is the recurring tension of payment reform: the very experimentation that drives progress also creates instability for the practices that bet on a given model. Reading CMMI’s strategy is therefore not academic — it directly determines which contracts a health system can sign next year.
From ACO REACH to LEAD: The Next Generation of Risk

No transition better illustrates the new era than the end of ACO REACH and the rise of its successor. The ACO REACH (Realizing Equity, Access, and Community Health) Model, launched in 2023, was the most advanced risk-bearing accountable care model in Traditional Medicare: it paired prospective, population-based payments with two-sided financial risk and provider-led governance. It will run for four performance years — 2023 through 2026 — and then conclude on December 31, 2026.

In its place, CMMI announced the Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model, a 10-year initiative with Performance Year 1 beginning January 1, 2027. The unusually long time horizon is itself the point: it signals that CMMI wants stable, durable risk arrangements rather than short demonstrations that expire and strand their participants. The obvious candidates for LEAD are the organizations already in ACO REACH — they have the risk experience, the contracts, and an existing model ending exactly when LEAD begins. REACH organizations that do not move into LEAD would revert to MSSP or to fee-for-service.

body.title: How the REACH-to-LEAD Transition Works

children.text: The 2026 updates to REACH preview the direction LEAD will extend. CMS added a 3% cap on Standard ACOs' cumulative risk-score growth from 2019 through 2026 (High Needs ACOs face an asymmetric 8% cap on 2023–2026 growth for newly voluntarily aligned beneficiaries), and it reduced the weight of the regional benchmark — shifting Standard ACOs toward a 60/40 blend favoring historical baselines. CMS’s financial operating guides now call the model’s Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment the "Population Adjustment"; for PY2026 it combines a new Community Deprivation Index with beneficiaries’ dual-eligibility and Part D Low-Income Subsidy status.
Prevention, Patient Empowerment, and Competition

The three pillars of the 2025 strategy are not slogans — each carries concrete design commitments that will shape the models providers actually operate under. The most striking is the prevention pillar: CMMI promised that prevention will be part of every model it tests, with mechanisms for providers to offer services such as exercise and nutritional support that promote healthier lifestyles. This embeds population health and upstream intervention into the structure of payment, rather than treating it as an optional add-on.

The empowerment pillar centers on data and incentives: models are expected to better connect people to their own health data, unlock data access across all models, and align financial incentives so patients are active participants rather than passive recipients. The choice-and-competition pillar aims to broaden participation in alternative payment models — with explicit attention to independent and rural providers, the practices most at risk of being squeezed out of a market dominated by large consolidated systems.

body.title: How the Emphasis Shifted

children.text: What This Means for the Decade Ahead

Pulling the threads together, several durable trends emerge from the noise of any single administration’s rebranding. First, risk is going up. The trajectory from shared-savings-only arrangements toward two-sided risk and long-horizon models like LEAD is consistent across strategies — providers will increasingly be accountable for total cost and outcomes, not merely rewarded for bonus performance. Second, primary care and accountable care remain the foundation even as the specific models churn; the MSSP, as a permanent program, is the stable anchor toward which beneficiaries are repeatedly funneled.

Third, prevention and patient-reported data are moving from periphery to core. A strategy that puts prevention in every model, combined with the strategy’s push to connect people to their own health data, means the definition of "value" is broadening beyond cost and clinical metrics to include what patients experience and whether illness is avoided in the first place. Fourth, the politics of value-based care are real and consequential: strategies, model names, and benchmarks change with administrations, and successful organizations build the underlying capabilities — risk management, data infrastructure, care coordination — that transfer across whatever model is in vogue.

body.analogy: Chasing individual payment models is like trying to catch each wave at the beach — exhausting and unpredictable, because waves come and go. Building core value-based capabilities is like learning to swim: once you can manage financial risk, use your data, and coordinate care, you stay afloat no matter which wave (REACH, LEAD, MSSP, the next acronym) arrives.
body.concept: Adapting to a changing VBC model landscape

children.text: For a state like Vermont — which has pursued some of the nation’s most ambitious payment reform through all-payer accountable care — these federal currents are not abstract. The fate of national models, the rise of long-horizon designs like LEAD, and the prevention-first framing all shape what is possible at the state level. The organizations that will thrive are not those that guess the next model correctly, but those that build the durable muscle of taking accountability for a population’s health and cost — the one capability every version of value-based care demands.

CMMI reset its portfolio toward fewer, more demanding models with clearer savings logic and greater downside financial risk, terminating Primary Care First and Making Care Primary early and funneling beneficiaries toward the permanent Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP).

The earlier goal of placing essentially all Traditional Medicare beneficiaries in accountable care relationships by 2030 has not been restated, marking a shift from maximizing participation to demonstrating savings.
ACO REACH — the leading two-sided-risk model in Traditional Medicare — runs through performance year 2026 and ends December 31, 2026.
Its successor, the Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model, is a 10-year initiative beginning January 1, 2027; REACH organizations not moving into LEAD revert to MSSP or fee-for-service.

PY2026 REACH previewed the tougher era with caps on risk-score growth (a 3% cumulative cap from 2019–2026), a reduced regional-benchmark weight (60/40 for Standard ACOs), while CMS’s guides now call the Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment the "Population Adjustment."
CMMI committed that prevention will be part of every model it tests, and that models will unlock patient data access and align incentives to empower patients — broadening the definition of "value."

The durable trends — rising risk, primary care as foundation, prevention and patient data access at the core, and politically volatile model names — mean success comes from building transferable capabilities, not betting on any single model.

title: Where Value-Based Care Is Heading: Primary Care, Risk & the Next Decade

children.text: What Are Vermont’s Designated Agencies?

Vermont organizes its public behavioral health system around a network of Designated Agencies (DAs) — private, nonprofit, community-based organizations that the state formally designates to deliver mental health, substance use, and developmental disability services in defined geographic regions. There are 10 Designated Agencies, with the state designating one to serve each region, so that every part of Vermont has a clear, accountable local provider of these services.

Alongside the 10 DAs, Vermont works with two Specialized Service Agencies (SSAs): Pathways Vermont, which serves adults, and NFI Vermont (the Northeastern Family Institute), which serves children and families. Together the DAs and SSAs form the backbone of Vermont’s publicly funded behavioral health "System of Care."

The defining feature of this model is that responsibility is explicit and local. Rather than leaving it to chance whether a region has adequate community mental health services, Vermont assigns a designated, accountable agency to each region and funds it to serve everyone who needs care — a structure quite different from the fragmented patchwork found in many states.

A Designated Agency is a private nonprofit that Vermont formally designates to provide mental health, substance use, and developmental disability services for a specific region. Vermont has 10 DAs (one per region) plus two Specialized Service Agencies.

children.text: Roots in Deinstitutionalization

The Designated Agency model grew out of the deinstitutionalization movement of the mid-twentieth century. For decades, people with serious mental illness were confined in large state psychiatric hospitals — Vermont’s was the Vermont State Hospital in Waterbury — often for years or decades. The federal Community Mental Health Act, signed by President Kennedy in 1963, set out to replace this with community-based care, shifting resources toward local nonprofit services.

Vermont built its DA network as the community-based system that deinstitutionalization required. The logic was that local, community-rooted nonprofits would be better positioned than a distant state institution to support people living in their own communities. Over time the DAs became the primary home for community mental health, developmental disability, and substance use services across the state.

This history became vivid in 2011, when the Vermont State Hospital in Waterbury was severely damaged and effectively closed after flooding from Tropical Storm Irene, capping years of decertification and quality problems. Its closure accelerated Vermont’s reliance on a more distributed, community-based system — making the strength of the DA network a matter of statewide importance.

body.content:
The Vermont State Hospital in Waterbury, the state’s long-standing psychiatric institution, was forced to close in 2011 following flooding from Tropical Storm Irene, on top of earlier decertification and quality concerns.
Its closure pushed Vermont toward an even more decentralized model, increasing the importance of the community-based Designated Agencies that care for people outside of institutional walls.
body.title: The Closure of the Vermont State Hospital

children.text: How Designation Works

Designation is a formal, statutory process. Under Vermont law (18 V.S.A. § 8907 and related statutes), the state’s commissioners ensure that community services for people with mental health conditions, psychiatric disabilities, and developmental disabilities are provided through designated community agencies, and they designate the public or private nonprofit agencies to provide or arrange for those services in each area.

Designation is not permanent or automatic — agencies must be periodically recertified, meeting state standards to keep their designated status. This gives the state ongoing leverage over quality and accountability: a Designated Agency holds a defined responsibility for its region, and that responsibility is reviewed and renewed rather than granted indefinitely.

Many of the DAs are organized collaboratively through Vermont Care Partners, a network combining the Vermont Council of Developmental and Mental Health Services and the Vermont Care Network — a collaboration of sixteen nonprofit community-based member agencies serving Vermonters affected by developmental disabilities, mental health conditions, and substance use disorders. This shared infrastructure helps the agencies coordinate, advocate, and operate consistently statewide.

children.text: How the Agencies Are Funded

Funding is what makes the model work — and it reflects the same move away from pure fee-for-service discussed earlier in this course. Rather than billing per visit, DAs are largely funded through case rates and a capitation arrangement: the Department of Vermont Health Access (DVHA), Vermont’s Medicaid agency, makes per-member-per-month payments to the Department of Mental Health, which in turn pays the agencies, supplemented by additional state and federal funds for services and people not covered by Medicaid.

This capitated, case-rate structure gives agencies flexibility to provide comprehensive services — case management, crisis response, community support — without the financial pressure of fee-for-service to limit care to the most billable activities. It is, in effect, a value-based approach that predates much of the national value-based payment movement. Much of the Department of Mental Health’s budget — about $347 million (all funds) in the state's FY2027 request — flows to these agencies, much of it from federal Medicaid funds.

Because so much funding and responsibility is concentrated in the DAs, their financial health and workforce capacity are recurring statewide concerns. When DAs face staffing shortages or funding pressure, the effects ripple across Vermont’s entire behavioral health safety net — which is why the agencies feature prominently in the state’s legislative and budget debates.

Vermont funds its Designated Agencies largely through Medicaid case rates and capitation rather than fee-for-service — a value-based approach that gives agencies the flexibility to deliver comprehensive community care.
Why Vermont’s System Is Studied

Vermont’s Designated Agency model is frequently cited as a comparatively organized approach to community behavioral health. By assigning clear regional responsibility, funding agencies flexibly, and building a comprehensive local presence, the state achieves a level of coordination and coverage that fragmented systems in other states often lack. A single agency like the Howard Center, the Designated Agency for Chittenden County, can run dozens of programs and serve many thousands of people across mental health, substance use, and developmental disability needs.

The model is not without strain. Like behavioral health systems everywhere, the DAs face workforce shortages, rising demand, and funding pressures, and Vermont continues to reform and supplement the system — including by adding Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic funding in 2024, layering a national model on top of its existing infrastructure. The DA system is a strong foundation, not a finished solution.

For this course, the Designated Agencies illustrate in concrete, real-world form many of the principles covered earlier: community-based care, integration of mental health and substance use services, accountable regional responsibility, and value-based funding. They set the stage for Vermont’s equally distinctive opioid treatment system — the Hub-and-Spoke model — examined in the next lesson.

children.text: A Statewide System for Opioid Use Disorder

Vermont’s Hub-and-Spoke model is one of the most influential state responses to the opioid crisis in the United States. It is a statewide system designed to do exactly what the earlier lesson on opioid treatment identified as the central challenge: get more people onto medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) by extending treatment from specialty clinics into mainstream, community-based care.

The model emerged from Vermont’s Blueprint for Health — the state’s broader initiative to reform primary care and chronic disease management. A key conceptual move was to treat opioid use disorder as a chronic condition, like diabetes or heart disease, that benefits from a coordinated network linking specialty expertise with everyday primary care. Addiction medicine physicians and public health leaders built this into the "Care Alliance for Opioid Addiction," which became the Hub-and-Spoke system.

Vermont divided the state into five geographic regions and began a staggered rollout of the system in January 2013. The result was a coordinated, statewide treatment infrastructure rather than a scattering of unconnected clinics — a structure that closely mirrors the integration principles at the heart of this course.

Vermont’s Hub-and-Spoke model treats opioid use disorder as a chronic condition and builds a statewide network linking specialty addiction "hubs" with primary-care "spokes." It launched across five regions in January 2013 under the Blueprint for Health.
The Hubs: Specialty Addiction Treatment

The "hubs" are regional specialty centers built around Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs) — the SAMHSA-certified clinics that, as covered earlier, are the only settings legally able to dispense methadone for opioid use disorder. Each of Vermont’s five regions has a hub clinic that provides daily dosing, can offer either methadone or buprenorphine, and delivers more intensive therapeutic services.

Hubs serve two main functions. First, they treat the patients who need the most intensive, structured care — including those starting treatment, those with complex needs, or those who are not stable enough for a primary care setting. Second, they act as the regional center of addiction expertise: hub staff assess patients at intake and determine the most appropriate placement, including referral out to a primary-care spoke when a patient is stable.

Entry into the hubs comes from many directions — hospitals and emergency rooms (especially after an overdose reversal), residential programs, the Department of Corrections, and community mental health programs — making the hub a true regional gateway into treatment for opioid use disorder.

body.content:
Each hub is organized around an existing Opioid Treatment Program with the authority to dispense both methadone and buprenorphine, providing daily dosing and intensive services for patients with the most complex needs.
Hub staff assess every patient at intake and decide whether they should be treated at the hub or transferred to a primary-care spoke — making the hub the clinical anchor for its region.
body.title: The Hub as Regional Center of Expertise

children.text: The Spokes: Office-Based Treatment in the Community

The "spokes" are general medical settings — primary care practices and other office-based providers — that deliver office-based opioid treatment (OBOT), prescribing buprenorphine and seeing patients weekly or monthly rather than daily. The spokes are how the model reaches patients close to home, in the same primary care relationships where the rest of their health care happens. This is the integration this course champions, applied directly to addiction.

The model’s signature innovation is the support given to spoke prescribers. Each spoke is backed by a "MAT team" — staffing of roughly one full-time registered nurse and one master’s-level licensed behavioral health or addictions provider for every 100 Medicaid office-based patients. This team provides nursing, counseling, and care management; the nurse handles intake tasks, prescription refills, urine drug testing, and diversion monitoring, freeing the physician to manage a panel of patients without being overwhelmed.

Crucially, this MAT team support is provided to the practice at no direct cost, funded through a Medicaid Health Home arrangement (a 90/10 federal–state funding split enabled by the Affordable Care Act). By removing both the workload burden and the cost barrier, Vermont made it realistic for ordinary primary care providers to treat opioid use disorder — directly attacking the prescriber-shortage problem.

body.title: How a Patient Moves Through Hub-and-Spoke

children.text: A Bidirectional, Coordinated Network

The genius of the model is that patients flow in both directions. The arrangement deliberately mirrors how other chronic diseases are managed — for example, the way a complex cardiac patient might be stabilized by a cardiology center and then managed by their primary care doctor, returning to the specialist if they destabilize. Opioid use disorder is treated the same way: hubs and spokes form one connected system, not separate silos.

When a patient stabilizes, they can step down from the hub to a spoke for more convenient, less intensive care; when a patient struggles, they can step back up to the hub for more support. This "robust bidirectional transfer based on clinical need" is what makes the network coherent, and it echoes the ASAM principle that placement should follow the patient’s changing clinical status rather than being fixed.

This design also expanded the prescriber workforce dramatically. By making office-based treatment feasible and supported, the model drove large increases in the number of buprenorphine prescribers and in patients served per prescriber — multiplying the state’s capacity to treat opioid use disorder.

children.text: Outcomes and National Influence

The results have made Vermont a national reference point. By around 2017, Vermont had the highest capacity for treating opioid use disorder in the country — on the order of 10.56 people in treatment per 1,000 population. The system substantially expanded treatment access in a largely rural state where access is otherwise hard to achieve.

A state evaluation found significant positive impacts for patients in treatment: less frequent opioid use, an elimination of overdoses among the study group, fewer emergency department visits, fewer police stops and arrests, and less illegal activity — alongside improved wellbeing, less family conflict, and reduced depression, anger, and anxiety. These are exactly the outcomes the opioid response aims for, achieved by getting and keeping people on effective medication.

Researchers have concluded that the Hub-and-Spoke system contributed substantially to Vermont’s expanded treatment capacity and "may serve as a model for other states grappling with the opioid epidemic." It demonstrates, in one rural state, the central thesis of this course: that integrating specialty and primary care — backed by the right payment and team support — dramatically expands access to lifesaving treatment.

children.text: When Doing the Right Thing Costs You Money

Imagine a hospital that runs a brilliant program to keep heart-failure patients healthy at home. The program works: admissions for those patients drop sharply. Under fee-for-service, this clinical triumph is a financial disaster — every avoided admission is lost revenue, while the hospital’s fixed costs (the building, the staff, the equipment) remain. The hospital did exactly what good medicine demands and was punished for it by its own payment system. This is the central, uncomfortable truth of the volume-to-value transition, and it is the reason that transition is so financially treacherous.

Value-based care asks hospitals to deliver less of the high-margin, volume-driven care that fee-for-service rewards — fewer admissions, fewer readmissions, fewer unnecessary procedures — in exchange for payments tied to keeping populations healthy. But the shift does not happen overnight, and during the long in-between, hospitals must operate under two contradictory payment logics at once. The financial implications of that contradiction are the subject of this lesson.

This is not abstract. It determines whether a hospital can afford to pursue value-based contracts, how fast it can move, and whether its mission to improve health aligns with or fights against its need to stay solvent. For a field built on the promise of paying for outcomes instead of volume, the messy economics of getting there are where most hospitals actually live.

Key Concept: Under fee-for-service, reducing unnecessary care reduces revenue while fixed costs remain — so a hospital succeeding at value-based care can lose money on the very utilization it eliminated. Managing this contradiction during the transition is the core financial challenge of moving from volume to value.

children.text: The Two Canoes Problem

The transition’s defining metaphor is the "two canoes" problem: a hospital stands with one foot in the fee-for-service canoe and one foot in the value-based-care canoe, and the two canoes are drifting apart because their incentives point in opposite directions. Value-based contracts demand very different business and clinical practices than those that maximize fee-for-service revenue — yet with most income still anchored to volume, hospitals often cannot afford a wholesale pivot to cost-conscious care. They must straddle both worlds, and straddling is precarious.

The financial mechanics of the straddle are genuinely hard to model. A health system CFO asked "what is the financial impact of reducing chronic-disease admissions by 25%?" faces a brutal calculation: the saved direct care costs are real, but so is the lost reimbursement, and the overhead that those admissions used to cover does not disappear. The published research is blunt about the consequence — because preventing a hospitalization leaves overhead costs uncovered, the loss of reimbursement revenue can actually mitigate a hospital’s incentive to reduce readmissions in the first place. The payment system fights the clinical goal.

body.message: Value-based contracts return a portion of the savings a hospital generates — but that share frequently does not fully offset the fee-for-service revenue lost when admissions and procedures fall. A hospital can improve care, generate system-wide savings, and still come out behind financially if it has not shifted enough of its revenue to value-based payment.
body.title: Shared Savings Often Don’t Cover the Loss

children.text: Where the Revenue Goes: The Migration of Care

The volume-to-value shift is not only about eliminating care — it is also about moving it. Procedures that once required expensive inpatient stays are migrating to lower-cost outpatient settings, and the financial footprint follows. Inpatient primary knee replacements fell 21.2% year over year as those cases moved to outpatient sites. Each of these shifts trims the high-revenue inpatient business that hospitals were built around, even when overall volumes remain healthy.

Paradoxically, this is happening during a period of strong hospital revenue. Through 2024, hospitals posted 20 consecutive months of year-over-year revenue increases, with outpatient revenue up 8.0% — outpacing inpatient growth of 6.1% — and full-year median operating margins holding above 4.5% and reaching 6% by December. The headline numbers look healthy, but underneath them the revenue base is migrating from inpatient to outpatient and from volume toward value, reshaping where and how hospitals earn their money.

body.content:
A teaching hospital invests in a care-transitions program that successfully prevents readmissions. Clinically and ethically, this is unambiguously good — and under the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program, avoiding readmissions also dodges penalties of up to 3% of Medicare payments.

But under fee-for-service, each prevented readmission is also a lost admission: revenue the hospital would have collected, gone, while the fixed overhead remains. Whether the program helps or hurts the hospital financially depends entirely on its payment mix — how much of its revenue is value-based (rewarding the prevention) versus fee-for-service (penalizing the lost volume). The same clinical action is a financial win or loss depending on which canoe carries more of the hospital’s weight.
body.title: The Avoided Readmission Paradox

children.text: Managing the Straddle: Tipping Points and Bridges

If straddling two canoes is dangerous, how do hospitals survive it? The strategic answer centers on the concept of a tipping point: the share of revenue under value-based contracts at which it becomes financially rational to fully embrace cost-conscious care. Below that threshold, a hospital that aggressively cuts volume bleeds fee-for-service revenue faster than its value-based payments grow. Above it, reducing unnecessary utilization finally rewards the hospital more than it costs. Much of value-based strategy is about deliberately managing the pace of the shift so the two sides cross over without the hospital capsizing in between.

Hospitals use several bridges to tie the canoes closer together during the crossing. Expanded fee-for-service reimbursement — new billing codes for care coordination, remote patient monitoring, and chronic-care management — lets a hospital get paid for value-promoting activities even while still in the fee-for-service world, acting like bungee cords that keep the canoes from drifting too far apart. Hospitals also sequence their risk-taking, starting with upside-only shared savings before accepting downside risk, and concentrate value-based efforts on the populations and service lines where they can succeed first.

body.title: Navigating the Volume-to-Value Transition

children.text: Why This Is the Hardest Problem in Hospital Finance

The volume-to-value transition is uniquely difficult because it asks an organization to undermine its current business model in order to build its future one — while keeping the lights on throughout. Every other industry that has been disrupted got to fail and be replaced; hospitals must transform themselves without interruption, because the community cannot go without a hospital while it figures out its finances. The two-canoes problem is not a temporary inconvenience but a structural feature of a decades-long, incomplete transition.

body.analogy: Moving from volume to value is like a store that earns most of its money selling cigarettes being told its future is selling gym memberships. As long as cigarettes pay the bills, every successful fitness program cannibalizes the store’s own revenue. It cannot simply stop selling cigarettes (it would go bankrupt) nor ignore the future (memberships are where the market is going). It has to grow the new business fast enough to replace the old one before the old one is taken away — exactly the tightrope hospitals walk.
body.concept: The volume-to-value financial transition

children.text: External pressure is compressing the timeline. Hospitals are bracing for major revenue hits beginning in 2027 from provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), pushing many to cut expenses and rethink their revenue base now. As fee-for-service reimbursement grows less sustainable and government payments tighten, the calculus increasingly favors moving toward value — not because value-based contracts are lucrative, but because the volume-based alternative is eroding. The two canoes are being pulled toward the value side whether hospitals are ready or not.

For the student of hospital finance, this lesson reframes everything that came before. Payer mix, margins, cost accounting, and capital structure all take on new meaning when revenue can be reduced by success rather than failure. The hospitals that navigate the transition will be those that understand their cost structure precisely (hence the emphasis on activity-based costing), manage the pace of risk deliberately, and build the population-health capabilities that make value-based payment a strength rather than a threat. The next lessons — on shared savings and risk, and on the business case for population health — are about exactly how to do that.

Research shows that because a prevented hospitalization leaves overhead uncovered, the loss of reimbursement can actually mitigate a hospital’s incentive to reduce readmissions — the payment system fighting the clinical goal.

Shared savings frequently fail to fully offset the fee-for-service revenue lost from reduced utilization, so a hospital can generate system savings and still come out behind if too little of its revenue is value-based.

Care is migrating as well as shrinking — inpatient knee replacements fell 21.2% year over year to outpatient settings — even amid strong overall revenue (20 straight months of growth, outpatient up 8.0%, margins reaching 6% in late 2024).
Hospitals manage the straddle by working toward a tipping point: the share of value-based revenue at which cutting unnecessary volume finally rewards more than it costs.

Transitional bridges — new billing codes for care coordination, remote monitoring, and chronic-care management, plus sequencing from upside-only to two-sided risk — tie the canoes together during the crossing.

The transition is uniquely hard because hospitals must undermine their current business model to build the future one without interruption, and external pressures like OBBBA revenue cuts beginning in 2027 are compressing the timeline.

children.text: A Different Unit of Concern

Most of medicine focuses on one patient at a time: this person, this visit, this diagnosis. Population health flips the unit of concern from the individual to the group. It asks not "how do we treat this patient?" but "how healthy is this whole population, and what is driving its health?"

The foundational definition comes from a 2003 paper by David Kindig and Greg Stoddart in the American Journal of Public Health. They defined population health as "the health outcomes of a group of individuals, including the distribution of such outcomes within the group." That definition is more subtle than it looks, and unpacking it is the key to the whole field.

The phrase "distribution of such outcomes" is doing heavy lifting. It means population health is not satisfied with an average — a population can have good average health while a subgroup suffers terribly. Built into the very definition is a concern with equity: how health is spread across the group, not just its mean. This is why population health and health equity are inseparable.

Population health (Kindig & Stoddart, 2003) is "the health outcomes of a group of individuals, including the distribution of such outcomes within the group." The unit of concern is the group, and the focus on distribution makes equity intrinsic.
Three Elements and the Determinants of Health

Kindig and Stoddart described the field as having three connected elements: health outcomes, the patterns of health determinants that produce those outcomes, and the policies and interventions that link the two. In other words, population health is not just measuring how healthy a group is — it is understanding why, and acting on it.

The "why" lives in the determinants of health. The authors list them as medical care, public health interventions, aspects of the social environment (income, education, employment, social support, culture), aspects of the physical environment (urban design, clean air and water), genetics, and individual behavior. Strikingly, only one of those six — medical care — is what we usually think of as "health care."

This is the most important and counterintuitive idea in population health: most of what determines a group's health happens outside the doctor's office. The conditions people live in, their behaviors, their early-life circumstances, and their environment shape health far more than medical care does. A field focused on population health must therefore look well beyond the clinic.

children.text: The Triple Aim

Population health entered the mainstream of U.S. health policy through the Triple Aim. In 2008, Don Berwick, Tom Nolan, and John Whittington of the Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI) described three goals to pursue simultaneously: improving the patient experience of care, improving the health of populations, and reducing the per capita cost of care.

The Triple Aim was transformative because it made "the health of populations" an explicit, co-equal goal of the health system — alongside individual care quality and cost. It became the organizing framework for the U.S. National Quality Strategy and for countless health-system strategies. IHI describes the Triple Aim itself as having given leaders a "North Star" for building value-based models of care for populations.

The framework's power is that the three aims pull on each other. You cannot durably reduce per capita cost without improving population health (sicker populations cost more), and you cannot improve population health by focusing only on the patients who happen to show up. The Triple Aim pushed health systems to think beyond their own walls to the health of the communities they serve.

children.text: Population Health vs. Population Health Management

A crucial distinction runs through this course: population health versus population health management (PHM). Population health is the broad concept — the health outcomes and determinants of a group, in the academic Kindig-Stoddart sense, which can mean an entire community or nation. Population health management adds a strong, operational management component: it is what a specific health-care organization actually does to improve outcomes for a defined group it is responsible for.

The key word is "defined." A PHM program operates on a defined population — usually the patients attributed to a practice, the members of a health plan, or the employees of an employer. Most PHM models rest on an attribution method that assigns a panel of patients to a provider or organization, which is then accountable for that panel's health.

This distinction matters because this course is mostly about management — the practical work of improving the health of a defined, attributed population. When we say "population health" going forward, we usually mean PHM: a concrete organization, a concrete panel, and concrete interventions, all measured against the Triple Aim.

children.text: Proactive, Whole-Population Care

The defining behavior of population health management is that it is proactive and whole-population, not reactive and visit-based. Traditional care is reactive: it treats the patients who walk in the door. PHM attends to the entire defined population — including the patients who have NOT come in, who are often the ones at highest risk.

This is the logic of "panel management": a practice systematically identifies and tracks the care needs of every patient on its panel, whether or not they are showing up for appointments. The diabetic patient who has not been seen in a year, the woman overdue for a mammogram, the person with rising blood pressure who never schedules a visit — population health is designed to find and reach exactly those people.

This proactive stance is also why population health is bound up with value-based care. Under fee-for-service, there is little incentive to chase the patients who are not generating visits. Under value-based payment, where the organization is accountable for the cost and quality of a whole population, preventing expensive downstream events (an avoidable ER visit, an uncontrolled chronic disease) becomes the whole game. Value-based care is the economic engine that makes population health management worth doing — and the rest of this course builds out how it is actually done.

body.message: The biggest mental shift in population health is attending to the whole defined panel — especially the high-risk patients who are not coming in for care. Reactive, visit-based medicine misses exactly the people who most need outreach. PHM is proactive by design.

children.text: The Money Side of Care

Every time a patient receives care, two things happen in parallel. There is the clinical story — the diagnosis, the treatment, the outcome. And there is a financial story — someone has to be billed, an insurer has to be charged, and the provider has to actually get paid for the work. Revenue cycle management (RCM) is the discipline that governs that second story.

Formally, the revenue cycle is comprised of all the administrative and clinical functions that contribute to the capture, management, and collection of patient service revenue. In plainer terms: it is everything a healthcare organization does to get paid for the care it delivers — from the moment a patient schedules an appointment to the moment the final dollar is collected.

This matters enormously because, in American health care, getting paid is genuinely hard. Care is delivered first and billed later; payment flows through a maze of insurers each with their own rules; and a single error anywhere in the chain can mean the provider is never paid at all. RCM exists to manage that complexity so that providers stay financially viable and can keep their doors open.

Revenue cycle management (RCM) is the set of administrative and clinical functions that capture, manage, and collect the revenue a provider earns for patient care — everything involved in getting paid, from scheduling to final collection.
Why RCM Is Such a Big Deal

The scale of the money and effort involved is staggering. Administrative costs — much of which is billing- and insurance-related work — are estimated at roughly 15 to 25 percent of total U.S. national health expenditures (Chernew and Mintz, JAMA, 2021). The largest single category of healthcare "waste," about $266 billion a year, comes from administrative complexity.

That complexity translates into real money lost when RCM fails. A Change Healthcare analysis found that about $262 billion in hospital claims were initially denied in 2016, and in 2024 payers initially denied about 11.8 percent of the dollars billed on hospital claims (Kodiak Solutions) — roughly one in eight dollars, even though most were eventually paid after rework. Each denied claim costs somewhere between $25 and $181 just to rework.

Unsurprisingly, RCM has become a massive industry in its own right. The U.S. revenue cycle management market is measured in the tens of billions of dollars and growing at double-digit rates, as providers invest heavily in people, software, and outsourced services to capture revenue they would otherwise lose. RCM is not back-office trivia — it is central to whether a hospital or practice survives.

children.text: The Three Phases of the Revenue Cycle

The revenue cycle is conventionally divided into three phases, and this front-to-back structure is the map for the entire course. The first is the front-end: everything that happens before and at the point of care — scheduling, registration, insurance verification, prior authorization, and financial counseling.

The second is the mid-cycle, where clinical care meets the financial process. This is where the care delivered during the visit gets translated into billable form: clinical documentation, medical coding (ICD-10, CPT, HCPCS), and charge capture. The mid-cycle is the bridge — what happens here directly determines how much the provider can bill and how cleanly.

The third is the back-end: everything after the bill is created — claim submission, payment posting, denial management, appeals, accounts receivable follow-up, and patient collections. A useful way to remember it: the front-end sets up the claim, the mid-cycle builds the claim, and the back-end collects on the claim.

children.text: Where Clinical Meets Financial

One of the most important ideas in RCM is that it is not purely a financial function — it is deeply clinical. The mid-cycle makes this explicit: what a clinician documents during a visit directly affects how much the organization gets paid and how quickly. A service that was delivered but not documented, or documented but not coded, simply does not get billed.

This clinical-financial link runs throughout the cycle. A registration clerk who mistypes an insurance ID, a physician who under-documents a complex visit, a coder who selects the wrong code — each is a clinical-adjacent action with direct financial consequences downstream. RCM is therefore a team sport spanning the entire organization, not the job of a billing department alone.

This is also why RCM is increasingly understood as a quality-and-finance discipline together. Accurate documentation and coding are simultaneously about getting paid correctly and about reflecting the care actually delivered. The same data that drives a clean claim also feeds quality measurement, which connects RCM to the broader work of running a health system well.

body.analogy: Think of RCM like a relay race. The front-end runner gets the baton cleanly off the line (correct patient and insurance info). The mid-cycle runner carries it through the hard middle stretch (documentation and coding). The back-end runner sprints to the finish (claims and collections). Drop the baton at any handoff and the whole team loses the race — no matter how fast the other runners are.
body.concept: How the phases of the revenue cycle depend on each other

children.text: Who Does RCM and How It Is Measured

RCM is performed by a wide cast: schedulers and registrars, financial counselors, medical coders, billing specialists, denial and appeals analysts, and accounts-receivable teams, all supported by software and often by outsourced vendors. Many organizations now blend in-house staff with specialized RCM companies and technology platforms.

Because RCM determines whether a provider gets paid, it is measured rigorously. The Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) maintains a set of standardized revenue-cycle metrics known as MAP Keys, which establish industry benchmarks for revenue cycle excellence across hospitals, physician groups, and other provider types. Later lessons in this course dive into these key performance indicators in detail.

The goal of all this measurement and effort is simple to state and hard to achieve: get paid the right amount, for the right care, as quickly as possible, with as little waste and rework as possible. Every lesson that follows is, at bottom, about improving one piece of that goal — and this course walks the full cycle from scheduling to collections.

children.text: The Inevitable Reality of Denials

No matter how clean the front-end and mid-cycle, some claims will come back denied. Denial management is the back-end discipline of dealing with that reality, and it begins with a deceptively simple question: why was this claim denied? Understanding the root-cause categories of denials is the foundation for both fixing individual claims and preventing the next batch.

The scale makes this urgent. Payers initially denied about 11.8 percent of hospital claims in 2024 (Kodiak Solutions), and an earlier Change Healthcare analysis estimated that roughly $262 billion in hospital claims — about 9 percent of charges — were initially denied in 2016. Denials are not an edge case — they are a constant, massive drain that every organization must actively manage.

The single most important fact about denials, though, is hopeful: Change Healthcare’s 2020 Denials Index found that 86 percent of denials are potentially avoidable. The vast majority of denials trace to fixable, upstream causes — which means understanding the categories is the first step to driving the denial rate down.

Denials are a constant: initial denial rates hit ~11.8% in 2024. But about 86% of denials are potentially avoidable, so understanding root-cause categories is the key to both fixing claims and preventing future denials.
Soft Denials vs. Hard Denials

A foundational distinction shapes how a denial is handled: soft versus hard. A soft denial is temporary — it can often be reversed by submitting additional information or correcting and resubmitting the claim. The money is recoverable if the team acts. A duplicate claim or a missing-information denial is typically soft.

A hard denial is final — it generally results in lost revenue and cannot simply be corrected and resubmitted (though some can still be appealed). A denial for a service that was genuinely not covered, or one where the timely filing deadline has irrevocably passed, is typically hard. Hard denials are the ones that become write-offs.

This distinction drives triage. Soft denials should be worked quickly, because they are recoverable with effort; hard denials require judgment about whether an appeal is worth pursuing or whether to write off. Knowing which is which prevents teams from wasting effort on unrecoverable claims while letting recoverable ones age past the point of recovery.

children.text: The Major Root-Cause Categories

Denials cluster into a recognizable set of root causes, and learning them is essential because each maps to a different prevention strategy upstream. Missing or inaccurate information (wrong demographics, missing fields) and prior authorization problems consistently rank as the top causes in industry surveys, followed closely by eligibility/coverage issues.

The other major categories: medical necessity (the documentation did not justify the service — research has found this among the top denial reasons); coding errors (mismatched diagnosis and procedure, wrong modifiers, invalid codes); timely filing violations (the claim was submitted past the payer's deadline); duplicate claims (the same service billed twice); and coordination-of-benefits problems (billed the wrong payer first).

Notice that nearly every category traces back to an earlier lesson in this course: missing info and eligibility to the front-end; prior auth to its own lesson; medical necessity to documentation; coding errors to coding; timely filing to payer contracts. This is the practical proof of the "back-end denial is a front-end failure" principle — the denial categories are essentially a catalog of where upstream processes broke.

children.text: Reading the Denial: CARC and RARC Codes

Payers do not deny claims with a written paragraph — they use standardized codes. The primary one is the Claim Adjustment Reason Code (CARC), which states the reason for an adjustment or denial. CARCs appear on the remittance, telling the provider exactly why the claim was not paid in full. X12 maintains several hundred CARCs.

Alongside CARCs are Remittance Advice Remark Codes (RARCs), which provide supplementary explanation and instructions. The rule of thumb: the CARC tells you what happened to your claim, and the RARC adds context or next steps. RARCs are not always present — they appear when extra explanation is needed.

A handful of CARCs account for the majority of denials, so learning the common ones is high-leverage. Examples include CO-16 (claim lacks information), CO-18 (duplicate claim), CO-50 (deemed not medically necessary), CO-97 (service included/not separately covered), and CO-22 (coordination of benefits needed). The "CO" prefix indicates a contractual obligation (provider write-off), while a "PR" prefix indicates patient responsibility — the prefix itself tells you who owes the balance.

body.title: Common CARC Denial Codes

children.text: From Categorizing to Preventing

Categorizing denials is not bookkeeping — it is the engine of prevention. Because roughly 86 percent of denials are potentially avoidable, the path to a lower denial rate runs through systematically tracking which categories and CARCs are driving an organization's denials, then fixing the upstream process responsible.

This is classic root-cause analysis applied to revenue. If "no prior authorization" denials spike, the fix is in the front-end authorization workflow, not the appeals team. If "missing information" denials dominate, the fix is registration data quality. If "medical necessity" denials rise, the fix is documentation. The CARC distribution is essentially a diagnostic readout of where the revenue cycle is leaking.

This is why reducing denials became a top priority for so many organizations — and why denial root-cause analysis sits at the center of the back-end. Understanding why claims are denied is the prerequisite for the next two lessons: building a workflow to work denials efficiently, and appealing the ones that were wrong. But the ultimate goal is always to drive the denial rate down by preventing the categories at their source.

body.message: Fixing an individual denied claim recovers one payment; fixing the root-cause category prevents hundreds of future denials. Because about 86% of denials are potentially avoidable, tracking CARC patterns to find and fix the upstream process is far higher-leverage than working denials one at a time.
body.title: Work the Category, Not Just the Claim

children.text: The Problem Hiding in Plain Sight

For most of the 20th century, American medicine assumed that well-trained doctors working in good hospitals delivered good care, and there was little systematic effort to check. Quality was treated as a matter of individual competence and professional reputation, not something you measured, reported, or improved as a system.

That assumption shattered at the turn of the century, when a pair of landmark reports forced the country to confront how often care fell short. The realization was uncomfortable: the gap between the care people should receive and the care they actually received was enormous, and largely invisible because no one was measuring it.

Clinical quality measurement is the response to that problem. It is the discipline of defining what good care looks like, turning it into standardized metrics, and using the resulting data to hold the system accountable and drive improvement. This lesson explains why that discipline exists and why it matters.
Clinical quality measurement is the systematic practice of defining good care, converting it into standardized metrics, and using the data to improve outcomes and hold the health system accountable.
To Err Is Human: The Wake-Up Call

In November 1999, the Institute of Medicine (IOM) released "To Err Is Human: Building a Safer Health System." Its central finding stunned the public and the profession: between 44,000 and 98,000 Americans were dying each year as a result of preventable medical errors in hospitals.

To put that in perspective, even the lower estimate would have made medical error the eighth leading cause of death in the United States — killing more people than motor vehicle accidents, breast cancer, or AIDS. The report estimated that medication errors alone accounted for about 7,000 deaths annually, and that the economic cost of preventable adverse events ran to tens of billions of dollars.

Crucially, the report reframed the problem. It argued that most errors were not the fault of bad individuals but of bad systems — poorly designed processes that set up competent people to fail. The solution, therefore, was not to blame and punish, but to measure, learn, and redesign. That insight launched the modern patient-safety and quality-measurement movements.

children.text: Crossing the Quality Chasm: The Six Aims

Two years later, in 2001, the IOM followed up with "Crossing the Quality Chasm: A New Health System for the 21st Century." Where the first report focused on safety, this one widened the lens to the entire quality gap — the chasm between the care we know how to deliver and the care patients actually get.

Its lasting contribution was a definition of quality itself. The report proposed six "Aims for Improvement" that still anchor quality measurement today: care should be safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, and equitable. These six aims gave the field a shared vocabulary — any quality measure can be mapped to one or more of them.

The inclusion of equity as a core aim was especially consequential. By naming equitable care — care that does not vary in quality based on personal characteristics like race, gender, geography, or income — as a defining feature of quality, the report planted the seed for the equity-focused measurement work that has become central to the field.

children.text: How Big Is the Gap? The Evidence

The IOM reports made the case conceptually; a landmark study soon quantified it. In 2003, Elizabeth McGlynn and colleagues published a study in the New England Journal of Medicine examining whether adults actually received recommended care.

The researchers reviewed the medical records of nearly 7,000 adults across 12 metropolitan areas, scoring care against 439 clinical indicators for 30 conditions plus preventive care. The headline result: on average, participants received just 54.9 percent of recommended care — barely more than a coin flip.

The variation was striking. Performance ranged from about 79 percent of recommended care for senile cataracts down to just 10.5 percent for alcohol dependence. The study made the abstract "quality chasm" concrete and measurable, and demonstrated exactly why the field needed standardized measures: you cannot close a gap you cannot see.

body.content:
McGlynn and colleagues found U.S. adults received only about 55% of recommended care, with wide variation by condition — from ~79% for cataracts to ~10.5% for alcohol dependence.
Published in the New England Journal of Medicine, it became one of the most-cited demonstrations that the quality gap was real, large, and unevenly distributed — strengthening the case for systematic measurement.
body.title: The McGlynn "Quality of Health Care" Study (2003)

children.text: Why Measurement Drives Improvement

The premise behind quality measurement is often summarized as "what gets measured gets managed." When performance is quantified, problems become visible, comparisons become possible, and attention concentrates where the data points. Measurement creates accountability and transparency that professional good intentions alone cannot.

In practice, measurement now drives improvement through several channels: internal quality improvement teams use it to target their efforts, public reporting lets patients and purchasers compare providers, and value-based payment programs tie reimbursement directly to measured performance. Each channel depends on having trustworthy, standardized measures.

But measurement is a tool, not a guarantee. Measuring the wrong things, or measuring well-intentioned things poorly, can distract clinicians, create administrative burden, and even harm care by encouraging "teaching to the test." The rest of this course is about doing measurement well — choosing meaningful measures, calculating them correctly, and using them to genuinely improve care rather than just generate reports.

body.message: "What gets measured gets managed" cuts both ways. Poorly chosen measures can divert attention from what matters, add documentation burden, and incentivize gaming the metric instead of improving care. Good measurement requires choosing the right measures, not just more of them.
body.title: Measurement Can Backfire

children.text: The Quiet Revolution in How America Covers the Poor

Medicaid is the largest health insurance program in the United States, covering tens of millions of low-income children, adults, seniors, and people with disabilities. But the way most of those people actually receive their care has been transformed over the past three decades, largely out of public view. Today, the dominant model is not the government paying doctors and hospitals directly for each service — it is the state paying private managed care organizations (MCOs) a fixed amount per enrollee to take responsibility for their care. As of July 2024, over 66 million Medicaid enrollees — about 78% of all enrollees — received their care through risk-based MCOs.

This shift from traditional fee-for-service Medicaid to managed care is one of the most consequential and least understood changes in American health policy. It reshaped the relationships among states, the federal government, private insurers, and providers, and it created an entire industry of Medicaid managed care plans operating in most states. Understanding why states made this move — and what they gained and gave up — is the foundation for everything else in Medicaid managed care operations.

The story is not a simple one of cost savings. As we will see, the evidence on whether managed care actually saves money or improves quality is surprisingly mixed. The clearest thing states gained was something subtler but, to a state budget officer, enormously valuable: predictability. This lesson traces the history of the move to managed care and the real rationale behind it.

Key Concept: Medicaid managed care means a state pays a private managed care organization (MCO) a fixed, capitated amount per enrollee to provide their care, shifting financial risk to the MCO — in contrast to traditional fee-for-service Medicaid, where the state pays providers directly for each service.

children.text: From Experiment to Dominant Model: A Brief History

Medicaid began in 1965 as a fee-for-service program: providers delivered care and billed the state, which paid them for each service. By the late 1980s and early 1990s, Medicaid costs were rising sharply, and states began experimenting with more cost-effective ways to deliver care. The answer they reached for was managed care — borrowing the model spreading through private insurance, in which a plan accepts a fixed payment and takes responsibility for managing a population’s care and cost.

The growth was rapid. In 1991, about 2.7 million beneficiaries were enrolled in some form of Medicaid managed care — roughly 10% of the program; by 1996, nearly 40% of Medicaid beneficiaries were enrolled in managed care plans. A key legal turning point came with the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, which eliminated the requirement that states obtain a federal waiver before launching mandatory Medicaid managed care programs. That change removed a major bureaucratic hurdle and accelerated adoption, helping push managed care toward the near-universal model it is today.

Before 1997, and still today for certain populations and program designs, states needed federal permission to depart from traditional Medicaid rules — typically through Section 1915 or Section 1115 waivers, which grant exemptions from standard Medicaid guidelines. These waivers remain central to Medicaid managed care and are covered in depth later in this course. The history matters because it shows managed care was not imposed from Washington; it grew from states’ own efforts to control costs, enabled by federal flexibility.

body.title: The Path to Managed Care Dominance

children.text: The Real Rationale: Predictability and Coordination

Why did states embrace managed care so thoroughly? Two rationales are cited most often: increasing the predictability of spending and improving the coordination of care. The predictability argument is the more powerful one in practice. Under fee-for-service, a state’s Medicaid spending is the unpredictable sum of millions of individual claims — if utilization spikes, so does the bill, often after the budget is set. Under managed care, the state pays MCOs a capitated rate per person per month, so it knows its per-enrollee cost in advance. This lets state policymakers predict and manage Medicaid budgets far more reliably.

For a state budget officer, this predictability is enormously valuable. Medicaid is one of the largest items in every state budget, and states (unlike the federal government) must generally balance their budgets each year. Converting an open-ended, volatile fee-for-service liability into a fixed per-member payment transfers the risk of cost overruns to the MCO and gives the state a number it can plan around. The capitation payment effectively caps the state’s per-enrollee exposure.

The second rationale, care coordination, holds that an MCO responsible for a member’s total care — and bearing the financial risk for it — has both the incentive and the tools to coordinate that care, manage chronic conditions, emphasize prevention, and steer members away from costly avoidable utilization. In theory, the same capitation that delivers budget predictability also aligns the plan’s incentives with keeping members healthy. Whether that theory holds up in practice is a separate and contested question.
Did It Deliver? The Honest Evidence

Given how completely managed care has taken over Medicaid, one might assume the evidence for its benefits is overwhelming. It is not. Research has repeatedly challenged whether managed care has delivered on its promises. While states have reliably achieved more predictability in their Medicaid budgets, only a very small number of studies show that managed care has actually helped states lower costs or improve quality. The most confident claim that can be made is about predictability — not savings, and not better outcomes.

Even the predictability gain is more limited than it appears. Research has found that managed care use has been concentrated among the enrollees with the most stable spending — historically healthier children and families — which means the budget predictability gains were smaller than hoped, because the unpredictable, high-cost populations (the aged and people with disabilities) were often kept in fee-for-service. As states increasingly move these complex populations into MCOs, the stakes — and the difficulty — rise.

body.message: Capitated managed care can create an incentive to avoid expensive members. Plans have been criticized for prioritizing cost containment over necessary care and for directly or indirectly selecting healthier enrollees or avoiding patients with complex needs. Guarding against this is a central purpose of the oversight, risk adjustment, and contract rules covered later in this course.
body.title: The Cherry-Picking Concern

children.text: Where Managed Care Stands Today

Despite the mixed evidence, Medicaid managed care is now the dominant delivery model and continues to expand. As of 2024, thirty MCO states covered at least 75% of their Medicaid beneficiaries through MCOs. The populations enrolled tell an important story: children and ACA expansion adults are the most likely to be in comprehensive MCOs (around 90% and 86% respectively), while people eligible through a disability pathway and adults 65 and older have historically been less likely to be enrolled — though states are steadily moving these higher-need groups into managed care too.

body.analogy: A state moving Medicaid to managed care is like a company switching from paying every employee’s medical bills directly to buying a fixed-price health plan for all of them. The company no longer faces a surprise bill when costs spike — it pays a known premium and the insurer absorbs the risk. That predictability is the main attraction. But the company also gives up direct control, and must now watch carefully that the insurer doesn’t skimp on care or shun its sickest workers to protect its own margin.
body.concept: Why states adopt Medicaid managed care

children.text: This trajectory sets up the rest of the course. Because states have handed responsibility for most of their Medicaid populations to private MCOs, the critical questions become operational: How do states choose which MCOs to contract with? How are the capitation rates calculated so they are adequate but not excessive? How do states hold plans accountable for network adequacy, quality, and fair treatment of complex members? Each of these exists precisely because the move to managed care transferred enormous responsibility — and public dollars — to private organizations that must be carefully governed.

The fundamental tension introduced here runs through everything that follows. Managed care offers states budget predictability and the promise of coordinated care, but it does so by giving private plans a financial incentive that can cut against members’ interests. The entire apparatus of Medicaid managed care operations — procurement, rate-setting, network standards, oversight, quality measurement, and value-based purchasing — exists to capture the benefits of the model while guarding against its risks. Understanding why states made this move is understanding why all that machinery is necessary.

points: Medicaid managed care means a state pays private managed care organizations (MCOs) a fixed capitated amount per enrollee to provide care, shifting financial risk to the MCO instead of paying providers per service as in fee-for-service.
It is now the dominant model: over 66 million enrollees (~78%) received care through risk-based MCOs as of July 2024, and 30 states cover at least 75% of beneficiaries in MCOs.

Managed care grew rapidly in the 1990s (from ~10% of beneficiaries in 1991 to nearly 40% by 1996), accelerated by the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, which eliminated the waiver requirement for mandatory managed care.

The two most-cited rationales are increasing budget predictability and improving care coordination, with predictability the most powerful in practice because it converts volatile fee-for-service costs into a fixed per-member payment.

Budget predictability matters because Medicaid is a huge share of state budgets that must generally balance annually, so capitation caps the state’s per-enrollee exposure and transfers overrun risk to the MCO.

The evidence is mixed: states reliably gained predictability, but few studies show managed care lowered costs or improved quality, and predictability gains were limited because managed care first covered the most stable-spending populations.
Capitation creates a cherry-picking risk — incentives to avoid expensive, complex members — which oversight, risk adjustment, and contract rules are designed to counter.

The transfer of most Medicaid populations and dollars to private MCOs is exactly why the rest of Medicaid managed care operations (procurement, rate-setting, network standards, oversight, quality, value-based purchasing) is necessary.
